**Amethyst**, <gloss>not-drunken</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ἀμέθυστος"; the name reflects the ancient belief that the stone prevented intoxication</note>, <gloss>An Amethyst</gloss> / is a gemstone of a violet color. Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman naturalist</note> says the **Amethyst** approaches the color of wine: but before it fully takes on that hue, the brilliance of its purple ends in a violet—not entirely fiery, but fading into the color of wine. According to the same author, the homeland of the amethyst is India. Those that come from there are the best and possess an absolute purple color; workshops direct their dyeing efforts toward this standard. Furthermore, there is another species which borders on the hyacinth <note>a blue-violet stone</note>, a color which the Indians call *Sacron*, and they call that gem *Socodion*. There is a third species which is more diluted <note>paler</note> and is called *sapinor* and *paranitor*. A fourth species has the color of wine. Its fifth species descends toward the likeness of crystal, with the purple tint fading into white; some call such stones *paederotas* <note>youthful love</note>, others *anterotas* <note>reciprocal love</note>. Many also call it the "Gem of Venus." The homeland of the Amethyst is also found in Arabia, Petraea, Armenia, Egypt, Galatia, Tarsus, and Cyprus. However, these are of the most foul and cheap quality. The vanity of the Magi <note>astrologers and magicians</note> claims that amethysts resist drunkenness and evil thoughts; likewise, they resist sorcery, provide favor to those approaching kings, and turn away hail. Regarding what specific color the Amethyst is, consult the same Pliny in Book 20, Chapter 8, and Chapters 38 and 41 of Book 9. Cheaper Amethysts are found in many places in Bohemia; there are also "fluores" <note>fluorites or vein-stones</note> in the mines similar to these. Such stones are considered inferior to those from the East.

**Amalgamation** is the calcination <term>calcination: the reduction of a metal to a fine powder (calx) through heat or chemical action</term> of familiar metals by means of mercury <note>original: *hydrargyrum*</note>. For although we do not always strive toward the final state of a powder <note>original: *calcis*</note> in this way—and it is sufficient for the metal to be so dissolved that it can be worked like the pulp or soft mass <term>malagma: a paste used by goldsmiths</term>—nevertheless, corrosion occurs through this process, reducing it into a very fine powder, which they likewise call a "calx" or lime. Alternatively: **Amalgamation** is the calcination of a metal through mercury. It occurs when a metal—having been drawn out into thin parts, leaves, or plates—is mixed and united with six, nine, or twelve parts of mercury, so that a mass is formed that is uniform throughout; in this way the metal is broken down and calcined. For once the mercury is washed away through evaporation over a slow fire, the metal is left behind in the form of a fine powder <note>original: *calx*</note>.

<meta>catchword: Aman-</meta>

**Amandine stone** <note>original: *Amandinus lapis*</note> is a gemstone of various colors. It extinguishes and represses all poisons; for this reason, it is not a stone to be looked down upon. Regarding this, consult Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century scholar famous for his works on minerals and alchemy</note>.

**Amassa**, that is, prepare or mix; hence the term *amassare* <note>to knead or work into a mass</note>.

**Amber** <note>original: *Ambra*</note> is "whale seed" <note>original: *sperma Ceti*; at the time, ambergris—a substance from the digestive tract of sperm whales—was often confused with spermaceti or thought to be whale sperm</note>.

**Amene**, that is, common salt, or "the Apostle" <note>a symbolic or coded name for common salt in alchemical texts</note>.

**Amentum**, that is, split alum <note>original: *alumen scissum*; a fibrous or feathery variety of alum</note>.

**Amethyst**, <gloss>An Amethyst</gloss> is a gemstone of a violet color.

<margin>Pliny, Book 37, Chapter 9.</margin>
Pliny says that the **Amethyst** approaches the color of wine. However, before it fully reaches that shade, that purple brilliance fades into a violet, not entirely fiery, but declining into a wine-like color. According to the same author, the homeland of the amethyst is India. Those that come from there are the best, having an absolute purple color; it is toward this shade that dye-shops direct their efforts when creating pigments. Furthermore, there is another species of it which leans toward hyacinths <note>referring to a reddish-orange gemstone, likely zircon</note>, a color which the Indians call *Sacron*, and they call that gem *Socodion*. There is a third species, which is more diluted and is called *sapinor* and *paranitor*. The fourth species has the color of wine. The fifth species descends toward the appearance of crystal, with a whitening of the purple tone; some call these *paederotas* <note>meaning "youthful beauty"</note>, others *anterotas* <note>meaning "reciprocated love"</note>. Many also call it the **Gem of Venus**. The amethyst is also native to Arabia, Petraea, Armenia, Egypt, Galatia, Tarsus, and Cyprus. However, these are of the most foul and cheapest quality. The "vanity of the Magi" <note>Pliny's phrase for the claims of ancient Persian priests</note> says that amethysts resist drunkenness and evil thoughts; likewise, they resist witchcraft, aid those about to approach kings, and turn away hail. Regarding what color the Amethyst may be, consult the same Pliny in Book 20, Chapter 8, and Chapters 38 and 41 of Book 9. Cheaper amethysts are found in many places in Bohemia; there are also "fluors" <note>minerals used as flux, such as fluorite</note> in the mines that are similar to these. These are considered cheaper than the Oriental ones.

<margin>Of Meissen, which comes from the Undehensteini mine, which consists of amethyst.</margin> <note>Meissen is a famous mining region in Saxony</note>

**Amianthus stone** <note>original: *Amianthus lapis*; this is the mineral we now know as asbestos</note>, according to the testimony of Dioscorides <note>a famous 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, originates in Cyprus. It is similar to split alum <note>a fibrous variety of alum</note>, and because it is flexible, veils and cloths are made from it for the sake of spectacle; these, when thrown into fires, appear to burn, but when the flames are removed, they emerge even more brilliant. The Germans call such a stone **Feather-white** <note>original: *Federweiss*</note> or **Earth-flax** <note>original: *Erdflachs*</note>, and they tell tales that it grows from the hair of the Salamander, because it is not consumed by fire, just like the Salamander <note>a mythical creature believed to live in or endure fire</note>. 

Indeed, **Amianthus** is without a doubt our plume alum <note>original: *alumen plumosum*; a fibrous mineral</note>, and from this an eternal candle <note>a wick that does not burn away</note> can be made. Otherwise, amianthus is not of great medicinal virtue, though it does have a drying effect. Pliny, in Book 36, Chapter 19, says that amianthus is similar to alum and loses nothing in fire, and that it resists all the sorceries of magicians specifically. 

Truly, if we consider it sharply, we ourselves have a certain species of amianthus; namely, this metallic substance is found in metal mines, and we call it mica <note>original: *mica*</note>, or in German **Glimmer** or **Cat’s Silver** <note>original: *Katzensilber*</note>. It has the color of silver. It is called **Cat’s Silver** <note>original: *Felicum argentum*</note> by similarity, because their eyes shine at night in such a way; or perhaps because it is empty and useless, for it bears no fruit <note>meaning it yields no precious metal</note>, but is consumed according to the common opinion. But if you consider it sharply, it is not consumed, just like true amianthus; rather, it is only purified and assumes another color; other things...

**Spirit:** afterward, at the end, the **Soul** and **Spirit** lie hidden beneath the **Body**: for first, you see only **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium*</note>.

In these, there is a great kinship of salt to nitre and, conversely, of nitre to salt; likewise, between the froth of salt and the froth of nitre. Furthermore, the froth of nitre—called **aphronitrum**, the flower of stone, or the flower of the wall (just like the froth of salt)—is a very light, rounded, and crumbly substance, frothy and biting, almost purple in color; this is the best variety. We call the froth of nitre **Aphronitrum**, and specifically the "frothy aphronitrum" that grows on walls and stones—a saltpeter that grows on walls and cliffs. In certain places, they call it marl. <note>original: *Mergell*; a lime-rich mud or mudstone</note>. Indeed, the froth of nitre varies according to the stones and walls where it grows, and its power is similar to burnt salt. **Aphronitrum** (that is, froth of nitre), the flower of stone, and the flower of Asian stone (of which we speak in its own place below) are almost the same thing; yet they differ slightly in substance. For if it is dissolved by fire, it is the flower of Asian stone; if it is not dissolved, it is our froth of nitre.

**IN JENA** in Thuringia, which is a noble place for medicinal herbs <note>original: *simplicium*; single medicinal plants or "simples"</note>, a most beautiful species of Aphronitrum is found, which corresponds very closely to the flower of Asian stone described by Dioscorides. <note>historical: Dioscorides|An ancient Greek physician whose work on herbal medicine was the standard for 1,500 years</note>.

...[Alphidi]us wants it to be understood in many cases as Mercury precipitate. **In the Art, an Eagle is used for Sal Ammoniac and precipitate.** <note>The "Eagle" is a common alchemical symbol for the process of sublimation—the transition of a substance from solid to vapor—because it "flies" upward in the flask.</note>

**Eagle**—*Aquila*—is the "Bird of Glue" or viscous slime which appears reddish in the first coagulation and is found in Istria. It is also the spirit turned into earth; that is, the spirit of Mercury, the Stone itself.

The *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," is one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between ancient sages.</note> says on page 73: The perfection of every thing is in the number 10, according to its governance. Therefore the *Senior* <note>Senior Zadith, a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose works were highly regarded in the West.</note> sets forth ten eagles, etc. It is also said to be Sal Ammoniac and fixed sulfur.

**The Eagle of the Philosophers** <note>original: *Aquila philosophorum*</note> is the Mercury of the metals; that is, a metal reduced to its first matter. **The Philosophical Eagle is the Mercury derived from the metals and lovely beings when the ores are brought back to their primordial state.**

**Eagle**, that is, Arsenic or sulfur.

**Eagle**, that is, gold—dripping, faithful, noble, and settled. <note>The original German uses a rhythmic string of descriptors: *guttendo, fidelo, edel, sedalo*.</note>

**Aquillo**, the North-east wind. <note>original: *Mittelner Tost*, an archaic German term for the wind between North (Midnight) and East.</note>

**Water**—*Aqua*—that is, a liquid. **This Water is also always "of the substance"; however, it is not cloud-water <note>common rain water</note> but a dry, mineral, primordial, Universal Water <note>original: *Catholisch Wasser*, referring to *Aqua Catholica*, the universal solvent or "Mercury of the Wise."</note> which dissolves all metals and turns them into water, just as ice becomes water again. It is almost like a blackish oil, says R. B.** <note>Roger Bacon, the 13th-century English philosopher and scientist.</note>

<margin>1.</margin> **This Water cleanses, washes, expands, makes porous and fluid; and yet it also dries and fixes, makes white and red—and then it is called fire <note>original: *ignis*</note>. Therefore Geber <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath considered the "father of chemistry."</note> says: "Burn it in water and wash it in fire."**

<margin>2.</margin> **Hermes <note>original: *Termis*; likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> describes this Water in the letter to Thomas of Bologna. Just as common water boiled with herbs takes on the nature and power of those herbs, so too does Mercury with the metals.**

<margin>3.</margin> **Everything grows out of water and receives its nourishment from it. This Water unites itself with metals like no other water.**

<summary>This page defines the alchemical symbols of the "Eagle" (Aquila) and "Water" (Aqua), identifying the former with Sal Ammoniac and Mercury, and the latter with a universal, primordial solvent used to dissolve metals.</summary>

-># MARTIN RULAND'S DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY #<-
->### 48 ###<-

**The Flying Dragon** / <term>spiritus</term> <note>the volatile essence or soul of a substance</note>, etc. is of a heavenly nature; it divides the elements in bodies and joins them together again; it finally becomes thick, like honey-white, and also green, which is why it is called **the Green Bird**.

**Nourishing Water** <note>original: "Aqua alma"</note> is water that is made from wine through sublimation <note>the process of vaporizing and condensing</note>.

**Alregi Water** <note>original: "Aqua alregi"</note>, that is, **lime water** <note>original: "aqua calcis"; a solution of calcium hydroxide</note>.

**Heavenly Water** <note>original: "Aqua cœlestis"</note> is rectified or sublimated wine <note>high-proof alcohol or brandy</note>, so that it takes on the nature and likeness of heaven in some way, after many revolutions <note>repeated distillations</note> have been completed. **Heavenly Water** is sublimated wine.

**Celestial Water** <note>original: "Aqua cœlestina"</note>, that is, **Mercurial water**.

**Water of the Brain** <note>original: "Aqua cerebri"</note>, that is, **Water of Tartar** <note>a solution made from the potassium bitartrate deposits found in wine barrels</note>.

**Corroding Water** <note>original: "Aqua corrodens"</note> is vinegar and every corrosive liquid. That which dissolves is called **Dissolving Water** or **Biting Water**, such as vinegar and others.

**Elfabon Water** <note>original: "Aqua Elfabon"</note>, that is, water of common salt.

**Water of Wine Dregs** <note>original: "Aqua fæcum vini"</note> is made when the dregs are dried and whitened by calcining <note>heating to a high temperature to remove volatile substances</note>, and then dissolved on a marble slab into a water in the manner of **Oil of Tartar**. **Wine-dreg water**.

**Stinking Water** <note>original: "Aqua fœtida"</note>, that is, **Water of Mercury**, also known as **the Ostrich’s Stomach** <note>A metaphor for a powerful solvent, as the ostrich was legendary for its ability to digest even iron</note>.

**Aqua Fortis** <note>Strong Water; usually nitric acid</note> is that which is distilled over violent fires from salts <note>original: "auibus" (likely a typo for "salibus") or volatile substances</note> and corrosives mixed in a certain proportion, having a powerful fiery strength for corroding. That which is most powerful is called **Stygian Water** <note>named after the River Styx in the underworld</note>, which directs **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note> with the rest so that gold may be dissolved in it <note>this mixture is known as *Aqua Regia*</note>. Others are made with different virtues, the mixture being increased according to the requirement, so that it is suited to certain things. It is called **Gradating Water** <note>original: "Gradatoria"</note> when it is used for "gradating" <note>improving the color or purity of</note> tinctures, etc. And these are made like the "strong waters" from the same material, but with dyeing agents added, such as **cinnabar** <note>mercury sulfide</note> and **alum**. In these, it must be noted that nothing dyes unless having been made...

The **Enduring Water**, or the **Philosophers' Mercury**, is when both metals—Sun and Moon—are dissolved and bound together with water. Or **Permanent Water** is the incombustible oil, the harshest of all vinegars, a sharp and penetrating water that dissolves bodies and the spiritual power. It is called **Mercury** because it is hot and clear, possessing mercurial power and properties. It is called **Mas** <note>male</note> or **Man**, **White Smoke** <note>original: "fumus albus"</note> because it rises up, and also the **Tail of the Dragon**, or the **Flying Bird**.

**Philosophical Water** <note>original: "Aqua philosophica"</note> is called by some **sublimated vinegar**; by others **circulated wine** <note>wine repeatedly distilled in a closed vessel</note>; and by others **Everlasting Water**, which does not wet the hands.

**Palestine Water** <note>original: "Aqua palaestina"</note>, that is, the **flower of copper**, or **verdigris** <note>original: "Grünspan"; the green crust that forms on copper or brass</note>.

**Rain Water** <note>original: "Aqua pluvialis"</note>, that is, fresh water.

->### 50 ###<-

**Reddish water** <note>original: "Aqua rubicunda"</note>, **megi water**, **segi water**, that is, **water of vitriol** <note>vitriol refers to various metal sulfates, such as iron or copper sulfate</note>.

**Salmatine Water** <note>original: "Aqua Salmatina"</note>, that is, made from salt.

**Saturnine Water** <note>original: "Aqua Saturnia"</note> is water generated from the **three primes** <note>the Tria Prima: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, the fundamental building blocks of matter in Paracelsian alchemy</note> in the passages of the earth, dissolved into transparent stones, such as rooted acidic waters <note>original: "aquæ radicatæ acetoſæ"</note>. <gloss>Mineral Spring</gloss> <note>original German gloss: "Saurbrunnen"</note>. Or Saturnine Water is that which retains within itself the nature of the three primes; such as the waters of hot springs, which are called "naturally medicated" by nature because of the substances through which they pass.

**Distilled water** <note>original: "Aqua ſtillatitia"</note> is a specific extract of a watery consistency and division, produced by the condensation of vapors <note>original: "halituum"</note> drawn from substances through the process of distillation. It is twofold: the **solvent** and the **simply distilled**.

**Simply distilled waters** are material **specific secrets** <note>original: "arcana ſpecifica materialia"</note> distilled from things in such a way that, although they possess a secret power within them, they are nevertheless milder than solvent waters. They possess a more diluted substance, closer to the **phlegmatic element** <note>in distillation, "phlegm" is the watery, tasteless, and often inert part of the substance being processed</note>. Or: **Simply distilled waters** are those that are milder, more diluted in power and consistency, and produced by a simpler distillation. For the phlegmatic element is coarser and less subtle, differing very little from common external water. Indeed, a simply distilled water has less fire and more wateriness than a solvent; but it has more fire and less coarseness than phlegm.

And although every "water" is created by distilling, the former [the solvent] receives the name of **solvent** because of its function and its superior purpose. It differs from a simply distilled water by its penetrating fiery sharpness, or its acidity <note>original: "acumine"</note>, and by a more laborious distillation, so that it contains as little as possible of the simple watery element, but rather a fiery fluidity—as if they were watery fires, **burning waters** <note>original: "aquæ ardentes"</note>, and so on. Therefore, it is named **sharp water** <note>original: "aqua acuta"</note> by **Geber** <note>an influential 8th-century alchemist and chemist</note>, and by others it is called the **key of the philosophers** <note>original: "clauis philoſophorum"</note>. In certain things, the power of this water is achieved by the whole substance of **mercury** <note>original: "hydrargyrus"</note>; just as other things sometimes perform the same task, such as

**Aracon**, is **Laton** <note>Laton usually refers to brass, or in alchemical stages, the "blackened" metal that must be washed to become white</note>.

**The Tree of the Sea** <note>original: "Arbor maris"</note> is a metal which grows and flourishes in the sea like a shrub. Otherwise known as corals, *curallion*, *Gorgonion*, *Dendrites*, *Lithodendron*. <gloss>Corals or beads.</gloss>

**Trees** <note>original: "Arbores"</note> is a spotted defilement of smooth skin: at the beginning there is no ulceration, but it occurs in the process of time; it is the same as morphea <note>a skin condition causing discolored patches</note>. <gloss>A type of leprosy.</gloss>

**Arcanum** is a thing secret, incorporeal, and immortal, which cannot be known by man except through experience. For it is the virtue <note>the inner power or essence</note> of each thing, which works a thousand times more than [the material body...]

Waters that are simply distilled are specific material secrets <note>original: "arcana"</note> distilled from substances in such a way that, while they possess a secret power, they are nonetheless milder than solvent waters and have a more diluted substance, closer to the element of phlegm <note>in alchemy, the cold and moist "watery" component of a substance</note>. Alternatively: Waters that are simply distilled are those that are milder, weaker in power and consistency, and produced by a simpler method of distillation. For the "phlegmatic" element is cruder and less refined, differing very little from common water. Indeed, a simply distilled water contains less fire and more wateriness than a solvent water; yet it has more fire and less crudeness than phlegm. And although every water is produced by distillation, the former type is called "solvent" because of its function and its more powerful purpose. It differs from simply distilled water by its penetrating fiery sharpness, or its acidity and the more laborious distillation required to produce it, so that it contains as little as possible of the simple watery element, but rather a fiery fluidity—as if they were "watery fires," "burning waters," and so on. Therefore, it is called **sharp water** <note>original: "aqua acuta"</note> by Geber <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note>; by others it is also called the **key of the philosophers** <note>original: "clavis philosophorum"</note>. In some cases, **mercury** <note>original: "hydrargyrus"</note> achieves this same power through its entire substance; just as other things sometimes perform the same role, such as **lyes**,

<meta>This page continues the definitions of alchemical principles, specifically transitioning from the different types of "Arcanum" (secret virtues) into terms like "Archates" and the "Archaeus," which are foundational concepts in Paracelsian alchemy regarding the vital forces of nature.</meta>

-># MARTIN'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY #<-

...the thing itself. <gloss>German: It is a secret, incomprehensible, and immortal thing, which man cannot know without experience; it is the virtue of every single thing, with a thousandfold improvement.</gloss>

**Material Arcanum** <note>original: "Arcanum materiale"</note> is a specific extract closer to the matter of the body. Since, however, the matter of composite bodies consists of a twofold element—namely, the moist and the dry (for air and fire are formal principles rather than matter, and act as the efficient cause)—this Arcanum likewise shares their nature and is twofold: a distilled water and a specific coagulum <note>a substance thickened or solidified from a liquid state</note>.

**Specific Arcanum** <note>original: "Arcanum specificum"</note> is an extract of the inner nature, representing the substance of each species more closely so that it may be recognized therein. Therefore, it must be worked with such industry that the substantial temperament <note>original: "crasis" — the unique balance of elements in a body</note> does not perish. For this reason, it is called "specific." It differs from the **quintessence** <note>original: "essentia quinta"</note>, which, because of its extreme subtlety and nobility, seems almost to have departed from its own species to join the rank of ethereal things. But the specific Arcanum presents the substance, form, and specific difference of composite things, produced from the innermost part of the body. The specific Arcanum is twofold: one is more "formal" and is called the **astral**; the other is more "material."

**Archates**, like columns of the earth, are the foundations of the earth according to Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who revolutionized medicine</note>, because they do not seem to be sustained by their own kind, but by another greatness <note>original: "magnali"</note> and secret of God. See this very thing: they call it **Archallem**, <gloss>German: "that same being which truly bears the Earth, for the other elements do not bear it."</gloss>

**Archaeus** <note>the vital force or internal chemist that directs the functions of life</note>, <gloss>German: "is the separator of the elements, who orders and governs them, each to its own place, kind, and being."</gloss>

**Archeus** is the highest, exalted, and invisible spirit, which is separated from bodies, is exalted, and ascends; it is the hidden power of nature, common to all things, the craftsman, and the physician. Likewise **archiatros**, the supreme physician of nature, who [assigns] to every thing its own Archeus...

19. Ash-colored sand.

21. Sea sand, **sea-sand**.
22. Thicker lake sand. **Slimy sand**.
23. Rich <note>original: "Pinguis" — literally "fat," used to describe minerals high in oily or metallic content</note> metallic sand.

...peculiarly disposes it, so that it may put on its own specific nature, and not that of another. Therefore, the difference between these three most beautifully and divinely ordered things in nature must be noted—to speak according to the distinctions used in the schools. **Ares** is the Spirit in Nature which, out of the three principles, gives to all things their special Form, Genus, and Substance. These three, then, are: **Iliastes**, **Archeus**, and **Ares**. 

**Iliastes** is the substance of the most general genus, consisting in the universal first matter of all things. It first organizes this into three genera: namely, sulfur, mercury, and salt. The **Iliastes**, or the **Fundamental Character** <note>original German: *Grundzeach*. In Paracelsian thought, this refers to the primordial state of matter</note>, is the first matter of all things, arising out of these three principles: Mercury, Salt, and Sulfur. 

**Archeus** is the primary dispenser of nature, and from there it produces all things into their proximate genera <note>the next level of classification below the universal</note>. The **Archeus** is the beginner who nurtures and creates, as the master-craftsman, all things out of this nature. 

**Ares** bestows upon each species its own peculiar nature and a form distinct from others, as is seen in plants, each of which has a unique root, stalk, flower, leaves, and the like. The **Ares**, or the **Assigner**, then assigns to each its particular nature, form, and shape, so that it may be recognized as distinct from others; as seen in herbs alone, where each has its particular root, stem, flower, and leaves.

**Arfar**, that is, <term>Arsenic</term> <note>a brittle, steel-gray metalloid, often used in alchemical processes for "whitening" metals</note>, **Arfag**.

**Silver** <note>original Latin: *Argentum*</note> is called **Luna** <note>the Moon</note> by the Alchemists, to whom it is also attributed. It is the metal closest to gold; it is white with a pure whiteness, clean, hard, and resonant. Its tincture of whiteness comes from pure <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note>, which is almost fixed <note>non-volatile; resistant to heat</note>, clear, and white; and from a similar **Sulfur**—clean, fixed, white, and clear—which has fallen upon the substance of the quicksilver. It lacks only a small amount of fixation, color, and weight [to be gold]. It is, as it were, the daughter of Nature when she intends to produce gold, through the joining of quicksilver and a white, non-burning sulfur.

Silver is also found in our mines. 1. That which is immediately its own <note>meaning it exists in a pure state</note>, which is produced without the work of furnaces, and is found pure in veins. This is **native silver** <note>original German: *gediegen Silber*</note>; it is such as it is without smelting, for it was generated that way at its birth, possessing its own color. Almost always some bit of stone from the valley where it was taken still clings to it, as we see when it is dug from the mines. Pliny was ignorant of this when he said in Book 33, Chapter 6: "It is only found in pits, and is born with no signs of itself, having no shining sparks as gold does; the earth is sometimes red, sometimes ashen." So says Pliny. But this pure silver clings to the stone in the thinnest leaves; sometimes it even takes on the appearance of hair, **like little hairs** <note>original German: *wie Härlein*</note>; sometimes like rods, **like balls of thread or little twigs from trees** <note>original German: *wie Zwirnklouweln / oder Reißlein von den Bäumen*</note>. Sometimes it takes the shape of a globe, as if wound with white or red threads, **like a ball of twine or a small ball of red silk, and at times like spiderwebs** <note>original German: *wie ein Zwinckloul oder von roter Seiden ein Klöulein / zu zeiten wie die Spinnweblein*</note>. Sometimes it presents the appearance of a tree, a tool, mountains, herbs, and other things. I myself have seen a whole fish, I have seen Christ crucified with the Blessed Mary, I have seen a serpent, I have seen a scorpion, etc., formed thus from pure silver in the bowels of the earth.

2. Raw silver, called by the Germans **Silver Ore** <note>original German: *Silbererz*</note>; in our mines this is of various types, namely of a red, leaden, black, purple, ashen, or reddish color, which we shall now treat in order.

3. That which is smelted from metals, such as pyrite or galena <term>plumbagine|a lead-bearing ore, often referring to galena</term>, called by the Germans **smelted silver from pyrites and galena** <note>original German: *geschmeltzt Silber / auß dem Kiß / vnd Glantz*</note>; of which we speak below in their proper places.

### DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULANDUS

Bermannus <note>A character in Georgius Agricola’s famous 1530 dialogue on mining, who represents the expert knowledge of the Saxon miners</note> distinguishes those varieties excellently. Let us return to the task at hand. I speak of **red raw silver** <note>silver ore</note> of a leaden color; it resembles galena <term>galena: the natural mineral form of lead sulfide, often appearing as shiny grey cubes</term> in appearance. But it differs in this: Galena is brittle, and when struck by a knife, it shatters. This raw silver, however, cannot be ground; it is split by a knife just like lead, and indeed, when squeezed by the teeth, it spreads out <note>indicating the metal's ductility or softness</note>; which galena does not do at all. This species of raw silver of leaden color is found as masses of wonderful size in the very channels of the veins, as if in a nest. 

Secondly, masses of it are found in the shape of tree buds; sometimes they cling to rocks with an admirable roundness and are contained within them. Its masses also take the form of little rods or other certain figures. Thus Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola, the "Father of Mineralogy," who wrote *De Re Metallica*</note> testifies that he saw pickaxes and small hammers—metallic tools—cast and dug up from it <note>This likely refers to "native" metal that has naturally formed into shapes resembling tools</note>. I have seen little fish in some pieces, and also the tracks of a lion or a wolf; so busy is nature in the very bowels of the earth, even in the darkness. Sometimes even its thinnest plates <note>original: *bracteæ*, thin leaf-like layers</note> embrace some kind of stone.

**Black raw silver** is the third kind of raw silver, called by the Germans **Black Silver Ore** <note>original: *Schwarz Silber Erz*</note>. Within its blackness, the second kind sometimes shines, which resembles galena of a leaden color. Sometimes it also contains sparks of red raw silver, as well as sparks of naturally white silver; and the more it abounds in those sparks, the more silver it yields when it is smelted <note>original: *excoquitur*, literally "cooked out"</note>. This was unknown to Pliny and the ancients. If indeed it is sterile, which happens sometimes, then it is simply to be considered black earth, as discussed in its own place concerning earths.

**Purple raw silver** is the fourth kind of raw silver, called by the Germans **Brown Ore** <note>original: *Braun Erz*</note>; this was also unknown to Pliny and the ancients. Moreover, this also contains no small amount of silver. In the valley, in the mines of the mountain named Tarcicus <note>possibly referring to a specific mine in the Erzgebirge mountains of Germany/Czechia</note>, this raw silver can be shown.

Ash-gray and reddish raw silver is the fifth kind of raw silver; it is called **Gray Ore** <note>original: *Graw Ertz*</note> by the Germans. The sixth kind is entirely reddish in color. The more silver it contains compared to other types, the greater the abundance of silver that can be smelted from it. Indeed, we see that the ash-gray type is very often rich in silver, especially when it is quite hard, so that it can even be cut with a knife, or if it is soft and tiny flakes of silver—the color of lead—shine within it. If it is not of this color, it is worth very little and contains less silver. 

Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman author of *Natural History*</note> (in Book 33, Chapter 6) seems to have known these two types when he says: "One earth is reddish, another is ash-gray." Otherwise, I find little mention of them; yet these were known to the ancients. These are the six species of raw silver known to German mining men. Perhaps there are more, if someone observes the mines diligently, as we shall investigate when we have more leisure time than we have had until now.

Silver dross, which they also call slag, or *helcysma* <note>original: *Helcyfma*, a Greek term for the dross of metal</note>, or *encauma* <note>original: *Encauma*, meaning something "burnt-in" or a byproduct of fire</note>, is called **Silver Slag** <note>original: *Silberschlacken*</note> by the Germans. This is what remains after the silver has been smelted, or what is usually drawn from the furnaces where the silver is refined. Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note> (Book 5, Chapter 51) says that silver dross has the power of litharge <note>original: *molybdenæ*, a lead-based mineral used in ancient medicine</note>, and that it draws together and extracts. For this reason, it ought to be added to plasters used to cover scars and those which they call *epheas* <note>original: *pheas*, referring to medications for skin conditions</note>. 

Consider, however, dear reader, what kind of silver dross you might want from us. For among us (as mentioned), silver is smelted from pyrite—that is, from copper, called **Copper Slag** <note>original: *Kupfferschlacken*</note>—and from lead-ore, called **Lead Slag** <note>original: *Bleyschlacken*</note>, of which we will speak in their proper place. As for this true silver dross, **Silver Slag** <note>original: *Silberschlacken*</note>, from silver or **Silver Ore** <note>original: *Silber Ertz*</note>, which is truly our silver dross—you must judge for yourself whether Dioscorides meant that. Certainly, Dioscorides did not know those species of silver; how then could he have known the true dross of silver? But let us leave these matters aside. Concerning silver dross, see

Silver foam, also called **Litharge** <note>original: *Lithargyron* or *lithargyrion* from the Greek terms meaning 'silver stone'</note>, is known generally by the Germans as **Litharge** <note>original: *Glette*</note>. 1.  **Molybditis**, which is smelted from sand in the furnaces until it glows perfectly in the fire.

2.  **From Lead**, which is made from lead plates. Dioscorides praises the varieties from Attica <note>the region around Athens, Greece</note> and Spain, and then that which is made at Baiae and Puteoli <note>ancient Roman resort and port cities</note> in Campania, as well as in Sicily.

3.  **From Silver**, which is produced during refining; this type is again twofold: **Argyritis** and **Chrysitis**. **Argyritis** <note>from the Greek 'argyros' for silver</note> is made from silver and is silver-colored; the Germans call it **Silver Litharge** <note>original: *Silberglette*</note>. We still use this today in its raw, unprepared state. **Chrysitis** <note>from the Greek 'chrysos' for gold</note> is gold-colored and is called **Gold Litharge** <note>original: *Goldglett*</note> by the Germans; not because it is made of gold, but because it is made of silver and reflects the color of gold. These species are known to us today. As Dioscorides teaches, they have the power to bind, soften, fill <note>referring to filling wounds with new flesh</note>, repel, and cool.

# THE PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN RULAND

...silver <note>original: *argento*</note>, that is produced. 3. **Molybditis**, which is the smelting of lead itself, from which it also takes its name <note>The name is derived from the Greek *molybdos*, meaning lead</note>.

From these sources it is clear: according to Pliny, **molybditis** is made from the smelting of lead itself; however, according to Dioscorides, it is made from smelted sand—unless a second species, made from lead plates, was also once called *molybditis*. See the rest in the same Pliny, who, in his usual manner, transferred all of Dioscorides' writing on silver foam into his own work. He also says that foam differs from slag <note>original: *scoria*</note> as much as foam differs from dregs <note>original: *fæce*</note>. Some have also identified types of litharge <note>original: *lithargyri*</note> called **sterelitis** and **pneumenis**.

Moreover, silver foam <note>litharge</note> is a potent poison when swallowed, as the same Dioscorides teaches in Book 6, chapter 27. And Nicander (from whom Dioscorides transferred most of his 6th book) in his 22nd poem on *alexipharmics* <term>alexipharmic: a remedy or preservative against poison and venom</term>; you may consult these authors yourself regarding the symptoms and antidotes. See also Serapion on this in his *Book of Aggregations* under the chapter *Marechet*, and Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century medical encyclopedist</note> as well as Galen in Book 9 of *On Simple Medicines* regarding its properties.

Silver is otherwise divided thus:

1. **Raw white silver**, clotted, from Schneeberg: which can be cut with a small knife and worked with a hammer. <note>German: *Paur Ertz / Schnee-weiß gediegen Silber / dicht Silber* — Pure ore / snow-white native silver / dense silver</note>.
2. **Silver from Annaberg**, white, found in the whitest metallic marble. <note>German: *Ein Stüfflein gediegen Silber in weiſſem Spadt* — A small piece of native silver in white spar</note> <term>spar: a general term used by miners for any non-metallic, lustrous, crystalline mineral like calcite or quartz</term>.

->Hair-like silver:<-

1. **White hair-like silver from Annaberg**. <note>German: *weiß gediegen häricht Silber* — white native hair-like silver</note>.
2. **Silver condensed into many hairs** like a braid or tangle. <note>German: *Gediegen häricht Silber / Büſchel weiſe zuſammen gewachſen* — Native hair-silver / grown together in clusters</note>.
3. **Very white silver**, which consists of a ball of the finest silver threads. <note>German: *Ein Wimmer von härichtem Silber* — A knot or burl of hair-silver</note>.

4. Purple-colored silver dug from the same vein. **Brown silver.** <note>original: "Braun Silber"</note>
5. A silver-bearing stone. **A silver specimen.** <term>Specimen: The original German *Stufe* refers to a piece of ore or mineral sufficiently beautiful or representative to be kept for a collection.</term>
6. A vein of silver with very hard nodules. **Gritty nut-shaped lumps.**
7. A rich silver vein to which the "hide" or crust adheres. **A hand-sized specimen still attached to the host rock.** <note>original: "Handstein / daran noch der Bergk ist." Miners used the term "hide" to describe the outer layer of rock surrounding a rich vein.</note>
8. Silver combined with lead, separated from copper. **Work.** <term>Work: Known as *Werck* in German, this is the silver-bearing lead produced during the first stage of smelting before the silver is fully refined.</term>
9. Mixed with lead, that is, tin. **Black lead, or Work.** <note>In early metallurgy, terms for lead and tin were often overlapping; "black lead" usually referred to common lead.</note>
10. A rich mixture with lead. **Lead or Work that contains much silver.**
11. Of middling quality. **Light-streak work.**
12. Poor in quality. **Fresh-streak work.** <note>The "streak" (Strich) refers to the marks or traces left during the testing or smelting process.</note>
13. Hard cakes, which contain more silver within them. **Rich, hard work.**
14. Soft cakes, in which there is more "black lead" (common lead). **Soft, dry work.**
15. A small piece of silver. **A silver sample.**
16. A cake of pure silver. **Flash-silver.** <term>Flash-silver: Known as *Blicksilber*, this is silver that has just reached purity during cupellation. The name comes from the "flash" or "brightening" that occurs the moment the last film of lead oxide disappears.</term>
17. Ash-colored dross of gold. **Gray silver-slag.**
18. Nearly ash-colored. **Black silver-slag.**
19. Silver-scum. **Silver-litharge.** <term>Litharge: A byproduct of silver refining (lead oxide), often used as a pigment or in glass-making.</term>
20. Smelted silver, yet still mixed with lead. **Work, or lead-rich silver.**
21. Separated from other metals. **Refined silver.**
22. Thoroughly purified. **Burnt silver.** <note>original: "Gebrandt Silber." "Burning" was a common term for high-heat purification.</note>
23. Pure from the smelting-furnace. **Fine silver.**
24. Stamped or marked. **Minted or coined silver.**
25. Gilded. **Gilt silver.**
26. Drawn into threads. **Spun silver.**
27. Beaten into thin sheets. **Battered or leaf silver.**

To separate silver from copper. **Liquation.** <term>Liquation: A process (Seifferen or Saigern) where silver is separated from copper by using lead as a solvent at a controlled temperature.</term>

**Vocabulary:** Silver, Work (Lead-silver alloy), Lead, Silver-slag, Litharge, Hand-specimen, Liquation.

->[MARTIN] RULAND, DOCTOR OF PHILOSOPHY AND MEDICINE.<-
->I 2<-

To dissolve silver into little spheres. **Silver grains.** <note>original: "Silberkörnern"</note>

People's silver, that is, **bitter salt.** <note>In alchemy, *sal amarum* (bitter salt) often refers to magnesium sulfate or similar crystalline salts that were sometimes compared to silver due to their white luster.</note>

Quicksilver is what the Chemists call **Mercury.** It is nothing other than a viscous water found in the bowels of the earth, a subtle substance of white earth, united by a very temperate heat into a total union through its smallest parts, until the moist has been balanced by the dry, and the dry by the moist equally. According to the Chemists, quicksilver is one of the two parts of the **Philosophers’ Stone.** <term>Philosophers’ Stone: The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold; in alchemy, it was thought to be composed of a "perfected" marriage of Mercury and Sulfur.</term> It is also the other principle and the mother of all metals. Depending on how it unites with the "father"—its masculine sulfur—it causes either perfection or imperfection in the resulting metals. Metals, like a fetus, take more from their "mother" (so to speak) than from their father; thus, they mostly draw their origin from it, and are mostly resolved back into it. Quicksilver is of two kinds: native and artificial.

**Native quicksilver** retains its own color without needing to be smelted; it is found within metals in pools where it has flowed out from the fibers of the rock. **A truly natural quicksilver.** <note>original: "Ein recht natürlich Quecksilber"</note> That is, the mother and element of metals. The Roman naturalist Pliny knew of this in Book 33, Chapter 6, where he says: "There is also a stone in these veins, whose vomit of eternal liquid is called quicksilver." <note>original: "Est & lapis in iis venis, cuius vomica liquoris æterni, argentum viuum appellatur."</note> The Greek physician Dioscorides perhaps did not see it himself, as he says in Book 5, Chapter 60: "Even quicksilver is found in the shells of silver mines, collected drop by drop; others report it to be found by itself in metals."

**Artificial quicksilver** is that which is made or "cooked" from cinnabar itself (the native stone) or from a vein of cinnabar ore: **From the mountain cinnabar, or quicksilver ore.** <note>original: "Auß dem Berg Zinober / oder Quecksilber Ertz"</note> This is also found in our own mines. This artificial kind, produced from cinnabar, was known to Dioscorides, as is evident in Book 5, Chapter 60. He teaches its preservation, use, its nature as a poison, and its antidotes; you may also consult Pliny in the place cited above, as well as Book 20, Chapter 5, and Book 28, Chapters 9 and 10, among others.

<meta>catchword: 12. An-</meta>

Furthermore, take note of this: the Greeks call both the artificial and the natural forms "hydrargyron." <note>original Greek: υδράργυρον; literally "water-silver."</note> Pliny, however, uses the name "argentum vivum" <note>literally "living silver" or quicksilver</note> only for the natural variety—that which nature created by its own power and accord, as is clear from the passage cited above. But that which artifice produces from minium <note>red lead or cinnabar ore</note> or from a vein of minium, he calls "hydrargyron" in, if I am not mistaken, the same 33rd book. For this reason, he is also corrected by the most learned Leonicenus. <note>Niccolò Leoniceno (1428–1524) was an Italian physician and humanist known for correcting botanical and medicinal errors in the works of Pliny the Elder.</note> Finally, this should also be noted: while it is liquid, it is called "crude quicksilver" in our apothecary shops; but when it has been "mortified" <term>mortification: an alchemical process of "killing" a metal by stripping it of its outward metallic properties, often through chemical change or solidification</term>, they call it "calcined" in the shops, or "sublimated" by some. Quicksilver is hot and moist in the fourth degree. <note>In the humoral theory of the time, the "fourth degree" was the most intense level of a quality.</note> Some, however, maintain it is cold in the fourth degree. The Chemists categorize it as cold and moist in the fourth degree, liquid in the third, white in the second, and dark in the first degree. Others speak differently.

Others enumerate these species of quicksilver:

<margin>1.</margin> Quicksilver, that is, the Spirit, or Mercury, also known as the fugitive servant, asoc, ydrogiros, Sanlarum, anzatyg, asoc, Zaylat, Azehoc, Kyregiros, white smoke, alsohoc, asob, ayor, azcc, alozet, azoar, aurarid, and the dragon. <note>These are various Arabic and esoteric alchemical synonyms for mercury. It is called the "fugitive servant" because it evaporates (flees) easily when heated.</note>
<margin>2.</margin> That which is found pure within metals without needing to be smelted: **A pure quicksilver.** <note>original: "Ein rein Quecksilber"</note>
<margin>3.</margin> That which is smelted from a vein of minium: **smelted quicksilver.** <note>original: "geschmelzt Quecksilber"</note>
<margin>4.</margin> Sublimated, as they call it.
<margin>5.</margin> Precipitated.
<margin>6.</margin> Mortified: **Deadened.** <note>original: "Getödt"</note>
<margin>7.</margin> That which has been solidified by the chemical art: **A quicksilver that has been made "fixed."** <note>original: "Ein Quecksilber das fix gemacht"</note> <term>Fixed: A substance that has been made resistant to fire so that it no longer evaporates.</term>
<margin>8.</margin> Native minium: **Mountain cinnabar.** <note>original: "Berckzinober"</note>
<margin>9.</margin> Hard and spherical, which the Arabs call Cinnabar: **Cinnabar.** <note>original: "Zinober"</note>
<margin>10.</margin> Friable: **soft cinnabar.** <note>original: "weicher Zinober"</note>
<margin>11.</margin> Artificial: **Manufactured cinnabar.** <note>original: "Gemachter Zinober"</note>

**Arthoicum** or **Pannonium**: a red oil expressed from the roots of herbs that have been digested with bread in dung. **Asaphatum**, a skin eruption, creeping sore, or lichen: these are related skin ulcers or defects. **Intertwined shingles or ringworm.** <note>German: *Geflochten zittermalsflecht / Hayrwurm*. These terms describe various fungal or parasitic skin conditions.</note>

**Afeb** or **Afep**, that is, alum <term>a versatile mineral salt</term>, in German **Alaun**. It is a metallic substance, or a vein of earth, which has a substance midway between vitriol and salt, and is found in mines. It is a saltiness, as it were, of the earth, as Pliny says in Book 35, Chapter 15. It is formed from water and mud—that is, from the nature of overflowing earth. Gathered together in winter, it is matured by the summer suns. It is a vein, as if of the earth, which is turned into a white color by excessive heat. And all vitriol contains alum. The name is now applied to a certain artificial alum; although we know several species of natural alum from the learned. Alum is primarily formed in hot regions, and especially in sulfurous and fiery places. Because alum has many species, we will set them forth in the usual manner for the sake of those studying these things.

**Afeb**, **Febel**, **Alpar**, **Alumaic** in Arabic; **Scipterea** in Greek; **Alumen** in Latin; **Alaun** in German. It is hot and dry in the 4th degree according to Avicenna <note>The Persian physician Ibn Sina; "degrees" refer to the Galenic system of medicinal potency.</note>. Others say it is hot and dry in the 3rd degree. It is found naturally in mines, a saltiness of the earth formed from water and mud. It is either White or:

# THE WORKS OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.

Liquid alum, which they call rock alum <note>original: *alumen de Rocha* or *rocca*</note>, or Liparean alum <note>original: *liparinum*; named for the Lipari Islands, known for volcanic minerals</note>.

Broken alum is of three kinds: Lumpy,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Round,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and Fissile (Split).

1. **Lumpy alum** is again twofold: the mined kind and the
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;man-made kind, of which there are one or two
species. These are boiled (mostly produced from the native mined kind) and they solidify. Of all these species, we only possess this man-made lumpy kind.

2. **Round Sugary alum**, called so because of its resemblance to sugar, is
again twofold: Mined and
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Man-made.

The Mined kind is what they call *strongylen* or *strigilim* <note>original: *strongylen*, from the Greek for "round"</note>. Of this there are again two species: Spongy and
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Pumice-like.

The Spongy kind is easily dissolved in anyone's mouth and is entirely rejected as worthless.

The Pumice-like kind is better; it is round and similar to the porous tubes of a sponge. It is nearly pure white, has a certain fattiness, and is crumbly without being sandy. It does not stain things black and is of Egyptian or Melian origin <note>original: *Melinum*, referring to the island of Melos</note>.

The Man-made kind is that which is shaped by hand, and it is rejected.

3. **Fissile alum** is, as it were, the flower of the lumpy kind, which was called *Schistion* by Pliny in Book 35, Chapter 15. It is a split variety that gapes open into whitening, hair-like filaments, hence the name *trichitin* <term>from the Greek 'trichos', meaning hair-like</term>. This is also prepared and adulterated from fissile stone; it is now called feather alum <note>original: *alumen plumosum*</note>, or *alumen de pluma*, or commonly *scaiola* <note>likely referring to scagliola, a plaster made of selenite or similar minerals</note>. Without a doubt, this is the *amianthus* <term>a fibrous, fire-resistant mineral like asbestos</term> which we mentioned above as our feather alum. They also call it *chalcitin* or *trichitin*, as it is alum, or rather the "sweat" of the stone itself, coagulated into a foam. Some also call it copper-alum <note>original: *alumen ærarium*</note>, because in pyrite...

->### MARTIN RULAND’S ALCHEMICAL LEXICON.<-

...it hardens. Hence, sometimes copper-stone <note>original: *chalcitis*; a mineral of copper and iron sulfates</note> is called "hardened alum." This alum, however, does not possess a binding power, but only dries. It is also called *sciptereon*; hence also *scipteria* of the rock-rose <note>original: *cistis*; possibly referring to the Cistus plant where certain salts were found</note>, and Yemenite alum <note>original: *alumen Iamenum*</note>, and fissile (split) alum. When the term "alum" is used on its own, this fissile variety is usually understood. Yemenite alum is brought from Babylon; and because it does not bind, but only dries, it is not truly alum—not even the fissile kind—but merely has the appearance of alum. On this point, see the error of Musa <note>referring to Antonius Musa, the Roman physician, or a similar ancient authority</note>.

Liquid alum, which they call rock alum <note>original: *alumen de Rocha*, *rocca*, or *liparinum*</note>, is of two kinds:
1. Soft, fatty, clear, and milky, which they call *phormion*. Pliny teaches that its adulteration can be detected by using pomegranate juice.
2. Pale and rough, which is stained by gall-nuts, and is called *paraphoron*. 
The powers of these are to bind, to harden, and to corrode. They are produced in Spain, Egypt, Armenia, Macedonia, Pontus, Africa, and the islands of Sardinia, Melos, Lipara, and Strongyle. Their nature is to heat, bind, cleanse, and thin. They are prepared by burning, in the same manner as copper-stone. For their other medical virtues, their places of origin, and their identifying signs, consult Dioscorides book 5, chapter 72; Pliny book 35, chapter 15; Serapion in the *Book of Aggregates*; C. Seben.; and Avicenna book 2.

**Alum.** The round, fissile, and liquid varieties are suitable for Medicine.

There is also another species of alum which they call *affar* alum, or *Usnen* in Arabic <note>likely *ushnan*, referring to alkali-rich plant ash</note>, known in Latin as "sparrow dung" <note>original: *stercus passerinum*</note>, or *haren*. You will find many more species of this in the works of Serapion and Avicenna. Some call it alkali salt; some categorize it not as a species of alum, but as a species of salt.

**Ased**, that is, the Lion <note>In alchemy, the 'Lion' often symbolizes mercury, gold, or a powerful acid/solvent depending on the context</note>.

**Asedenigi**, that is, Hematite <note>Bloodstone</note>.

**Asegen**, that is, Dragon’s Blood <note>a bright red resin or cinnabar</note>; *azogen* is the same.

**Asenec**, that is, a leaf <note>original: *fol.*, abbreviation for *folium*</note>.

**Aseph**, that is, fissile (split) alum.

**Asingar** or **asugar**, **asiniar**, **asigi**, that is, verdigris <note>the green crust on weathered copper</note>. Verdigris <note>original: *Grünspan*</note>.

**Asmaga**, that is, a mixing or a commingling of certain metals with one another.

Asoper, that is, soot, **Soot.**

Assaliae are worms growing inside planks, such as wood-grubs, woodworms, termites, wood-lice, and wood-eaters: **Woodworms that grow between the boards.**
Assanegi, Assanirgi, afaragi: **the powder that falls from the walls of salt [mines].**

2. Female Astroite, shaped like a half-sphere, in which (unlike the male) there are not stars to be seen, but marks resembling caterpillars or worms; thus the stars are packed together tightly by nature herself: **Upon it, stars are not to be seen, but rather streaks like caterpillars.**
3. Beads made from star-stone, with which prayers were formerly counted: **A rosary made of such victory-stones.**
A Star <note>original: *astrum*</note> is a celestial constellation. In this context, "Star" is used to mean the virtue and power of things acquired through chemical preparations; for example, the "Star of Sulfur" is its ignition, by which it is turned into a most excellent oil.

# MARTIN RULAND’S DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY #

Likewise, the **Star of Salt** is its resolution into water or oil, by which it simultaneously takes on greater powers than it had previously possessed. Similarly, the **Star of Mercury** is its sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collecting the purified solid that forms as it cools</note>, by which it acquires a wonderful strength and power, greater and more subtle than its natural state. *Astrum* or *Astrũ* means the constellation or "Star." But in our Chemical Art, it signifies the nature and power that a thing receives from its preparation. For instance, when Mercury is sublimated, or when sulfur is ignited with a tiny spark of fire, or when Salt is spontaneously dissolved and resolved, they become "Astral" or "Star-like"; this is then called the Star of Mercury, of Sulfur, or of Salt. Or the **Star** is the *alkol* <note>original: *alkol*; in this context, the finest, most purified essence</note>, or the **Fifth Essence** <term>Quinta Essentia: the most purified and potent form of a substance, believed to be the "fifth element" beyond earth, air, fire, and water</term>, the pure and clearest power, the Extract, the seed, the nature, and the property of the thing, as Bacchus <note>likely referring to an alchemical author or a pseudonym used in the Hermetic tradition</note> says.

**Afub**, that is, the galaxy, the dispersal of the stars.
**Afubedegi**, that is, a stone that cuts other stones.
**Asulci**, that is, **Lapis Lazuli**, or Azure-stone.
**Asuoli**, that is, ink or vitriol <note>original: *atramentum*; used for both black ink and various metallic sulfates</note>; it is also called soot.
**Atac**, that is, talc or nitre <note>potassium nitrate or saltpeter</note>.
**Atanor**, that is, a perforated pot.
**Atebras**, a bronze water-vessel <note>original: *vneus aquinus*, likely a corruption of *aeneus aquarius*</note>, that is, a vessel used for sublimation.
**Athanor**, which is also called the "Philosophical" and "Secret" furnace, is a furnace constructed to provide a suitable heat for working the secret **Stone of the Philosophers** <term>Lapis Philosophorum: the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals and healing all illnesses</term>; in this furnace, the fire does not directly touch the vessel. Many people have imagined many ways of building such furnaces. However, it seemed appropriate to include here one of our own invention, which excels all others both because of the proximity of the fire and the temperature control it provides. However, it is necessary that on some face of this middle part, a space be left empty through which material can be put in and taken out. For in this middle part is the **Workroom** <term>Ergasterium: the internal laboratory space or chamber of a furnace where the chemical reaction takes place</term>, where the material is processed in its vessel placed upon a **tripod**. To fill and seal this empty space, a stopper is properly formed and applied that closes it tightly, so that no air is drawn in from there. Four fingers wide above this second vaulting of the furnace, four vents are left at its base with their stoppers, by which the heat can be increased or decreased...

...spirits, which are the opposite of fluxes. <note>original Latin: *fluoribus*. In early chemistry, a flux is a substance that helps a mineral melt or flow, while spirits were the volatile components.</note> Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and author of the foundational herbal 'De Materia Medica'.</note> (Book 5, Chapter 64) says that in genus, **shoemaker’s black** <term>atramentum</term> <note>original: *atramentum sutorium*</note> is one and the same—both soft and solid—but in species, it is threefold:

That which solidifies from moisture gathered drop by drop in mining shafts, which they call **dripping vitriol** <term>stillatitium vitriolum</term> <note>original: *stillatitium vitriolum*</note>, used by those who refine Cyprian metals [copper]. Others call it *pinarion* or *stalacticon*, meaning "dripped." By the Germans, this species is called **Göckelgut** <note>original German: *Göckelgut*, referring to vitriol found in stalactite form.</note>.

That which forms in caves and is later poured by a simple method into excavated pits, where it takes on a solid form; they call this *pecton*, that is, **solidified** or **frozen vitriol**.

And these two species are natural, differing in their lumps and their manner of formation. By the Germans, they are called **Kupfferrauch** <note>original German: *Kupfferrauch*, literally "copper-smoke," a term for copper-based sublimates or crusts.</note>, as if it were the smoke of copper, or pyrite solidified or frozen within the mines themselves.

The powers of these are suitable for medicine: for they are astringent, warming, and they produce scabs <note>original: *crustas inducunt*, referring to the medicinal ability to form a protective layer over a wound or sore.</note>. According to their colors, however, there are three species of natural shoemaker’s black or vitriol, namely:

Furthermore, the "white violet" <note>original: *leucoion*</note> of Theophrastus and Dioscorides is a flower well known to physicians. 

2. **Green**.

# DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND

### 32.
The refuse of **atrament** <note>original: *Atramenti recrementum*. "Atrament" was a broad term for black pigments or vitriols (metal sulfates).</note>, from which sulfur is later extracted at Radeberg <note>A town in Saxony, Germany, famous for its historical mining and chemical processing.</note>.

**Atrament**, that is, *duenec*, *malagislaca*, **Black Chalk** / **Krieschbech** <note>original German: *Schwarz Kreid / Krieschbech*. These refer to carbon-based or pitchy substances used for marking or dyeing.</note>.

**Green atrament**, that is, **Chalcantum** <term>Chalcantum</term> <note>From the Greek *chalkanthon* (flower of copper). Usually refers to green vitriol (iron sulfate) or blue vitriol (copper sulfate).</note>, or **Roman Vitriol**.

**Shoemaker’s blacking** <note>original: *Atramentum sutorium*</note> is nothing other than **vitriol**, that is, **Chalcantum**—which is to say, as it were, the "flower of copper." However, it is not the "flower of copper" <note>original Greek: *χαλκοῦ ἄνθος* (chalkou anthos)</note> as two distinct words—meaning the literal shavings or flakes of copper which we discussed above—but rather the **verdigris of copper** <note>original: *aerugo aeris*</note>, which is also called the "flower of copper" by more recent authors. But this *chalcantum* is called the "flower of copper" by analogy. For the actual flower of copper (or the verdigris known by that name) is one thing, and the substance *chalcantum* (that is, vitriol) is quite another.

Hence Pliny (Book 34, Chapter 10) says:
> The Greeks created a relationship, by the name of copper, with shoemaker's blacking; for they call it **chalcantum**. Just as there is a certain kinship between the vitriols and the verdigris of copper, which they also call the flower of copper.

**Shoemaker’s blacking** itself is called vitriol because in former times shoemakers and other craftsmen who use leather used to dye their hides with it. But because its acidity easily eats away at footwear, another blacking was devised by shoemakers for dyeing leather, specifically made from iron; **Our Shoemaker's Black** <note>original German: *Unser Schuster Schwärtz*</note>.

But among the ancients, **atrament** must be understood as that metallic vitriol, which is nothing other than congealed water that has taken on the nature of copper, having a diverse nature and form according to the nature of the stone to which it adheres. Seneca, in his excellent discourse on springs and rivers, says:
> The earth contains various humors, and it also possesses spirits just like the human body, wherein there are various kinds of humors; namely, some that are necessary, some corrupt, some fattier, and others that are hardened in due time.

From this source comes the entire nature of metals, such as gold, silver, and those which are dissolved from a liquid into stone. Such are those metals which the Chemists, not without reason, call

Pliny also divides **chalcanthum** <note>A term derived from the Greek for "copper flower," referring to blue vitriol.</note>—that is, **vitriol** and **shoemaker's blacking** <note>original: *atramentum sutorium*; used in the ancient world for darkening leather.</note>—into:

*   **Natural (mined)**

    2. That which is formed in stone basins.

*   **Artificial:** That which is made in Spain from wells or pools that contain the same kind of water from which the natural forms are produced.

# Metamorphosis, transmutation, or transformation of such minerals by nature’s own craftsmanship.

->There is a great kinship between the **flower of copper** <note>original: *floris æris*</note>—that is, **verdigris**, according to the moderns—and **chrysocolla** <note>In this context, likely a green copper mineral like malachite used for soldering gold</note>, the **vitriols**, and the rest of its species.<-

---

**I.**

**Green Zeg** <note>An Arabic-derived term used by Ruland for vitriol or copperas.</note>, or **shoemaker's blacking**, or **vitriol**, or **natural copper-flower** <note>original: *chalchanthum natiuum*</note> changes or passes into:

*   On the outer part, while the inside still remains shoemaker's blacking, through the long passage of time:
    *   **1. Misy** <note>A yellow mineral, likely an oxidized form of iron pyrite or a basic iron sulfate.</note> (formed easily).
*   Thread-like fibers, when they age, become **artificial chalcitis**; and again, copper-flower changed into chalcitis becomes **artificial misy**:
    *   **2. Chalcitis** <note>A brassy-colored mineral, often an intermediate state between pyrite and vitriol.</note>
        *   Chalcitis is a **lemon-yellow** or **honey-colored Zeg** according to Pliny; it is the "heat of copper" <note>original: *caloris æris*</note> according to Dioscorides; it is **Colcothar** <note>The red oxide of iron remaining after the distillation of vitriol.</note>, or Zeg according to the Arabs. It is a substance midway between **marcasite** (that is, black Zeg, or pyrites, or black ink) and **vitriol** (that is, green Zeg or copper-flower). When it has aged, it changes and passes into:
            *   **Sory** <note>A dark, porous mineral related to vitriol, often used in ancient medicine.</note> (formed easily).
            *   **Sory** and **melanteria** <note>A black mineral substance or ink-stone.</note> conversely pass into **White Copper-flower** <note>original: *Chalchanthum leucon*</note>, that is, **white vitriol**.

<margin>The Arabs call ink <note>original: *atramentum*; here referring to mineral-based pigments or vitriols</note> simply "zeg," and they distinguish these species of ink.</margin>

1.  **Black Zeg**, that is, **black ink**: And this is **marcasite** <note>original: *marchasita*</note>, which is to say, **pyrites** <note>Iron disulfide minerals. Ruland is explaining how these minerals were used to create black pigments and inks</note>. For marcasite, or dissolved pyrites, produces the ink which is called **Black Zeg** by Serapio <note>A name attributed to influential medieval medical authors; likely referring here to the author of the *Treatise on Simple Medicines*</note>. It is dissolved with wine and vinegar into a black color. Avicenna <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose works on medicine and chemistry were foundational in Europe</note>, in Book 2 of his chapter *On Ink*, calls it **white ink**, because when it is not yet dissolved, it appears to be white in color.

2.  **Colcothar Zeg**, or **chalcitis**, or **zegi**, which we will discuss shortly. This Zeg is **lemon-yellow** <note>original: *citrini*</note> in color, or the color of copper according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose *De Materia Medica* was the primary authority on medicinal substances</note>. It is called **citrine ink**. From this is made a fourth species, which is called **Red Zeg**, that is, **Red Ink**, and it is also named **Asuria**.

3.  **Green Zeg**, or **green ink**: This is **chalcanthum** <note>The Greek-derived term for "flower of copper" or vitriol</note>, that is, **vitriol**, which is the subject we are currently treating. This is also known as **shoemaker's blacking** <note>original: *atramentum sutorium*; a common name for ferrous sulfate used in tanning and dyeing leather</note>.

->### OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.<-

L 3

Serapio <note>likely Serapio the Younger, a 12th-century author of a celebrated work on simple medicines</note>, in his chapter on *zeg* <note>an Arabic-derived term for vitriol or mineral-based inks</note>, testifies that he has seen in the mines **black zeg**, that is, **marcasite**, which is to say, **pyrites**. And alongside it, **Colcothar**, that is, **chalcitis**, and **green zeg**, that is, **vitriol** or **chalcanthum**, all found together.

And he says these three species differ from one another in their refinement and density. Since, he says, the densest of these is **black zeg** (pyrites), the most refined is **green zeg** (chalcanthum, or **shoemaker's ink** <note>original: *atramentum sutorium*; a common name for green vitriol used in dyeing leather</note>). **Colcothar** (chalcitis) exists as a medium between these two. Furthermore, **green zeg** (chalcanthum) and **colcothar** (chalcitis) are dissolved and liquefied by fire; however, **black zeg** (marcasite) is not easily dissolved or liquefied.

**Green zeg** (chalcanthum or shoemaker's ink) is solid, being more refined—especially the Cyprian variety. It is easily changed into **misy** <note>a yellow mineral, likely a basic iron sulfate</note>, and sometimes over time its outer part transforms into **chalcitis** <note>a reddish-bronze mineral ore</note> while the interior remains shoemaker's ink. This mutual transformation is most beautiful. Such native metals <note>referring here to "metalla" in the broad sense of mineral ores or salts</note> include white, green, or blue **chalcanthum** (based on its color); then also **chalcitis**, which has the color of copper; **misy**, which is like gold; and **sory** <note>a grey or black mineral salt</note>, which is almost the color of **melanteria** <note>a black pigment or mineral ink; original: *melanteriæ*</note>. Galen <note>the famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note> mentions these many times and uses them in plasters, as did other ancient writers. Once, these were highly praised and common in Cyprus. I do not know if they are now found in our silver mines, though I do not deny they might be found there if one searched diligently. But they are found (though not frequently) in copper mines, such as at Goslar <note>a famous mining town in Germany</note> and other places.

It is a marvel, however, that wherever **marcasite** (pyrites) is found, all these minerals are formed: **chalcanthum**, **chalcitis**, **misy**, and **sory**. And all these species migrate <note>meaning they change or degrade into one another through oxidation or weathering</note>; for this reason, they are called **inks** <note>original: *atramenta*</note>. Furthermore, **chalcanthum** is hot and dry in the fourth degree <note>in the Galenic system, the "fourth degree" is the highest intensity of a quality, often indicating it can sear or destroy tissue</note> according to Paul <note>referring to Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century medical authority</note>. As for what **shoemaker's ink** was to the ancients, and what it is to us now,

We have previously discussed these matters: here, however, we shall briefly address writing ink along with Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a 1st-century Greek physician and pharmacologist whose work was the primary source for medicinal substances for 1,500 years</note>. **On Ink or Black** <note>original: *Von der Dinten oder Black*</note>, as the Saxons call it. However, the methods taught by Dioscorides for how ink is made are now entirely obsolete. For we now compose our ink much differently, using vitriol <note>iron sulfate</note>, oak gall <note>growths on oak trees used for their tannin content</note>, and gum <note>gum arabic, used as a binder</note>, as well as other methods known to scribes; therefore, its quality is variable depending on the ingredients. Artificial ink according to Dioscorides is made: 1. From soot cooked from pine torches. 2. From the soot of resins, and the painters' soot used for corroding. From various soots. 6. From vitriol, oak gall, and gum. Pliny, in Book 35, Chapter 6, also teaches other methods by which writing inks were formerly composed, namely from earths of a sulfurous color, from charcoal found in tombs, and from soot.

<header>LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND.</header>

...only sandarac <note>original: *sandaracam*; here referring to realgar or red arsenic sulfide</note>: And yellow arsenic <note>original: *arsenicum luteum*</note>, which we call orpiment <note>original: *auripigmentum*; a deep yellow mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy</note>. Avicenna <note>a prominent 11th-century Persian physician and philosopher</note> also recognizes white arsenic, but since the white form is never found as a mineral <note>original: *fossile*; something dug from the earth</note>, Avicenna seems to have been referring to another kind, perhaps a synthetic variety, of which one is yellow and the other is white, which the Chemists <note>original: *Chymistæ*</note> produce, and which today are called by the name of arsenic alone.

# DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY - M

<page-num>90</page-num>

<header>DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY - M.</header>

<margin>* Concerning all these species, see Serapio in the *Book of Aggregates*, chapter *Harmech*, and Avicenna in the chapter on Arsenic: there you will find information on its quality and harmfulness. For the sublimate, which they otherwise call "salt of arsenic," is lethal. And the white variety among them is lethal by itself. They are poisons, as Dioscorides teaches in Book 6.</margin>

**Orpiment** <term>Auripigmentum: A yellow arsenic sulfide mineral, often used as a pigment and a key ingredient in the attempt to create gold.</term> is the blood of the stone. The *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," a famous early alchemical text.</note> on page 10 calls it the "female" which we use to color the Sun <note>The alchemical symbol and name for Gold.</note> and to cook with Mercury. It is, however, truly Sulfur, according to the *Assembly* on page 66. Mercury orpiment is sulfur which rises from the mixed composite; it is the Red Stone.

**Orpiment** <term>lempinas</term> water of the lily.
**Orpiment** crystalline. Shimmering or scaly <note>original: "Schiffriecht."</note>.
**Orpiment** lumpy. Choking or suffocating Orpiment <note>original: "Stickicht Operment," referring to the dangerous fumes of arsenic.</note>.
**Orpiment** lumpy, mixed with sandarac <note>In this context, a red arsenic mineral.</note>. Mixed with red-arsenic <note>original: "Reschgelb."</note>.
**Orpiment** red, that is, Realgar <term>Realgar: A red arsenic sulfide mineral.</term>.
**Orpiment** sublimated white, which is distinguished by yellowish-white veins. White sublimated Orpiment.
**Orpiment** sublimated, that is, varied with black, reddish, and yellow veins.

**Gold**, called *Gold* by the Germans and *Sol* <note>The Sun</note> by the Chemists, is attributed to the Sun. It is the most balanced of all metals; they say it is hot and dry in the second degree, and fixed and red in the third degree. It is a metallic body, lemon-yellow, shining, heavy, and evenly "digested" <note>Matured or ripened by the earth's heat.</note> in the belly of the earth, washed for a very long time by mineral water. It is composed of pure quicksilver (mercury) that is fixed, clear, and red, and of clean, fixed, red sulfur that does not burn. In short, gold is the most refined substance of quicksilver. For we see that quicksilver most easily receives gold because it is closest to its own nature, just as a mother receives her son. Furthermore, gold [is made] from a small substance...
