**Lime of Mercury** is precipitated Mercury.

**Lime of Venus** <note>Venus is the alchemical symbol for Copper</note> is verdigris, **Spanish green.**

**Lime of Mars** <note>Mars is the alchemical symbol for Iron or Steel</note>, that is, the saffron of steel or iron, **the redness of iron.** <note>The "saffron of Mars" refers to iron oxide or rust used in various preparations.</note>

**Lime of Jupiter** <note>Jupiter is the alchemical symbol for Tin</note> is the spirit of Jupiter, **Tin-lime, in which the spirit of tin is contained.**

**Lime of Saturn** <note>Saturn is the alchemical symbol for Lead</note>, minium, **or lead-yellow.** <term>Minium: red lead (lead tetroxide), though here the author also associates it with yellow lead oxide.</term>

**Lime of pilgrims** is tartar. <term>Tartar: the potassium bitartrate crust that forms in wine barrels, frequently used as a flux or reagent.</term>

**Greater Lime**, **from eggs.**

**Roasted Lime**, alum from apples.

Among these, those which shine more feebly and with a leaden hue are called *liuicontas*, and they are much larger than the true *carchedonii*. The best carbuncles are the *methystizontes* <note>original: "methystizontes", from the Greek for "amethyst-like"</note>, that is, those whose outermost spark fades into the violet of an amethyst.

Next to these are the *syrrytæ* <note>original: "syrrytæ"</note>, radiating with a feathered brilliance. Callistratus (as cited by Pliny) asserted that the brilliance of a carbuncle ought to be white, clouding at the edge of the vision: and if it is lifted up in such a way, it blazes forth, which is why it is called a "white carbuncle." Finally, Pliny in Book 37, Chapter 8, identifies a type of carbuncle as *anthracitis* <note>original: "anthracitim"</note>, found as a fossil in Thesprotia <note>A region in ancient Epirus, Greece</note>, which resembles burning coals. It is clear that the Greeks call many things *anthracas* <note>Greek: ἄνθραξ, meaning coal or charcoal</note>: namely, the vein of cinnabar <note>original: "minii"</note>, the hematite gem, and the carbuncle itself: of which the **ruby** <note>original: "rubinus"</note> is undoubtedly a species, which we may otherwise call *lychnites* <term>Lychnites: From the Greek 'lychnos' (lamp), referring to a stone that seems to glow with its own light</term>, etc. Regarding this *anthracitis*, the same Pliny says there is a species encircled by white veins, and the color of these stones is like those mentioned above; yet when thrown into fire they are extinguished as if dead, whereas when drenched with water they blaze up. And related to these is the Indian gem *sandastron* <note>original: "sandastron", likely a variety of aventurine or sunstone</note>, or *garamantiten*, which is also found in Arabia: within its transparency, golden droplets shine from the inside. Finally, he teaches that *lychnites* belongs to this class, which is found in Caria and Orchosia, and is most esteemed in India; it is a milder Carbuncle, one variety of which radiates with purple, another with scarlet, and when warmed by the rubbing of fingers or by the Sun, they attract straws. <note>This refers to the pyroelectric or static properties of certain gems, which Ruland uses to identify the species.</note> I call our **ruby** a species of *lychnites*. And Albertus [Magnus] himself testifies that the Carbuncle is called *anthrax* by the Greeks, and that it shines in the dark like a coal when clear, bright water is poured over it in a glass vessel that is clean and polished; its species vary according to their country of origin, their brilliance, and their substance. Furthermore, it possesses the virtues of all other stones: especially as a defense against venom and poisons. Among us, in our mines, gem-

# LEXICON OF ALCHEMY #

->**DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMICAL TERMS**<-

**Catma**, gold filings.

**Catrobil**, that is, earth.

**An Ash-Cup** <note>original: "Catillus cinereus," also known as a cupel, used in the process of assaying to separate precious metals from base metals.</note> is a melting vessel made from two parts of the ashes of light wood—which have been leached and purified of all charcoal and other impurities—and one part of the ashes of bones that lack marrow (though one should avoid pig bones, which cause the greatest loss). These are finely ground and moistened with good beer until they form a mass, then thoroughly mixed together in its own little mortar. This small mortar is filled with the moistened ashes, and a pestle (commonly called a **monk**) is driven into it with three strikes of a wooden mallet. Finally, ashes from the heads of calves or the horns of stags are sprinkled through a hair sieve, and one or two more strikes are added before it is removed to dry. A larger version of the ash-cup is also made, which is formed in an iron corner-mold.

**Cathochites**. Just as the Magnet attracts iron, the Sagda stone attracts wood, and Jet and Amber attract and hold straw; so does the **Cathochites** hold onto flesh and hands by means of an innate, extremely sticky gum or glue. It is found in the fields of Corsica, according to the testimony of Solinus in the *Polyhistor*, chapter 9, and Pliny, book 37, chapter 10.

**Caua**, <term>Small pits</term> / <term>Small hollows</term> <note>German: Tälcklein / Grüblein.</note>.

**Caudafollium vectis**, <term>Bellows-lever</term> <note>German: Balgsterckel; the handle used to pump air into a furnace.</note>.

**Tail of the Reddish Fox**, this is **minium** <note>Red lead (lead tetroxide), often used as a pigment or in glassmaking.</note> made from lead.

**Small Cavities of the Veins**, <term>Crystal cavities</term> <note>German: Drüsen. In mining, these are "vugs" or cavities in a rock lined with crystals.</note>.

**Cauerna**, <term>Council-chamber</term> <note>German: Rahtstube. Likely referring to a large natural cavern or a meeting point of ore veins.</note>.

**Cauernosum**, <term>Glandular or Pitted</term> <note>German: Drüsig.</note>.

**Caurus**, <term>The West-northwest wind</term>.

**Precaution** in the <term>spagyric art</term> <note>The alchemical-medical practice of "separating and recombining" substances to create purified medicines.</note> is a certain industriousness gained through habit, by which the professors of this art perform and complete their operations more easily.

**Cauterium**, or **Cautery**, is a tool used by surgeons with which they open...

# MARTIN RULAND'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY #

<page-num>133</page-num>

...it is, so that they may have a flowing medicine which (to use the words of **Geber** <note>Geber, or Jabir ibn Hayyan, was a legendary 8th-century Islamic alchemist whose works were foundational to European alchemy</note>) suddenly adheres to it in its depths before it can flee, and is joined to it through its smallest parts, and thickens it, and preserves it in the fire by its own **fixation** <note>term: "fixione" — the process of making a volatile substance stable in heat</note>, until a greater tolerance of fire arrives to consume its humidity. Through this artifice, it converts the substance in a moment into a true sun-making and moisture-making agent <note>original Latin: "solificum & humificum"</note>, according to that for which the medicine was prepared. 

**Ceratio** (Ceration) occurs when a dry and hard body is drenched with its own moisture through frequent and repeated <term>imbibition</term> <note>the process of a solid absorbing a liquid</note>. **Arnoldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a prominent 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> describes the sign of perfect ceration for us in the second book of his *Great Rosary*, chapter 27: namely, if the medicine is cast upon a red-hot plate and it dissolves very quickly like wax, without smoke. But I leave that to the philosophers. 

**Ceratio**; This is a refinement or a "making-subtle" of the parts, so that their virtue and power may be poured upon and spread into the bodies and the moisture, which is necessary in the Art for the "complement" or fulfillment. And such ceration happens only through division and sprinkling, so that it becomes like a wax that begins to melt or become soft in a tempered heat. And note that such ceration or "waxing" was entirely discovered by those Masters.

**Cerare**, that is, to incorporate, or to mix.

**Cerebrum arietis** (Brain of the ram), Water of egg white.

**Cerebrum bouis** (Brain of the ox), that is, burned <term>tartar</term> <note>original: "tartarum combustum" — potassium bitartrate, a byproduct of winemaking used as a chemical reagent</note>.

**Cerober**, that is, water.

**Ceruiculæ spiritus** (Spirit of the neck) is the bone from the heart of a deer <note>the *os de corde cervi*, a bone-like cartilage found in a stag's heart, historically used in medicine</note>.

**Cerusa** (Ceruse), that is, the rust of lead, White Lead <note>original German: "Bleyweiß"</note>. In Greek it is called *psimytim* or *psimmythion*, or *aphidegi*. It is a poison when taken into the body, as **Dioscorides** and **Nicander** teach; it is cold and dry in the second degree. Ceruse is known to almost everyone, and it retains its name in the pharmacies: White Lead. For a powder is made from lead, whether white or black:

### THE WRITINGS OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND DOCTOR ###

<page-num>139</page-num>

...or, as others also wish, <term>verdigris</term> <note>original: "ærugo," a green pigment typically formed on copper</note>, or <term>white lead</term> <note>original: "cerussa"</note>. For they define it thus: that white lead is either verdigris or the ash of lead. If it is made from white lead <note>original: "plumbo albo," which in classical contexts often refers to tin, though here Ruland discusses it in the context of lead pigments</note>, it is called **Spanish**, and it is the whitest of all. Today we see it being made in Venice and Nuremberg. In ancient times, the most praised kind was prepared in **Rhodes**, **Corinth**, and **Sparta** <note>original: "Lacedæmone"</note>. But how it ought to be made, the same **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> teaches in book 5, chapter 53. He adds also how it may be roasted until it becomes similar to <term>sandaraca</term> <note>a red arsenic sulfide mineral, often called realgar</note>, which he then calls <term>sandix</term>. Among the Germans, this is known as *red cosmetic* <note>original: "rote Schmincke"</note>, and it is a type of artificial sandaraca, the *mountain red* <note>original: "der Berck-rote"</note>, as **Vitruvius** <note>The famous Roman architect and engineer</note> maintains. Furthermore, **red orpiment** <note>another arsenic sulfide mineral</note> has the appearance of our <term>minium</term> <note>red lead or cinnabar</note>. See **Serapio** <note>An influential Arabic medical author</note> in the *Book of Aggregation*, chapter Asteg.

Thus you see that **Sandix** is not only a plant, as some have wished to believe. Indeed, **Servius** <note>A 4th-century grammarian</note> himself, commenting on that line of **Virgil** in the *Pollio* <note>The Fourth Eclogue</note>:

> Of its own accord, the sandix shall clothe the grazing lambs.

->And Propertius:<-

> And let her be [clothed] in the common garment of sandix.

Perhaps this follows **Pliny**, book 21, chapter 15—where, however, one reads <term>scandix</term> <note>wild chervil</note> rather than **sandix**—and book 35, chapter 6. But you also see that sandix is a metallic substance, specifically white lead roasted by a certain artifice to resemble sandaraca. Pliny calls this white lead "adulterated" in book 35, chapter 6. For the rest, on how white lead is washed, consult the same **Dioscorides**; and for its powers, see also **Serapio** in the *Book of Aggregation*, chapter Affidhegi; **Avicenna**, book 2, chapter "White Lead"; and **Pliny**, book 34, chapter 18, and book 35, chapter 6. The lightest of all white lead is also used for the whitening of women's complexions. Whence **Ovid**, in his work *On Facial Cosmetics*, says:

> Neither let white lead be lacking, nor the foam of red nitre <note>original: "vitrispuma," literally glass-foam, often referring to a cleansing agent or soda</note>, etc.

**Ceraunia** <note>A "thunderstone" or a type of gemstone believed to fall from the sky</note>. Among the white-glowing gems, let the following be noted:

First, the **Asteria** <note>Star-stone</note> gem from **Pliny**, book 37, chapter 9. The Asteria is a gem which holds an enclosed light in the manner of a pupil, and pours it across when tilted; it is born in **India** and **Carmania**. Another is the **Astrios**, similar to **Crystal**, born in India and on the shores of **Pallene**; from within its center, a star shines as if with the brightness of a full moon. When held opposite the stars, it seizes their brightness and reflects it back. The best are born in Carmania.

A variety of this, which is inferior, is called by some **thunderstones** <note>original: "ceraunias"</note>. The worst is the one that looks like the light of lamps. There is another called **star-stone** <note>original: "astroitis"</note> which resembles fish eyes. It shines with a brightness like the sun. There is also a white variety among them called a thunderstone, which captures the brilliance of the stars; it is crystalline with a blue luster and originates in **Carmania** <note>An ancient province of the Persian Empire</note>. **Zenothemis** <note>A Greek geographer mentioned by Pliny</note>, according to **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*</note> in the passage cited, says it is white but has a wandering star within it. **Sotacus** <note>An early Greek writer on the properties of stones</note> adds other varieties of thunderstone, namely black and reddish ones, and claims they are found nowhere else but in places struck by lightning. These thunderstones are the stones the Germans call **Donnerstein** <note>literally "thunderstones"; historically, these were often prehistoric stone tools or fossilized belemnites believed to have fallen from the sky during storms</note>. They fall from the clouds with thunder. They are found in **Grania** <note>likely referring to a region in Germany or Spain</note> as well as in Spain, having a glowing color almost like fire.

They are also found here and there in Germany, especially by rivers such as the **Elbe** <note>original: "Albim"</note>, where I have happened to find thunderstone gems similar to crystal with a blueish tint, of various shapes—sometimes like clubs, sometimes like a pyramid, so that they resemble a **sugarloaf** <note>original: "caput Zuccarinum"</note>, as they call it,
-> **A sugarloaf**. <- <note>original German: "Ein Zuckerhut"</note>

However, it is never possible to find them whole, perhaps because of the force of the river current, the force by which they are cast out from the clouds, and their impact upon the earth. It is claimed that their power is to induce sweet sleep and to be effective against lightning strikes; likewise, they are useful for winning battles and legal cases. See also **Solinus** <note>A 3rd-century Roman geographer</note>, chapter 23, concerning thunderstones.

### Chambar, Poison <note>original German: "Gifft"</note>, is the fruit or magnesia.
The *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note> on page 66 says it is the **white stone**, and on page 92 calls it <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auripigmentum," a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, **Zendrio**, **absemech**, and **chalul**. But when it becomes white and harmless, it is then called <term>lead</term> <note>original: "plumbum"</note>, **exobmich**, <term>magnesia</term> <note>In alchemy, "magnesia" refers to a primordial substance or a mineral mixture rather than modern magnesium</note>, **martech**, and **white copper** <note>original: "æs album"</note>.

<header>THE WRITINGS OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.</header>

<page-num>141</page-num>

<margin>
**Copper-stone** <note>original: "Chalcitis"</note>
</margin>
The translation by **Marcello Virgilio** <note>An Italian scholar and translator of Dioscorides (1464–1521)</note> mistakes a specific type for the whole category when he says in Book 5, chapter 65: "Chalcitis is the stone from which copper is smelted." In fact, many different substances and types are understood and signified by this general name. One type is the copper-stone <note>original: "lapis chalcitis"</note>—that is, the ore-stone, which is **Marcasite** or the **Pyrite** itself from which copper is smelted. **Macer** and **Mesue** <note>Aemilius Macer and Mesue the Elder, influential medieval medical authorities</note> call this the **Starry Stone** <note>original: "lapidem Stellatum"</note>, as was noted in the entry for pyrite.

The second meaning of *chalcitis* refers to **hair-like alum** <note>original: "trichitin, id est, alumen capillare"</note> and copper-alum, which forms within pyrite. For this reason, *chalcitis* is sometimes called **fissile alum** <note>original: "alumen concretum, schiston"</note>. On this, see **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman natural philosopher</note>, Book 35, chapter 15. Because of this, Arabic authors sometimes mention **colcothar** <note>An alchemical term for the red oxide of iron remaining after the distillation of vitriol</note> (which is the *chalcitis* we are discussing here) alongside the *chalcitis* that is alum. This is seen in the works of **Serapion** and **Mesue**; the latter, if I am not mistaken, includes *colcothar* in his saffron lozenges, referring to both the *chalcitis* we discuss here and the *chalcitis* that is fissile alum. Likewise, **Dioscorides** <note>The primary ancient Greek authority on pharmacology</note> says that *chalcitan* (alum) is prepared by fire in the same manner as the *chalcitis* we are treating here.

The final and proper meaning of *chalcitis* is the specific substance we are discussing in this section. It is a variety of **copper-flower** <note>original: "chalcanthi"</note>, which is to say, a type of **shoemaker’s ink** <note>original: "atramenti sutorii"; historically referring to copper or iron sulfates used for dyeing leather</note>—specifically, the bright variety. It stands as a middle ground between **vitriol** <note>Sulfuric acid salts</note> and **marcasite** (or pyrite). This specific type of *chalcitis* comes in two forms: natural and man-made. The natural variety is further divided into **Cyprian** and **Babylonian**.

The **Cyprian** variety has the reddish hue of copper, from which it takes its name, as Pliny teaches in Book 37, chapter 11. Dioscorides describes it in the passage cited above as being similar to copper, easily crumbled (not stony), and not too aged, marked by long, shining veins running through it. Because of this, it should perhaps be called "Starry Stone" rather than marcasite. This substance is **zeg** <note>An Arabic term for vitriol</note>, which is a yellow-colored ink.

<header>MARTIN’S DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY.</header>

<page-num>142</page-num>

...[threefold], either yellow <note>original: "citrini"</note>, or of copper, and it is of colcothar or zeg <note>an Arabic term for vitriol</note>. From this, the Arabs say that the fourth species becomes Asuria, a red vitriol <note>original: "atramentum rubeum"</note>. But this colcothar—the yellow vitriol—is properly red vitriol, **red Vitriol**, and not sory <note>Sory is a mineral described by ancients as a further stage of decomposed or "ripened" vitriol</note>: although the Arabs call only red vitriol "Sory." Truly, it is an easy mistake to make. For chalcitis, which is red vitriol, eventually becomes sory.

However, I have never found this chalcitis in silver mines (as I have mentioned before); yet it is found in copper mines and at Goslar <note>A famous mining town in the Harz Mountains of Germany</note>. Pliny describes this native chalcitis in Book 34, chapter 12. He notes that it contains within itself three kinds: namely copper, misy <note>Yellow vitriol or iron sulfate</note>, and sory; and that it has long veins of copper. He adds that the best kind is honey-colored, crumbly with a delicate path of veins, not stony, and fresh—since when it is aged, it becomes Sory.

You may see for yourself how the same Pliny distinguishes chalcitis from Cadmia <note>A term often used for zinc ores or furnace deposits</note>; then what he understands as Cadmia and what as chalcitis, from which copper is smelted—namely marcasite (that is, pyrite) and native Cadmia (that is, **our Cobalt**). Both types of chalcitis are now unknown to the common people, and indeed even to the apothecaries themselves. Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist</note> and the same Pliny testify that the power of the native mineral is to cleanse, to warm, and to form scabs over ulcers.

Furthermore, he teaches how the vitriol <note>original: "chalcanthum"</note> itself ought to be burned with honey, and for what purpose. Finally, he describes how a medicine called *phoricon* is made from it, which helps with leprosy, though it is not prepared today; it possesses the same power as chalcitis, which Paul of Aegina <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note> and others say is of the third degree <note>referring to the Galenic system of medicinal potency</note>. There is also the Babylonian variety, which Serapio <note>An influential Arabic medical writer</note> discusses (see the entry for *zeg*), which is hard and, when broken, shows white spots inside. There is also the artificial variety, which is made from old vitriol that has turned into filaments.

### Other Types of Chalcitis

1.  Hard Chalcitis. It is called by this name because of the rust, which is its true and native color: **Hard red vitriol.**
2.  Friable Chalcitis: **Soft red vitriol.** <note>original: "Milch rot atrament"</note>
3.  Hard Chalcitis, containing misy: **red vitriol, containing yellow vitriol.**
4.  Hard Chalcitis, containing sory: **red vitriol containing black vitriol.**
5.  Hard Chalcitis mixed with pyrite: **which is fissile** <note>original: "das fissig ist," meaning it splits into layers or splinters</note>.
6.  Cyprian Chalcitis: **red vitriol from Cyprus.**

**Chalcute**, burnt copper <note>original: "æs uſtum"</note>.

**Chalcopyrites**, is lead <note>original: "Bley"</note>, according to Synecius <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist and alchemist</note>.

**Chalchos**, that is, copper <note>original: "æs"</note>.

**Chalchitor** is marcasite <note>A term often used in this period for various metallic sulfides like pyrite</note>.

**Chambelech** is the Elixir.

**Chaomantia** <note>Chaomancy</note> is the art by which a prophecy is drawn from the air. When the <term>stars of the air</term> <note>referring to atmospheric phenomena or spirits</note> open themselves and allow themselves to be seen, so that one sees and prophesies something through the air.

**Chaos**, besides the confusion of all things, the heap and the formless matter, is "Air" according to Theophrastus <note>Paracelsus</note>. It is also taken for <term>Iliaste</term> or <term>Iliastro</term> <note>Paracelsian terms for the prime matter of the elements or the spiritual force of the universe</note>. A coarse, mixed matter. Likewise: Air and Iliaster.

**Charatra**, a water-gap or gully <note>original: "Waſſerriß"</note>.

**Cheizi** <note>Likely a variation of "Cheiri," the wallflower</note> is a Paracelsian term used in an absolute sense: if the discussion is about minerals, it denotes <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note>; if, however, it is about vegetables, it denotes vegetable flowers. When it is found with an addition, such as "flower of Cheiri," it signifies the **white elixir** made from silver, or its quintessence; just as "flower of anthos" <note>original: "flos anthos"</note> refers to the **red elixir** of gold. Others maintain it is <term>potable gold</term>; others say it is Antimony.

**Chelæ**, claws or shears <note>original: "Scheren"</note>.

**Chelidonia** is gold.

**Chanchedeſt**, steel.

**Chelidonius lapis** <note>The Swallow-stone</note> or the chelidonia gem is found in the bellies of swallows. If young swallows are captured when the Moon is waxing—as Dioscorides claims in Book 2, chapter 47—specifically those from the first brood, and their bellies are cut open, two small stones are found. They are the size and shape of linseed, as I have seen myself. One appears black, the other red; or, as Dioscorides prefers, one is variegated in color and the other pure. Pliny teaches in Book 37, chapter 10, that they are the color of swallows—purple in one part, with black spots interrupting.

I have seen such small black and red stones <note>Referring to the "swallow-stones" mentioned on the previous page</note>. The red or purple kind is said to be effective against insanity and epilepsy; it is also said to win favor. **Chelonitis** <note>The "turtle-stone," usually referring to fossilized remains such as sea urchins or shells that resemble a tortoise back</note>. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note>, in Book 37, Chapter 10, also mentions the gemstone *chelonitis*, which resembles turtles. In the Old March <note>The Altmark region in modern-day Germany</note> at the mouth of the Tanger <note>original: "Tangræ"</note>, where the river Tanger flows into the Elbe <note>original: "Albi"</note>, where once the royal seat of Charles IV <note>Holy Roman Emperor, 1316–1378</note> was located, along the Elbe below the town near the village founded by Charles and bearing his name—now commonly called *Calpu*, though it should properly be called *Caroli Gepern* <note>Likely referring to the area around Tangermünde</note>—where there is the source of a spring rushing into the Elbe, the place is most pleasant and fertile in various gemstones. In that place also, the double *chelonitis* has been found, though of various types. First, there was found the *chelonitis* that entirely represented the form of sea-snails, *like a Jacob’s shell* <note>original: "Wie ein Jacobs Muschel"; a scallop shell associated with St. James</note>. Sometimes the *chelonitis* is perfect and alone; sometimes it is barely begun; sometimes it is perfect, yet adhering in part to another stone. Occasionally two or three, perfect or imperfect, were joined together. Sometimes they are the size of a bean; sometimes so small they almost escape the sight. Some are tawny-white, shining in the manner of an onyx; some are black with remarkable lines expressed in the manner of a sea-snail. There is another form of *chelonitis*, namely one resembling an oblong, turned aquatic shell, which is found here and there by rivers, such as the Elbe. These *chelonitides* also seem to have the power of <term>ostracitis</term> <note>A shell-like stone used in ancient medicine as an astringent or to treat sores</note>. Pliny also, if I am not mistaken, describes a species of *chelonitis* as having golden drops. A white *chelonitis* like onyx is found with certain small drops. Others claim the *chelonitis* is found in the heart of a turtle. But Pliny calls that one *chelonia*, and says it is the eye of the Indian turtle.

->### MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.<-

### Alchemy <note>original: "Chemia"</note>

Some linguists say that **Alchemy** is and should be called a smelting and casting art, or a craft of separation. They say that the prefix *Al* is an emphatic and completing particle <note>original: "particula emphatica & completiua"</note>. For example, as the word *Manach* means to count, so one says *Almanach* <note>Almanac</note>, in which the entire year and all the days are counted, and many other things are calculated. Others wish to derive the name from the Greek, suggesting it should be called *Archimia* or *Archodunia*, meaning the chief wisdom and principal knowledge <note>original: "sophia & sapientia principalis"</note>, as it contains within itself the highest and most wonderful secrets, and easily holds the prize above all other arts.

**Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus (1493–1541)</note> says in his *Book of Nature* <note>original: "lib. naturæ"</note> that in ancient times it was called *Vsopus* and *Vsopaica*. It is a smelting and casting art that the world cannot do without, as from it comes all goods and wealth, the art of medicine, handicrafts, and commerce. It is also called **Spagyrica** <note>Spagyrics; the Paracelsian term for alchemy, from the Greek words for "separating" and "combining"</note>, a craft of separation through which one learns to recognize the nature and properties of all minerals, their principles, causes, and effects <note>original: "principia caussas effectus"</note>: how they grow, and are purified, improved, changed, destroyed, mixed, united, and also how they are increased and diminished.

The common definition <note>original: "definitio"</note> reads as follows: *Alchemy is the art of separating essences from any mixture, and of preparing the master-works of the artisans. It teaches how to remove that which lowers the grade, or which hinders and obstructs. It teaches how to separate the false from the legitimate, and to lead things toward perfection.* <note>original: "Chemia est ars separandi, ex quolibet mixto essentias, concinnandique magisteria artificum. Docet id auferre, quod gradum diminuit, detinet & impedit. Docet falsum a legitimo separare, & ad perfectionem res adducere."</note>

**Theophrastus** says in Book 3, Paragraph: The third foundation of Medicine is alchemy. Nature brings nothing to light that is complete in its state; rather, man must complete it. This completion is called **Alchemy**. Therefore, a baker is an alchemist when he bakes bread; the vintner, when he presses wine; the weaver, when he makes cloth. Thus, whatever grows out of nature for the use of man—whoever brings it to the point for which it was ordained by nature, that person is an alchemist. How coarse and unskilled would he be, who...

<sig>T</sig>

<summary>This page defines Alchemy (Chemia), exploring its etymological roots and its role as a "craft of separation." Following Paracelsian thought, it argues that alchemy is not just laboratory work, but the process by which humans complete what nature has left unfinished, such as baking bread or making wine.</summary>

# LEXICON OF ALCHEMY [BY] MART[IN RULAND] #

I have seen such black and reddish small stones. The reddish or purple one is said to be effective against insanity and epilepsy; it is also said to win favor <note>original: "conciliare gratiam"</note>. The black one calms anger and works against fevers and bad humors <term>humors: in pre-modern medicine, the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to govern health and personality.</term>, and is good for the eyes; I omit the remaining magical properties. 

**Chelonitis** <term>Chelonitis: a gemstone or fossilized shell named for its resemblance to a turtle (Greek: *chelone*).</term>. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> in Book 37, Chapter 10, also mentions the chelonitis gem, which resembles turtles. In the **Old March** <note>The Altmark region in modern Saxony-Anhalt, Germany.</note> at the mouth of the **Tanger** <note>original: "Tangræ"</note>, where the Tanger River flows into the **Elbe** <note>original: "Albi"</note>, where once was the royal seat of **Charles IV** <note>Holy Roman Emperor (1316–1378); he held court at Tangermünde.</note>, along the Elbe below the town near the village which was founded by Charles and bears his name, and is now vulgarly called **Calpu**, although it should properly be called **Caroligepau** <note>Likely referring to a site near Tangermünde, possibly Karlsbau.</note>, where there is the source of a certain spring rushing into the Elbe, the place is most pleasant and fertile with various gems. In that place also a double chelonitis was found, though of various species. 

First, there was found the chelonitis which in its form completely represented sea snails, *like a scallop shell* <note>original German: "Wie ein Jacobs Muschel"</note>. Sometimes the chelonitis is perfect and stands alone, sometimes it is scarcely begun, and sometimes it is perfect but attached in part to another stone. Occasionally two or three, perfect or imperfect, were joined together. Sometimes they are the size of a bean; sometimes so small that they almost escape the sight. Sometimes they are yellowish-white and shining in the manner of an **onyx**; sometimes black with excellent lines expressed in the manner of a sea snail. There is also another form of chelonitis, namely one resembling an oblong, polished water-shell, which is found here and there along rivers, such as the Elbe. These chelonitides also seem to have the power of **ostracitis** <term>Ostracitis: a fossilized shell or stone resembling a crust, believed to have medicinal properties.</term>. Pliny also, if I am not mistaken, describes a species of chelonitis having golden drops. A whitening chelonitis is found like onyx, with certain small drops. Others claim that the chelonitis is found in the heart of a turtle. But Pliny calls that stone *chelonia*, and says it is the eye of an Indian turtle.

# RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND DOCTOR #

### Chemistry (Alchemy)
Several language experts say that *Chemia* <note>original: "Chemia"</note> is and should be called a smelting and casting art, a separation art <note>German: "schmeltz vnd giesseKunst / ein scheidkunst"</note>, and that the prefix *Al-* is an emphatic and completing particle <note>Latin: "particula emphatica & completiua"</note>. This is similar to how the word *Manach* means to count, and so one says *Almanach*, in which the entire year and every day is counted and many other things are calculated. Some wish to derive it from the Greek, suggesting it should be called *Archimia* or *Archodunia*, meaning "principal wisdom and knowledge" <note>original: "sophia & sapientia principalis"</note>, as it contains the highest and most wondrous mysteries within itself and easily holds the prize above all other arts.

**Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), the famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist.</note> says in his *Book of Nature* that in ancient times it was called *Vsopus* and *Vsopaica*. It is a smelting and casting art which the world cannot do without, as from it comes all goods and wealth, the art of medicine <note>German: "ArtzneyKunst"</note>, crafts, and trade. It is also called **Spagyrica** <term>Spagyric: derived from the Greek words for "to tear apart" and "to bind together," referring to the alchemical process of separation and purification followed by recombination.</term>, a separation art by which one learns to recognize the nature and properties of all minerals, their principles, causes, and effects <note>Latin: "principia caussas effectus"</note>, how they grow, are purified, improved, altered, corrupted, mixed, united, and also how they are increased and diminished.

The common definition reads as follows: "Chemistry is the art of separating essences from any mixture, and preparing the magisteries of the craftsmen. It teaches one to remove that which diminishes, detains, or hinders progress. It teaches the separation of the false from the legitimate, and the bringing of things to perfection." <note>original Latin: "Chemia est ars separandi, ex quolibet mixto essentias, concinnandique magisteria artificum. Docet id auferre, quod gradum diminuit, detinet & impedit. Docet falsum a legitimo separare, & ad perfectionem res adducere."</note>

**Theophrastus** says in Book 3: The third foundation of medicine is alchemy <note>original: "alchemia"</note>. Nature brings nothing to light that is finished in its place; rather, man must complete it, and this completion is called Alchemy. For an Alchemist is like a baker when he bakes bread, a vine-dresser when he presses wine, or a weaver when he makes cloth. Thus, whatever grows out of nature for the use of man—whoever brings it to the state for which it was ordained by nature is an Alchemist. How crude and unskilled would he be, who...

Some call this natural variety "borax," but it is not the "Toad-stone" <note>original: "borax de buffonibus"; a mythical stone thought to be found in the heads of toads</note>. It is, as it were, a species of nitre. **Pliny** <note>Natural historian of the 1st century AD</note> in Book 33, Chapter 5, defines natural chrysocolla as a liquid found in shafts, flowing through a vein of gold, where the mud thickens and reaches hardness due to the winter frosts...

In swine-stone <note>original: "suina"; likely referring to *Lapis Suillus* or "stinkstone," a variety of calcite</note>, he calls a crumbling vein **Chrysocolla**. Thus you see there are certain species of both artificial and natural **Chryſocolla**. Indeed, the finest gold is smelted from natural chrysocolla and blue <note>original: "cæruleo"</note>. Note also that in that stone where green earth (that is, *kyanos* <note>original: κύανον; a deep blue or greenish-blue mineral</note>) is present, a certain third white substance shines in the manner of sparks, which the miners call **mica**, and **cat’s silver**; in German: **Glymmer or Katzensilber**. Nature wished to delight herself with these colors in the innermost parts of the earth. Furthermore, concerning **chryſocolla**, see Serapion in the *Aggregator*, the chapter on **Tincar**, who also calls natural **chryſocolla**...

### LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND

[It is] said to be found on the shores of the sea; and it is among the species of salt, hot and dry in the 4th degree. Furthermore, for its use in medicines and how it should be washed, consult the cited work of Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note>. There is also a poisonous chrysocolla if taken in more than the proper dose. It is also called **Azoth** <note>the universal solvent or essential agent in alchemy</note>; **Rebis** <note>the "dual-matter" or alchemical hermaphrodite</note>; water of sulfur; wine of the soul; the Flower; and the **Soul / Spirit** <note>original German: "Seel / Geiſt"</note>. There are indeed various types:

1. Pure natural Chrysocolla collected in the Carpathian Mountains: **pure mountain-green** <note>original: "rein Bergkgrün"</note>.
2. Natural variety from Schneeberg in Meissen, found in metallic copper stone: **mountain-green in a copper ore** <note>original: "Bergkgrün in einem Kupffer Ertz"</note>.
3. Natural variety from the Rhaetian Alps, deposited in layers with malachite: **A blackish mountain-green, mixed with malachite layer by layer** <note>original: "Ein Schwartzisch Bergkgrün/ miteinem Malachit ſchicht weiſe vermenget"</note>.
4. In the fissile stone of Eisleben: **A mountain-green in Eisleben shale** <note>original: "Ein Bergkgrün in Eiſlebiſchen Schifer"</note>.
5. The grassy variety, which after dyeing is called in the common tongue: **shale-green** <note>original: "Schifergrün"</note>.
6. The artificial variety: **manufactured mountain-green** <note>original: "gemacht Bergkgrün"</note>.

**Chrysos** or **Chrysion**, that is, gold.

**Chrysolite** <note>a golden-hued gem, often modern peridot or yellow topaz</note> is a gem sent from Ethiopia along with the hyacinth <note>likely a blue or yellow zircon</note>, etc., having a translucent golden color. Whence it also takes its name, according to Pliny, Book 33, Chapters 9 and 12. Solinus, in the *Polyhistor*, Chapter 33, seems to call the same thing **Chrysolampis** <note>literally "golden lamp"</note>, which Pliny (in the same book, Chapter 10) says is born in Ethiopia; it is of a pale color by day and fiery by night. Likewise, Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century philosopher and scientist</note> says that the golden-colored chrysolite gem appears most beautiful in the morning hours; at other hours it is not so beautiful, appearing unlike itself, and it is destroyed and put to flight by fire because it is set ablaze by it. He also considers a species of it to be golden marcasite, which he also calls another stone of blue and red color.

The **Power** of Chrysolite is to excite good spirits, to oppose melancholy and nocturnal ghosts <note>original: "lemuribus nocturnis"; refers to nightmares or restless spirits</note>, to cure mange and ulcers, and to mitigate the heat of fever. Ovid, in the second book of the *Metamorphoses*, imagines the chariot of the Sun as being beautifully made of chrysolite when he says:
> The axle was of gold, the pole was gold, and the gold of the highest... <note>original Latin: "Aureus axis erat, temo aureus, aurea ſummæ"</note>

It also signifies arsenic, the Achesian stone.
**Chemistry** <gloss>from the word "to pour" - original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ χέω</gloss> I pour. Whence <gloss>juice - original Greek: χυμὸς</gloss> juice, and chemistry is the art of making juice, or of dissolving solids into juice. But by a "synecdoche of the more difficult part" <gloss>preeminently - original Greek: κατ’ ἐξοχὴν</gloss>, coagulation is also understood by the ancient chemists under the term "solution": hence that very common saying: *solve et coagula* <note>meaning: dissolve and at the same time solidify; the fundamental cycle of alchemical transformation</note>. Suidas and Cedrenus <note>Byzantine chroniclers and lexicographers</note> called it <gloss>chemistry - original Greek: χημείαν</gloss>.

The Arabs, noting its excellence, added the article *Al*, and called it **Alchemy**; just as Caelius Rhodiginus called it *Archimia*, which they named <gloss>the chemistry of silver - original Greek: ἀργύρου χημείαν</gloss>. It is also called **Spagyric** <gloss>from the words "to draw out" and "to gather" - original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ σπάω & ἀγείρειν</gloss>, from the processes of extracting and combining; it is likewise called the *Separatory* art, as well as *Usopaic* <note>possibly from a term for cleansing or washing</note> from washing, sequestering, and purifying. Chemistry, therefore, is a physical art of separating the pure from the impure, adapted for the preparation of medicines to heal human bodies as well as for bringing metallic bodies to their highest perfection.

**Chymus**, that is, a mass. Likewise, the dregs or lees.

**Cianum**, <term>Lapis Lazuli - original German: Laſurſtein</term>.

**Cibatio** [Feeding], that is, incorporation <note>the process of adding liquid to a dry substance to give it "body"</note>.

**Cibur** or **Chybur** is sulfur.

**Cicatrizing**, <term>that which heals or burns away blisters - original German: Was Blättern brennet</term>.

**Cicinum oil**, Radish oil <note>usually referring to castor oil, derived from the *Ricinus* plant, sometimes confused with radish oil in old texts</note>.

# MARTIN RULAND’S DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY

**Cinnabar** <note>original Latin: *Cinnabaris* or *cinnabari*</note> is twofold:

**True Cinnabar**, which we shall treat in this present section. The ancients called True Cinnabar **"Dragon’s Blood"** <note>original Latin: *sanguinem Draconis*</note>, and it still retains that name today. It is itself twofold: namely, **Metallic** <note>original Latin: *Metallicum*</note>, which we shall treat in the following section.

1.  **Red** <note>original Latin: *Rubeum*</note>, like sandarac <note>a resin or sometimes a mineral pigment</note> and minium <note>red lead</note>; these consist of small lumps. These are used by painters in Venice because they imitate the color of blood, and they are also used by Physicians in antidotes.

2.  **Dark** <note>original Latin: *Atrum*</note>, which is brought to us formed in the shape of a globe, though it is compressed and not protruding; this variety is adulterated. The evidence of this is its excessive stickiness. Indeed, it appears that certain particles of true cinnabar are mixed with gum, which can be seen; and the Apothecaries <note>original Latin: *Medicamentarii*</note> sell this as the true substance.

As for what True Cinnabar actually is, there are various opinions. Pliny, in Book 33, Chapter 7, calls it "Indian Cinnabar" <note>original Latin: *Indiacum cinnabarim*</note> for the sake of distinction; he says it is the **gore of a crushed dragon** <note>original Latin: *faniem draconis illisi*</note>, under the weight of dying elephants, mixed with the blood of both animals. Solinus agrees with him. Leonicenus <note>a Renaissance physician and scholar</note>, however, considers it to be a metallic substance, since Dioscorides <note>the famous Greek pharmacologist</note> reckons it among the metals. The Arabs claim it is a juice. Serapio <note>likely Serapion the Younger, an Arabic medical author</note> claims it comes from the **Achilles’ Ironwort** <note>original Latin: *Sideritidis Achilleæ*</note>. On the other hand, Dioscorides, though he describes that herb diligently, makes no mention of such a juice. Nevertheless, I lean toward the opinion of those who maintain that cinnabar is the juice or "tear" <note>sap or resin</note> of some herb or tree, because even

->### MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN. 151<-

...as even the taste and flavor themselves indicate. They say there is a tall tree in Libya and neighboring regions from which that **Dragon’s Blood** flows, just as in the Rhetian Alps it flows from the larch, and among us from our spruce and fir in the springtime—namely resin, which the Italian apothecaries <note>original Latin: *medicamentarii*</note> even sell as turpentine resin, although true Turpentine is said to be similar in color to Chian mastic <note>a high-quality resin from the mastic tree</note>. Thus Platearius <note>a 12th-century medical writer</note> also believes that Dragon’s Blood is the juice of a tree or herb in India or Persia.

<margin>Metallic Cinnabar.</margin>
The other kind of cinnabar is metallic; it is called *nulton* or even *minium* <note>historically, this term was used for both red lead and cinnabar (mercury sulfide)</note>, and is called *cinnabaris* by the Greeks. Metallic cinnabar is twofold: namely, artificial and natural minium. The natural variety is called <term>BergkZinnober</term> <note>literally "Mountain Cinnabar" in German</note>; when it is broken down, it becomes quicksilver <note>mercury</note> and sulfur. In other places it is called natural minium, and it is red in color like sandarac <note>a red pigment, either a resin or a mineral like realgar</note>. It is found in silver mines, as Pliny writes. Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a 16th-century botanist and pharmacologist</note> indicated that this natural minium is also found near the Rhine, at Eberburg, just as a great quantity is found at Schneeberg <note>original: *Schonbachi*</note>. In the mines of Meissen <note>original: *Misnensibus*</note> we have a vein of it, <term>Quecksilber Erß</term> <note>literally "Quicksilver Ore" in German</note>, which was once of such great value among the Romans, as Pliny writes in Book 33, Chapter 7. Hence Virgil also says in his tenth Eclogue:

> Pan, also, reddened with minium.

And Pliny calls it now a "vein of minium," and now a "minium stone." And as we see, it adheres to the type of fissile stone in such a way that it seems innate to it. For so Pliny says in Book 33, Chapter 6: "And there is a stone in those veins, the fluid of whose eternal 'blister' <note>original: *vomica*</note> is called quicksilver." Vitruvius writes that this natural minium is called *anthrax* <note>the Greek word for "coal"</note>, or <term>das Quecksilber Erß</term> <note>the Quicksilver Ore</note>, for the vein is similar to a glowing coal. These are the words of Vitruvius himself: "I shall now begin to explain the nature of minium. It is said to have been first discovered in the Cilbian fields of the Ephesians; both the substance and its nature are a source of considerable wonder. For a clod is dug up, which is called *anthrax*, before it reaches the state of minium through processing..."

### Metallic Cinnabar <note>original: *Cinnabaris metallicus*</note>

The other type of cinnabar is metallic; it is called *nulton* <note>a medieval term for mineral cinnabar</note> or even *minium*, and it is called *cinnabaris* by the Greeks. There are two metallic types: namely, artificial and natural minium.
Natural Cinnabar (in German: **Mountain Cinnabar** <note>original: *Bergkzinober*</note>), when broken down, becomes quicksilver <note>mercury</note> and sulfur. It is otherwise known as natural minium and is red in color, like sandarac <note>a red mineral pigment, likely realgar</note>. It is found in silver mines, as Pliny writes. Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a 16th-century botanist</note> noted that this natural minium is also found near the Rhine, at Eberburg, and a great abundance is found at Schönbach. In the mines of Meissen, we have a vein of it called **Mercury Ore** <note>original: *Quecksilber Ertz*</note>, which was once of such high value among the Romans, as Pliny writes in Book 33, Chapter 7. Hence, Virgil says in his tenth Eclogue:

> ->*Pan, reddened with minium.*<- <note>original: *Pana minioque rubentem*</note>

And Pliny calls it sometimes a "vein of minium" and sometimes a "minium stone." As we see, it adheres to the type of fissile stone <note>stone that splits into layers, like slate</note> so closely that it seems to be born within it. Indeed, Pliny says in Book 33, Chapter 6: "There is a stone in these veins whose 'pimple' <note>original: *vomica*; referring to a pocket or inclusion</note> of eternal liquid is called quicksilver." Vitruvius <note>the Roman architect</note> writes that this natural minium, or **Mercury Ore** <note>original: *Quecksilber Ertz*</note>, is called *anthrax* <note>Greek for coal or charcoal</note>, for the vein is similar to a glowing coal. These are the words of Vitruvius himself: "I shall now begin to explain the nature of minium. It is said to have been first discovered in the Cilbian fields of the Ephesians. Both the substance and its nature are quite wonderful. For a clod is dug up, which is called *anthrax* <note>charcoal</note>, before it reaches the state of minium through processing."

<margin>Cinnabar or cinnabari is twofold</margin>

**Cinnabar**
*   **Genuine**, which we shall treat in this present section. Genuine cinnabar is further divided into two types:
    *   1. **Red**
    *   2. **Black**
*   **Metallic**, which we shall treat in the following section.

Genuine cinnabar is what the ancients called **Dragon’s Blood** <note>original: *sanguinem Draconis*</note>, and it still retains that name today. It is also of two types:

> 1. **Red**, such as **Sandarac** <note>a red mineral, likely realgar or a resin</note> and **minium** <note>red lead</note>; these are found in small clumps. Painters in Venice use them because they imitate the color of blood, and physicians also use them in antidotes.
>
> 2. **Black**, which is brought to us formed into the shape of a ball; however, these are compressed and do not rise, which is a sign of an adulterated <note>fake or diluted</note> substance. The proof of this is its excessive stickiness. For it seems that certain particles of true cinnabar are mixed with gum—which can be seen—and pharmacists sell this as the genuine article.

**Metallic Cinnabar**, which we shall treat in the section following.

---

Regarding what **Genuine Cinnabar** actually is, there are various opinions. **Pliny** (Book 33, Chapter 7) calls it **Indian Cinnabar** to differentiate it; he says it is the gore of a dragon crushed by the weight of dying elephants, a mixture of the blood of both animals. **Solinus** agrees with him. **Leonicenus**, however, judges it to be something metallic, as **Dioscorides** <note>a famous 1st-century Greek physician</note> reckons it among the metals. The Arabs claim it is a juice. **Serapio** <note>an Arabic medical authority</note> claims it comes from the plant *Sideritis Achillea* <note>likely a species of Ironwort or Yarrow</note>. But Dioscorides, on the other hand, makes no mention of such a juice when he describes that herb in detail. However, I am inclined toward the opinion of those who hold that cinnabar is the juice or "tear" of some herb or rather a tree, because even

## Metallic Cinnabar

The other kind is **Metallic Cinnabar**; it is called *nulton* or also **minium** <note>red lead or cinnabar; in antiquity, these terms were often used interchangeably for red pigments</note>, and the Greeks call it *cinnabaris*. The metallic form is twofold: namely, artificial and native.

**Native cinnabar** is called in German <term>Bergk Zinnober</term> <note>Mountain Cinnabar</note>; when it is broken down, it becomes quicksilver <note>mercury</note> and sulfur. Otherwise it is called native *minium*, and it is red in color, like sandarac <note>here referring to the red mineral realgar</note>. It is found in silver mines, as Pliny writes. Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a famous 16th-century botanist and physician</note> indicated that this native *minium* is also found by the Rhine, at Eberburg, just as a great abundance is found at Schneeberg. In the Meissen mines, we have a vein of it, <term>Quecksilber Erß</term> <note>Mercury Ore</note>, which was once of such great value among the Romans, as Pliny writes in Book 33, Chapter 7. Whence also Virgil says in the tenth Eclogue:

> Pan reddened with *minium*. <note>original: *Pana minioque rubentem*</note>

And Pliny calls it now a "vein of *minium*," now "stone *minium*." And as we see, it adheres to the type of fissile <note>layered or slaty</note> stone in such a way that it appears innate to it. For so Pliny says in Book 33, Chapter 6: "And there is a stone in those veins, whose discharge of eternal liquid is called quicksilver." Vitruvius writes that this native *minium* is called *anthrax* <note>from the Greek for coal or ember</note>—<term>das Quecksilber Erß</term>—for the vein is similar to a glowing coal. These are the words of Vitruvius himself: "I shall now proceed to explain the nature of *minium*: it is said to have been first discovered in the Cilbian fields of the Ephesians; its substance and nature are quite worthy of admiration. For a clod is dug up, which is called *anthrax* <note>original: *gleba, quae anthrax dicitur*</note>, before it reaches the state of *minium* through processing..."

...a reddish iron vein having a red powder around it. When it is dug from the sites of ironworks, it emits frequent tears of quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, which are immediately collected by the miners. This is according to Vitruvius <note>a Roman architect and engineer of the 1st century BCE</note>. But note that the Greeks, because of the similarity in color, called many things *anthracas* <note>original: *anthracas*; the Greek *anthrax* means "coal," but also referred to deep red gems that look like glowing embers</note>, such as:

1. The vein of minium <note>original: *vena minii*; here referring to cinnabar, the ore of mercury</note>, as the words of Vitruvius himself declare here.
2. The hematite gem <note>original: *hæmatites*</note> according to Pliny, Book 36, Chapter 20, which we discussed above.
3. That most noble gem which Pliny calls the Carbuncle <note>original: *Carbunculum*; likely a ruby or garnet</note>, if I am not mistaken, in Book 37, Chapter 7.
4. A type of earth mentioned by writers on rural affairs; I believe it is that earth which the Saxons dig up in several places, dry in the sun, and use instead of wood. It is then used for tending the fire, and is undoubtedly a species of bitumen. The Saxons call it <term>peat</term> <note>original: *thorff*</note>. It is a bitumen dried outside the earth by the heat of the Sun; it is undoubtedly the "mother" of stone coal, which is bitumen hardened by heat within the earth. They call it <term>peat</term> <note>original: *thorff*</note>, perhaps because it is "torrefied" <note>dried or scorched</note> by the Sun.
5. It is that which Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note> describes when he says:

> Regarding those which they call "coals" <note>original: *carbones*</note> among the things dug up for use, they must be considered earthy. They are consumed and ignited by fire just like charcoal.

Among us, a certain type is found, so "cooked" by the heat of the earth that it is black and light just like charcoal. Nevertheless, it is fatty <note>rich in hydrocarbons</note> and used by blacksmiths; in German it is called <term>Stone-coal</term> <note>original: *Steinkolen*</note>, or as it were "stone-anthracites" <note>original: *lithanthrakes*</note>. Theophrastus calls them "crumbly" <note>original: *psathyras*</note> because they are so light that they float on water, which seems to be because they are a parched and porous earth. In the territory of Liège <note>in modern-day Belgium, famous for its coal mines</note>, heavy ones are dug up, which would be called "stone-anthracites." Pliny has nothing on these. The Greeks, however, used the word *anthrax* for both glowing embers and extinguished coals.

**Coals: they are extinguished and black, or glowing and red; such are the first.**

2. Species of *anthrax* <note>original: *anthrakas*; referring to the list of red minerals from the previous page</note>, like glowing coals, and the last two are like black, extinguished coals. From minium, whether already refined or raw, quicksilver <note>mercury</note> is often produced, as has been said; this can by no means be done from sandaraca. Indeed, while the vein of minium is washed so that it may later be ground, part of it changes into quicksilver; and this, once dried and ground again, returns to its own color. The artificial kind, which is made from quicksilver and sulfur by the Chemists, is called *Zinnober* <note>cinnabar</note> by the Germans and *Cinnabari* by the Latins. This is our common artificial cinnabar. There is also another adulterated minium, different from what they call cinnabar—namely, that which today alone retains the name of minium <note>red lead</note>, and it is made from lead. There is also a third adulterated type found in silver and lead mines, made from a certain burnt stone found in the veins, about which Pliny wrote in Book 33, Chapter 7. Pliny seems to have transcribed from Theophrastus the method by which minium is actually made.

**Incineration** <note>original: *Cinefactio*</note> is the process by which ashes are made. Therefore, although metallic soot and Alkali are sometimes called ashes, the term properly belongs to combustible or flammable things. For the remains of these burnt things are properly called ashes. The administration of this process is twofold: closed and open.

**Ash** <note>original: *Cinis*</note>, the impure body. When Mercury kills the luminaries <note>alchemical shorthand for mercury dissolving gold and silver</note>, a precious ash remains; this is called calcination or sifting <note>original: *calcinatio*, *cribratio*</note>. The ash is a white powder.

**Ivy ash**, that is, Potash <note>original: *Cinis clauellatus*; a salt captured from the ashes of wood, used as a powerful alkali</note>.
**Potash**, that is, Alkali.
**Ash from ash** is a salt or an extracted liquid <note>original: *aqua extracta*</note>; it is a "fixed" or stable ash in which the "ash of ash" resides. It is called "frozen coagulant" <note>original: *congelatum coagulans*</note>, because it solidifies water into earth. It is also called the "ferment of ferment," meaning it ferments gold, as Rosinus <note>A common Latinization of the name of the early alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis</note> says.
Senior <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a famous 10th-century Arabic alchemist</note> on page 40: the purified ash becomes dregs; for we no longer have need of the dross, and it is then called Lime, Glass, Litharge <note>original: *Silberglett*; a lead oxide byproduct of silver refining</note>, Pure Water, or Ash, once it has been cleaned of its "windows" <note>likely referring to its transparent or glassy impurities</note>. For the crude earthiness is cast away, and these are its leaves and flowers—namely, the Spirit and the Soul.
**Vine-shoot ash** is called *Rebenasch* or *Weinrebenasch* by the Germans. This ash is not only useful to physicians and surgeons, but also to Chemists. Pliny and Dioscorides <note>famous ancient authorities on natural history and medicine</note> list its extraordinary powers. It contains the power of salt, but milder. It corrodes fleshy growths. Its virtue, however, varies according to the difference and quality of the material burned. See Serapion's *Book of Aggregations*, the chapter "Mamad", and Galen, *On Simple Medicines*, book 8.
**Ash-ified** <note>original: *Cinificatum*</note>, that is, calcined <note>reduced to powder through heat</note>.
**Vein of ash**, simply Ash.
**Cupel** <note>original: *Cinericium*</note>. This is a goldsmith’s shard or testing-bowl <note>original: *Scherb*</note> in which gold or silver is refined by burning away impurities.
**Cementing material** <note>original: *Cineritium*</note> is a "cement" used for refining gold or silver; it is called the "regal" substance <note>referring to *regale*, a process used to separate silver from gold</note> by some.
**To cement**. To join together in the manner of a cement.
**Circius**. The West-North-West wind.
**Circulation** is the "exaltation" <note>the process of refining a substance to a higher power</note> of a pure liquid through a continuous cycle of dissolving and solidifying within a Pelican <note>a specialized alchemical flask with two curved side-arms that return the distilled vapors back into the base</note> by the action of heat. ...especially extractions, by which essences are made. Therefore, it also not infrequently performs the duty of rectification <note>The process of purifying a liquid by repeated distillation</note>, since through it liquors become not only thinner, but also purer, more effective, and more transparent. Several operations concur in its administration, such as digestion (whence sometimes digestion in a **pelican** <note>A specialized alchemical flask with two curved "arms" that return the condensed vapor back to the main body, allowing for continuous reflux</note> and circulation are considered the same thing), sublimation, and vicarious distillation.

For example: Much work and study is spent on the true extraction of the **spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritus vini*; ethanol or concentrated alcohol</note>, so that it can be obtained without any **phlegm** <note>original: *phlegmate*; the watery, inactive part of a substance that remains after the "spirit" is removed</note>. For whenever it is raised through heat, it always carries some phlegm with it. 

Hence, we will demonstrate the method of circulation using this example. One takes the most noble wine that can be found and pours it into a spacious **circulatory vessel**. With the opening sealed, it is placed in a **water bath** <note>original: *balneo maris*; literally "Bath of Mary," a double-boiler used for gentle heating</note> for fourteen days, so that the water boils continuously. Afterward, it is removed and poured into a vial. In the winter time, while still warm, it is placed in cold snow-water—the **alembic** <note>A distillation apparatus consisting of a cap and a delivery tube</note> being attached and glued to a receiver—or in the summer, it is placed in a cellar in a vessel containing ice. The pure spirit, free from all phlegm, will transcend the alembic and slip down into the receiver. 

When nothing more ascends, the receiver is removed, and the vial is taken out with the wine, which now contains no true spirit, but only **burnt wine** <note>original: *vinum adustum*; a term used by Paracelsus (Theophrastus) to describe the residue left after the spirit has been extracted</note>. This spirit of wine, while still in the circulatory vessel, is rotated so long until it can no longer be poured from glass to glass, but must be advanced by distillation or moist elevation. But when the material upon which it ought to act is placed in the receiver, it easily embraces it and ceases its flight <note>meaning it stops evaporating away and begins to interact with the target substance</note>.

**Circulatory**, is a glass vessel where the infused liquor, by ascending and descending, is rotated as if in a circle. Its use is found in subtilizations <note>The process of making a substance more refined or volatile</note> and circulations. Various vessels of this kind have been devised by various minds, out of which number only two of great importance and use please us: namely, the **Pelican** and the **Diota** <note>A vessel with two handles, resembling an ancient Greek vase, used for similar reflux processes</note>.

**Circle** is a round instrument for cutting glass...

Therefore, **Clyssus** can encompass the entire essence of a thing, since, once the impurities and dregs have been discarded, whatever is essential in it is reduced into a single compound. Or, it is the extraction of the subtle essence of all parts of a plant, joining together into a common existence. It can be united in two ways: either so that all the essences extracted from the various parts are joined and incorporated; or, so that the oil is in one gourd-shaped vessel <term>cucurbit: a glass or clay vessel used in distillation</term>, the salt in a second, and the liquid in a third, and thus placed under a single **alembic** <term>alembic: the lid or "head" of a still used to condense vapors</term> they are distilled through a common pipe, and so united. But this will not succeed so easily. For waters and salts do not rise <note>vaporize</note> in the same way. Therefore, this might better be done in different oils and waters.

**Coadunatio** <note>Uniting together</note> is a process by which things that were separated are joined. It is sometimes called **Coagulation**, the name of a more excellent species. From this arises that dogma of the philosophers, that the alchemical art <note>original: *Chymicū artificium*</note> consists of solution and coagulation; however, this refers more to the mystery of the **Stone** <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note>. Thus, coadunation is the reduction of a solution in those things where it is possible. There are two types: Composition and Coagulation.

->### MART[IN RULAND'S] LEXICON OF ALCHEMY<-

...and a driving together <note>original: *coactio*</note> into a solid. Therefore, those things which have been thinned by watery, airy, or fiery dissolution are, through this process, reduced into a homogeneous body. And thus coagulation accompanies many operations, such as evaporation <note>original: *divaporationem*</note>, exaltation, sublimation, distillation, etc. It is performed in two ways: by **Segregation** and by **Comprehension**. It is also either **cold** or **hot**.

**Cold Coagulation** is when things dissolved in heat are coagulated in the cold.

**Hot Coagulation** is when, by means of suitable heat, dissolved things are coagulated.

**Coagulation by Segregation** is when, once certain parts are separated, the remainder grows together. Thus it could also primarily be called concretion or *sympexis* <note>original Greek: σύμπηξις; a binding or joining together</note>. It is accomplished by heat, which gradually evaporates or exhales the moisture that was the cause of the flow.

**Coagulum** <note>or Rennet</note>. Rennet <note>original German: *Lip/Geypß*</note> is made from milk and causes the milk to curdle <note>original German: *zusammen rinnet*</note>; it is also a ferment. Mercury is the milk; our Mercury is the rennet with its sulfur. Maria the Prophetess <note>a legendary female alchemist of antiquity</note> calls the "coagulating coagulant" the Sulfur of the Philosophers, the soul of the *prime matter* <term>prima materia: the fundamental, formless substance from which all things are made</term> and "our gold." For that same sulfur coagulates Mercury. "Ash from Ashes" <note>original German: *Esch auß Eschen*</note>—that is, the Earth—is also called the "ferment of the ferment" because it coagulates the spirit.

**Specific Coagulant** is a material earthy essence, hardened into a dry consistency through coagulation.

**Coagulum**, that is, Mercury.

**Coagulation by Comprehension** is when the whole substance is simultaneously compressed and remixed into a uniform substance.

**Cobastoli**, that is, ash.

**The smoke of Cobatiorum**, which is Cobalt <note>likely referring to the mineral or the arsenic-rich fumes produced by smelting cobalt ores</note>.

**Cochlea**, a screw <note>original German: *Schraubet*</note>.

**Cochleare**, a ladle <note>original German: *Kelle*</note>.

**White Cochleare**, a shovel or scoop <note>original German: *Schuffe*</note>.

**Cocilio**, that is, a weight of 11 ounces.

**Codax**, Braids <note>original German: *Zopffe*; likely referring to the braided appearance of certain roots or mineral structures</note>.

**Heaven** <note>original: *Cœlum*</note>. It is a heavenly spirit which pours in the essential forms of things, and thereby weds and unites them. In the planets are their own special spheres. This lower heaven has earth and water; these must be separated and purified and put back together again, so that heaven becomes light and fire, life and movement.

**Heaven of the Philosophers** <note>original: *Cœlum philosophorum*</note> is the name given to that which far transcends the nature of ordinary elements, such as the **Philosopher's Stone** or the **Universal Medicine** <note>original: *medicina catholica*</note>.

**Heavens of the Planets** <note>original: *Cœli Planetarum*</note> according to Paracelsus <note>a famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist</note> are their own orbits and spheres, not imaginary ones, to which movements are attributed by non-believers, who recognized them in the heavens just as they could on earth. Pliny and Empedocles <note>ancient natural philosophers</note> investigated these pagan "conflagrations." If they were ignorant of what is on earth, which is separated by such an immense distance, how could they judge well otherwise than through deceptive conjectures? Indeed, because of their lack of faith, it is only fair that they were participants in no truth from their own speculations and imaginations; for true visions of meditation are reserved by God for the faithful alone. False visions, on the other hand, proceed from the enemy of truth and follow the speculations of the unfaithful, to whom that portion falls as their lot.

**Mud** <note>original: *Cœnum*</note>, that is, dung.

The corrosive species are pulverized and moistened with vinegar, urine, or **strong water** <term>aqua forti: nitric acid</term> so that they become like a paste <note>some people use these dry</note>. ->### MARTIN RULAND'S DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY ###<-

...a portion is placed in the cementing box <note>a crucible or heat-resistant container</note>, and a plate is placed over it, and another portion of powder is sprinkled on the plate; this is called **stratification** <term>stratificatio: the process of arranging materials in alternating layers</term> and **layer upon layer** <note>original: *stratum super stratum*</note>. Another plate follows this, and so on, until the box is full or no plates remain; finally, it is closed with powder on top, and the joints of the fortified box are sealed with some tenacious clay. It is then placed in the fire or (more ideally) in its own furnace, and is cemented according to the degrees of heat for four, six, eight, twelve, or 24 hours; indeed, it is kept there for several days depending on the situation <note>original: *pro re nata*</note>. 

For example: If the intent is to prepare **Saffron of Mars** <term>Crocus Martis: a red powder produced by the oxidation of iron, used in medicines and pigments</term> or of steel, and that through cementation, then I take as much fresh **quicklime** <note>original: *calcis viuæ*</note> as is needed, and I moisten it for a while with male urine until it becomes like a pulp. Afterward, I cover the bottom of the cementing box with this pulp to the thickness of a finger's breadth, and I add plates of steel upon it, filling the vessel (as said above) and sealing it with clay. When all is properly prepared, I place the box in our cementing furnace and maintain a continuous fire of the third degree <note>a high heat, but not the absolute maximum</note> for 4 to 24 hours. Finally, having removed the vessel, I thoroughly crush the material contained within it in a mortar and pass it through a hair-sieve so that it becomes a very fine powder. I then wash away all the lime from the steel with hot water, dry the residue, and I receive the most excellent Saffron of Mars. In the same way, **Saffron of Venus** <term>Crocus Veneris: a copper oxide produced by a similar heating process</term> is made, which can serve many operations.

**Azure** <note>original: *Cœruleum*</note>, called *kyanthos* or *kyanon* by the Greeks, and *cœruleum* by the Latins because of its color; **Lapis Lazuli**. This is the same as the poisonous color called *Lasur* by the Germans. All these terms seem to imitate the Arabs, who call it *Lasuli*.

<margin>
Native fossil, properly called Lapis Lazuli <note>original: *Lasur*</note>, which is also of two types.
</margin>

Found in the mines of Cyprus according to Dioscorides <note>Book 5, Chapter 56</note>, originating from copper mines. It is also found in our gold and copper mines, such as at Lauterberg in Saxony, near the Harz mountains, and at Goldberg in Silesia; the finest species is produced there and is called **slate-blue** <note>original: *schiferblaw*</note>. It also occurs in Hungary and Lorraine. It is like a fine sand, stone, or earth which adheres to fissile stone <term>fissile stone: stone that easily splits into layers, like slate</term> alongside **Chrysocolla** <term>Chrysocolla: a green copper carbonate mineral</term>. Hence Theophrastus also rightly says: "Native Azure is that which contains Chrysocolla within itself." Gold is smelted from this azure at Lauterberg and at Goldberg in Silesia. Its power in medicine is for dispersing <note>referring to the "discutient" property of breaking up humors or swellings</note>, although it is somewhat astringent. It is prepared by burning, like **chalcitis** <term>chalcitis: a copper-bearing mineral or "copper-stone"</term>, and washed like **Cadmia** <term>Cadmia: a term used for various zinc or cobalt ores and their residues</term>; you must beware of using it in its raw state. Pliny <note>Book 33, Chapter 13</note> identifies three kinds of it: Egyptian, Scythian, and Cyprian, to which have been added Puteolan and Spanish. He then teaches how to prepare **lomentum** <term>lomentum: a high-quality blue pigment</term> from it by washing and burning. Indeed, there is a very great kinship between Azure and Chrysocolla, which is called **slate-green** or **mountain-green** <note>original: *Schifergrūn, Bergrūn*</note>. This Azure is called **Lapis Lazuli**, **slate-blue**, or **mountain-blue** <note>original: *Lasur, Schiferblaw, Bergblaw*</note>. He says one should choose an azure that is saturated with color, hard, resistant to iron, and free from marble and **marcasite** <term>marcasite: here likely referring to iron pyrites</term>; for the varieties that have a beautiful color but are crumbly and impure are of little use. Furthermore, concerning Azure, see also Serapion <note>in the *Book of Aggregation*</note>, Alzanard, and Mesue on the **Lapis Lazuli**. Some consider it hot and dry in the third degree; others say hot in the second and dry in the third degree. It possesses astringency combined with sharpness. Its dose is from one scruple up to one and a half drams. Dioscorides, in the place cited above, also makes mention of **Armenian Stone** alongside Azure; he notes that Armenian Stone is light and blue in color, or as Pliny insists, mostly green, sharing its color with Azure. This is now brought forward as a substitute for **Emerald** <term>Smaragdus: Emerald</term>, and we use it in place of the Emerald itself, though incorrectly. *It is not as hard as an Emerald* <note>original: *Er ist nit so hart/alß ein Smaragd*</note>; otherwise, Armenian Stone is not recognized. It enters, if I am not mistaken, into the composition of **Diasenna** <term>Diasenna: a medicinal electuary or purgative based on the senna plant</term>. See concerning it Pliny <note>Book 35, Chapter 6</note>, Avicenna <note>Book 1</note>, Mesue, and others. I wanted to include these few notes for the sake of students regarding Armenian Stone. Finally, regarding the **Ganean stone**, see also Pliny <note>Book 37, Chapter 9</note> and Solinus <note>Chapter 30</note>.

<margin>
There is another kind of Azure.
</margin>
Found in the hollowed-out caves of the sea, made from shore-sand.

<margin>
Artificial Azure, of which there are again many kinds, and indeed precious ones among the Chemists. Currently, pills are prepared from artificial azure—a great error—whereas they ought to be prepared from the native and Armenian varieties. Aetius wrote about its purging power in his work on Nechepso.
</margin>
