->## OF MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN ##<-

**Cohob**, is sand or dust.

**Cohobation** <note>original: *Cohobatio*</note> is the frequent drawing off of a liquid that has been poured many times back over a substance <note>this refers to the alchemical process of redistilling a liquid back onto its residue to increase its potency</note>. Hence we say "to cohobate" or "to pour through cohob."

**Cohoph** is a term most familiar to Paracelsus <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, 1493–1541, a seminal figure in alchemy and medicine</note>, and **Cohobate** occurs when a material is frequently soaked with a liquid, and the liquid is then drawn off again by distillation. Similarly: it is when herbs are reduced to juice by pounding; then they are putrefied in the same glass vessel in a <term>B. M.</term> <note>original: *Balneum Mariae* or Mary’s Bath; a water-heated vessel for gentle warmth</note> for four days, until the pure can be separated from the impure. The liquid added is either the material’s own natural moisture, or it is an added vehicle. When the herbs are pounded in their own juice, then putrefied and decayed in a glass in a Mary’s Bath (otherwise called a sea-bath or dung-bath) until one can separate the pure from the impure. Also, when one frequently draws the juice or the fruits off from the material and pours it back on, that is called cohobating.

**Cohos** is whatever the skin encloses in the entire body. It is an allusion made to **Chaos** <note>the primordial state of matter</note>, which, having been reduced to order by divine power—and not being formless as before—comprehends all created things for the benefit of the smaller ordered chaos or *Cohos* <note>Paracelsus used "Cohos" to describe the human body as a microcosm, or "small chaos," containing all the elements of the universe</note>. It is what the skin covers in the whole body.

**Colcotar**, properly according to Paracelsus, is <term>fixed vitriol</term> <term>fixed vitriol: vitriol (metal sulfate) that has been treated with heat until it no longer evaporates</term>. This occurs when the phlegm is drawn off from the vitriol by distillation, and this is done so many times until the *colcotar* has soaked up all the phlegm or water, and no more water drips out during distillation, even if it is urged by a strong fire. It is called the **green serpent** or **lizard** which has devoured its own tail <note>an Ouroboros symbol, representing the cycle of distillation and re-absorption</note>. Fixed Vitriol. More commonly it is understood as <term>caput mortuum</term> <term>caput mortuum: "dead head," the useless residue left after distillation</term>, which is vitriol made red in a simple way without cohobation; or it is red or yellow ink. Red Vitriol, copper-red, or red copper-water. Vitriol calcined <note>burned to a powder</note> until it is red. It is ironically called **Red Henry** <note>original: *Heinricus rubeus*</note> in mockery of certain deceitful surgeons and charlatans, who...

...with this medicine alone they tried to cure all ulcers and wounds, and they leaned upon this single remedy as if it were a sacred anchor <note>original: *sacrae anchorae*; a metaphor for a final resort or a person's last hope</note>, losing their patients rather than saving them.

<term>Coleritium</term> is a liquid composed of corrosive materials extremely hostile to metals, by which gold is tested by rubbing it against a touchstone <note>original: *Lydium lapidem*, or Lydian stone; a dark jasper or basalt used since antiquity to determine the purity of gold by the color of the streak it leaves</note>. No metal except gold can resist it. Thus, it is recognized immediately whether something else is mixed with the gold; all of this other material soon vanishes, changing color in the area where the *coleritium* was applied, while the rest—not having been moistened—keeps the color of the rubbed gold. However, that which is pure and clean is not changed at all by that liquid.

A hill rising up around the house of the machine: **Halde** <note>a German mining term, still used today as *Halde*, referring to a heap of waste rock or slag</note>.

<term>Colliquation</term> <note>original: *Colliquatio*</note>, or melting-together, is the joining of several meltable substances in a fire into a single compound through fiery liquefaction.

<term>Colophony</term> <note>original: *Colofonia*</note>, that is, Greek pitch, the gum or resin of the pine tree.

<term>Coloritium</term> is a gradation of color achieved through a sharp paste, which they also call *coleritium*. Therefore, it is a method of tinting, primarily intended for metals. It is only effective on the surface. For it cannot penetrate deeply because of its thickness <note>original: *corpulentiam*, referring here to the density or physical body of the paste</note>, unless the paste is diluted with a large amount of liquid and thus changed into the form of a lye <note>original: *lixivii*; a solution of alkaline salts</note>.

<term>Coloration by the absorption of an entering liquid</term> is a very frequent method of coloring by means of a liquid tincture, which the things to be colored are forced to "drink" or soak up. This occurs according to their diverse natures. Those things that are porous are soaked in the liquid tincture; or they are even cooked together, or watered and drenched frequently (with drying periods in between) until the color is satisfactory. In this way, people commonly dye fleeces, linens, silks, cloths, and so on.

<term>External Coloration</term> occurs when the color is only raised <note>The text ends mid-word with "exal-", completed by the catchword "tatur" as *exaltatur*</note> on the surfaces...

**Coloration by heat alone** is a method of coloring where the color is drawn out from potentiality into act, or from the hidden into the manifest, by using only alterative heat. Nor is this done only for the principal purpose of extraction, but it also serves secret tinctures.

**Coloration by washing** is when spiritual darknesses and other impurities that obscure or change the color are washed away with sharp waters <note>original: *aquis acribus*; typically referring to acidic or caustic solutions used for cleaning the surfaces of metals</note>, and thus the color is brightened or exalted.

**Colic** is tartar dissolved in the intestines, and a disease fixed in the colon. A colicky disposition: **Abdominal gripes / the Mother / colicampas** <note>The German *die Mutter* (the Mother) historically referred to "suffocation of the mother" or hysteria, which was often thought to manifest as abdominal or uterine distress; *colicampas* is a corrupt or archaic medical term for severe intestinal pain</note>.

**To demand a contribution from the Lords**, **To demand an additional payment.**

**Combustion** is ignition, reducing bodies into lime <note>original: *calcem*; referring to "calx," the fine powder or ash produced after a metal or mineral has been thoroughly heated or "calcined"</note> by burning. This is either incineration or vitrification <note>the process of turning a substance into glass through heat</note>.

**Cometz** is a half-drop.

**Comisdi**, that is, gum Arabic.

**Comminution** <note>the process of reducing a substance to very small particles</note> is when we reduce a thing into the smallest parts by striking it against something. Sometimes the drying, roasting, or sifting of the thing serves this purpose. In Latin, it is called *Corallium*, and by some, "stone-tree" <note>original: *λιθόδενδρον* (lithodendron)</note>. Methrodorus calls it "gorgian" <note>original: *γοργίαν*</note>, perhaps because of its legendary origin from the head of the Gorgon. Pliny, in Book 32, Chapter 2, says it is called *Corallum* because it is caught or pulled up with nets, or cut off with a sharp iron tool. For this reason, it is also called *caeralium, ciralium, curalum* by some.

It is, however, Coral and nothing else but a marine shrub, which, when drawn from the deep, hardens as it emerges and immediately solidifies upon exposure to the air. Regarding the origin of corals, Ovid in the 4th book of *Metamorphoses* offers a most beautiful fable, namely this: When Perseus placed the severed head of Medusa on the shore upon a bed of leaves and twigs, the twigs hardened at the touch of the head. When the sea nymphs saw this happen, and saw it occurring with many twigs, they scattered those twigs here and there through the sea, which remained as the seeds of coral. Thus the same poet skillfully says in that place:

> *Now also coral retains the same nature,*
> *Taking on hardness from contact with the air: and that which*
> *Was a supple twig in the water, becomes stone above the waves.*

Likewise in Book 15, he says:

> *So also coral, at the very moment it first touches the breezes,*
> *Hardens: it was a soft plant beneath the waves.*

In the same way, the lynx-stone <note>term: *lapis lyncirinus* | a gemstone (often identified as amber or tourmaline) believed by the ancients to be the solidified urine of a lynx</note> is congealed from the urine of the lynx by the air, and coral by the air into a gem; and just as (according to Pliny and Solinus) pearls <note>term: *uniones* | large, high-quality pearls found singly</note> are soft in the waters but immediately harden when taken out into the air. # THE WRITINGS OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN #

### You may see the river Sarno turn things to stone ###

-> Under the blue spring, the alder, and handfuls of fern, <-
-> And twisted stalks of straw with pliant willow-twigs. <-
<note>These lines describe how organic materials like wood and leaves appear to transform into stone when submerged in mineral-rich waters.</note>

For just as the coral plant, when frozen by the air, becomes stone, so too the alder tree and the fern herb become stones in the water of the Sarno spring <note>A river in Campania, Italy, known in antiquity for its petrifying properties</note>. Seneca testifies that the same happens in other places in Italy: if a branch or foliage is submerged, a stone is drawn out after a few days. This occurs because it is perhaps surrounded by mud, which gradually smears onto the body. Thus Ovid, in the 15th book of the *Metamorphoses*, teaches that the river of the Cicones <note>A Thracian tribe</note> causes the "fleshy innards" to turn to stone if the water is drunk. Similarly, among us, black oaks are formed in rivers and, as it were, turn to stone. 

However, it is not well established what kind of plant or herb it is, or what kind of branches they are, from which corals harden in this way. Pliny, in Book 32, Chapter 2, says the plant is green in color, with berries that are white and soft under the water; when removed, they immediately harden and turn red, appearing like cultivated cornel cherries. 

There are, however, three species of coral now known:
1. White coral <note>original German: *weiß Corallen*</note>, which was entirely unknown to Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist</note>.
2. Red coral <note>original German: *rot Corallen*</note>, also called the "stone-tree" <note>original: *lithodendron*</note>.
3. Black coral <note>original German: *schwartz Corallen*</note>, also called *antipallas*. When this is of the darkest black color, it is currently held in high price because it is rare.

It is a most powerful remedy against the disease of frenzy <note>original: *phrenesin*, an acute fever with delirium</note>. It is said to have first been discovered in the Ligurian Sea. Dioscorides (Book 5, Chapter 86) celebrates the red and the black varieties. He teaches that Syracuse is the homeland of the red. He also discusses which coral is best or bad, and what its medical virtues are. 

Pliny, in the place cited, teaches that among the Indians, coral is of the highest price among all things, because their soothsayers and prophets wear coral berries as a religious amulet <note>original: *gestamen*</note> to ward off dangers. He also notes that the Gauls once adorned their swords, shields, and helmets with them; and that twigs tied to infants were believed to provide protection. Our matrons <note>referring to mothers or midwives of Ruland's time</note> still retain this custom, for they hang corals on boys against I-know-not-what diseases. Indeed, formerly...

# MARTIN RULAND'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY #

Corals were the common ornament of matrons and noble girls, worn to win favor and grace; for they declare that this power resides within them. In Stendal, the capital of the Old March <note>original: *Marchiæ*; referring to the Altmark region in modern-day Saxony-Anhalt, Germany</note>, noble women still adorn themselves with corals, which are inlaid with silver by a certain specialized craftsmanship. The ancient mages also, who sacrificed to each of the planets in their own way with things dedicated to them, offered storax and mastic to the Sun, and corals to Venus—as she is the Goddess of Grace—as a substance that would procure favor.

But now these are "golden ages." Despising corals, our young women make themselves pleasing with gold, and thus procure beauty for themselves. Solinus <note>A 3rd-century Latin grammarian and compiler</note>, in chapter 8, cites Metrodorus and Zoroaster regarding corals, and enumerates I know not what fabulous powers of coral against lightning and whirlwinds <note>original: *typhones*</note>. If you wish, see Serapion <note>A 9th-century Christian physician from Damascus</note> in the *Aggregator*, the chapter on *Bassath*. He calls the root of the coral shrub *Nigen* and *Mergen*, while on the other hand, he calls the branches themselves *Bassath*. Avicenna <note>The famous Persian polymath Ibn Sina</note> also treats corals. These authors attribute to corals power against epilepsy, bleeding, bad dreams, and use them in medicines.

However much these things may seem like fables, experience testifies that red corals turn white whenever they are worn by a person who is already close to death or suffering from a dangerous disease; not to mention that corals, especially burnt red corals, have the greatest power (of which I speak from experience) in breaking stones in the bladder <note>original: *calculo vesicæ*</note>. For their other powers, consult L.C. <note>Likely a reference to a specific medical compendium or author known to Ruland</note>.

I also did not want this to escape you: Pliny, in Book 36, Chapter 19, says that coral is called *pyrites* <note>meaning "fire-stone"</note> because it contains a great deal of fire; but this is not the *pyrites*—that is, the <term>marcasite</term>—of which we treated above in Book 1. For Pliny, *pyrites* is a genus <note>a broad category</note>, not a species. To him, *pyrites* refers to every stone from which fire can be struck.

Finally, there were those who taught, contrary to the opinion of all these authors whom we have cited, that coral is of an earthy substance and is found in marine places and mountains, especially in cavernous locations existing in the sea. They claim it is formed from a glutinous and humid viscosity of the earth adhering to stones, which becomes condensed...

->OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.<-

...both by its own nature and by the heat and dryness of the sea, it is transformed into a stony substance. This occurs in such a way that whatever contains more wateriness becomes clear or white, being colder than the red variety; thus, nature forms it in the shape of tree branches. To these arguments, I do not have a ready answer at the moment. It is difficult to depart from the opinion of the most learned men I have already cited. Furthermore, the very form of the coral, representing a shrub with branches, indicates that it arises from a bush. For instance, I once saw a coral of immense size in Munich. On the other hand, near the mouth of the Tanger <note>The Tanger is a small river that flows into the Elbe at Tangermünde</note> on the Elbe River, I found true white coral. This had undoubtedly been formed in such a manner from the viscosity of the earth, hardened by its own heat and the water. In that same place, I also found ferns <note>original: *filices*; likely referring to fossilized plants or coral-like mineral formations</note> distinguished by their branches. What if nature makes such a noble gem in both ways—from a shrub hardened by the air, and from the viscosity of the earth—so that it might not fail despite its frequent use? Perhaps it is formed through the vigor of internal principles, participating in much salt and sulfur <note>In alchemical theory, salt, sulfur, and mercury were considered the three primary building blocks of all matter</note>, and thus by the power of "fruiting spirits"? 

Just as we often see things created in various ways—as I have observed with those slippery aquatic creatures, the lamprey <note>original German: *die Neunauge*, literally "the nine-eye"</note>, as well as eels and morays—which are generated first from the viscosity of the earth; secondly, from mutual rubbing and the slimy discharge they produce; and thirdly, from eggs, in the manner of other fish. As soon as they are hatched, they are taken up into the gills and cherished there (as Nicander <note>A Greek poet and physician from the 2nd century BC</note> says of the cuttlefish and the sea hare) by the "ploceno" fish, so to speak—the roach <note>original German: *von den Plozen*</note>. Also by those fish which are called "Red-eyes" <note>original German: *Rotaugen*; likely the common rudd or roach</note> because of the redness of their eyes. Likewise by the "mouse-catching" fish, known as "devils" <note>original German: *von den Deueln*; likely the European bullhead, known for its large head and wide mouth</note>, which devour water mice. Also by the white bream and the *Beckelaugs* <note>local German names for species of the carp family</note> of that name, as the fishermen at the mouth of the Tanger have often shown me. Similarly, little "water wolves" <note>original: *lupuli aquatici*; young pike, known for their predatory nature</note>, once hatched from the egg, are cherished in the gills of these fish; for this reason, the adult water wolves do not eat or harm such fish, so they do not return "bad thanks" to their nurses. Eels, however...

### MARTIN RULAND'S DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY

Art also, by imitating nature, makes corals. For artificial corals are found which very well mimic natural ones. Consult certain Alchemists <note>original: *Chymistas*</note> who know how to compose them properly.

**Skin of the earth** <note>original: *Corium terræ*</note>, Earth.

**Cornelian** <note>original: *Cornelius* or *corneolus*</note>, or rather carnelian, is a gem or stone whose homeland is coastal Italy, and now Germany. It is found, according to the testimony of Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century polymath</note>, near the Rhine. It is a well-known gem in Germany because of the seals on rings, which are frequently made from it; it is called **A Cornelian** <note>original German: *Ein Corneol*</note>. To me, it seems almost to be a species of Jasper. But one Cornelian stone is marked by a deep redness, another is paler, the color of flesh—whence some wish it to be called "Carneolus" <note>From the Latin *caro*, meaning flesh.</note>. Another is marked with white flakes <note>original: *pinnulis*, literally "little feathers."</note>, another with white lines; another is completely dark in its redness, while another shines greatly, like vermillion. Moreover, the power of the carnelian is to bind the blood, and to stop the menses and hemorrhoids. It is also said to soothe anger, and when used in a tooth-powder, it cleanses the teeth.

...is ferment and tincture; the white is imperfect, the red is perfect. 3. **Body** <note>original German: *Corpus*</note> is the Earth which remains at the bottom, as if dead; then the power ascends with the Spirit. 4. The **Soul** <note>original German: *Seel*</note> is the power of the body which is sublimated <note>A process of turning a solid into vapor and back to solid to purify it.</note> with the Spirit; it is the **Oil of the body**. The **Spirit** <note>original German: *Geist*</note> is the **water of Mercury** <note>original Latin: *aqua Mercurii*</note>, which draws up and sublimates the soul.

The **Invisible Body** <note>original: *Corpus inuisibile*</note> is the soul; for it holds the middle ground between the visible body—for which reason it is called "body" in that respect—and the invisible, because it participates in the invisible spirit. These are physical <note>Ruland uses "physical" in the sense of natural science or alchemy, rather than modern physics.</note> definitions, not theological ones.

The **Physical Body** <note>original: *Corpus physicum*</note> is the subject of nature.

**Super-celestial Bodies** <note>original: *Corpora supercoelestia*</note> are those which are recognized through the mind in the imagination alone, and not through the eyes of the flesh. They are the subjects of the wonderful works of the **Spagyrists** <note>original: *Spagyrorum*; followers of Paracelsus who used chemical methods to separate and recombine substances.</note>.

**Stag’s Horn** <note>original: *Cornu cervi*</note> in chemical matters is the beak of the **alembic** <note>The distillation head used in alchemy.</note>, **The beak of the distillation head** <note>original German: *Der Schnabel am Alembick*</note>. In the medicinal works of **Paracelsus** <note>The famous 16th-century physician who revolutionized medicine with chemistry.</note>, it is also a wound-healing herb, so named because the natural similarity of its leaves alludes to such horns, being signed by nature <note>original: *ex arte signata*; referring to the "Doctrine of Signatures," the belief that a plant's physical appearance reveals its healing purpose.</note>.

**Corrosion** <note>original: *Corrosio*</note> is a form of **calcination** <note>Reduction of a substance to powder through heat or chemicals.</note> that reduces coagulated things into a powder <note>original: *calcem*; literally "lime" or "ash"</note> by means of corrosive spirits. It is either vaporous or immersive.

**Corrosion by Stratification** <note>original: *Corrosio Stratificatione*</note> occurs through calcination when that which is to be corroded is laid down in a vessel layer-by-layer <note>original: *vicissim*</note> with corrosive powders. The material is either drawn out into thin plates, broken, or crushed into suitable small particles, such as filings, etc.

**Corrosion by Paste** <note>original: *Corrosio per pastam*</note> occurs when plates of metal or stone, etc., are coated with a colored paste <note>original: *pulticula coloritii*</note> and, as it were, plastered over. For this reason, this work can be called **plastering** <note>original: *emplastratio*</note>. The coated plate is set aside somewhere until it is corroded. It is necessary, however, that the paste be made of separable substances, such as salts, **vitriol** <note>original: *chalcantho*; copper or iron sulfate</note>, and vinegar.

**Corrosives** <note>original: *Corrosiva*</note> are the medications of surgeons which eat away and consume callous and superfluous flesh; these include **cathæretics** <note>substances that eat away warts or growths</note> and **septic** <note>original: *nemomena septica*; agents that cause tissue to break down</note> remedies. **Etching things, biting through or eating through** <note>original German: *Etzende Ding/durchbeissend oder durchfressendt*</note>.

->## LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND<-

[Cry]stal has a medical use in cauterizing the body <note>original Latin: *cremandis corporibus*; early physicians used crystal spheres to focus sunlight and burn away diseased tissue or wounds</note>. Placed under the tongue, it is said to quench thirst. Ground and mixed with honey, it increases the supply of milk in nursing women. It possesses other powers and uses as well. Consult Solinus regarding crystal in his *Polyhistor*, chapter 20. The ancient astrologers dedicated crystal to the Sun.

In Alchemy, **Crystal** (or ice) is a brittle stone made through chemical coagulation. Coagulation of this kind occurs when the watery moisture recedes and the coagulable juice thickens into the form of a small stone; this can happen even in a cellar without any evident heat. If, however, part of the wateriness is dissipated by evaporation, the work proceeds faster. Therefore, the lye <note>original Latin: *lixivia*</note> of the ice is usually boiled down to a soapy thickness, or the sediment is allowed to form while the watery part floats on top and is poured off. The remainder then coagulates more easily.

There are many types of **Crystal**:
1. The purest hexagonal crystal from the Alps. <gloss>Crystals such as those found in the Alps and high mountain ranges.</gloss>
2. Hexagonal translucent crystals from Bohemia found with pyrite.
3. Those dug from the mountain of the Kriebstein fortress in Meissen. <gloss>As clear and beautiful as pure spring water.</gloss>
4. Hexagonal and impure. <gloss>Cloudy and dirty.</gloss>
5. Shining with the color of citrus. <gloss>Yellowish.</gloss>
6. Polished and formed into various shapes. <gloss>Cut or polished.</gloss>
7. Combined and dyed with cinnabar. <gloss>Weylandic Cubil <note>Likely a regional name for a specific red mineral or prepared pigment</note>, red earth.</gloss>

**Cuculatum**, also called the Greater *Aqua Vitae*. <gloss>Brandy; literally "burnt wine."</gloss>

**Cucurbita** <term>a gourd-shaped flask</term>. <gloss>A flask or retort.</gloss> It is a vessel, usually top-shaped, swelling out in the middle like a gourd or pear. Some flasks are provided with a rounded bottom, while others have a flat one.

**Wild Gourd** <note>original Latin: *Cucurbita agrestis*</note>. <gloss>Earth-apple <note>In this period, "Erdapfel" (earth-apple) could refer to various tubers, including the potato or cyclamen</note>.</gloss>

**Blind Gourd** <note>original Latin: *Cucurbita coeca*</note>. A vessel in which solutions of salts and other things are filtered or strained by means of vapor <note>A "blind" vessel is one that is sealed or has no outlet, used to circulate vapors</note>.

**Culatum**, that is, **Calcined** <note>Reduced to a powder by the action of heat</note>.

**Deliquium** <note>deliquescence</note> is a "cold descent." This occurs when substances that have been "coagulated" (solidified) are placed in a cellar, exposed to the air, or put in a pit or another cold and damp place. They are laid upon a marble slab, a glass table, or in a "Hippocrates' Sleeve" (as they call it) <note>a conical fabric filter bag used by apothecaries</note>. With the help of the external moisture that joins itself to these substances, they resolve into a liquid, and they flow down and drip into a vessel placed beneath. Especially calcined powders, salts, and other such bodies that share the nature of salts, are resolved in the cold. However, all things that are resolved in the cold are coagulated (made solid) again in the heat.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical lexicon of alchemical and medical terms by Martin Ruland the Elder. Having concluded brief definitions for terms beginning with D (such as *dehenez*), Ruland now provides a lengthy, systematic explanation of the term *Deliquium* (liquefaction or deliquescence), detailing its types and the methods used by chemists to achieve a liquid state from solid matter.</meta>

<page-num>181</page-num>
<header>OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.</header>

**Deliquium** <term>Deliquium: from the Latin *deliquescere*, meaning to melt or dissolve; in alchemy, it refers to the process of a solid substance turning into a liquid</term> in the air is the melting of a solidified mass, which occurs when external moisture creeps in and dissolves the dryness, causing it to flow. What is thus dissolved is called a **liquor**, and it possesses a watery consistency. (For although limestone rocks may crumble when exposed to atmospheric or watery moisture, this is neither a true melting, nor is the resulting substance called a **liquor**.) **Deliquium** is of two kinds: **Vaporous** and **Embaptic**.

**Vaporous deliquium** occurs when a substance, having been reduced to a fine powder, is exposed to moist air and, by becoming damp, is dissolved into a liquor. That moist air is sometimes warmer and sometimes colder, such as that found in damp underground places <note>original Latin: *subterraneorum irriguorum*; likely referring to cellars or caves where alchemists placed salts to "melt" naturally</note>. And unless the substance to be dissolved is naturally suited for this, it is processed—chiefly through **calcination** <note>heating a substance to a high temperature to make it brittle or powdery</note>—until it takes on the nature of a salt or something similar, or until it is reduced to such a state of dryness that it greedily drinks in external moisture and quickly flows away. For it is necessary that the firm internal structure be broken down and a certain salt-like brittleness be introduced.

**Embaptic deliquium** <term>Embaptic: from the Greek *embaptikos*, meaning "related to dipping" or "immersion"</term> is when a substance is submerged in a liquid and kept there until it has melted. This is done in two ways. Either the substance is placed within a small vessel and submerged so that the liquid itself does not come into direct contact with it—or at most only a very fine "sweat" [vapor] permeates through—such as when it is placed in a wax container or an ox bladder and, once it has melted, is extracted. If the surrounding liquid is hot (as is usually the case), this process is a form of a **bath** <note>original Latin: *simulacrum balnei*; a reference to the *balneum Mariae* or water-bath, a fundamental tool for gentle heating in alchemy</note>. Or, the substance is allowed to diffuse directly into the liquid itself, either bare or with a piece of linen cloth placed between them, so that impurities may be filtered out at the same time. In this case, too, the liquor used may be cold—the method by which **gums** and thickened juices, such as **sugar** and the like, can be dissolved—or it may require heating, as is the case with **manna** <note>a sweet secretion from trees used as a mild laxative</note> and similar substances that contain fats or a stubborn, sticky sap. That liquid, which serves as the medium of the solution, must be of such a nature that, if we wish to remove it later, it can easily be separated again; nor should it introduce any foreign quality into the dissolved substance, unless we are intentionally seeking such an alteration.

**Deliquium** <term>Deliquium: The process of a solid substance absorbing enough atmospheric moisture to dissolve into a liquid</term> is a "cold descent." This occurs when solidified bodies—having been placed in a cellar, the open air, a well, or some other cold and humid place—are set upon marble, a glass plate, or within a "Hippocrates' Sleeve" (as they call it) <note>a conical cloth filter bag</note>. With the aid of external moisture joining itself to these bodies, they are resolved into a liquid, and they flow down and drip into a vessel placed beneath. It is primarily calcinated powders, salts, and other such bodies that share the nature of salts that are resolved in the cold. However, all things that are dissolved in the cold are coagulated again when subjected to heat.

It marks a shift from simple nomenclature to procedural theory.</meta>

<page-num>181</page-num>
-># OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN<-

Deliquescence <note>original: *Deliquium*; the process where a substance absorbs moisture from the air until it dissolves into a liquid</note> in the air is the liquefaction of a solid substance, which occurs as external moisture creeps in and dissolves the dryness, causing it to flow. That which is thus dissolved is called a liquor, and it has a watery consistency. (For although limestone rocks may crumble due to atmospheric or aquatic moisture, this is neither called liquefaction, nor is the resulting substance called a liquor.) Deliquescence is of two types: **Vaporous** and **Embaptic** <note>original: *Embapticum*; derived from the Greek *embaptein*, meaning "to dip in" or submerge</note>.

**Vaporous deliquescence** occurs when a substance reduced to a fine powder is exposed to moist air and, by becoming damp, is dissolved into a liquor. This moist air is sometimes warmer and sometimes colder, such as is found in damp underground places <note>this refers to the practice of placing chemicals in cellars or caves where the natural humidity would trigger the reaction</note>. And unless the substance to be dissolved is naturally suited to this process, it is brought by processing to the nature of a salt or something similar; this is done chiefly by **calcination** <term>calcination|the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or reduce it to a crumbly powder</term>, or by reducing it to such a state of dryness that it greedily drinks in external moisture and promptly melts away. For it is necessary that the tenacious structure of the matter be broken down and a certain salt-like friability be induced.

**Embaptic deliquescence** is when a substance is submerged in a liquid and kept there continuously until it has melted away. This happens in two ways. For the substance, contained in a small vessel, is either submerged so that the liquid itself does not touch it, or at least only a very thin "sweat" permeates it—as when it is placed in a waxen vessel or a bull’s bladder—and when it has melted, it is extracted; this process, if the liquid is hot (as is usually the case), is a form of bath <note>original: *simulacrum balnei*; a "likeness of a bath," referring to indirect heating methods similar to a modern bain-marie or water bath</note>. Or, the substance is allowed to diffuse directly into the liquid itself, either bare or through a linen cloth, which simultaneously separates out the impurities. And here too, the liquor may be cold—in which way gums and thickened juices, such as sugar and the like, can be dissolved—or it may require heating, as with **manna** <note>a sweet, medicinal resin collected from trees</note> and similar substances containing fat or a tenacious juice. That liquid which serves as the medium of the solution must be of such a kind that, if we desire it to be removed, it can easily be separated again; nor should it introduce any foreign quality into the dissolved substance, unless we are intentionally seeking such an alteration.

**Cold descent** <note>original: *Descensio frigida*</note> occurs when a dissolved liquid descends in the cold. It is either **deliquescence** <term>deliquescence|the process where a substance absorbs moisture from the air until it dissolves into a liquid</term> or filtration.

**Descensum**; **descensorium**; a furnace, a chemical furnace in which the liquid, separated from the coarse matter, descends downward. <note>German: *Ein Ofen, darin man unter sich treibt*</note>.

**To descend** means to make liquid or to melt together.

**To descend by steps cut into the rock**, to enter a mine by hewn steps <gloss>steps</gloss>.

**Distillation** is a purification and clarification.

**Distillation** is a drawing-out by which the essence is extracted in the form of a liquid; once condensed, it is carried down drop by drop, transferred from the vessel containing the matter into a receiver placed below. Therefore, whatever is to be distilled must be capable of being resolved into a moist consistency, or be combined with moisture, whether that moisture is innate or added from the outside. Such things are mostly vaporous and possess oily spirits. Hence, if substances are not such by nature, they must be brought to that state by the chemist's art. Distillation was invented principally for the sake of extracting the essence, although it also serves for abstractions, purifications, and similar operations.

**Distillation by ascent** is when, before the extract distills, it is raised up in an aerial form <note>as a vapor or gas</note>. This must be a continuous process; if the work is interrupted between the beginning and the end, the remaining material will scarcely ascend.

**Distillation by descent** is when the drawn-out moisture distills downward without first being raised up.

**Distillation by inclination** is that which is performed by tilting the vessel containing the matter to the side, with the beak pointing downward. Because that vessel is usually a **retort** <term>retort|a glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</term>, this is also called "distillation by the retort." The second kind of diphryges is artificial, which is again twofold. The first is nothing other than the dross settling from perfected copper—just as artificial *molybdena* <term>molybdena|the lead-like dross or scum that forms during the refining of silver</term> is the dross of silver, from which **quicksilver** <note>original Greek: *ὑδράργυρος* (hydrargyros)</note> is made, as we taught above.

In short, the first artificial species of diphryges is the dross of perfected copper that settles; it is made at the same time as the flower of copper, <term>when one cools the ore or copper|Wann man das Erß oder Kupfer abkühlet</term> by the pouring on of cold water. Once the copper is removed, it is found clinging to the bottom of the furnaces, having the astringency and taste of copper. However, whether in our own time the dross of copper is still produced this way alongside the flower of copper, as Dioscorides <note>A famous 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> claims, you should ask the copper-boilers, the <term>smelters|Schmelzern</term>.

The second artificial kind of diphryges is simply when pyrite is burnt like lime in a furnace until it turns red like red ochre. Dioscorides records that this species is also made, according to some, from the raw material itself that produces the copper-stone when it is roasted. This species is often adulterated with burnt ochre. But they can be distinguished by taste, namely thus: the species of diphryges burnt from the pyrite itself, or from its raw material, has the taste of copper and verdigris, astringent and drying to the tongue. Burnt ochre, however, has no such taste or power. **Diphryges:**
1. That which remains at the bottom of the furnace after the copper <note>original: *æs*</note> has flowed out; <gloss>Lower furnace-slag</gloss>.

**Digestion**, <gloss>signifies the changing of one thing into another through the warming and cooking of Nature</gloss>.

**Digestion** is a simple ripening, by which raw things are digested in a digestive heat. For to "digest" is to cook thoroughly—after the manner of the natural digestion of food in the stomach—using a suitable heat for each thing, and to make it ready to exert its power. Thus, even intractable materials, by digesting, become milder and suitable for work. And if any part is half-cooked, it is brought to the condition of finished parts, so that afterwards the harvest of the essence may be more abundant. Under this name, "digestion" sometimes serves in the processing; and it is also called by another word, **Maceration**. In the works of Mesué <note>Johannes Mesué, an influential medieval medical authority</note> it is also called **Nutrition** (as when dross is said to be "nourished" with vinegar for a long time, meaning to be macerated). For the harsh part, or the juice, is as it were tamed so that it becomes mild; this not only increases the essence, but allows it to be easily drawn away from the inactive dregs. For maceration has a certain power of penetrating, unlocking, and freeing from impurities. Or:

# RYLAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN #

...[by the separa]tion of the pure from the impure: <note>original: *Wenn mā ein Ding kocht im Glaß vnd in ein ander Wesen bringt*</note> When one cooks a thing in glass and brings it into another essence. Sometimes it stands for the glass in which this mastery is fulfilled, or for the furnace. Or:

**Digestion** is a thinning <gloss>that is, of things</gloss> dissolving raw materials in a digestive heat. And it is either putrefaction or extraction.

**Digestion** occurs in the **athanor** <term>athanor|a self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a constant temperature over long periods; the name comes from the Arabic *al-tannur* (the oven)</term>, when, the tower of the athanor having been filled to the top with coals, we light a fire in the hearth, and with an iron spatula or regulator <note>original: *registro*; a sliding plate used to control airflow</note>, we open or close the small door at our discretion, transmitting heat to the chambers. However, the opinion of the Philosophers is divided on how that heat should be directed—that is, when it ought to be milder or more intense. For some, emulating (as they say) the operation of nature, contend that a continuous and identical heat is required from the beginning of the action until the end. Others divide it into degrees: namely, the first degree at the beginning until whiteness <note>original: *albedo*; the purifying second stage of the alchemical process</note>, then the second until yellowness <note>original: *flavedo*</note>, and for the end, which is of the richest redness <note>original: *rubedo*; the final stage signifying the perfection of the Philosopher's Stone</note>, the third degree is employed. We, led by many authorities as well as reasons, agree with this second opinion, leaving the other view to its own authors.

**Separation** <note>original: *discessus*</note> occurs when things that were deeply united are separated and depart, primarily through the efficacy of a dissolving heat. This is accomplished by exhalation and by the resolution of mixed things.

**Separation** by exhalation <note>original: *exspiratio*</note> is when a part, thinned into a spirit, departs. And it is called "exhalation" principally when it rises into the open air and is released. When it is not released, but caught, it is called **distillation** or **sublimation**—operations which sometimes also serve the purpose of exhalation. Moreover, exhalation occurs in moist and vaporous things.

**Discerners:** <term>Erapucha</term> <note>likely a corruption of an Arabic medical term for medicines that purge or "discern" humors in the bowels</note>.

**Disk of the Sun** <note>original: *discus solis*</note> is quicksilver [extracted] from gold.

**To Despoil** <note>original: *dispoliare*</note> is <term>to dissolve</term> / <term>to kill</term> / to corrupt.

**Distillation:** <term>dripping</term> / <term>distilling</term>.

**Distillation**, or upright moist elevation, is that by which the more subtle moist parts are raised into the ether and, adhering to the cold chambers of the alembic...

# RYLAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN #

...[vapors] rising <note>original: *aſcendentes*; the OCR *reſcētes* is the end of this word continued from the previous page</note> condense into moisture, and through the same channel drip down and flow away into a vessel placed nearby. It is done in this way: The material to be distilled is placed in a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit|a gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the lower part of a still</term> not less tall but sufficiently wide (for the height of the vessel hinders the craftsman, while width helps him), and a large **alembic** <term>alembic|the "head" or cap of the still that collects and cools vapors</term> is placed on top, which may more easily catch the rising spirits <note>original: *spiritus*; in this context, the gaseous or vaporous form of a substance</note> and resolve them into liquid. Afterward, according to the nature of the thing to be raised, it is placed in an appropriate heat, with a **receiver** <term>receiver|the flask attached to the still to collect the final distilled product</term> attached to receive the flowing liquid. When all joints have been properly sealed, a fire is lit and applied according to degrees, until all the moisture has descended through the alembic.

We shall provide an example from the plant kingdom. I fill a cucurbit to the third part with fresh roses and place it in a **bain-marie** <term>bain-marie|a water bath (literally 'Mary's bath') used for gentle, indirect heating</term> while the water is still cold. Then I fill the rose alembic with red rose petals, from which the yellow points <note>original: *aculei lutei*; likely referring to the stamens or the yellow base of the petals which would discolor the final product</note> have been plucked, and place it on the cucurbit. Having attached the receiver and sealed the joints with **lute** <term>lute|a clay or paste used to make the connections between glass vessels airtight</term>, I light the fire. Then the rising moisture fills the alembic and extracts the tincture from the roses; having condensed into water, it drips into the receiver as a rosy liquid. It must be noted, however, that if the yellow points are not plucked away, the water cannot extract a purely red tincture. I continue with the heat for as long as it takes until no more water crosses over and the roses in the alembic turn white. I have brought this up because of the skill required in extracting a tincture from roses using their own water. This method of **elevation** <note>original: *eleuationis*; the process of vaporizing a substance so it "rises"</note> is of very frequent use. For we use it when we draw something out through a **vesica** <term>vesica|a copper boiling vessel, often shaped like a bladder, used in large-scale distillation</term>, and also when we elevate something through an alembic attached to a cucurbit.

**Oblique moist distillation and elevation** is when the moisture is raised while the vessel lies at an angle. This is done either through the side or by means of a **retort** <term>retort|a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck, used for distilling substances that require higher heat</term>.

**Distraction** is that by which parts are pulled apart, while each remains within its own homogeneous nature. Thus, it is as if a certain tearing apart of diverse things occurs here,

**Dracatium**, that is, Saturn <note>in alchemy, Saturn usually represents the metal Lead</note>.

It is the Earth of the Sun’s body; it is killed when it loses its soul, and resurrected when the soul returns. It devours Mercury like a poison and dies, then drinks it again and returns to life; in this way, it casts off all impurity, for it becomes white and lives. This is also called the "Woman" who kills her husband, for which reason she herself is killed in turn.

### E

**Ebel**, that is, Sage or juniper seed.

**Eclipsis** <note>literally "Eclipse"</note> is the **Raven’s Head** <term>Raven’s Head|In alchemy, the *Caput Corvi* or Raven's Head refers to the 'Nigredo' stage, where the material in the flask turns black, signifying the death of the old forms before rebirth</term>.

**Echis**, that is, the male viper.

**Echidna**, that is, the female viper.

**Echies** are the cubs, or the offspring of the viper. The *echis* is a serpent which we call **an Adder or Viper** <note>original German: *ein Natter oder Atter*</note>. Its homeland is near houses, though it specifically dwells in thickets near water. Nicander describes its form most beautifully in his *Theriaca* <note>Nicander of Colophon was a 2nd-century BCE Greek physician whose poem *Theriaca* dealt with the nature of venomous creatures and their antidotes</note>. Regarding its mating, a few things are recounted here: The male viper, at the time of coitus, inserts his head into the mouth of the female viper, thus pouring his seed into her. The female viper—whether foreseeing the future danger, or moved by the sweetness of pleasure while swallowing the seed, or perhaps because she knows her husband is an adulterer who frequently mates with the lamprey <note>a common medieval folk belief was that vipers and lampreys cross-bred</note>—clings to him with an impetuous bite and cuts off her husband's head with her teeth.

But the young vipers <note>original: *echites*</note> already conceived in the womb—for the viper alone among serpents carries its young within itself, prepares eggs, and broods them so they become living creatures, whereas other serpents everywhere lay eggs and, in a gathered nest like birds, using dung near hedges and thickets, they warm their scaly offspring, as Nicander says—when they have drawn the first breath of life and the time for birth approaches, they avenge the death of their parent. They burst forth by gnawing through the soft parts of their mother, and are born into the world as matricides. Nor are these idle tales. I once saw such a mother viper gnawed through, and the cubs lying alive in the sun around her, where copper is smelted, like little earthworms.

From the viper (*echis*), the gemstone **echites** <note>also known as the Viper-stone or Adder-stone</note> takes its name, either because it is similar in color to the viper, or in shape, having viper-like spots. Regarding this, consult Pliny, book thirty-seven, chapter eleven, and Solinus, chapter forty; it is called by the Germans **an Adder-stone** <note>original German: *ein Natterstein*</note>. Its power is said to be effective against poisons. The tongues of vipers have the same power when snatched from the palpitating throat <note>original: *farci*, likely a typo for *fauci* (throat/jaws)</note> of a still-living viper; likewise...

**Elaboration** <note>original: *Elaboratio*</note> is a manual operation by which a thing is worked upon and changed in its substance, particularly its material. For we call it "elaborating" when we draw out the most excellent part by removing the baser parts of the matter—those which either cling to it incidentally or provide a support for the essence in some way. Thus, the separation of the pure from the impure is most active here. Elaboration is either a dissolution <note>original: *solutio*</note> or a joining together <note>original: *coadunatio*</note>.

**Elanula**, a hard alum, like iron <note>original German: *Ist hart alumen, wie Eisen*</note>.

**Electrum** is amber, the gum of a tree.

**Electrum**, is also **gold**. Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman naturalist</note> says: *It is gold which contains a fifth part silver.* The book *Alchemia* (page 130) says: *It is called Electrum because, when placed against the radiance of the sun, it shines more brightly than gold or silver. It is found in mines, and it is also manufactured.*

**Electrum**, according to Theophrastus <note>referring to Paracelsus</note>, is a mixture of a composite metal melted into one body from all seven Planets <term>seven Planets|In the Hermetic tradition, the seven metals (Gold, Silver, Mercury, Copper, Iron, Tin, and Lead) correspond to the seven celestial bodies</term>: *A gathering together of the seven metals according to the union of the planets; otherwise, a mixture of gold and silver, in which...*

It is not so in manifest nature, in which the more specific—indeed, the baser and more degenerate—parts exist the further they recede from their whole. # MARTIN'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY #

...I place the vessel in a perforated opening, coat it with lute <note>A specialized sealant or "chemical cement" made of clay, dung, or hair, used to airtight seal laboratory apparatus.</note>, and secure it so that the spirits or the parts being sublimated cannot escape. Then I place it in a sand bath, with three fingers of sand filling the space between the bottom and the sides, or I place it over an open fire, and I increase the heat by degrees. At the first degree of heat, it is necessary for all moisture to depart; I easily test for this by placing a smooth iron plate over the glass. For as long as any moisture remains, it will stick to that plate, but when all moisture has departed, the dry spirits ascend; at this point, I close the opening of the alembic <note>The "head" or cap of a still where vapors condense.</note> with a piece of glass fitted with good lute, so that the spirits do not escape. Finally, I maintain the fire until all the material to be sublimated has risen. Some, instead of a <term>cucurbita</term> <note>A gourd-shaped glass flask used as the base of a still.</note>, use a bowl or an earthenware dish to hold the material, with a glass cone properly fitted to the walls of the lower vessel.

For example: I take 2 lbs of well-purified <term>yellow sulfur</term> <note>original: "sulphuris citrini"</note>. I take half a pound each of <term>common salt</term> <note>original: "Salis communis"</note> and slightly calcined <term>Hungarian vitriol</term> <note>original: "vitrioli Vngarici"; likely copper or iron sulfate.</note>. Having powdered these individually and mixed them together, I place them into a <term>cucurbita</term>, and having attached a "blind" <term>alembic</term> <note>An alembic without a discharge tube or spout.</note> that is perforated at the top, I light a fire of the first degree until the moisture has vanished. Then, with the orifice closed, I proceed by degrees until all the finer <term>sulfur</term> has ascended. This sulfur (called <term>Flowers of Sulfur</term> <note>original: "Flores sulphuris"</note> by Chemists), once removed from the <term>alembic</term>, is refined a second or even a third time—always adding a fourth part of salt and vitriol—restored by <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a solid until it becomes a gas and then cooling it back into a solid form, used for purification.</note>. Thus, I obtain the most beautiful flowers of sulfur, which are resistant to many ailments.

**Moist Elevation** (commonly called by the more familiar name <term>distillation</term> <note>original: "destillatio"</note>) is the refining of moist parts, thinned into vapors, from dry and gross parts. It is either "straight" or "oblique."

**Elevation by the side** occurs when the moisture is drawn out of a vessel tilted to the side.

**Elevation by retort** occurs when the moisture is driven out of a retort...

## BY RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN ##

...used. Each of these methods has its use in matters involving heavier and more persistent spirits.

**Elidrium**, that is, gum or mastic <note>A resin obtained from the mastic tree, used as a binder or medicine.</note>.

**Elidrion** is Mercury, similar to <term>Rha</term> <note>Likely referring to a specific mineral or botanical substance, sometimes associated with rhubarb or a particular red earth.</note>.

**Elidrium** is a preparation <note>original German: "confect"</note> of gold or silver; it is made from two parts of silver, one part of gold, and one part of copper.

**Elixir, Elei**, that is, a Medicine.

**Elixir** is an incomparable medicine dedicated to preserving life and driving away diseases. ->Or:<-

**Elixir** is a ferment, the smallest quantity of which penetrates and binds a vast mass of its own kind into a paste like itself. In this context, "paste" refers to the spirit of human life and the internal balsam of life; it is the internal preserver of the body in whatever state it finds it. The Elixir, however, is an external balsam sought and prepared by art into a <term>spagyric</term> <note>An alchemical term for medicine produced by separating and then recombining the components of a substance to increase its potency.</note> ferment. ->Or:<-

**Elixir** is also a fermented medicine made either from gold alone or from the seven metals <note>The seven traditional metals: Gold, Silver, Copper, Iron, Tin, Lead, and Mercury.</note>. It is a medicine prepared with Gold or all seven Metals. It is just like a leaven <note>original German: "Hefel"</note>, of which a tiny bit penetrates an entire dough. ->Or:<-

**Elixir** is a species composed of many simple ingredients of different kinds. Thus, when oil of turpentine is combined with flowers of sulfur and oil of myrrh; or when a tincture of saffron is mixed with the <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence," the most purified and potent form of a substance.</note> of wine; or when vegetable <term>magisteries</term> <note>A concentrated extract or precipitate of a substance, believed to contain its full medicinal power.</note> are united with mineral magisteries, essences, or other extracts, and similar things are joined into a composite medicine, it is called an elixir. Liquid elixirs especially excel, which by their form represent <term>bezoardic waters</term> <note>Medicinal waters believed to act as an antidote to poison, named after the bezoar stone.</note> and other composite distilled waters, with which they share a name due to their kinship. To others, an elixir differs from all other essences because it is made from many ingredients and is given either to maintain health in its current state, or to ward off impending diseases and preserve the body from decay <note>original: "putredine"</note>. ->Or:<-

### MARTIN’S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY ###

**Elixir** is the ferment, the origin, the sharp agent, or the leaven; it is that which is produced from Water. For **Yxir** is Water; it is a colored water mixed with bodies. It is also the White Stone, Oil, and Powder—for these are all one and the same thing. It is also called the Treasure; it is also called <term>prima materia</term> <note>The "First Matter," the formless base of all substance that alchemists sought to transform.</note>. It is an <term>imperfect Elixir</term>; once it is <term>perfected</term> and prepared, it is truly a treasure. Lacinius <note>Janus Lacinius, a 16th-century Calabrian editor of alchemical texts.</note> says: Elixir is made from three: <term>Sol</term> <note>Gold</note>, <term>Luna</term> <note>Silver</note>, and <term>Mercury</term> <note>Quicksilver</note>. It should, however, be of a medium consistency, between hard and soft—softer and more subtle than Mercury; otherwise, the gold produced from it will be brittle. From the Elixir comes <term>Azoth</term> <note>The essential agent of transformation; the universal solvent.</note>, and this is the first part of the Work. Thus, the Elixir is of two kinds, white and red. When it is red, the <term>ferment</term> is added, and it is <term>multiplied</term> <note>The process of increasing the quantity or the transmutative power of the alchemical medicine.</note>. ->Or:<-

**Elixir** or **Xir** is a penetrating medicine, and it is made from <term>vegetables</term> <note>In this context, "vegetable" refers to the four "spirits" of alchemy (mercury, sulfur, arsenic, and sal ammoniac) rather than literal plants.</note>, that is, the four spirits, with the addition of a <term>body</term> <note>A metal</note>, which body acts as the ferment of the medicine.

**Eloanx** is <term>auripigmentum</term> <note>Orpiment, a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral often used as a pigment or in alchemical experiments.</note>.
**Elome**, that is, <term>auripigmentum</term>.
**Elopitinum** is tragacanth <note>A natural gum</note> or vitriol.
**Elos maris**, that is, burnt lead.
**Elpis**, that is, silver dross <note>original German: "Silberschlacken"; the impurities or scum left after smelting silver.</note>.
**Eltz**, that is, the flower of copper <note>The green or blue oxidation (verdigris) found on the surface of copper.</note>.
**Elzimar**, that is, the flower of copper.
**Ema**, that is, blood.
**Hematites**, that is, the bloodstone <note>An iron oxide mineral used for its supposed ability to stop bleeding and its red color.</note>.
**Embula** is a vessel, similar to a pipe—that is, a tube or reed.
**Emunctorium** is the place through which the expulsion of corruption or disease occurs; it is the spot through which the sickness cleanses itself.
**Endica** is the impurity, the <term>feces</term> <note>The dregs or sediment remaining at the bottom of a vessel after distillation or filtration.</note> at the bottom. Morienes <note>Morienus, a legendary hermit and alchemist often cited in medieval texts.</note> says: Look for **Endica** in glass vessels, and set them in a hidden place

<term>Elixir</term> is the ferment, the origin, the caustic leaven; it is that which comes from Water. For <term>Yxir</term> is Water; it is a colored water mingled with the bodies. ### MARTIN'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY
<meta>catchword: separation</meta>

...through the **separation** <note>original: "separatio"; the first part of the word appeared as a catchword on the previous page</note> of diverse substances: and it is brought about by heat, not only actual <note>direct heat, like a flame</note> but also potential <note>chemical heat, like that from corrosive substances</note>.

**Dry Epipolasis** <note>A term for a surface "bloom" or a type of sublimation where matter rises to the top</note> occurs when the sublimated matter blossoms immediately out of the thing itself, and adheres closely to it in a dry state. It is carried out in various ways through the work of elevating heat, and by opening the enclosures to loosen the way for its exit.

**Eposilinga**, that is, **iron scales** <note>The flakes of oxide that fall from red-hot iron when it is hammered</note>.

**Erodinium** is a sign of some future thing or history, which remains hidden from men for a time until it arrives; then at last, what was uncertain is called known, and a more certain presage.

**Erysipelas**, "the Beauty" or "the Clouds" <note>original German: "die Schöne/die Wolcken"; archaic folk names for this red skin inflammation, also known as St. Anthony’s Fire</note>.

**Essarz** are small scabby pustules, like blisters, except that they have protruding flesh, such as the pustules caused by a nettle; small, broad blisters, as if someone had burned themselves with nettles <note>original German: "kleine breite Bläterlein/ alß wenn sich einer mit Nesseln brendt het"</note>.

**Potential Essatum** <note>A term used by Paracelsus to describe the inherent "being" or power of a thing</note> is the force, power, and virtue that resides in vegetables and minerals: the power and virtue in wood, herbs, stone, etc. <note>original German: "krafft vñ tugent in Holtz/Kräuter/Stein/&c."</note>

**Essenced Wine** <note>original: "Essatum vinum"</note> is when herbs are added to distilled and rectified wine so that it may extract their essences, such as wine of lemon balm <note>original: "melissa"</note>, which is excellent for asthma; likewise wine of lungwort: for the liquid, not the herb, does the same thing as the lemon balm. This is when one puts herbs into distilled wine so that their power may be extracted <note>original German: "Wenn man zu distillirtem Wein Kräutter thut/daß ihre Krafft außgezogen werde."</note>.

**Escura** or **Estphara** <note>An eschar or scab</note>, is black, dead, bruised flesh, which is separated and falls away from the good and living flesh by means of a cautery or corrosive medicine: a battered, black, and killed flesh <note>original German: "Ein zerschlage/ schwarz vnd getödtet Fleisch."</note>.

**Esebon**, **Alsabon**, that is, **common salt**.

**Essence** is a simple extract produced from things that are perfected in their whole nature. And it is called an essence because, being born and contained within elementary compartments, it is a perfect part of the mixture of the whole substance, instructed by nature and essential reason, and by virtue. It can be made from every kind of mixture—mineral, vegetable, and animal—with great profit.

**Essence** is twofold: **Juice** and **Mystery**.

**Quintessence** <note>literally "the fifth essence"</note> is the corporal matter from all things in which life resides...

### RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN
Cc

...separated from all impurities, and most subtly purged of all things corruptible, in which is all the power of things and medicine <note>original Latin: "separata ab omnib. impuritatibus, ac corruptibilitatibus subtilissime purgata, in qua omnis rerum potentia est & medicina"</note>: It is a matter that is corporally extracted from all plants and everything in which there is life, separated from all uncleanness, and refined to the highest degree of purity <note>original German: "Ist ein Materi/ die corporalisch wirdt außgezogen/ auß allen Gewächsen/ vnd allem dem/ in dem Leben ist/ gescheiden von aller Vnreinigkeit/ gesubtilt auff das aller reinest."</note>.

**Fifth Essence** <term>Essentia quinta</term> is so named because it is something beyond the four elements <note>earth, air, fire, and water</note>, nor does it arise from their mixture; it is divine both in its author and in its effects.

**Effodinum** is a certain presage of a future thing based on an indication: A certain sign of a thing yet to come.

**Efthiomenus** is the complete corruption of a limb, which devours the entire part, such as "the wolf" <note>Lupus, a corrosive skin disease</note>, a spreading herpes, a devouring ulcer, shingles, the "creeping" disease, a type of "holy fire" <note>ignis sacer or erysipelas</note>, *herpedon*, or *zoster*: An open sore that eats entire limbs, such as "the wolf" or the "bursting fire" <note>original German: "Ein offener Schaden/ der da gantze Glieder frist/ alß der Wolff/ das gespreng Fewer."</note>.

**Etesian Winds** <term>Etesiæ</term>, West or West-Northwest.

**Ethesian Stone** <term>Ethesius lapis</term> is Chrysolite.

**Ethees** is Rhenish gold, or precious gold.

**Ethel** is blackness, and also fire. Reference: *The Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original Latin: "Turba," referring to the Turba Philosophorum</note> folio 61. **Ethelia** is the burnt body, dry and impoverished; it is red and white *auricolla* <note>gold-glue or solder</note>, fire, and herbs. Reference: folios 41, 81, 83. It is a herb or a silver vessel that binds together the "Water of Mercury." Reference: folio 22. **Ethelia** is also the red tincture. It is also the white flower of gold; it is called "seething" when the blackness rises upward.

**Euentilatio** is the airing or tossing of linens.

**Euestrum** is the perpetual of the firmament within the four worlds of the elements. # THE WORKS OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN
### page 203

...you will dissolve the purer parts, captured by some poured-on solvent <term>menstruum</term>, leaving the dregs behind. For example: I take as much rhubarb as I wish, and upon that powdered root I pour enough spirit <note>a distilled alcohol or solvent</note> so that it floats four fingers deep above it. Having closed the vessel, I place it in a water bath <term>balneum</term> for four days to undergo digestion <note>a process of gentle, consistent heat to encourage chemical change</note>. Afterwards, having opened the vessel, I separate the colored spirit from the root by decanting <note>tilting the vessel to pour off liquid while leaving solids</note>, and having poured on fresh spirit, I again place the closed vessel for digestion. I continue this until the spirit is no longer colored. For then all the tincture and essence has been extracted from the rhubarb. Furthermore, having mixed all these extractions together, I draw off the spirit in a water bath <term>B. M.</term> <note>original Latin: Balneum Mariae, a double-boiler or "Mary's Bath"</note>, and I keep the remaining essence in a glass vessel for use. This essence is very powerful in purging bile and for other ailments. Or:

<margin>Extraction</margin>
*Extraction* <term>Extractio</term> *is the separation of an essence which is drawn out from its body.* Here there occurs both a pulling apart and, most especially, the dissolving of mixed substances <term>resolutio</term> aids it; sometimes also calcination <note>heating to the point of reduction to ash</note>, boiling, and similar methods are used. The essence is understood to be extracted as a concentrated whole—as if folded together—even though this does not happen without the breaking of the physical structure and a tearing apart. Thus, it is clear that extractions are more noble than mere separations, although they sometimes serve other processes or take their place.

<margin>An Extract</margin>
*An Extract* <term>Extractum</term> *is that which is drawn out from a physical mass, leaving the elemental dross behind.* This is, as it were, the marrow and the most noble part of the whole substance produced within the elements. It is like a seed sown there, preserved in their bosom, and nourished toward the perfection of its nobility. It indeed has its roots to some extent in the elements—from which there exists a kinship of birth and sustenance—but it depends principally upon the creative power of God <note>original: "avi creatis Dei," likely "a vi creatrice Dei"</note>, and through the hidden influences of the heavens, and further upon the preservative power within nature. Hence extracts, especially the more noble ones, are said to rival the ethereal and celestial nature. When well-prepared and skillfully applied for human health, with God’s blessing, they have great power in medicine. Since most of these are very precisely liberated from the elements or their matrices <note>the "womb" or surrounding source material</note> (for the degree of refinement varies even among these), it is clear from this how...

### page 204

...[essences] differ from **magisteries** <term>magisteria</term> <note>In alchemy, a "magistery" refers to a preparation where the entire substance is refined and exalted without losing its elemental parts, whereas an "extraction" separates the pure from the impure</note>, in which the elements remain for the most part (unless something is occasionally overlooked or separates during the process of purification). Nevertheless, these magisteries are exalted so as to rival extracts. Furthermore, one should consider the great advantages they possess in providing rapid healing, due to the penetrating subtlety of the essence which reaches through the entire body.

These substances are called by such names—not because the extracts do not clearly belong to the elements, but because when compared to the coarse and heavy parts of a substance, the other part appears noble. It is seen as the **soul** <term>anima</term>, the **balsam of life** <term>balsamus vitae</term>, the **purest essence**, and a **celestial nature** (though it also truly derives something from the heavens). This is true even in a material sense, if we give any credit to those who—following **Plato**—believe that when the celestial light was separated from the dark earth, not all of the ethereal substance departed. Or, at the very least, they believe that later, during the birth of mixed things, some of that light was reclaimed. This reasoning is confirmed by the way the heavenly bodies <note>the stars and planets</note> act upon these lower, earthly things.

# LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND

### IRON

**Iron** <note>original: "Ferrum"</note> is a metal, very livid, slightly red, sharing in an impure whiteness, and hard. For if fixed, earthy sulfur is mixed with fixed, earthy quicksilver, and both of these are of an impure, livid whiteness—if the sulfur predominates, it becomes iron. In short, if the quicksilver is porous, earthy, and unclean, and the sulfur is also unclean, foul-smelling, and earthy, and of a fixed substance (as if an almost diseased father copulates with a menstruating mother), iron is generated. This metal is attributed by the Alchemists to **Mars**, and it is called Mars, since its use is most frequent in war. The Germans call it **Iron** <note>original: "Eisen"</note>. The Greeks call it **Sideros** <note>original: "σίδηρος"</note>. Some call the stone **sideritis**, which is iron slag. It is also known by the name **Magnets** <note>The author likely refers to magnetite or lodestone here</note>, which attract iron.

Furthermore, iron is of two types: namely, Native, and Smelted or Refined. **Native iron** is pure and is found in mines, appearing like grains or a mass; the Germans call it **Native Iron** <note>original: "gediegen Eisen"</note>. The other kind, smelted or refined, is that which is melted down in ironworks, **At the Hammer-Smiths** <note>original: "Vff den Hammerschmitten"</note>. This occurs in two ways among us in Germany: either from iron-stones, **from the iron-stone** <note>original: "auß dem eisen Stein"</note>, as is done in the valley that takes its name from kings <note>Likely referring to Joachimsthal or a similar royal mining district</note>, and in many other places. It should also be noted that in the same vein of iron, gemstone-like magnets are not infrequently found: so great is their harmony with iron. 

Secondly, iron is also smelted from a red earth, which is as if damaged by rust; the Germans call it **Iron Earth** <note>original: "Eisen Erde"</note>. This occurs in Silesia, and likewise in the March <note>The March of Brandenburg</note>, as I once saw not far from **Berlin**, where the seat of the Margraves is, in a workshop which was called **Niciana** by the craftsman. Indeed, I would almost dare to say that just as one type of pyrite is solid, unified, and hard, while another is brittle and easily ground, so that stone of iron is in one case solid and more refined, and hardened by heat; in the other case it is brittle, and like earth damaged by rust, not yet hardened into an iron-stone due to the weakness of the heat, although it is just as fruitful for producing iron as that solid stone,

# OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN

...as those from Silesia and the March of Nicia <note>Nicia likely refers to the region around Niesky or Meissen</note>. There are also iron mines—very ancient mines, as Tacitus relates—who teaches that the Gothini <note>An ancient Celtic or Germanic tribe</note> worked iron mines and used the Gallic tongue. In Germany, the first mines were iron mines. However, as to which iron is good or which is bad, I leave that to the judgment of the blacksmiths. In Thuringia, if I am not mistaken, Dylmeracense iron <note>Likely referring to iron from the Schmalkalden district</note> is praised; on the other hand, the "glassy" type is condemned—which they call **Glass-Iron** <term>Glaß Eisen</term>—because it breaks easily on the anvil when struck. Concerning the types of good iron and ferrous metals, consult Pliny himself (Book 34, chapters 14 and 15, etc.). Dioscorides (Book 5, chapter 46) discusses iron rust—**Iron Rust** <term>von dem eisen Rost</term>—and its powers. For iron rust has excellent medicinal power for restricting, binding, and drying. It is hot and dry in the second degree. Achilles is said to have healed Telephus with this <note>According to myth, Achilles healed the wound he gave Telephus by scraping the rust from his spear into the injury</note>. Ovid alludes to this in Book 1 of his *Tristia*, first elegy:

> For either no one, or only he who caused me the wounds, 
> alone can take them away in the manner of Achilles.

Furthermore, Dioscorides in the place cited also treats the dross of iron—**Iron Slag** <term>von dem Eisen Schlacken</term>—which they also call scoria and the "dung" of iron, and the "siderite stone"; the Saxons call it **Sunderstein**. Just as all those major metals have dross—**Slag** <term>Schlacken</term>—when they are cooked, so too does iron. Thus we say:

| | |
|----------|----------|
| | dross of copper, <term>Kupfferschlacken</term>. |
| | dross of silver, <term>Silberschlacken</term>. |
| Dross <note>original: "Recrementum"</note> | dross of iron, <term>Eisenschlacken</term>. |
| | dross of lead, <term>Bleyschlacken</term>. |

The dross of iron has the same power as rust, but it is less effective. So too does the scale of iron—that wide and thin piece that flies off from the iron when it is struck—the **Hammer-slag** <term>der Hammerschlack</term>. Concerning these and their powers, consult also the Arabs, Serapion in the *Book of Aggregation* <note>original: "Lib. Aggreg."</note>, chapter Haid. Nicander calls iron slag the "dregs of iron" and declares it effective against monkshood <term>aconiten</term> <note>A potent herbal poison</note>. Dioscorides, in his usual manner, also transferred this into his own work.

1. Pure iron of its own color, found in its own veins within white flint, **Pure native Iron Ore** <term>Rein gediegen Eisen Erz</term>.

->### MARTIN RULAND'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY###<-

**Iron** is a metallic substance, very livid <note>The Latin 'lividum' refers to a bluish-grey or leaden color</note>, slightly reddish, possessing an impure whiteness, and is hard. For if fixed, earthy sulfur is mixed with fixed, earthy quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>, and both of these are of a livid rather than pure whiteness, iron is produced if the sulfur predominates. In short, if the quicksilver is porous, earthy, and unclean, and the sulfur is likewise unclean, foul-smelling, and earthy, and of a fixed substance, iron is generated—much as if a nearly diseased father mates with a menstruating mother <note>Ruland uses this common alchemical metaphor to explain why iron was considered a "base" or "imperfect" metal compared to gold, resulting from "impure" starting materials</note>.

This metal is assigned by the Alchemists to **Mars**, and is called Mars, because its use is most frequent in war. The Germans call it **Iron** <term>Eisen</term>, and the Greeks call it **Sideron** <note>original: σιδηρον</note>. Some call this stone "siderite," which is the slag of iron. However, the magnet <note>lodestone</note> which attracts iron is also called by this name.

Furthermore, iron is twofold: namely, **Native**, and **Smelted** or **Refined**. Native iron is pure and is found in mines in grains or masses; the Germans call this **Native Iron** <term>gediegen Eisen</term>. The other, smelted or refined, is that which is boiled out in iron workshops—**at the hammer-smithies** <term>Uff den Hammerschmitten</term>. In our land of Germany, this is done in two ways: either from iron stones—**from the iron-stone** <term>auß dem eisen Stein</term> or **ore** <term>Erz</term>—as occurs in the valley which takes its name from kings <note>Likely referring to Königsthal</note>, and in very many other places. It should also be noted that in the same vein of iron, magnet-stones <note>lodestones</note> are often found; so great is their harmony with iron.

Secondly, iron is also smelted from a red earth, as if damaged by rust; the Germans call this **Iron-Earth** <term>Eisen Erde</term>. This occurs in Silesia, and likewise in the March <note>The Margraviate of Brandenburg</note>, as I once saw not far from Berlin (the seat of the Margraves), in a workshop which was called "Niciana" by the craftsman. Indeed, I would almost dare to say that just as one type of pyrite is solid, unified, and hard, while another is brittle and easily ground, so too is that iron-stone: one type is solid and more refined, hardened by heat; the other is brittle, like earth stained with rust, not yet hardened into stone due to a weakness of heat—although this earth is just as fruitful for producing iron as that solid stone.
