->### RULANDUS, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN ###<-

4. Fragments that fly off from a hot iron mass when it is condensed and hammered into a mass with wooden mallets. **Iron that chips off when it is compacted.**

5. Scales that fly off from iron when they forge rods with great hammers, which smiths later use to harden iron. **Large hammer-scale, which smiths use for steeling.** <note>Hammer-scale consists of iron oxides (mostly magnetite) produced during hot forging; it was historically reused in various metallurgical processes.</note>

**Iron dust or filings. Iron filings.**

**Iron rust**, that is, the dross of iron, the excrement of iron. **Cinder-stone.** <note>original: *Sindelstein*. This refers to the slag or "cinder" produced in the forge.</note>

**Iron rust**, the defect and decay of iron. **Rust.**

**Fermentation** is the exaltation of a thing in its substance through the admission of a ferment, which—by a power distributed through the spirit—penetrates the entire mass and transforms it into its own matter. For this reason, it was discovered so that from a common and less effective state, a most noble substance might be created by the "medicine" of the ferment, reaching the perfection intended by nature. This occurs most especially in metals, whose nature is inclined toward mutual transformation, and it takes its name from the imitation of fermented dough. Alternatively: **Fermentation** is the incorporation of the ferment with the substance to be fermented. It is called "ferment" by analogy. For just as a little leaven can convert a great deal of flour and dough into its own nature, so too does the chemical ferment assimilate the substance to which it is joined. Therefore, as the ferment is, so shall the fermented result be. Furthermore, the Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists, the "Philosophers of Fire."</note> understand "ferment" to be a true body and a true matter which, when joined to its own Mercury, converts it into its own nature. They also claim the Stone itself to be the ferment of the perfect body. Since the Stone is so subtle (as the Philosophers assert) that when cast upon an imperfect body, it floats on the surface like oil and does not mix with it, there is a need for some body—possessing a primary affinity with the Stone—which may receive it and introduce it into other bodies. For as soon as that first body is "infected" and fermented by the Stone, it immediately transforms into a tincture. <note>A "tincture" in alchemy is a substance capable of "staining" or transforming the internal nature of a base metal into gold or silver.</note>

**White Ferment**, that is, silver. **Felda.** <note>An alchemical name for silver when used as the starting point for the "White Work," the creation of silver from base metals.</note>

**Ferment. Ferment is the Elixir, Sourdough, Leaven, or Yeast.**

# ALCHEMICAL LEXICON OF MARTIN RULAND #

1. Or "leaven," as it is called; it makes the body porous <note>original: *luck*</note> so that it opens up and the spirit finds a place, making it ready for baking. Just as flour is not leaven by itself, but flour and water and the whole dough become soured and turn entirely into leaven, so here the Stone itself is the ferment. However, Gold and Mercury are also called "ferment."

2. **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says: Ferment guides the Work; otherwise, nothing comes of it.

3. **Geber** <note>An influential 8th-century chemist and alchemist, also known as Jabir ibn Hayyan.</note> in the *Book of Forms*, chapter 19: Dissolve the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note> in dry water, which is called Mercury; such that 12 parts of the water contain one part of the perfect body. After 40 days, you will find the body dissolved into water. The sign of complete dissolution is the blackness that appears on top <note>The *nigredo* or "black stage," indicating the death and decomposition of the metal before its rebirth.</note>; this is "our Mercury," which we take as the ferment.

4. The paste <note>original: *pastam*</note> that we wish to ferment is drawn from the imperfect bodies: the White from Saturn <note>Lead</note> and Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, and the Red from Mars <note>Iron</note> and Venus <note>Copper</note>. But each body should be dissolved by itself within the ferment.

5. **Richard of England** <note>A 14th-century alchemist.</note>: For the white <note>the process of making silver</note>, take white ferment; for the red <note>the process of making gold</note>, red; though the red can also produce white.

6. **Geber**: After fermentation, it should be sealed; thus the work is completed for the white in 40 days, and for the red in 90 days, in a single vessel and a single operation.

7. **Lullus** <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note>: Common gold cannot be the ferment, for it must have an active <note>original: *actualem*</note> power and be full of spirit to possess that power. Nevertheless, it is still called "ferment," and Silver is called "white ferment."

->Or:<-

*Ferment is a firm matter, as if fixed, which prepares the material of its own nature for its own fixed condition—a condition which it [the material] did not have before preparation any more than it [the ferment] had—just as the leaven of bread is...* <note>The original Latin text "ut fermentum panis est fa-" cuts off here; it likely intended to complete the bread analogy.</note>

2. When he is born, he must have food and nourishment; the nourishment is the **increase** <note>original: *augment*</note>, when the material is honored by the **leaven** <note>original: *ferment*</note>, then the Child becomes a seed again.

<header>MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.</header>

**Filtration** is the withdrawal of liquid through a filter: this is a chemical strainer, and thus it can also be called straining or percolation. It is performed primarily on damp substances, from which a thin watery part passes through, while the thick and oily parts are held back. The practice of it is mainly as follows: **Filter paper** <note>original: *Carta emporetica*; literally "merchant’s paper," used for wrapping or straining</note> is rolled or folded; or in its place, a **shaggy cloth** is sewn into the shape of a bag, or applied to a vessel, such as a funnel, etc. The poured liquor is allowed to drip little by little into the receiving vessel; hence this operation is called **distillation by filter**. Alternatively: Filtration is a **cold descent** <note>a method of separating liquids from solids without heat</note>, letting watery humors pass through a filter—whether rolled or folded filter paper in the manner of a funnel—leaving the dregs behind in the filter. But besides the filter, other things are also used, such as **Hippocrates’ Sleeve** <note>original: *manica Hippocratis*; a conical woolen filter bag</note>, or cloths made of wool, linen, or bristles.
<gloss>To filter: To purify through a felt or woolen cloth.</gloss>

**Arsenical thread** <note>original: *Filum arsenicale*</note>: sublimated arsenic.
**Thread of plumed alum**: Virgin’s Thread <note>original: *Jungfraw Faden*; likely referring to a fibrous form of asbestos or alum</note>.
**Horse dung**: Horse manure <note>original: *Pferdemist*</note>; it provides a moist heat <note>often used for gentle, sustained digestion in a ‘manure bath’</note>.
**Phial**: A glass with a long neck.
**Firex**: That is, oil.
**Firfir**: That is, a red color.
**Firmament**: That is, Azure or Lapis Lazuli.
**Fisarum**: That is, a preparation of Sal Ammoniac.
**Fistula**: A narrow, long, and callous cavity; a syringe or pipe; the fistula.
**Fistula**: A mold, pipe, or tube.
**To drive or strike cracks**: To carve fissures.
**Fixing**, or **Fixation**: To make stable; to fix.
**Fixation** is the habituation to the fire of a substance that usually flees from it <note>a volatile substance</note>, so that it no longer flees, but remains fixed within the fire. This is achieved whether through **calcination** <note>reduction to powder by heat</note>, or through a slow and long **decoction** <note>boiling</note>, or through frequent **sublimation**, or through many repeated cycles of **solution and coagulation**, or finally, it is perfected by the addition of a fixed substance.
<gloss>When it becomes entirely dry and solid, so that it no longer dissolves in water, but withstands the fire.</gloss>

<vocab>Filtratio, colum chymicum, Carta emporetica, manica Hip., Filum arsenicale, Fimus equinus, Fiola, Firex, Firfir, Firmamentum, Fisarum, Fistula, Fixatio</vocab>

<page-num>216</page-num>
<header>MARTIN RULAND’S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY</header>

<term>Fixation</term> <note>original: *Fixio*</note>, taming or making stable <note>German: *Zähmachung oder Stetmachung*; the process of making a volatile substance solid and resistant to fire</note>.
<term>Fyada</term>, that is, Mercury, or white smoke.
<term>Flammula</term> <note>literally "little flame"</note>, Crowfoot <note>German: *Hahnenfuß*; a plant of the *Ranunculus* genus</note>.
<term>Flagae</term> are spirits who know the secrets of men, or spirits appearing from things in a mirror. They are something we do not see, yet they are with us in our hidden words and deeds.
<term>Phlegmon</term> <note>original: *Flegmon*</note>, a common abscess or boil <note>German: *Bluteis*</note>.
<term>Flower</term> <note>original: *Flos*</note> is a mass extracted through sublimation <note>a process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then collected again as a solid</note>. Therefore, it must be raised from the center and the lowest parts and brought upward, so that a dry form coagulates at the summit. A "flower" is the spiritual substance of a thing; whereas "Turbith" <note>an alchemical precipitate</note> is more earthy. Every flower is naturally volatile and spiritual, although through the skill of a master it can be fixed and sometimes brought to the nature of Turbith.
<term>To flowerify</term> <note>original: *Florificiren*</note>, to make "flowers" or sublimated extracts.
<term>Flower of copper</term> <note>original: *Flos æris*</note>, that is, verdigris <note>the green crust that forms on copper</note>.
<term>Flower of copper</term> <note>original: *Flos æris*</note> is the coagulum, "bite," or "lip." The "man" who acts upon the "woman" is the spirit of the man who completes the work <note>alchemical allegory for the interaction of active and passive substances</note>. A "flower" is the extract.
<term>Flower of cheiri</term> <note>original: *Flos cheiri*</note> is the essence of gold <note>*Cheiri* often refers to the wallflower, used here for its yellow color</note>.
<term>Flower of salt</term> <note>original: *Flos salis*</note>, salt-flower; in Greek, *halos anthos*.
<term>Flower of sector Croe</note>: others wish this to be saffron flowers <note>Crocus</note>, because of the addition of "croe," thinking it an error by those who did not read Paracelsus’s handwriting exactly, mistaking "e" for "ci" <note>i.e., reading *croe* instead of *croci*</note>. However, through the transposition of letters, I have discovered it to be the flower of nutmeg <note>mace</note>, as the term *sonath anthos* denotes. Others say it is the extract of celandine.
<margin>Flowers</margin>
<term>Phlox</term> <note>original: *Flox*</note>, that is, a flame.
<term>Fluors</term> <note>original: *Fluores*</note>, from the German *Flüsse* [fluxes]. These stones from mines are similar to gemstones, but less hard. Miners call them *fluores* because they melt and flow in the heat of fire like ice in the sun. These fluors are, in a sense, the opposite of those intermediate or distant metals which dissolve into spirits and air. If Theophrastus <note>referring to the physician Paracelsus</note> had known them, he would have called them "that which comes from a flowing together" <note>original Greek: *ek syrrhoēs*</note>.

...because they are formed by a flow in the earth. But I believe they were entirely unknown to the ancients. However, so that you may better recognize the types of fluxes <note>original: *fluores*; these are minerals we now call fluorite, used to help metals melt and flow</note>, we will list them below for the sake of students. These are the rudiments of gems, and these fluxes <note>German: *die Flüße*</note> are similar to gemstones and are well known in the mines. They are:

1. **Of a red color.** At first glance they look like raw red silver, although this also occasionally appears translucent. They also look like carbuncles <note>a term for deep red gems like garnet or ruby</note>, but they shine with a weaker clarity. Those that are not translucent are distinguished from carbuncles by that very fact. Furthermore, all types of fluors flow away <note>melt</note> as soon as they feel the heat of the fire. Carbuncles, however, do not liquefy in fire.

2. **Of a paler purple color.** They appear to be greener amethysts, such as are found in many places in Bohemia; certainly they are not much different from them. For this reason, the common folk are often deceived by them, as they do not know real amethysts. Wicked men set them in rings and sell them as amethysts.

3. **Of a white color.** They appear to be crystals.

4. **Of a yellow color.** They appear almost to be topazes.

5. **Of an ash-gray color.**

6. **Of a blackish color.** There are also fluors of other colors, if one were to look more carefully. Now, the use of fluors is in the smelting of metals; they are employed and thrown into the furnace. For they make the material more fluid in the fire, just like a type of stone made from pyrite. I believe the best pigments could be made from such fluors, if someone were to experiment.

<margin>Red Fluors.</margin>
1. Long ones, red on a white background, hexagonal and transparent.
2. Long red ones, shaped like an upright beam, to which are attached small black stones from which white lead <note>original: *plumbum candidum*; in this period, this refers to tin, specifically the ore cassiterite</note> is made.
3. Quadrangular and hexagonal pyramids <note>German: *Spitzige eckiche Fluße* - sharp, cornered fluxes</note>.
4. Hexagonal ones, glowing red in white stone, like a sea-urchin <note>original: *echino*</note>...

...suitable for coals and vessels. There is also another kind of tongs with which we lift vessels out of the fire, which folds together like a pair of forceps.

**Forms of things** <note>original: *Formæ rerum*</note>; that is, the influences of the heavens, which lower things receive from higher things: the hidden power, force, and virtue of each thing.

**Formicae** <note>literally "Ants"; a medical term for a type of wart</note>; these are wart-like or leek-like abscesses, low-lying warts, "creeping" growths, or "ant-infestations" <note>original: *myrmeciæ*</note>. <gloss>Deep-rooted warts; ant-warts.</gloss>

**Furnace** <note>original: *Fornax*</note>. <gloss>An oven or furnace; there are many kinds:</gloss>

**The primary furnace of glassmakers**, and also that in which the veins of ore are thoroughly smelted. <gloss>Melting furnace.</gloss>

**The furnace** in which lead is separated from silver. <gloss>Refining hearth.</gloss> <note>original: *Treibherd*; used in the process of cupellation.</note>

**The furnace** in which silver and lead are separated from copper. <gloss>Liquation furnace.</gloss> <note>original: *Seigeroffen*; part of the "Saiger" process for extracting silver from copper ore.</note>

**The furnace** in which iron is smelted. <gloss>Bloomery hearth.</gloss> <note>original: *Rennherd*.</note>

**The furnace** in which roasted copper loaves are cooked. <gloss>Refining hearths.</gloss> <note>original: *Gerherde*; *panes ærei* or "copper loaves" refers to the raw ingots of copper.</note>

**The furnace** in which copper loaves are heated. <gloss>Heating oven.</gloss>

**The furnace** into which the wind is blown through openings. <gloss>Wind furnace.</gloss>

**A furnace** similar to a baker's oven. <gloss>Splitting furnace.</gloss> <note>original: *Epleiß Offen*, likely a variant of *Spleißofen*.</note>

**The wind-furnace** <note>original: *Fornax anemia*; likely from the Greek for "without bellows," relying on natural draft</note> is made of iron in the shape of a tripod, with an ash-pit and a hearth; these two regions are separated by a grate. The ash-pit is closed by an iron door through which the air enters from below. However, the hearth is open and lined on the inside with thick clay. The workspace <note>original: *Ergaſtulū*</note> is an open space. Generally, the work is managed using a frying pan, a pot, a triangular crucible <note>original: *catinū triangularē*</note>, or similar vessels, so that they sit upon the coals or are lowered slightly into them. Although the fire is sometimes intensified with a hand-fan or bellows, the power of the air or wind entering from below is the most effective. Therefore, it must be placed in a location where the door of the ash-pit is exposed to the wind or the movement of the air, and there should be no other exit anywhere—with windows and other parts closed—except for the chimney tending upward, so that the air is forced to escape through the coals. This is done especially when we wish to melt something with a great fire or to calcine it <note>reduce it to powder through heat</note>.

**Master of the furnace.** <gloss>Refining master.</gloss> <note>original: *Garmacher*.</note>

**Hidden Ditch** <note>original: *Fossa occulta*; German: *Felort*</note>. <gloss>A "field-place" or a dead-end workspace in a mine.</gloss>

**Latent Ditch** <note>original: *Fossa latens*; German: *Leng/Querschlag*</note>. <gloss>A longitudinal gallery or a crosscut in a mine.</gloss>

**Latent Ditch near a Pit** <note>original: *Fossa latens iuxta lacunam*; German: *Außgeworffen Ortlein*</note>. <gloss>A small discarded niche or side-chamber.</gloss>

**To build an underground trench** <note>original: *Fossam latentem substruere*; German: *Kasten schlagen*</note>. <gloss>To construct mine-timbering or a shaft-box to support the earth.</gloss>

**To drive an open ditch** <note>original: *Fossam patentem ducere*; German: *Rosch treiben*</note>. <gloss>To excavate a drainage channel or watercourse.</gloss>

**To lead ditches** <note>original: *Fossos ducere*; German: *Scherpffen*</note>. <gloss>To sharpen or cut notches for drainage.</gloss>

**Digger** <note>original: *Fossor*; German: *Hauwer / Berghauwer*</note>. <gloss>A hewer or miner.</gloss>

**Diggers who collected twisted things** <note>original: *Fossores, qui collegerunt intorta*; German: *Krumbhalß*</note>. <gloss>Literally "Crook-necks"; a nickname for miners who work in cramped, bent positions.</gloss>

**Laurel Leaves** <note>original: *Frondes lauri*; German: *Lorber blätter*</note>. <gloss>In alchemical symbolism, these refer to specific colors.</gloss>

**Fugile** <note>a medical term</note>; **Parotis**; **an abscess near the ears** <note>German: *Ohrenmußl / Ohrimückl / Ohrenvottel*</note>. <gloss>A swelling or tumor located behind the ears.</gloss>

**Soot of Metals** <note>original: *Fuligo metallorum*</note>; specifically refers to **Arsenic**, and often also to **Mercury**.

**Soot** as used by painters <note>German: *Schmiß / Ram / schwersel*</note>. It is now produced in various ways and from many substances. Among us, it is made from torch-pine and is called **Pine-soot** or **Lampblack** <note>German: *Kötteltrohm / Kinrauch*</note>. Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician</note> describes soot gathered from **glassmaking workshops**, which has the medical power to bind <note>astringe</note> and wear away <note>erode</note> tissue. See also Pliny, Book 35, Chapter 16.

**Lightning** <note>original: *Fulmen*</note>. In this context, it refers to the "flowers" of silver that has been **cupelled** <note>refined in a special ash-vessel</note> during its purification with lead. Hence, **to fulminate metals** is the same as to purify them, especially those considered "perfect" <note>the noble metals, gold and silver</note>.

**Fulmination** is a metallurgical refinement involving smelting to absolute purity in a cupel <note>original: *cineritio*; a vessel made of bone-ash</note>. Its perfection is indicated by a sudden, flashing brilliance. The process takes its name from this, as a "flash" or "coruscation" occurs, much like a bolt of lightning appearing. For after the impurities have been consumed and separated (such as added fluxes, lead, and conjoined minerals), a certain sulfurous little cloud "rides" across the surface; following this, a purple brilliance shines forth, which they call the **Flash**, the **Lightning**, or even the **Flower**.

**Native Supports** or **Arches** <note>original: *Fulturæ natiue vel fornices*; German: *Bergveſten*</note>. <gloss>The natural pillars of rock left standing in a mine to support the roof.</gloss>

**Smoke** <note>original: *Fumus*</note> is the **dregs** <note>original: *fæx*; German: *Druſen*</note> at the bottom; yet properly it is that which rises and carries the **body** <note>the material substance</note> with it. For there are two kinds of Smoke: those which, mixed with the Earth, make the stars fall from heaven, and also create comets and rainbows around the Sun and the Moon. When the **vaporous vessel** <note>original: *batia*; likely referring to the rising steam or the vessel containing it</note> finds a mineral matter, it is mixed with it **intimately** <note>original: *per minima*; literally "by the smallest parts"</note>, and it also becomes **fixed** <note>stable under heat</note> and turns into a metal. If, however, it finds no such matter, it becomes **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*</note>. But the mineral power which it is meant to find is clear, washed **sulfur**, which is partly fixed and is found in extracted stones and in sand; it shines like silver, and since nothing is created without this, it is found everywhere that metals are born. Therefore, the metal that contains much sulfur is called the **lake of the generation of metals** <note>original: *lacus generationis metallorum*</note>.

**White Smoke** <note>original: *Fumus albus*</note> is **Mercury**, the Soul and the **Tincture** <note>the transforming essence</note>, Celestial Water, and the **quintessence of Venus** <note>original: *quinta essentia Veneris*; referring to the refined essence of copper</note>. This carries the color of gold, in a dry state, into the heights. There **the serpent climbs the tree** <note>A classic alchemical allegory for sublimation, where the volatile substance rises up the neck of the flask</note>, finds the mother with two young ones, and devours them all. That is to say: The Smoke rises above itself and finds two **sulfurs** with the Mercury; it dissolves them all, draws them into itself, and becomes **Fixed** and the **Stone** <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note>. The White Smoke is the Soul of the dissolved bodies; it gives life and brings about whiteness.

**Yellow Smoke** <note>original: *Fumus citrinus*</note> is yellow sulfur.

**Red Smoke** <note>original: *Fumus rubeus*</note> is red **orpiment** <note>original: *Auripigment*; arsenic trisulfide</note>. It is also called Gold, because it is esteemed <note>original: *hol*; perhaps meaning "hold" or "valued"</note>.

**Venomous Smoke** <note>original: *Fumus virosus, vel virus*; German: *Schwaden*</note>. <gloss>Poisonous damps or gases found in mines.</gloss>

**Furnace Smoke** <note>original: *Fumus casæ vel cassæ*; German: *Hütten Rauch*</note>. <gloss>Refers to "smelter's smoke" or arsenic trioxide collected from the flues of a furnace.</gloss>

**Fumigation** <note>original: *Fumigatio*</note> is **calcination** <note>the reduction of a substance to a powder through heat</note> performed by means of smoke and corrosive air. 
It is done in various ways. The nobler metals are rendered brittle by the vapor of molten lead or **mercury** <note>original: *hydrargyrum*</note>, and are afterwards reduced to small pieces by grinding them with salt.

**Hauling rope** <note>original: *Funis ductarius*; German: *Seil*</note>.

**Rope made from linden bark** <note>original: *Funis ex philyris tiliæ factus*; German: *Bast*</note>.

**Hempen cord** <note>original: *Funiculus canabinus*; German: *Schnur*</note>.

**White thieves** <note>original: *Fures candidi*</note>, that is, **Red Water** <note>original: *Rote Wasser*; likely referring to a corrosive solvent or reagent that "steals" the metal's form</note>.

**Furogi**, that is, a **cock** <note>original: *gallus*; a rooster, often a symbol for the active principle or sulfur</note>.

**Furnace** <note>original: *Furnus*</note> is a place in which fire is skillfully and conveniently adapted for the chemical treatment of matter. It is either **Open** or **Covered**.

**Open furnace** is one whose upper part is open. It is either an **Assay furnace** <note>original: *Probatorius*</note> or a **Blast furnace** <note>original: *Ventosus*; literally "windy," referring to the use of bellows</note>.

**Assay furnace** or **docimastic furnace** <note>original: *furnus docimasticus*; from the Greek for "testing"</note> is an open furnace in which the more perfect metals are purified, examined, or, to use a more common term to describe the matter, **fulminated** <note>the process of final purification where the precious metal suddenly "flashes" or shines brightly when the dross is removed</note>. This furnace is most often built from clay or iron plates, rarely from bricks, in the following manner: 

Take an iron plate, or one made of clay, and construct it into a square so that the width of the foundation is eleven parts (dividing one foot into twelve parts), and the length is sixteen parts. However, when the measurement has reached eight parts in length, the furnace must be gradually curved into a slope so that it finally becomes narrower by four parts, and the **crater** <note>the opening</note> at the top of the furnace retains a width of only seven parts. It is appropriate for the plates to have a thickness of one and a half parts, while the pavement and the bottom made of clay should contain three-quarters of one part. These things being thus constructed, three parts in height and four in width are to be taken upward from the floor to form the lower door. From the peak of this door...

...let the same wall be continued for two measures <note>original: *mensuras*; a standardized unit of length used in the construction of the apparatus</note>, which make up the space between the door already mentioned and the one following immediately after. From there, three and a half measures are to be repeated again, and four in width, from which a small door <note>original: *ostiolum*</note> is made, suitable for putting in, taking out, and directing the materials. From this point one must proceed, and after a distance of one measure, a small hole should be pierced in the middle, barely large enough to contain the little finger <note>original: *auricularem digitum*</note>, serving for the iron tools used to move the coals. Furthermore, three-quarters of one measure are to be set to the right and left under the edges of the small door, where two holes the width of a middle finger <note>original: *mediocrem digitum*</note> are made. Into these holes (to which two others must correspond in the opposite wall), iron bars are placed, which project four finger-widths <note>original: *digitos latos*</note> from the front wall.

Furthermore, doors or barriers <note>original: *obices*</note> with a handle should be adapted to each small door for regulating the fire, so that they may be removed and replaced. Of these, the upper door should contain an oblong hole so that, even when the door is closed, the view is not obstructed; the lower door, however, should be equipped with a larger, round hole so that it may draw in the air that feeds the fire. Above the bars, an earthen plate is placed, hollowed out on three sides to allow ash to pass through, but whole and straight on the fourth side where it touches the front wall. 

Next, the floor of the laboratory <note>original: *ergasterii*; the workspace or workshop</note> and the vaulted tiles are built upon it, which must be two and a half measures away from the sides and the back. Additionally, a round hole is hollowed out near the upper door to supply air. Once everything has been constructed in this manner, while the furnace is still soft, grooves and pits should be shaped on the outside to receive the iron plates <note>original: *bracteas ferreas*</note> that strengthen the furnace. Finally, once the furnace has dried in a sunny place, let it be properly fired <note>original: *coquatur*; literally "cooked" or baked</note> by a potter. 

This is a most suitable method for building a furnace, both because it is not easily blocked by ashes and is therefore sufficient for all assaying work <note>original: *docimastico negotio*; referring to "docimasy," the art of testing the purity of metals</note>, and because it far surpasses all others due to the skill with which the fire can be directed.

# LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MART[IN RULAND]
<meta>catchword: otherwise (original: secus)</meta>

A **wind furnace** <note>original: *furnus ventosus*</note>, or **anemia** <note>from the Greek *anemos*, referring to wind-powered airflow</note>, is an open furnace in which minerals are liquefied and melted by the benefit of the wind, which increases the power of the fire. If by chance the minerals are of a more difficult fusion, so that the wind cannot foster sufficient heat, or if the craftsman wishes to melt something more quickly, a bellows <note>original: *follis*</note> is conveniently attached to increase the fire and render the fusion faster. 

But a wind furnace with its bellows is constructed in this manner: Let four walls be raised, constructed with the sides lying flat, distant from each other by the interval of a foot, and a cubit <note>approximately 18 inches or 45 cm</note> in height, to create the **ash-pit** <note>original: *conisterium*, from the Greek for "place of dust," or *cinerarium*</note>. In one or the other wall of the ash-pit, let a small door <note>original: *ostiolum*</note> be made, through which the fire can draw air and the ash can be removed. 

Furthermore, above the ash-pit, iron fittings are placed for the grate <note>original: *craticula*</note>, which supports the coals and the vessel placed upon it. A finger's breadth below the grate, a small hole should be made through which the nozzle <note>original: *rostrum*</note> of the bellows may pass; it must be inserted there. The furnace should then be made with a slope of one foot from the grate to constitute the hearth <note>original: *focus*</note>. This, once sufficiently dried, is smeared with coal dust and clay diluted with water, and finally the bellows is applied. This furnace can also serve for calcination <note>the process of reducing a substance to a powder or friable state through heat</note> if necessity demands.

**Covered furnaces** <note>original: *furni tecti*</note> are those whose upper surface is covered.

A covered furnace is either **simple** or **composite**.

A **simple furnace** <note>original: *furnus simplex*</note> is one which consists simply and absolutely of the support of another; and it is either calcinatory or dissolutory.

A **calcinatory furnace** <note>original: *furnus calcinatorius*</note> is one which serves for the calcining of things: such as the cementing and reverberatory furnaces.

A **cementing furnace** <note>original: *furnus coementatorius*</note> is one in which the fire is expertly adapted for the cementing of materials <note><term>cementation</term>: a process where a solid metal is heated in contact with a powdered reagent to alter its properties, often used in purifying gold</note>. Various furnaces can be employed in the business of this operation; however, that one which I shall now describe—both because of the continuity of the fire and because of the convenient management of its degrees <note>referring to "degrees of heat," the alchemical practice of precisely controlling temperature</note>—pleases us above all others, and is erected in the following way. Let a wall be made of bricks in a square, which internally...

otherwise <note>original: *secus*</note>, let it be a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> wide laterally, and up to the first section let it be one foot high, to establish the **ash-pit** <note>original: *conisterium*</note>. The remaining doors and holes are properly closed with their stoppers, so that the furnace, according to the requirements of the work, can properly maintain a continuous lit fire for a period of twenty-four hours.

Once these are arranged, a floor <note>original: *solarium*; a raised platform or partition within the furnace</note> is made of bricks upon the wall, positioned so that it does not touch the back wall by a space of three fingers' width. This allows the flame to pass through that opening, where it is held back by the following chamber and forced to reverberate back onto the material. By these vents, the fire can be skillfully and conveniently directed, and its heat increased or decreased at will as the work requires. When everything has been constructed in this manner, we fashion a suitable plug for each little door, put it in place, and command the furnace to be ready for use.

The **Dissolving Furnace** <term>Furnus dissolutorius: a furnace used for "dissolution," the alchemical process of reducing a solid body into a liquid or extracting its "subtle" essence</term> is a simple device by which things are dissolved by passing the subtle from the coarse. It is either **Ascending** or **Descending**.

The **Ascending Furnace** is used when we dissolve by way of ascent <note>referring to heat or vapors rising through the substance</note>. It is either **Dry** or **Moist**.

The **Dry Furnace** is a vessel containing the material which is not placed in any water, but promotes dissolution without external moisture; this is done in a **bladder-vessel** <note>original: *vesica*; a copper or glass vessel shaped like a bladder, often used as the base of a still</note> or a **sand-bath** <note>original: *catino arenario*; a container filled with sand to provide even, indirect heat</note>.

The **Furnace of the Bladder-Vessel** is one that serves for dissolving a substance within the *vesica*. It is of this kind: Four walls are to be erected in a square of one foot in height (though the width may vary according to the capacity of the *vesica*) to serve as the **ash-pit** <note>original: *conisterium*</note>. However, on one side at the bottom, let two fragments suffice, placed at the corners so that an empty space for the ash-hole <note>original: *cinerario*</note>, six fingers wide and high, is formed in their midst; and above that, the rest of that side is to be leveled with the others. As far as the structure is concerned, it is no different from the former, except that instead of a bladder-vessel, we place a crucible or another vessel containing the material to be dissolved, and we keep watch over the furnace. 

If, however, besides the crucible, we wish to dissolve something over an open fire by tilting it or through the side, it is necessary for the furnace to have an empty space on one side, four or (as the case may require) six fingers wide, through which the vessel may project. This furnace is of the greatest use in almost all dissolutions, whether they are performed by means of ashes, sand, or iron <note>Refers to heating the vessel indirectly through a bed of ash, a sand-bath, or an iron plate</note>, or finally, whether they are completed over a naked fire.

The **Bath Furnace** <margin>Bath furnace</margin> is where we dissolve substances in a kettle containing warm water. This furnace is erected in the same way the previous ones were built, and in place of the bladder-vessel or crucible, a bronze kettle <term>ahenum: a copper or bronze pot, here serving as a water bath or "bain-marie"</term> specially fashioned for this purpose is placed upon it.

And above that <note>referring to the grate mentioned on the previous page</note>, let a wall one foot high be made for the hearth, which should have another small door above the aforementioned one, through which wood is cast in. With these things thus arranged, a platform <note>original: *solarium*; a raised floor or brick shelf</note> of bricks is constructed upon the wall, so that it does not touch the back wall by three fingers' breadth, so that the flame can pass through that opening and, being held back by the following chamber, be forced to **reverberate** <term>reverberare: to bounce heat or flame back onto the material, a technique used in "reverberatory" furnaces to provide intense, indirect heat</term> into the material. Furthermore, leaving a moderate door in the front wall above that platform, where the material to be reverberated can be put in and taken out, we close the remaining part of the furnace (which is a little lower than the others) with a firm vaulting <note>original: *concameratione*; a vaulted ceiling or arch</note>. And for both the back and front furnace, leaving two fingers' width on the face above the aforementioned upper door, we block it off with four vents <note>original: *ventilabris*; air-holes or dampers used to regulate the flow of oxygen and heat</note> placed next to each other, by which the fire can be directed skillfully and appropriately, and its heat increased or decreased at will as the task requires, strengthened with brick walls. Everything being built in this manner, we fashion a suitable plug for each small door, put it in, and command the furnace to serve its purpose.

The **Simple Dissolving Furnace** <note>original: *Furnus dissolutorius simplex*</note> is one by which substances are dissolved by passing the subtle from the gross. It is either **Ascending** or **Descending**.

An **Ascending Furnace** is when we dissolve by ascending <note>referring to upward distillation or vaporization</note>. This is either **Dry** or **Moist**.

A **Dry Furnace** is a vessel containing material that is not placed in any water, but promotes dissolution besides external moisture; this occurs in a **Bladder-vessel** <term>vesica: a copper or glass vessel shaped like a bladder or cucurbit, used as the base of a still</term> and a **Sand-dish** <note>original: *catino arenario*; a sand-bath used for even heating</note>.

The **Bladder Furnace** <note>original: *Furnus vesicæ*</note> is that which serves for the substance to be dissolved in a bladder-vessel. It is of this kind: Four walls are to be erected in a square a foot high (though the width may vary according to the capacity of the bladder) for the **Dust-chamber** <note>original: *conisterio*; from the Greek *konis*, the lower part of the furnace where ashes collect</note>. But on one side at the bottom, two fragments <note>bricks or stones</note> suffice, placed at the corners so that in the middle of them an empty space is established for the **Ash-pit** <note>original: *cinerario*</note> six fingers wide and high, and above that, the rest of that part is to be leveled with the others. <margin>**Crucible furnace,**</margin> by the aid of which we dissolve substances in a crucible, is managed in the same way as the one described above. Regarding its structure, it does not differ from the former in any way, except that in place of the bladder-vessel, we insert a crucible or another vessel containing the material to be dissolved, and we watch the furnace. If, however, besides the crucible, we wish to dissolve something by an open fire through inclination <note>pouring off or heating from the side</note> or through the side, it is necessary that the furnace have a vacant space on one side, four or (as the case requires) six fingers wide, of suitable capacity, through which the vessel may project. This furnace is of the greatest use in almost all dissolutions, whether they are performed through ashes, through sand, through iron <note>referring to heating in a pan of iron filings</note>, or finally, if they are completed by an open fire.

<margin>**Bath furnace**</margin> is where we dissolve substances in a cauldron containing hot water. This furnace is erected in the same manner as the previous furnaces were constructed, and in place of the bladder-vessel or crucible, a copper cauldron <note>original: *ahenum*; a bronze or copper pot</note> fashioned for that purpose is placed upon it. ...the joints should fit so precisely that they can be aptly closed and packed tight, lest even the slightest breath of air or vapor escape. From one side of this vessel, a pipe or a spout <term>epistomium: a nozzle or tap used to control the flow of liquid</term> projects, which reaches toward the copper kettle <term>ahenum: a bronze or copper boiling pot</term> with its lower lips, so that fresh water can be poured through it whenever necessity requires. Very near to this copper kettle, the vessel has a certain fold or rim all around it, to which a perforated plate—acting as a transverse partition—is fitted to hold the vessels placed within. It often happens that more items need to be digested at once than a single vessel of this kind can hold; therefore, to remedy this shortage, a second vessel can be placed upon the first, or even a third in time of need and when the quantity of items to be digested requires it. At the top of the vessel, we fit a copper lid that closes the joints appropriately, so that no vapor can escape from there. When, however, the intention is to distill something by means of a vapor bath <term>balneum roris: literally a "bath of dew," where a vessel is heated by steam rather than being submerged in water</term>, we do not need this specific vessel; instead, a gourd-shaped flask <term>cucurbita: a glass distillation vessel named for its gourd-like shape</term> is placed into a deeper copper kettle, though with this caution: that the water does not touch the glass. For it is necessary that only the vapor surrounds and heats it. Finally, it is sealed with a lid serving the bath so that the vapor cannot escape.

**The Descending Furnace** <note>original: *furnus descensorius*</note> is one by whose aid we dissolve a substance by driving the moisture downward. The walls are built up to the ash-pit <note>original: *conisterium*; the lower chamber where ashes are collected</note>, which holds a receiving vessel, kept safe from all violence of the fire. Upon the ash-pit is placed a grate <note>original: *craticula*</note> of such a kind that it has a round hole in the middle, through which the neck of the upper vessel may pass. The walls are then continued to the hearth, where the work-chamber <note>original: *ergasterium*; the internal space where the chemical reaction occurs</note> is also to be constructed; the said vessel is placed into this upside down, and the dissolution is undertaken as the situation requires, while observing the proper degrees of heat.

**Composite furnaces** are those where several furnaces are heated by a single fire; these include the **Athanor** <note>a furnace designed to provide consistent heat over long periods via a self-feeding fuel hopper</note> and the **Furnace of Sloth** <note>original: *Acediæ furnus*; another name for the Athanor, so called because the alchemist could "lazily" leave it unattended for long periods</note>.

The furnace of sloth or negligence, <margin>where several furnaces are heated.</margin> where several furnaces are heated by a single fire and with little labor. It takes its name from laziness; hence, it is called "Lazy Heinz" <note>original: *Ein fauler Heinze*</note> or "Lazy Henry" <note>original: *piger Henricus*</note> by the Germans. <note>This furnace, also known as an athanor, was designed with a large fuel reservoir so that it could burn for long periods without constant tending, which the author humorously attributes to the "sloth" of the chemist.</note> A round or square tower is erected in the manner described above, and above the grate <term>craticula: a metal grating used to support fuel in a furnace</term> we leave open three, four, or five holes—depending on the number of furnaces to be built—which carry the heat to the side furnaces. **Fusion** is the process of melting by means of heat.

**Fusion by means of antimony**, by which we separate true gold not only from imperfect metals, but even from silver itself. It is performed in this manner: I take gold mixed with other metals and mix it with three parts of powdered antimony. I place this in a crucible <term>crucibulum</term> within a wind-furnace <term>furnus ventosus: a furnace designed to create a strong draft of air for high temperatures</term> with a persistent fire. Afterward, when it is well melted—with the help of a bellows <term>follis</term> if desired—I pour it into a pre-heated cone-shaped mold <term>pyramis</term> smeared with tallow. When the edges of the mold have been struck with a hammer, the "regulus" <term>regulus: the metallic button or mass that settles at the bottom of a mold during smelting</term> containing the gold will settle at the bottom <note>literally "at the apex," as the mold is a cone</note>, which I then knock off with a hammer. Furthermore, I place the remaining antimony back into a crucible in the fire for a third time, proceeding in the aforementioned way, so that all the gold is forced out of the antimony. Finally, I place these individual reguli in an earthen cup <term>catillum</term> near the bellows, and having placed charcoal over them, I light a fire in the manner of a vault <term>fornix: an arched arrangement of coals to concentrate heat</term>, and for as long as...

->G<-

**Jet stone** <note>original: *Gagates lapis*</note>, and it should not be called *gagites*; for *gagites* is the eagle-stone <term>aetites: a stone traditionally believed to be found in the nests of eagles and possessing magical or medicinal properties</term> according to Pliny, Book 10, Chapter 3. Jet stone, which we are discussing here, is called by the Germans **a jet stone, amber stone, or fossil coal** <note>original: *Gagatstein / Gagestein / Agatstein / Bornstein*</note>. Jet is undoubtedly formed in the sea and rivers from petroleum—that is, from a refined naphtha <term>naphtha: a highly flammable liquid hydrocarbon</term> or natural liquid bitumen. Just as another species of jet, the Thracian stone, **black amber or jet stone** <note>original: *schwartz Bornstein / oder Agetstein*</note>, is formed from black naphtha or bitumen: when bitumen or liquid naphtha—that petroleum, as we shall soon say in the chapter on naphtha—drips or flows into the sea or rivers near the coast, I say it becomes jet. The Germans, however, frequently confuse jet stones with amber or *electrum* <term>electrum: here referring to amber, known for its ability to produce static electricity when rubbed, rather than the gold-silver alloy</term>, even though the material from which they are made is different; yet there is a certain kinship and affinity between them in the way they attract chaff. For both amber and jet, when warmed by friction, attract threads and straw, just as the magnet attracts iron, or the *sagda* <term>sagda: a legendary stone mentioned by ancient naturalists, said to attract wood</term> attracts wood. Furthermore, both of them burn when set on fire. But amber does not burn in water, although it burns to some extent in oil, because of the weakness of the resin from which it is made. Jet, however, because it is made of bitumen, burns all the more in water, and is even ignited by water because of the power of the bitumen, just as it is extinguished by oil. For amber, or electrum, is not bitumen, but only the "tears" <note>referring to the resinous sap</note> of poplar trees, or even pine trees, as you will hear shortly.

Moreover, the stone jet <note>original: *gagates*</note> is named after a place and a river called Gagas in Cilicia <note>a region in modern-day Turkey</note>. This stone is found at the river's mouth or its entrance to the sea near the city of Plagiopolis, as Dioscorides teaches in Book 5, Chapter 92. Or, as others maintain, it is named after Gangis, a city of Lycia (also called Gangitis), where this stone is found in large, green masses near the shores. Nicander, in his *Theriaca* <note>a poem on venomous creatures and antidotes</note>, calls it *Engangin* and *gangitin* after the Lycian city of Gangis; he teaches that the fumes of jet drive away serpents because of its smell of bitumen. For as I have said, its nature—because it is formed from bitumen—is to burn; it is ignited by water and extinguished by oil <note>This paradoxical property was a common belief in ancient mineralogy regarding certain bituminous substances</note>. Nicander says that even the force of a strong and consuming fire does not exhaust it. Hence Dioscorides also teaches that in the variety of jets, that which ignites quickly and gives off a smell of bitumen is to be preferred. Pliny, in Book 36, Chapter 29, likewise testifies that the stone jet takes its name from the place and river Gagas in Lycia, and that it is cast up by the sea and collected at Leucola.

# ALCHEMICAL LEXICON OF MARTIN RULAND

Galen (if I am not mistaken) says he does not know of that river in Lycia named Gagas. Yet it is possible that the name of the River Gagas has been exchanged for the name of another river into which it flows, as we often see happen. However, Strabo and other Cosmographers <note>Scholars who described the physical universe, combining geography and astronomy</note> agree with Dioscorides that such a river exists in Lycia. Therefore, we should not rely solely on Galen in this matter. What if the Gagas were a small river, and not well known to the common people, just as we see in our own lands? The Orla, the Schwarza, and the Tanger <note>original: *Pangera*; likely referring to the Tanger river in Germany</note> itself are most noble rivers; yet because they are small and have a short course, who knows them well except those who live nearby?

Furthermore, regarding the powers of jet <note>original: *gagates*</note>, consult Dioscorides and Pliny in the passages already cited. It puts serpents to flight with its scent. When burned as incense, it detects the "falling sickness" <note>original: *morbus fonticus*; an old term for epilepsy</note> and relieves the suffocation of the womb <note>original: *strangulationes vuluæ*; a condition historically associated with hysteria</note>. I speak from experience on this. For it has the power of softening and dispersing. In former times, jet stones were worn by matrons, and they would win favor for themselves with these little stones just as they did with corals. Even now, they are hung upon children in some places for the sake of ornament. Helmets, shields, and swords were also decorated with them.

I myself have seen a temple founded in a fortress at the mouth of the Tanger, decorated in marvelous ways with various gems by Emperor Charles IV, whose windows were fashioned from jet by a wonderful invention. I also saw in the same temple the dagger of Charles himself, whose hilt was fashioned from a single piece of jet stone with wonderful craftsmanship. Would that kings and princes now also cared for religion as that good Charles IV did.

But now, amber <note>original: *succinum*</note> is more commonly in use, as it has a more pleasant scent. Finally, jet has something in common with the eagle-stone <note>original: *aetites*; a stone believed to be found in eagles' nests with protective properties</note>, because both lose very little of their substance in fire. For this reason, the eagle-stone is also called *Gagitis*. But it is not jet, as we indicated at the beginning. Some also identify these as species of jet: namely, the jet that is similar in color to a lion’s hide. This is our common variety, the <term>Aagetstein</term> <note>A German term for agate or jet, used here to identify the local variety</note>. Second, the black variety with small white veins. Third, the black variety with saffron-colored veins; this is common in Crete.

Fourthly, a variegated kind found in India, appearing as if sprinkled with blood. Fifthly, a black kind similar to coral.

Jet <note>original: *Gagates*</note> stone is formed from naphtha, that is, petroleum. Likewise, another species of jet, which is the Thracian stone—**the black amber or jet** <note>original: *Der schwartze Bornstein / Agtstein*</note>—is formed from bitumen or black naphtha. Its varieties include stone-coals <note>original: *lithanthraces*; from the Greek for "stone-charcoal"</note> and fissile stone, **shale** <note>original: *der Schifer*</note>, as we have mentioned several times.

Amber <note>original: *succinum*</note>, however, is formed from the resin of the poplar tree, as Dioscorides maintains; it is distilled into the Eridanus <note>The ancient name for the River Po in Italy, though here associated with northern myths</note> and hardened by either its own heat or the heat of the water. Hence Ovid also says in the fable of the Heliades in the second book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> From there the tears flow, and distilled by the sun
> They harden from the new branches into amber <note>original: *electra*</note>, 
> Which the dark river receives and sends 
> To be worn by the brides of Rome.

For learned men call amber by other names: *electrum*, *glessum*, *chrysophoron*, and *chrysolectrum*. We Germans also have true amber, just as Tacitus writes of us. The Aesti <note>original: *Estin*</note>, **the Icelanders** <note>Ruland here identifies the ancient Baltic Aesti with the Icelanders</note>, still gather amber in the waves and on the shore. The Britons also gather it, so it is said. It is also gathered in parts of Prussia <note>original: *Borussiae*</note> **on the beach**, that is, on the shore; for this reason, there is an official called the Master of the Shore, **the Beach Master** <note>original: *der Strandmeister*</note>, who pays the amber-gatherers their wages, specifically in salt. 

Amber is indeed nothing other than the sap of trees, which, having fallen into the nearby sea, hardens and congeals; it can be lit like a torch, and it nourishes a flame with its oily fatness, which gives off a very pleasant scent. It is of two types: Amber or *Electrum*. The first is yellow and translucent, almost like glass. The ancients called this *glessum* because of the transparency of glass which it possesses. For Germans call those transparent vessels **glasses** <note>original: *Glässer*</note>. From this, the Glessinga and Glessaria islands, and the Glessarii people take their name, as Pliny also testifies in Book 37, Chapter 3, and Book 4, Chapter 16. The second type of *electrum* is dark and white, almost like bone, and is the most precious. The locals call it **bastard** <note>original: *Basthard*</note>. Truly, on that shore of Prussia and the neighboring regions, there are no poplars or al— <note>The text breaks off here</note>

...of the Prussians, but from fir trees and sea-pines, namely from a great abundance of resinous trees, which is where it likely comes from. That amber <note>original: *succinum*</note> is made from the resins of these trees is proven by its pine-like odor, both when it is rubbed and when it is set on fire. See Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, author of the *Natural History*</note>, in the cited book, and Solinus, chapter 23. Thus, amber is not only made from the alder or the poplar by the Eridanus <note>The ancient name for the River Po, often associated with the myth of Phaethon</note>, as Lucian also says in his work *On the Eridanus* that amber is not native there, but brought in from elsewhere. Therefore, everything the poets write is purely legendary. You should look at the explanation of Germany by Irenaeus, and also Tacitus.

Finally, that amber is a "tear" or resin of trees—especially the pine and sea-pine—is shown not only by its smell, color, and the substance itself when it is rubbed and burned, but also by this evidence: that it first dripped from trees as a liquid resin. We know this because we see trapped and visible through the amber flies, spiders, dust, ants, and other small creatures like gnats. These animals fell in by chance while the drop was dripping into the water, or while it was still hanging on the tree about to fall; thus they were joined with the mass and hardened, as witnessed by Tacitus and Pliny in the places mentioned.

Some, however—moved by I know not what reasons—wish amber to be the "prolific seed" <note>A historical theory that amber was the sperm of whales or large fish</note> of some fish or whale, found in the sea as a hard substance similar to a clod of earth, which then floats to the shore. Some want it to be brought from the Caspian Sea. Benedict of Verona <note>Benedetto Rini, a 16th-century physician</note>, in Book 13, Chapter 26 of his work on diseases, also describes amber as being mixed with white and black colors, light in weight, and having an unpleasant smell at the first sniff. This is unknown to me, unless it is a species of impure <term>Basthardus</term> <note>original: *Basthardi*; a term used by Ruland for an "impure" or hybrid variety of amber</note>.

In summary, there has been a great dispute among the learned until now—and there still is—as to what amber actually is. I say it is the resin of trees, and especially of the pine and sea-pine. Pliny also lists other types of amber <note>original: *electri*</note>: not only the white, which is our *Basthardus* of excellent scent; then the tawny, which is <term>glessum</term> <note>A Germanic word for amber used by Roman authors</note>; but also a type that is transparent with a soft glow, called <term>falernum</term> <note>named after Falernian wine due to its similar color</note> because it has the color of Falernian wine; and finally, a type in which the "lightness of honey" is pleasing. But these species are also found among our own ambers, if one considers <note>original: *confiderat*</note> them closely.

<summary>This page argues that amber is a fossilized tree resin rather than a mythical tear or whale seed, citing the presence of preserved insects (inclusions) and its pine-like scent as proof.</summary>

<keywords>amber, succinum, resin, pine, sea-pine, inclusions, Pliny, Tacitus, glessum, falernum, Basthardus, natural history</keywords>

# MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN #

...considers. However, as for the "electrum" <note>Electrum here refers to amber, though the term was also used for a gold-silver alloy.</note> that is said to be mined in Liguria, I simply believe it to be jet <note>original: *gagates*</note> derived from the bitumen of the earth, and not true amber. Or perhaps it is another gemstone, for there are many gems of similar colors, such as the topaz and the lynx-stone <note>original: *lapis lyncurinus*, a mythical stone thought to be formed from the urine of the lynx.</note>. In former times, matrons sought to win favor for themselves by wearing amber and jet; today, amber is even hung around the necks of children for similar reasons. Furthermore, this stone is effective against madness <note>original: *lymphatione*, a state of delirium or being "nymph-struck."</note> and serves as an amulet, as Pliny testifies. There is also no more immediate remedy for "suffocation of the womb" <note>original: *strangulatione vulvae*, a historical term for hysteria or respiratory distress believed to be caused by the movement of the uterus.</note> than burning amber and placing it beneath the nostrils. It is also beneficial for stomach ailments, sharpens the senses, and helps those suffering from the falling sickness <note>original: *comitialibus*, an old term for epilepsy.</note>. This argument carries great weight: all things that smell pleasant cheer the spirits; amber is pleasant-smelling (for it is of a most sweet and excellent odor); therefore, it cheers the spirits, and consequently benefits those with the falling sickness. For further information, consult Avicenna, Serapion, Paulus, Galen, and others concerning *Karabe* <note>The Arabic name for amber, meaning "that which attracts straw."</note>—that is, electrum or amber. Furthermore, when amber acquires the power of heat through friction, it attracts chaff, threads, and dry leaves to itself, just as jet does; much as a magnet pulls iron, and the *sagda* gem pulls wood. Concerning amber, see also Hesiod and Euripides. Apollonius, in the fourth book of his *Argonautica*, says the resin was born not from the tears of the Heliades <note>The daughters of the Sun who wept for their brother Phaethon.</note>, but from the tears of Apollo, shed when he was moved by grief for the death of Asclepius, or when he pastured the flocks of King Admetus. Consult also Solinus and Strabo regarding electrum, and the various opinions of authors in Pliny, Book 37, chapters 2 and 3.

Hardened stone: the species of which are stone-coals, and fissile stone, known as **Slate** <note>original: *Schifer*</note>.

# LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND #

**Amber** (Electrum). <note>original: *Succinum electrum*. Electrum here refers to amber, though the term was historically also used for a natural alloy of gold and silver.</note> The Germans improperly mix this with jet and call it **Amber / Burning-stone / Jet-stone**. <note>original: *Bornstein/Brennstein/Aagstein*. *Bornstein* is a variant of *Bernstein* (amber); *Brennstein* refers to its ability to burn; *Aagstein* usually refers to jet (*gagates*), illustrating the common historical confusion between the two substances.</note> It is in fact a gum or resin, or a hardened teardrop: 1. From the Poplar, according to Dioscorides, Ovid, and others—or from the Alder, though they treat the poplar and the alder as one and the same tree. 2. From the Pine. 3. From the Wild Pine. It is truly found in the Eridanus <note>The mythical name for the Po River in Italy.</note> (that is, the Po) and in the sea. It is yellow, honey-colored, transparent, white, or bone-colored; it is called by the Germans who collect it "Glass-amber" or **Bastard**. <note>original: *Glastum* (referring to a glass-like or blue-grey tint) and *Bastard* (denoting an impure or lower-grade variety).</note>

**Milk-stone** (Galactites). The stone is called Milk-stone because it exudes a milky juice; it is ash-colored and sweet to the taste, especially when placed in water. It is born in the earth in Saxony and increases there, as I have observed; however, I have not yet been able to "fish out" its German name. Concerning this, consult Dioscorides (in the cited location) and Pliny (Book 37, Chapter 20), who says that the *galaxias* or *galactites* is similar to the honey-apple <note>original: *epimeli*, likely referring to the color of a quince or medlar fruit.</note> but with red or white veins running through it. The Milk-stone, however, he says is of a single color like milk, and he also calls it **milk-bringer** <note>original: *leucogogeam*</note>, **white-marker** <note>original: *leucographiam*</note>, and **cloud-stone** <note>original: *synephiten*</note>. It is remarkable for its milky juice and flavor. When tied around the necks of nursing mothers, it is said to produce an abundance of milk; tied to infants, it is said to cause them to salivate <note>Used historically to aid teething.</note>. They also report that it melts in the mouth and takes away the memory. The Achelous River and the Nile send this stone. There are also those who call an Emerald bound with white veins a milk-stone. Regarding this, consult Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century philosopher and alchemist.</note>, who attributes I know not what magical powers to it; likewise Solinus in his *Polyhistor* (Chapter 13), who says it is a dark pebble that contains a white juice.

**Gala**, that is, milk.

**Galaxia**, **Star-coloring or Purification**. <note>original: *Sternenferbung oder Reinigung*. In an alchemical context, this may refer to a process of brightening or whitening a substance to a "star-like" luster.</note>

**Gallicus**, **North-North-East**. <note>original: *Nort Nort Ost*. This refers to the Gallic wind or a specific compass direction used in early modern orientation.</note>

**Gamathei** <note>Also known as *Gamaheu* or *Gamahez*; these were naturally patterned stones believed to hold supernatural signatures.</note> are stones upon which celestial powers and heavenly constellations are imprinted, marked with wondrous characters, images, and figures. Sometimes these are found fashioned by nature, dug out of mountains; at other times, according to...

# RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN #

Ripples of the waters: **A stone imprinted and formed with celestial figures.** <note>original: *Stein mit himmlischen Figuren imprimirt vnd verbildet*. This likely refers to stones with natural markings resembling stars or planets.</note>

Gangrene, the beginning of the mortification of an affected part. **Cold fire / Gangrene.** <note>original: *Kalt Brandt*. Historically, "cold fire" described gangrene because the limb lost its heat as it died.</note>

Gafar, that is, loam or slime. <gloss>Rotten flesh.</gloss> <note>original: *faul Fleisch*</note>

Gatrinum, that is, potash or salt of tartar. **Wood-ash.** <note>original: *WeydAsche*</note>

Treasure of smoke, that is, **Smelter’s soot.** <note>original: *Gaza fumi* / *HüttenRauch*. This refers to the metallic oxides, such as arsenic or zinc, that collect in the chimneys of smelting furnaces.</note>

Gebalum, that is, restoration. To coagulate is the same.

Gecharfun, *difdaha*, that is, a frog.

Gelion, leaf, *phyllon*, foliage, mane, **Leaf.** <note>original: *Gelion* (Hebrew), *phyllon* (Greek), *Blatt* (German).</note>

Geluta, that is, the Carline thistle. <note>original: *herba Carlina*</note>

The gem from a spider. Among us Germans, we have a domestic spider of immense size, which takes its name from a cross for some reason I do not know; thus we say, **a Cross-Spider.** <note>original: *ein Creutz-Spin*; the European Garden Spider (*Araneus diadematus*), identified by the white cross on its back.</note> Perhaps it is named from the shape of its web, or from the transverse colors of its body; it is considered a sin to harm such spiders. For they are said to draw all poisons out of houses, and in times of plague they are rarely or never seen. In the heads of these, they say a gem is found that is most effective against all poisons and enchantments. Truly, I have never seen it, nor have I dared to seek it by dissecting a spider. Nor is it strange that such a gem should have such power, since we see that the webs themselves of spiders are of great importance for many things. <note>In folk medicine, spider webs were often used to staunch bleeding.</note>

Tartaric gem, a general stone made from transparent tartar, **a type of stone.** <note>original: *ein Geschlecht deß Steins*. Tartar is the potassium bitartrate that deposits in wine barrels; in alchemy, it was a "stone" of the vegetable kingdom.</note>

Beryllian Gem. 1. Beryl, **a beryl.**
2. Chrysoberyl, **A yellowish beryl.**
3. Chrysoprase, **A green beryl.**

Prase Gem. A stone similar in color to a leek, **a Prase.** <note>original: *Ein Praß*. From the Greek *prason*, meaning leek.</note>

Opal Gem or *paederos*, **an Opal.** <note>original: *Ein Wesse*. *Paederos* is a classical name for opal meaning "lovely child" or "the bloom of youth."</note>

Ceraunian Gems (Thunder-stones). 1. Long Ceraunias, **a long and smooth Toad-stone.** <note>original: *Krottenstein*. *Cerauniae* were believed to be stones that fell from the sky during lightning strikes—often these were actually prehistoric stone tools or fossilized shark teeth.</note>

-> ### MART[IN RULAND'S] LEXICON OF ALCHEMY ### <-

2. Round, **A Round One.** <note>This likely refers to a classification of the shape of a specific mineral or "Gemma" mentioned on the previous page.</note>

**Iris Gem:** 1. The Iris is a six-sided, white stone, which when it receives the sun’s rays, casts a bow similar to the celestial one onto a wall. <gloss>**A stone that gives off a glow in the sun like a rainbow.**</gloss> <note>This describes clear quartz or rock crystal acting as a prism.</note>

2. Counterfeit Irises are those which imitate the true one. A polished and white <term>Brontia</term> <note>literally "thunder-stone," often a fossilized echinoid or a type of flint</note> does this. Likewise, translucent yellow <term>fluors</term> <note>fluorspar or fluorite</note>, such as I saw in the collection of our friend Fabricius. <note>Likely Georg Fabricius (1516–1571), a German humanist and physician known for his mineralogical interests.</note>

**Gems of the Toads.** The Phrynus, toad, or "rubeta"—**an earthy toad or "Pahte," as the Saxons call it**—a creature so foul, dwelling in caves, is not without its gems. For there is a species of this in France and Spain which is horned, with yellow and livid black spots, named *borax* <note>original: *borax*. In this medieval context, borax refers not to the chemical salt, but to the legendary "toadstone" supposedly found in the heads of toads.</note>, and it bears gems of the same name in its head: <gloss>**a toad-stone; its color is sometimes a darkish white**</gloss>; just as I saw such a thing in the possession of a certain nobleman. Sometimes it even has a blue eye in the middle, if it is extracted from a living *borax* while it is still palpitating. Sometimes it is black with livid black marks, as our toads are, and I once possessed such a one. In shape it was round, about the size of an average bean. Sometimes green, and sometimes multi-colored toadstones are also found. Commonly, people call such stones <term>crapodines</term>. Sometimes the form of a toad with outstretched legs appears within these stones. These are worn in rings by princes. For where poisons are present, such a stone, if nearby, changes color and emits drops as if sweating. And strangely, I have seen that these toadstones are sought after by our own toads, such that they strive to seize them with a leap; they also gather around the stone when it is placed on the ground. However, whether these toadstones are formed or born from the brain of the toad—as are <term>draconites</term> <note>legendary stones from the heads of dragons</note> or <term>echites</term> <note>viper-stones</note>—I leave to your judgment. Others claim that toadstones are born from the viscosity of foam, which the toads, gathered together in spring, blow onto the head of a singular, superior one, as if he were the King of the Toads. Our own toads are also said to "blow" such stones. Furthermore, regarding the <term>apocymi</term>—<gloss>**concerning the spikes in the toads**</gloss>—see Pliny. <note>Refers to Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*, Book 32, regarding substances derived from aquatic and amphibious animals.</note>

<page-num>243</page-num>

-> ### [THE WRITINGS] OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN ### <-

Pliny states: "Now also, let toads be hung in the air so that they may dry out; as a most immediate remedy, they stop all flow of blood." <note>Pliny the Elder was a Roman naturalist whose *Natural History* was a primary source for medieval and Renaissance science.</note>

<term>Genula</term> A deformity arising from the transplanting of parsnips. <gloss>A malformation of the parsnip that occurs when it is moved or replanted often.</gloss>

<term>Geographia</term> Geography. The art of investigating the earth; a description of the world.

<term>Geomantia</term> Geomancy. This is a very well-known art and science of the lands. But in this context, it is said to be when the stars of the earth reveal themselves to men, so that they may take from them a prophecy or omen which attains its effect. It is also called the "Astronomy of the Earth," which operates in two ways: either through astronomical calculations or through "points." <gloss>The art of measuring the earth through points.</gloss> <note>Geomancy was a method of divination that interpreted markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil or rocks.</note>

<term>Geometria</term> Geometry. Limitation, measuring with a ten-foot rod, or land-surveying. <gloss>The art of measuring, land-measure, or plot-measuring.</gloss>

<term>Gersa</term> That is, ceruse <note>original: *cerusa*. This refers to white lead, a pigment and cosmetic substance often used in alchemy.</note>.

<term>Gerhulle</term> A species of stone.

<term>Gesor</term> That is, galbanum <note>A bitter, aromatic gum resin used in incense and medicine.</note>.

<term>Gi</term> That is, earth. <gloss>That which painters use is the substance that attaches itself like a crust or lump in glass-furnaces, chimneys, or glass-works.</gloss>

<term>Gibum</term> That is, cheese.

<term>Gibar</term> That is, metallic medicine. <gloss>A type of medicine prepared from metals.</gloss>

<term>Gich, Gepsin</term> That is, gypsum.

<term>Gigantes</term> Giants. These are people elevated or tall beyond the measure of the "vessel" <note>likely referring to the human body as a vessel for the soul</note>, beyond the nature of man or the laws of nature.

<term>Gilla, grillus</term> This is vitriol <note>A sulfate of a metal; in alchemy, "Gilla" often specifically refers to a vomitive made from white vitriol or zinc sulfate</note> which has spontaneously dissolved into water; some think such a liquid is provided by nature. There are those who call the water of sal ammoniac by this name. It purges the stomach. <gloss>Vitriol that cleanses the stomach.</gloss>

<term>Gilvus, helvus</term> A color midway between white and red: honey-colored, tawny, reddish-yellow, or lemon-colored. <gloss>Citrine-colored, fallow, pale red, ball-colored, yellowish, or lemon-colored.</gloss>

# MARTIN RULAND'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY #

<term>Gipsum</term> Gypsum. That is, Armenian Earth or Plaster-lime <note>original: *Armenisch Erdtrich / Sparkalck*. Armenian earth was a silicate of aluminum often used as a base for pigments or in medicinal plasters.</note>.

<term>Gir, Gith</term> That is, quicklime <note>original: *calx viva*. Calcium oxide, a caustic substance produced by heating limestone.</note>.

<term>Girgies</term> These are white river stones, or little white creek-pebbles <note>original: *albi lapides fluminis, Weiß Bachkiſſelein*.</note>.

<term>Girmer</term> That is, tartar <note>original: *tartarum*. The potassium bitartrate crust found in wine vats, frequently used as a flux in alchemical processes.</note>.

<term>Gilisim</term> That is, gum.

<term>Girenon</term> That is, common bond, or common glue <note>original: *fatum commune, gemein Leim*.</note>.

<term>Glacies dura</term> Hard ice; that is, crystal <note>Ancient and medieval scholars often believed that rock crystal/quartz was water that had been frozen so intensely it could never melt.</note>.

<term>Glacialis</term> This is the "Icy Art," by which blades and swords are forged according to the course of the stars in the firmament—weapons which even anvils cannot resist; for this reason, the art is also called **Incusina** <note>original: *Incuſina*, derived from the Latin *incus*, meaning anvil.</note>.

<term>Glassa</term> A type of varnish, or dry varnish <note>original: *trockener Birniß*.</note>.

<term>Glisomargo</term> That is, bright white chalk <note>original: *creta candida, Schöne weiſſe Kreide*. It is a chalk used for lead pipes, mixed with a fatty hearth-clay.</note>.

**Glimmer or Cat-silver.** <note>original: *Glimmer oder Katzensilber*. This refers to the mineral Mica.</note> It indeed possesses the color of silver, but it is not silver. It is called "cat-silver" perhaps by similarity, because the eyes of cats shine at night in such a manner; or perhaps because it is something hollow and useless—for it yields no profit but is consumed by fire. Yet, if you consider it closely, it is not consumed at all, but merely purified (as I have observed several times), although it is a matter of little consequence. It assumes another color and is undoubtedly a species of amianth <note>original: *amianthi*, a form of asbestos known for its resistance to fire.</note>. Nature is accustomed to delighting herself with these colors in the innermost parts of the earth. Furthermore, regarding **chrysocalla** <note>original: *chryſocolla*, "gold-glue" or Malachite/borax</note>, see Serapion in his *Book of Aggregations*, chapter *Tincar*, who says that native chrysocalla is found on the shores of the sea and is of the species of salt, hot and dry in the fourth degree. Moreover, for its use in medicines and how it ought to be washed, see the same chapter in Dioscorides. Chrysocalla is also poisonous if taken in more than the proper dose.

<term>Glomer</term> That is, round.

<term>Gluten</term> That is, ox gall <note>original: *fel tauri, Ochſen Gall*. Used as a wetting agent in pigments and sometimes in alchemical preparations.</note>.

<term>Gluten</term> That which holds things together: glue or blood.

<term>Gluten, limonia, sinovia</term> Synovia is the noblest part of the body, subtle, and pure... <note>Ruland is beginning a definition for the lubricating fluid of the joints, comparing it to "glue" or "lemon-colored" fluid.</note>

->RVLANDI PHIL. ET MEDICI.<-

...pure, white, transparent, a dissolved sweet salt, and a natural moisture or liquid found in all the joints of the limbs, resembling the white of eggs. If <term>tartar</term> <note>original: *tartarus*. In Paracelsian medicine, tartar refers to stony or crystalline deposits in the body, such as kidney stones or the uric acid crystals of gout, named after the crust found in wine vats.</note> is generated in this transparent matter due to the dissolved salt it contains—which sometimes coagulates—the result is <term>gout</term> <note>original: *podagra*.</note>. **The tenacity of gluten** is a mineral resin, much like the resin of the turpentine tree. *A mineral resin.* <note>original: *ein Mineral Harz*.</note>

**Gluten** has the power and effectiveness of a tenacious pitch. *A sticky, resinous property.* <note>original: *eine zähe Harz Eigenschafft*.</note>

**Gnießt**, a species of stone.

**Gnomes** <note>original: *Gnomi*.</note> are said to be little men or corporeal spirits living beneath the earth; otherwise called pygmies, scarcely a cubit <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> in height. *Mountain-manikins.* <note>original: *Bergmännlein*.</note>
