**Gofel**, that is, a horned animal.

**Gradation** <note>original: *Gradatio*.</note> is the exaltation of metals in the degree of their properties, by which weight, color, and permanence <note>original: *constantia*.</note> are brought to an excellent degree. It does not have the power to transform the substance itself <note>meaning it is not a total transmutation of one metal into another</note>, but only raises its qualities or quantities in degree, or brings them from a hidden state into the manifest, without changing the original species. For instance, if nature has provided white gold, gradation makes it red; if it is volatile, gradation fixes it; if it is impure, gradation purifies it, and so on.

**Greek Magic** <note>original: *Græca magia*.</note> is a superstitious art invented, or at least practiced, by the Greeks. It deals with empty visions and was used to make things appear which did not truly exist. Through this, they sought to gain a great reputation for wisdom among the ignorant masses, though it was nothing more than a trick of the eyesight through clouding <note>original: *obfuscationem*.</note>, originating in the imaginations of men. Their belief was joined with a faithless effort to craft every kind of lie into a semblance of reality.

### MARTIN RULAND'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY

**Garnet** <note>original: *Granatus*, German: *ein Granätlin*.</note>. It perhaps takes its name from the pomegranate <note>original: *pomum granatum*</note>. It is undoubtedly a species of <term>carbuncle</term> <note>In historical mineralogy, "carbuncle" was a general term for any deep-red gemstone, usually garnets or rubies, thought to glow like a hot coal.</note>. It is a red, transparent gem, similar to wild pomegranate flowers <note>original: *balaustiis*</note>, of a rosy color, though darker than a carbuncle. Another species of it has a color scattered with the violet-red of the violet. For this reason, it is called a "violet garnet" or "violaceous." It is very similar to the amethyst-colored carbuncle. Its native land is Ethiopia and the sands of the sea. The garnet gladdens the heart and drives away sadness.

Men say that the female of this stone is the <term>Paeanitide</term> gem <note>original: *pæaniten*</note>, which is otherwise called the "Garnet of Michedon." They claim that at a certain time, it conceives and gives birth to a stone similar to itself, and that it is wonderfully beneficial for pregnant women. Pliny, in Book 37, Chapter 10, and Solinus, in Chapter 15, call it not *paeaniten*, but *paeantidem*. This *paeantides* is the gem that our people call the "consort-stone" <note>original German: *ein Gemahū*, likely *Gemahl* or spouse</note>. Pliny says it is also called *gemonides*. He testifies that it becomes pregnant and gives birth, and that it heals those conceiving and those in labor. It is found in Macedonia near the monument of Tiresias <note>The famous blind prophet of Greek mythology.</note>. It is a species of gem originating from frozen water, because it is also white.

**Green Grain** <note>original: *Granum viride*</note> is the fruit of the turpentine tree <note>original German: *Von Lerchbäumen Frucht*, fruit of the larch trees.</note>.

**Indigo Grain** <note>original: *Granum nil*</note> is the seed of Indigo, with which fabrics are dyed.

**Granulation** is the reduction of a substance into small grains. Melting <note>original: *fusio*</note> serves this process. It is a procedure specific to metals and is accomplished in various ways. Molten metals are poured into water, and by the force of the impact, they are scattered and break apart. They should be melted in a crucible or an iron ladle. Sometimes brushes made of thin twigs are placed in the water so that the metal scatters even better. In place of brushes, a board, a sieve with very narrow holes, or a crate may be used.

**To Granulate** <note>original German: *Granuliren*, *Körnen*</note>.

**Grassa**, that is, tincal or <term>borax</term> <note>Tincal is the historical name for crude, unrefined borax imported from Tibet.</note>.

**Gratiola** <note>Commonly known as Hedge-hyssop.</note> is a well-known herb. It was formerly brought to us at a high price; later, it was found around Nuremberg. It grows in great abundance in the territory of Strasbourg, very near the city.

<page-num>248</page-num>

->### LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MART. RULAND ###<-

Indeed, it does not ignite once it has been extinguished. Its nature is to bind and to obstruct; if swallowed, it causes suffocation. Consult Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD), author of "De Materia Medica."</note>, Book 5, Chapter 81, and Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist (23–79 AD), author of "Natural History."</note>, Book 36, Chapter 24, although in former times it was used to season wine. Its use is only for external application because of its excessive drying power and its tendency to cause suffocation.

There are truly two types of gypsum. One is fossilized and natural <note>original Latin: *fossile & natiuum*</note>, and it is dug out of the earth, though usually found near the very surface of the ground. It is a substance almost similar to nitre <note>Saltpeter</note>, occurring sometimes in wide veins. It was known to Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, known for his work on stones.</note> and Pliny, who followed Theophrastus’s description. It retains its name among us and is called **Gypsum** <note>original German: *Gyps*</note>. It is found in several places, and even near the Elbe <note>original Latin: *Albis*</note>. For when the Elbe overflows, it carries with it gypsum and specular stone <note>original Latin: *lapidem specularem*; a transparent, reflective mineral like mica or selenite</note>.

The second type of gypsum is artificial <note>original Latin: *factitium*</note>, and it is made or "cooked" (to use the word of Pliny) from a white stone similar to alabaster. Veins of this stone are found in the rocks of Jena, and near the Hercynian Forest <note>The Harz mountain range in Germany</note>; likewise at the mines in Saalfeld, and in Saxony by the rivers themselves. It seems to me that this stone is like the hardened marrow of the rock, **Stone-marrow** <note>original German: **Steinmarck**; likely referring to lithomarge or a similar soft clay mineral</note>; or it seems to be a species of <term>Aphronitrum</term> <note>Literally "froth of nitre," a salt-like efflorescence found on walls or rocks</note>, or true gypsum, or <term>Calamine stone</term> <note>Zinc ore, essential for making brass</note>. For this reason, certain Saxons also call this stone **Our Lady’s Ice** <note>original German: **Vnser lieben Frawen Eyß**</note>, although that name properly belongs to Calamine stone.

Secondly, artificial gypsum is produced from that cleavable specular stone which is called by the Germans **Spar-glass** <note>original German: **Sperglaß**</note>, **Mary’s Ice** <note>original Latin: *glacies Mariæ*</note>, or **Our Lady’s Ice** <note>original German: **Vnser lieben Frawen Eyß**</note>, because it resembles the form of ice. And this is the best gypsum, as Pliny testifies in Book 36, Chapter 24. Regarding specular stone, more will be said below under the entries for Arabian Stone and Selenite. Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century German Dominican friar and polymath who wrote extensively on alchemy and minerals.</note> considers the extremity of natural gypsum to be specular stone. For the rest, consult Pliny in the chapters already cited, as well as Book 35, Chapters 12 and 17, and also Serapion <note>An influential Arabic medical writer, likely Ibn Sarabi</note> in his *Book of Aggregation*, the chapter on Gypsum or *Iigetin*. There is also a very white, solid, Cyprian gypsum from which various cups and vessels are made to hold fragrances, called **White Gypsum from Cyprus** <note>original German: **Weiß Gyps auß Cypern**</note>.

## H

**Hadid** <term>Hadid: A term derived from Arabic</term>, that is, iron.

**Hematite**, called *Sedeneg* in Arabic, and *Blutstein* <note>original German: *Blutstein*, literally "blood-stone"</note> by the Germans because of its blood-red color with which it stains. It is particularly observed in its natural state within mines, and is also valued for its effect in stopping blood in any kind of hemorrhage. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist</note> identifies various species of it. Indeed, hematite differs according to the region of its birth: in Libya, Egypt, and Spain; in the lands of the Cherusci <note>An ancient Germanic tribe; here referring to the Harz region of Germany</note> near Nordhausen; likewise at Hasserode, and at Goslar in Saxony; in the Sudetes mountains at Annaberg and Geyer; and near the Saale river at Saalfeld, Saalburg, and Jena. Hematite is also distinguished by its softness or hardness. These, then, are the species known to me:

**Hematite** 1. The earth-dug variety <term>fossilis: Ruland uses this in the classical sense of "anything dug from the earth," not necessarily petrified remains</term>, which is celebrated by Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note> in Book 5, Chapter 90, and whose homeland is Egypt. It is black with a deep, saturated color, hard, brittle, uniform in its makeup, with no impurities mixed in and no bands or zones running through it. This first species is found among our native earth-dug hematites, but it is very rare; I have barely seen one or two, and it is generally unknown to most people.

2. A black variety found at Goslar which yields a saffron-yellow juice <note>This refers to the "streak" or powder color of the mineral</note>. It is extremely hard and unknown even to the apothecary shops. It is also found, though rarely, near the Hercynian Forest <note>The ancient name for the forested mountains of central and southern Germany</note> in the land of the Cherusci. This is, without a doubt, the black gem or "Median Stone" of Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century philosopher and alchemist</note>, which yields a saffron juice when ground. There is another species of it which is green. It is called "Median" because it is brought from the region of the Medes, and is found near the Phasis river <note>A river in the ancient region of Colchis, modern-day Georgia</note>.

3. An earth-dug variety in Hesse, found in many places, which is purple and fissile <term>fissile: easily split into thin layers, like slate</term> or slaty.

4. A very beautiful earth-dug variety is born in Geyer, Annaberg, and Saalfeld. Goldsmiths praise this because it is very hard against the whetstone and is used for polishing gems. It is black and somewhat top-shaped <note>original: *turbinatus*, referring to a conical or whorled structure</note>.

<meta>catchword: 5. Earth-dug [Fossilis]</meta>

5. This earth-dug variety is found in the same places; it is black and yields three colors when rubbed upon a whetstone. It may be called **Trichrus** <note>original Greek: *trichros*, meaning "three-colored"</note>. This three-colored stone of ours is also cone-shaped and hard.

It is found in the lands of the Cherusci <note>an ancient Germanic tribe inhabiting the Harz region</note>, at Nordhausen, and at Hasserode, in certain mountains; it provides the exact appearance of an exposed brain, and is by far the most beautiful. According to Sotacus <note>a Greek writer on stones cited by Pliny</note>, there are five kinds of it, besides the magnet.

<margin>The Hematites of Pliny.</margin>

1. **Ethiopian**, which is most useful for the eyes, being among those they call *panchrestas* <term>panchrestas: from the Greek for "all-healing" or "useful for everything"</term>. Our hematite found at Geyer <note>a town in the Ore Mountains of Saxony</note> corresponds closely to this, being very hard upon the whetstone and three-colored.

### H

**Hadid**, that is, iron. <note>original: *Hadid, id est, ferrum*. Hadid is the Arabic word for iron.</note>

**Hematite**, called *Sedeneg* in Arabic, and **Blutstein** in German <note>meaning "Bloodstone"</note>. It is so named because of its blood-like color with which it stains, and also because it is primarily observed as a mineral found in mines. It is further named for the effect it has in stopping blood in every kind of "bloody flux" <note>any excessive discharge of blood, such as a nosebleed or heavy menstruation</note>. Pliny describes several species of it. Indeed, hematite varies according to its place of origin: in Libya, Egypt, and Spain; in the lands of the Cherusci <note>an ancient Germanic tribe inhabiting the Harz region</note> at Nordhausen; likewise at Hasserode, and at Goslar in Saxony; in the mountains of the Sudetes at Annaberg and Gera; and along the Saale river at Saalfeld, Saalburg, and Jena. Hematite is also distinguished by its softness or hardness. These, therefore, are the species known to me:

**Hematite.** 1. The earth-dug variety, which is celebrated by Dioscorides <note>a 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note> in Book 5, Chapter 90, and whose homeland is Egypt. It is black, with a deep, saturated color, hard, brittle, uniform in its nature, with no impurities mixed in, and no patterns of bands or zones. This first species is found among our local minerals, but it is extremely rare; I have scarcely seen one or two, and otherwise it is generally unknown to the public.

2. A black variety is found at Goslar, which yields a saffron-yellow juice <note>The "juice" refers to the streak: the color of the powder produced when a mineral is rubbed across a surface</note>. It is extremely hard and unknown even in the apothecary shops. This type is also found, though rarely, in the Harz Forest in the lands of the Cherusci. It is, without a doubt, the black "Median Stone" of Albertus <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and alchemist</note>, which yields a saffron juice when crushed. There is another species of it that is green. It is called "Median" because it is brought from the region of the Medes and is found near the Phasis River <note>a river in ancient Colchis, modern-day Georgia</note>.

3. An earth-dug variety found in many places in Hesse, which is purple and fissile or "scissile" <note>meaning it can be easily split or layered</note>.

4. A most beautiful earth-dug variety occurs in Gera and Annaberg, and at Saalfeld. Goldsmiths praise this kind because it is very hard against the whetstone and is used for polishing gemstones. It is black and somewhat cone-shaped.

## H

**Hadid**, that is, iron <note>original: *ferrum*; *Hadid* is the Arabic word for iron</note>.

**Hematite**, called **Sedeneg** in Arabic, and by the Germans **Bloodstone** <note>German: *Blutstein*</note>; so named because of its blood-red color, with which it stains, and it is primarily observed as a mineral found in mines. It is also named for the effect it has in stopping blood in every kind of flux. Pliny describes several species of it. For hematite varies according to the regions where it originates: in Libya, Egypt, and Spain, and among the Cherusci <note>an ancient Germanic people of the Harz region</note> at Nordhausen; likewise at Hasserode, in Saxon Goslar, in the Jewish mountains <note>original: *Iudėtis montibus*; likely referring to the Jüdenberge near mining centers</note>, Annaberg and Geyer, at the Saale, Saalfeld, Saalburg, and Jena. Hematite is also distinct if you consider its softness or hardness. Therefore, these are the species known to me:

1. **The dug variety**, which is celebrated by Dioscorides in Book 5, Chapter 90, whose homeland is Egypt. It is black, deep in color, hard, brittle, uniform in its nature, with no impurities mixed in and no wandering bands or zones. This first species is found among our local dug hematites, but very rarely; I have scarcely seen one or two, and it is otherwise completely unknown to the common people.

2. **A black variety** found at Goslar, yielding a saffron-yellow juice <note>The "juice" refers to the mineral's streak—the color of the powder produced when it is rubbed on a hard surface</note>: it is very hard and unknown even to the apothecary shops. It is also found, though rarely, in the Hercynian Forest among the Cherusci. Without a doubt, this is the gem or "Median stone" of Albertus <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus and the *Lapis Medus*, a stone said to come from the land of the Medes</note>, which is black and ground to yield a saffron-yellow juice. Another species of it is green. It is called *Medus* because it is brought from the region of the Medes, and is found near the Phasis River.

3. **The dug variety in Hesse**, found in many places, which is a purple stone that is fissile or easily split.

4. **A most beautiful dug variety** born in Geyer and Annaberg, and at Saalfeld. Goldsmiths praise this because it is very hard against a whetstone and is used for polishing gemstones. It is black and somewhat top-shaped.

**Halcyonium.** To learn which birds are the halcyons beloved by Tethys <note>a sea goddess</note>, what their species are, when they breed, the method of preparing their nest, and what its shape is, see Pliny, Book 10, Chapter 32; Book 2, Chapter 49; and Book 18, Chapter 26; and also that most delightful fable in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* Book 11, and others who have written on such matters. <header>### THE PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN RULAND</header>

...of the sea, which we discussed above, although there is a certain relationship between them. For that "salt-foam" is the down or scrapings of the foaming sea coagulated upon the rocks. But this **Halcyonium** <note>original: *halcyoniū*</note> is the hardened sea-foam, brittle and spongy. It is called halcyonium because kingfisher birds <note>original: *halcyones aues*</note> build their nests hanging over the ocean—as the Poet says—from this spongy and hardened stone-like material, or near this hardened foam. Dioscorides <note>a famous Greek physician and botanist</note>, in Book 5, Chapter 83, lists five kinds of halcyonium; today scarcely one or two are kept, namely:

The **first halcyonium** is thick with a harsh taste, a spongy appearance, and a foul odor, smelling like fish—*it stinks severely* <note>original: *es stincket sehr*</note>. This is found on the shores of the sea and even by the Havel River <note>in Germany</note>, where there are kingfishers—which are called by the locals, though improperly, "Little Water-hens" <note>original: *Wasserhünlein*</note> and in another way properly, "Ice-birds" <note>original: *Eißvogel*</note>, because they nest and hatch their chicks in the icy winter. However, another bird is also called by that name, specifically the common kingfisher <note>original: *ispida*</note>.

The **second kind** of halcyonium is similar to the membranes of the eyes or a sponge; it is full of holes, light, and carries the scent of seaweed <note>original: *algæ*</note>. These first two kinds are used in women’s soaps and cleansers <note>original: *smegmata*</note>. *Hence Ovid says in his "Cosmetics for the Face":*

> *Medicines added from the querulous bird's nest,*
> *Drive spots from the face; they are called 'halcyonea.'*
> <note>original: *Addita de querulo volucrum medicamina nido, / Ore fugant maculas: halcyonea vocant.*</note>

The **third kind** is similar in form to a little worm and leans more toward purple; they call it "Milesian" <note>named after the city of Miletus</note>. It is a diuretic <note>promotes the production of urine</note>.

The **fourth kind** is not unlike unwashed fleeces <note>original: *succidis vellerib.*</note>; it is full of many gaps and is light.

The **fifth kind** exists in the shape of a mushroom, is odorless, and rough; it grows in the Propontis <note>the Sea of Marmara</note> near the island of Besbicon. In the local tongue, because it is salty and rough, they call it "sea-froth" <note>original: *halosachnem*</note>. It is suitable for whitening teeth. This is also used for cleansers <note>original: *smegmata*</note> and hair-removers <note>original: *psilothra*</note>.

For the rest, as to how halcyonia should be burned and washed, see Dioscorides in the cited book and Bulkasim <note>Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, a renowned medieval surgeon and chemist</note>. Pliny, in Book 32, Chapter 5, says that halcyonium is made from the actual nests of kingfishers.

**Heliotropium**, a **gemstone** that grows in Ethiopia, Africa, and Cyprus...

...[it is] of a leek-green color <note>original: *pracei coloris*</note>, similar to an emerald, yet it is marked with blood-red droplets.

**Heliotrope** <note>the stone today called Bloodstone</note> is so named because when it is cast into a vessel of water, it changes the brightness of the Sun into a blood-red reflection when struck by it, especially the Ethiopian variety. This same stone, when placed near water like a mirror, catches the Sun and detects eclipses by showing the Moon passing beneath it. The impudence of the Magi <note>referring to ancient Persian sorcerers or practitioners of magic</note> claims that the heliotrope stone, when anointed with the juice of the herb of the same name, prevents the wearer from being seen <note>renders them invisible</note>. They also claim it makes men wealthy and of good reputation, and is effective against poisons and the flow of blood. See Pliny, Book 37, chapter 10, and Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus</note> in his *Book of Stones*.

**Helnesed**, that is, **Coral**.

**Helunhai**, that is, the **ring of Solomon** in the art of Necromancy <note>black magic or spirit summoning</note>.

**Hemicyclium**, **A small sun-dial board** <note>original: *Sonlegebrättlein*</note>.

**Hesmic**, the **fourth part of a pound**.

**Hidus**, that is, **flower of copper** <note>a fine oxide formed by heating copper</note>.

**Hinnicula**, **genicula**, **gumicula**, **Valerian**. I believe this variation in names arises from the error of scribes.

**Hilsinat**, that is, **froth of silver** <note>litharge or lead oxide</note>.

**Hispanicum viride**, that is, **Seville green**, which is **verdigris** <note>the green pigment formed on copper</note>.

**Homo funem in brachium vel pectus inuoluens**, **A sack-puller** <note>original: *Sackzieher*; a laborer or porter who winds a rope around his arm or chest to haul loads</note>.

**Homunculi**, small images or little figures made in the likeness of man, which contain within themselves the invisible sidereal man <note>the "star-man" or astral body</note>; **Small humans or images made after humans, which have the invisible man of the stars within them**.

**Holsebon**, **helfaton**, **helsebon**, that is, **common salt, prepared**.

**Horizon**, the **mercury of gold**, **The mercury extracted from gold**.

**Hunc**, that is, **Jupiter**, **tin**, or *hucci*.

**Humor vitæ**, the **moisture of life** which sustains all living things so they do not dry up; the fuel and nourishment of the natural heat, otherwise known as the radical moisture: **That which keeps a living thing from withering and sustains it.**

<header>### MART[IN RULAND]’S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY</header>

**Receptacle of moisture**, a gutter or drain <note>original: *Azucht*, a term often referring to a conduit in a smelting-house or mine</note>.

**Hyarith**, that is, **Silver** <note>original: *Luna*</note>.

**Hyacinth** <note>a gemstone, often identifying varieties of zircon or garnet in antiquity</note>, a **Hyacinth**. It is a gemstone differing from the amethyst because the violet brightness gleaming in the amethyst is diluted in the hyacinth; it is pleasing at first sight, but it fades before it can satisfy the eye, wilting more quickly than the flower of its own name: as Pliny says in Book 37, chapter 9, and Solinus in chapter 33. Ethiopia, India, and Arabia produce hyacinths and chrysolites. The Arabs distinguish three species of it: namely, those of a red color, a citron-yellow color, and an antimony <note>a dark, metallic grey</note> color. Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus</note> distinguishes two kinds: namely, the aquatic, which turns white within the yellow or watery within the red. Then there is the sapphirine, which is very translucent and yellow. Hence we speak of the sapphirine hyacinth, which originates in Ethiopia. The power of the hyacinth is to induce sleep, to be effective against poisons, to gladden a person, and to strengthen the heart. The rest of its properties, which seem to me more than magical, I shall omit. Furthermore, the ancient astrologers dedicated the hyacinth to Jupiter.

1. **Hyacinth** which grows reddish in gold, a **burning Hyacinth**.
2. Of a **golden color**.
3. Inclining toward the color of amber <note>original: *electrum*</note>, a **pale Hyacinth**.
4. Rough or scaly, an **unclean Hyacinth**.
5. Counterfeit and artificial, made by applying a dye, a **false Hyacinth**.

**Hydropiper**, smartweed <note>original: *persicaria*</note> marked with red spots, **Red Water-pepper**.
The kind of smartweed without spots we call **Peach-wort** <note>original: *Pföhenkraut*</note>.

**Hydromancy** is an art derived from the stars of the water, occurring when they reveal themselves to men through unusual floods, fluctuations, and other appearances.

**Hydrophorbia**, a **water-gall** <note>original: *Wassergall*; likely referring to a marsh plant or a bubble/blister in the water</note>.

**Hypoglossum**, also known as *hippoglossum*, *epiglossum*, *epiphyllocarpon*, *uvularia*, *bonifacia*, *lingua pagana*, or *bis lingua*. **Outer-leaf**, **Uvula-wort**, **Grove-leaf**, **Bear-leaf**, **Tongue-leaf**, **Cabbage-wort**, or **Tapens-wort** <note>This refers to the plant *Ruscus hypoglossum*, known as Horse-tongue or Double-tongue, traditionally used for ailments of the throat and uvula</note>.

# I

**Iacens**, or the foundation of a mountain, the horizontal layer of the mountain <note>original: *Daß liegend deß Bergs*</note>.

**Iassa**, that is, the herb of the Trinity, the Jesus-flower or the Pansy <note>original: *Iesublümtlein / Dreyfaltigkeitsblümtlein*; referring to the *Viola tricolor*, often associated with the Holy Trinity due to its three colors</note>.

**Jasper**, **hematite**, **Bloodstone** <note>original: *Blutstein*</note>. There is another of a green color. 
**Jasper**, called a *Jasper* <note>original: *ein Iasp*</note> by the Germans, is a stone or gem of many species. For Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> enumerates seven species of it, namely: First, there is a green Jasper similar to an **Emerald** <note>original: *Smaragdus*</note>. Second, there is a Jasper similar to crystal, imitating the color of phlegm <note>original: *pituita*; a pale, watery discharge</note>. Third is a Jasper not unlike copper <note>original: *aerizusa*, meaning "sky-colored" or "copper-like"</note>. Fourth is a Jasper that appears as if stained by smoke, which is called **smoky** <note>original: *capnias*</note>. Fifth is a Jasper girded with white and shining lines, called **Assyrian** <note>original: *assyrios*</note>. Sixth is a Jasper similar to turpentine resin, which is called **turpentine-like** <note>original: *terebinthizusa*</note>. Seventh is a Jasper that rivals the **Callais** gem <note>a turquoise-like stone</note>, about which we spoke above in chapter 48. According to Dioscorides, all of these are used as amulets, and when bound to the thighs, they accelerate childbirth. Pliny, in Book 37, chapters 8 and 9, enumerates many species of Jasper based on their colors, country of origin, and quality, some of which we shall add here. First, according to Pliny, is the translucent green Jasper, similar to the Indian Emerald, which many nations possess. The entire Orient wears this as an amulet; when the stone is girded across its middle with a white line, it is called **lettered** <note>original: *grammatias*</note> or, by many, **many-lined** <note>original: *poligrammos*</note>. Second is a Jasper that Pliny describes as gray-green and oily, found in Cyprus. Third is a Jasper similar to copper found in Persia, and for that reason it is called **copper-like**; the Greeks call it **Borian** <note>original: *boria*</note> because it resembles the morning sky in autumn. Fourth is a blue Jasper found near the Thermodon river. Fifth is a purple Jasper in Phrygia. Sixth is of a purple-blue color that does not reflect light, found in Cappadocia. Seventh is a Jasper similar to the Indian variety found in Thrace. Eighth is a turbid or cloudy Jasper in Chalcis. Ninth is a violet Jasper...

...found in Sardis <note>an ancient city in Asia Minor; the text likely refers to the "Sardian Jasper" or Sard</note>. The tenth variety is similar to crystal or to phlegm <note>original: *pituita*; a clear or pale bodily discharge</note>. According to the same Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman naturalist</note>, the best Jasper is that which is purple, or similar to a rose, or to an emerald. In the same passage, Pliny also mentions the spotted onyx gem, which they call **Jasponyx** <note>original: *Iasphonychem*</note>: this stone appears as if it has embraced a cloud, imitating snow, and is starred with reddish points, looking similar to Megarian salt; when it is stained as if by smoke, it is called **Capnias** <note>original: *capnias*, meaning "smoky"</note>. 

Dioscorides, however, simply lists this spotted onyx among the Jaspers. Pliny, in the cited passage, seems to differ somewhat from both Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher known as the father of botany and mineralogy</note> and Dioscorides. But let us leave these disputes to be examined by the more learned. 

Without a doubt, that gem of such great value among us, which is called **Turquoise** <note>original: *turchus* or *turchoys*; German: *ein Türckes*</note>, is also a species of Jasper. Its color tends toward blue, but it is sometimes yellow, shining, or white, as if milk had permeated a yellow color. They believe its power is that it strengthens the sight and protects the wearer from various accidents. 

We also have a very beautiful species of Jasper in Germany: in Bohemia, there is a green variety with reddish lines and dots shining through it; it is also of a chestnut color <note>original: *spadicei coloris*; German: *Castanienbraun*</note> and possesses immense effects. It is found around Jena in Thuringia, at Altenburg in Meissen <note>original: *Misnia*</note>, and in other places. I have found by experience that Jasper is most effectively potent against bleeding and the menstrual flow. Likewise, it aids in childbirth and protects the conception <note>meaning it helps prevent miscarriage</note>.

1. Jasper, similar to a green Emerald on one side, and covered with fossil blue <note>likely Azurite or "Mountain Blue"</note> on the other. <note>German: *Ein Schwatziſcher Stein / halb Malachit / halb Bergk Lasur* — A Swabian stone, half Malachite, half Azurite.</note>
2. Similar to an Emerald, which is decorated with lines of fossil blue. <note>German: *Dardurch blawe Strich gehen* — Through which blue streaks pass.</note>
3. Blue within green. <note>German: *Ein blawlichter Jaspis* — A bluish Jasper.</note>
4. Black within green. <note>German: *Schwartzgrün* — Black-green.</note>
5. Green, suffused with milk. <note>German: *Weiſsgrün* — White-green.</note>

**Idraogiros**, that is: To pour into dung, or to place and set within dung. <note>original: "Unter ein Mist göllen / oder Mist setzen vnnd thun." This refers to the alchemical process of digestion using the natural, steady heat produced by fermenting horse manure.</note>

**Ifsides**, that is, white lead <note>original: *cerusa*</note> or lead ash.

**Ignis** [Fire], In the opinion of some, this is the oil that swims on top during distillation.

**Ignis.** — Fire for the Philosopher's Stone. <note>original: *Ignis pro lapide philos.*</note> Bernhardus <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist.</note> says: They have sworn to reveal this; however, they say nonetheless that one should make it with dung, lamps, or coals. The first degree occurs in water, the second in ash, the third in sand, the fourth in iron filings or in the flame.

2. Rosarius <note>Refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a key 16th-century alchemical text.</note> says: The fire of the dung works in the digestion, where the water-bath <note>original: *balneum*</note> is of no value. Therefore, some want one to put ash into the water-bath, and if one wants to increase the fire, one should put sand upon it.

3. They describe the government of the fire through the four seasons of the year. Aurora <note>Refers to the *Aurora Consurgens*, a medieval treatise attributed to Thomas Aquinas.</note> says: make a smoky fire <note>original: *Dampfficht*</note> that digests and cooks steadily, not tossing or boiling, subtle and enclosed, surrounded by air, so that nothing burns or changes, but rather penetrates; so also says Trevisanus.

4. The first degree of the fire lasts until the Whiteness <note>The *Albedo* or white stage of the alchemical process.</note> begins, and is produced with one lamp for three months. The second lasts until the Whiteness is completed, with two wicks for three months. The third lasts until the Whiteness is fixed <note>Stable and resistant to fire.</note> with three wicks for three months. The fourth is with coals until the end, for three months.

5. The flame should not touch the vessel.

6. The glass should not be taken out until everything is finished and completed; do not let others lead you astray.

7. When you wish to set the matter in, the glass and the matter should be warm so that it does not stick; then shake it well together so that it sinks to the bottom, and thus seal it. <note>original: *sigillirs*. This refers to creating a "hermetic seal" by melting the neck of the glass flask.</note>

<header># RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN #</header>

8. In distillation, the **alembic** <note>The top part of a still, used to condense vapors.</note> should be made of **glass** and sealed at all its joints.

9. **Teruis.** <note>Likely referring to Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist.</note> Cook it in such a way that the elements remain; govern the **fire** so that the **water** is not destroyed; likewise govern the **earth** so that the **air** is not ruined. For **ash** is a dead thing and cannot be awakened, but **calx** <note>original: *Kalck*; a powder produced by heating a substance to high temperatures, considered a "living" or "revivable" essence.</note> can be.

**Heat of fire** is either natural or artificial.
**Algir fire**, that is, a most powerful fire.
**Elementary fire**, that is, sulfur—but not the common kind.
**Fire of the wise**, that is, warm horse manure. <note>The heat generated by fermenting manure was used for gentle, long-term "digestion" of substances.</note>
**Brightly burning fire**, that is, sulfur.
**Extinguished fire**, that is, extinguished sulfur.
**Persian fire** <note>original: *Ignis Persicus*; also called *heiß Brande* or "hot burning."</note> is a burning ulcer that torments with a fiery heat. <note>In this context, it refers to a medical condition like shingles or anthrax, though Ruland often mixes medical and alchemical definitions.</note>
**Attained hoarfrost fire** <note>original: *Ignis pruinus adeptus*.</note> is the quintessence of wine (or of vitriol) rectified with tartar; this occurs when the fifth essence of **wine** is purified with tartar.
**Lion’s fire**, the element of fire, also called ether, *pyr*, *æthos*, *Jupiter argos*: **The element of fire.**

Four degrees of fire must be observed by practitioners, into which the fire is distributed. It is not only these degrees as wholes that must be watched, but also their beginnings, middles, and ends, just as it is established that the ancient Philosophers observed them. These are judged not only by the senses, but by the effect they have upon the substances themselves, and by judgment joined with the senses—most especially the sight and the touch. The first degree is the slowest, like a somewhat sluggish warmth; it is called the heat of a mild bath, of manure, of digestion, or of circulation, etc. This is described by touch as a heat that a human finger can always endure being held within; and although it has its own intensities and relaxations, it must never produce an obvious or sharp sensation. Of this kind is the vaporous fire of the Philoso-

<meta>This page continues the detailed classification of the "Four Degrees of Fire" used in alchemical operations, moving from the gentlest heats to destructive, high-temperature fires. It then transitions into the definitions for "Ignition" and the Paracelsian concept of "Ilech."</meta>

<page-num>262</page-num>

<header># MARTIN RULAND’S DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY #</header>

...[degrees of fire], the first of which is described as the warmth of a hen sitting upon her eggs to hatch chicks, or the natural heat of a healthy human body. This is generally such as is provided by the moderately heated furnace of a **vapor-bath** <note>original: *vaporarii*; a method of heating using steam or moist heat, similar to a modern food steamer.</note>, or like a **sand-bath** <note>original: *catini arenarii*; a container filled with sand which is heated to provide a steady, even temperature to a vessel placed inside.</note> placed upon a furnace, or a vessel placed within that sand-bath over a modest flame. 

The **second degree** is more intense, so that it is clearly felt by the touch, yet does not cause injury to the sense organ. They call this the **heat of ashes** <note>original: *calorem cinerum*</note>, because a moderate fire lit under a pan of ashes provides such heat; for ashes, due to their porous nature, do not hold much air. 

The **third degree** is reached when it causes injury to the touch, and is compared to boiling sand or iron filings—thus it is called the **fire of sand** <note>original: *ignis arenæ*</note> or iron filings, etc. 

The **fourth** is the highest degree, and is generally destructive. They call this the **fire of reverberation** <note>original: *ignem reuerberii*; a high-heat method where the flame is reflected or "reverberated" off the roof of the furnace onto the material.</note>, and it is produced by the live flame of wood or piled coals vigorously fanned with bellows. 

These degrees, when applied to their effects on specific substances, change significantly. Thus, what would be the final degree for a plant might be the first for **antimony** <note>original: *stibio*; a brittle, silvery-white metalloid used in various alchemical purifications.</note> or another firm substance. Furthermore, although the first degree is usually understood as the heat of a water-bath <note>original: *balnei*; often called a bain-marie.</note>, nevertheless all four degrees can have a place in operations involving a bath: the first is when the water is moderately warm, the second when it is already sharply felt, the third when it burns, and the fourth when it even destroys through maximum boiling—all of which are seen even more clearly when using oil.

**Ignition** <note>original: *Ignitio*</note> is **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or reduce it to powder.</note>, reducing bodies into lime <note>original: *calcem*; a fine powder or ash resulting from intense heating.</note> by the violence of fire; it includes both combustion and reverberation.

**First Ilech**, that is, the beginning; also called Ileias or Ileadus. **The first beginning.** <note>original: *Der erst Anfang*</note>

**Super-natural Ilech**, or the first from the stars, is the super-celestial conjunction and union of the stars of the firmament with the "stars" <note>In alchemical philosophy, "stars" often refer to the internal spiritual essence or "seeds" of earthly materials.</note> of lower things: **The first constellation, Ilech, is a super-celestial union of the upper stars of the firmament with the stars of lower, earthly things.** <note>original: *Das erst Gestirn Ilech, ist eine vberhimmlische Vereinigung deß obern firmamentischen Gestirns mit dem Gestirn der vndern irrdischens Dingen.*</note>

**Great Ilech** <note>original: *Ilech magnum*</note> is the ascendant, or the star of medicine, which we re-

We shall find nothing beyond these three, which exist individually within each of the elements. The ancients also handed these traditions down long ago; thus, Theophrastus was not the first to find them, but he called them back into the light from the shadows where they had been buried. ...is truly according to the four elements: the first is the Chaos <note>The primal, unformed state of matter.</note> of earth, the second the chaos of water, the third the chaos of air, and the fourth the chaos of fire. Likewise, there are four **Iliasters** <note>In Paracelsian philosophy, the Iliaster is the hidden virtue or life-force of nature.</note> belonging to men which concern a long life.

The first or innate **Iliaster** is the boundary of life, or rather life itself or its balsam <note>A vital fluid or spirit within the body that preserves it from decay.</note> within man: **The first or implanted Iliaster is life itself, the goal of life, the human, living balsam.**

The second or prepared **Iliaster** is the boundary of life which we obtain from the elements or from things composed of elements, and is life itself: **The second or prepared Iliaster is the arranged goal of life, the balsam which we derive from the elements or elemental things.**

The third **Iliaster** is the prepared boundary of the balsam which we obtain from the quintessence <note>The "fifth essence" or the purest, most concentrated part of a substance.</note> of things: **The third is the end of life and the balsam which we draw from the fifth essence.**

The fourth or Great **Iliaster** is the passing or rapture of the mind or soul into another world, as happened with Enoch, Elijah, and others: **The fourth or Great Iliaster is the ecstasy and displacement of the spirit, whereby a person is transported into another world, like Enoch, Elijah, and Paul.** <note>Enoch and Elijah are biblical figures described as being taken directly to heaven; Paul refers to the apostle's vision of the "third heaven."</note>

**Images** are metallic or wax effigies in which celestial powers operate: **Metallic or wax images in which the heavenly power works.** <note>This refers to the practice of creating "talismans" or "astrological images" intended to capture the influence of specific stars or planets.</note>

**Imagination** is a star within man, a celestial or supra-celestial body: **The star in man, the heavenly or super-heavenly body.** <note>For alchemists, imagination was not just "make-believe," but a creative force that linked the human soul to the stars.</note>

**To Imbibe** means to thicken [a substance] by grinding.

**Imbibition** is a washing, occurring when a liquid added to a body is raised [as vapor] and, finding no exit, falls back into the body; it washes the body with frequent moistenings for as long as it takes until it is coagulated with the pure part of it... <note>This describes a process of circular distillation or "pelican" digestion, where a solid is repeatedly saturated with its own distilled liquid until they merge into a single, purified substance.</note>

...strangled <note>Latin: *gulatus*. In alchemy, this often refers to a vessel with a restricted neck or one that has been hermetically sealed to prevent the "spirit" or vapor from escaping.</note>, it can no longer ascend, but remains entirely fixed. This is a clearly philosophical <note>The "philosophical" way refers to the high art of alchemy practiced by "philosophers," as opposed to "vulgar" or common chemistry.</note> operation and does not lower itself to common methods.

**Immersive corrosion** <note>Latin: *immersiua corrosio*</note> is when bodies <note>In alchemy, "bodies" usually refers to metals or solid substances.</note> are reduced to calx <note>A powder or lime-like substance resulting from the heating or corrosion of a metal.</note> by being submerged in other substances. It is either Wet or Dry.

**Impressions** <note>Latin: *impressiones*</note> are invisible fruits, such as those of the stars in lower things, not of the Sun and Moon. <gloss>The invisible fruit of the stars.</gloss> <note>original: *Unsichtbare Frucht deß Gestirns*</note>

**Impure alkali** is its foam, which is removed during the purification process after the substance has been constructed.

**Impure tartar** belongs to the alkali itself. <gloss>The scum of tartar; a raw salt.</gloss> <note>original: *Deß tartari abschaumet / ein rauch Saltz*</note>

**Inanimate ones**, that is, pygmies <note>In the Paracelsian tradition, "inanimates" or pygmies were considered elemental beings of the earth who lacked a human soul but possessed a form of life.</note>.

**Incarnatives** <note>Latin: *incarnatiua*</note> are medicines used by surgeons to cover wounds with skin or to cause the flesh to close. <gloss>These are medicines that make the flesh grow.</gloss> <note>original: *sindt Artzneyen / die das Fleisch machen wachsen*</note>

**Inceration** <note>Latin: *inceratio*</note> is the mixing of moisture with a dry substance through slow combustion until it reaches the consistency of softened wax. For this reason it is called *enkerosis* <note>original Greek: ἐγκήρωσις; literally "waxing."</note>; otherwise it is also called **imbibition**, which occurs through irrigation, where the dry substance "drinks" the moisture. This is no different from the "nourishing" used by physicians, by which **sarcocolla** <note>A Persian gum resin used for healing, literally "flesh-glue."</note>, **litharge** <note>Lead oxide.</note>, and other substances are gradually soaked in a certain juice and rendered suitable for use.

**Incilia** <gloss>Ditches lined with stones and plastered over.</gloss> <note>original: *Gräben mit Steinen außgemawrt / vnd verstrichen*</note>

**Incineration** <note>Latin: *incineratio*</note> is the process of ignition that converts bodies into ashes through a more vehement fire. Plant and animal matters are incinerated; however, minerals (to speak in the chemical fashion) are properly said to be reduced not to ashes, but to **calx**.

**Incineration and Whitening** <note>Latin: *dealbatio*</note> <gloss>is when the blackness begins to vanish and the matter starts to turn white like ash; then fire and water, or earth and water, mix and unite; the water departs and the earth increases until everything becomes completely parched, dry, and a powder.</gloss>

**Inclination** <note>Latin: *inclinatio*</note> is the force of nature, or that which reveals the nature of a person; <gloss>The power and inclination that shows the character and nature of a person.</gloss> <note>original: *Die Krafft vnd Neigung so der Menschen Art vnd Natur anzeiget.*</note>

**Incorporation** <note>Latin: *incorporatio*</note> is a mixing by which moist things are immediately combined with dry things into a single body in the form of a mass. Therefore, in this process, there is no slow nourishment, but as much moisture is added at once as is required for the consistency of the mixed body, so that it becomes like a paste; for this reason, it can also be called **impastation** <note>Latin: *impastatio*; the process of turning a substance into a dough or paste-like consistency.</note>, and in some cases, **subaction** <note>Latin: *subactio*; the act of working, kneading, or bringing a substance under control through physical processing.</note>. These incorporated things are then left in a digestive heat so that, through mutual action and passion, they may obtain a shared temperament <note>Latin: *crasin*; a Greek-derived term referring to the specific mixture or "constitution" of elements in a body.</note>.

**Incuba**, that is, the bride of the Sun <note>In alchemical allegory, the "Bride of the Sun" often refers to a substance that "marries" or reacts with Gold (the Sun).</note>.

**Incubus** is a nocturnal spirit that deceives and tricks women in sleep, acting as if they were having intercourse with it.

**Indian salt** <note>Latin: *indicum sal*</note>, that is, rock salt <note>Latin: *sal gemmae*; a transparent, crystalline common salt valued for its purity in chemical operations.</note>.

**Indian color**; <gloss>A wave-blue color.</gloss> <note>original: *Wellenblaw Farb.*</note>

**Indian foam** <note>Latin: *indicum spuma*; refers here to Indigo.</note> is of two species: namely, one is partly **Natural Indigo**, which grows of its own accord on certain reeds of India. The second species is **Artificial Indigo**, made in the workshops of dyers: it is a purple foam floating on the vats. The best of this artificial kind is that which presents a sky-blue appearance; for it contains a blue within a black color; in German they say, <gloss>Woad-flower or Dyer’s Indigo</gloss> <note>original: *Waidblum oder Färber Indich*</note>. It slightly binds, breaks, purges, and suppresses ulcers. Pliny, in Book 35, Chapter 6, says that Natural Indigo is of an unexplored origin. However, the artificial kind is made from the black "flower" <note>The "flower" here refers to the fine scum or froth that rises to the top of a liquid during a process.</note> that adheres to copper vats. Others simply call it the juice of a herb with which cloths are now dyed, which they call Indigo—that is, woad <note>Latin: *glastum*; a plant (Isatis tinctoria) used to produce blue dye before tropical indigo became widely available.</note>—though that is a different, domestic...

<margin>Influence is</margin> when, through our imagination and mind, we attract the nature and virtues of the higher stars and planets into ourselves. <note>original German: **Influence is when we, through the strength of our imagination, draw the virtue and nature of the upper stars and planets to and into ourselves.**</note> It is of two kinds: The True, which comes to us through created things, such as the influence of the heavens through the firmament; the other is that which is given to us without mediation, namely from God alone. **To Inter** <note>original Latin: *Inhumare*</note>, to bury under the earth for the purpose of putrefying <note>the process of breaking down a substance through rot to prepare it for transformation</note>, or also to turn something into earth. ### BY MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN ###

...indicates its quality. They claim it is born from a watery juice that flows from the matter of the stone, which is generated in red mud. Indeed, it is called **Iris** because in its center it represents the rainbow <note>original Latin: *Irin meteoron*; referring to the atmospheric phenomenon</note> with distinct little veins; or because when the stone is struck by sunlight under a roof, it casts the appearances and colors of the celestial rainbow upon the nearby walls, according to Pliny, Book 37 <note>original: *L. C.*, likely referring to *Liber* 37 of Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*</note>. The same Pliny adds that some have rough sides and unequal angles, which, when placed in the open sun, cause shimmering rays to run through them; some even illuminate their surroundings with a brightness projected before them. Finally, he adds another Iris similar to wax, very hard, which is born in Persia; and a gemstone similar to this in appearance, but not of the same effect, which is called **zeros** <note>original: *zeros*</note>, a crystal distinguished by a black and white line running across it. If you wish, you may also refer here to the **Demon Stone** <note>original: *lapidem dæmonis*</note> of Albertus <note>referring to the medieval scholar Albertus Magnus</note>, which is also two-colored like the Iris, and which is beneficial for those suffering from fevers and drives away poisonous things. Regarding the Iris stone, see also Solinus in *Polyhistor*, chapter 36.

**Iva arthetica** or **muscata** <note>a medicinal herb, likely Ground Pine or Bugle</note>: **A medicine for paralyzed or weakened limbs.** <note>original German: *Ein Arzney zu den lamen Gliedern*</note>
**Drinkable Iva**: **A drink that restores paralyzed limbs to health.** <note>original German: *Ein Tranc/ so die lamen Glieder widerumb zu recht bringet*</note>
**Mining Judge** <note>original Latin: *Iudex metallicus*; German: *Berg Richter*</note>.
**Iumnisum** or **Iumnizum**: that is, **ferment** or **leaven** <note>original Latin: *fermentum*; a substance used to trigger a transformation in the alchemical Work</note>.
**Jupiter**: that is, **tin** <note>original Latin: *stannum*; in alchemical tradition, the seven metals were linked to the seven planets</note>.
**Sworn seller of shares**: a **broker of mining shares**. <note>original Latin: *Iuratus partium venditor*; German: *Kränckler*</note>
**Iussa**: that is, **gypsum stone** <note>original Latin: *lapis gipsius*</note>.

# K

**Kachimia** or **Kakimia**, is the immature ore of any metal, or a semi-perfect metal, which still lies hidden in its primary Being <term>Ens: the first or essential state of a substance</term>, like an infant in the mother’s womb. Thirty species of it are known. <note>German text: An untimely, half-grown ore that still lies in the impurities of the earth, like a child in the mother's womb; there are over thirty kinds of it.</note>

**Kaib**, Curdled sour milk.

**Kal**, that is, Salt from the stream.

**Kald**, that is, vinegar.

**Kali**, that is, potash <note>original Latin: *cinis clauellatus*</note> or alkali. It is a salty herb or plant which, when burned, causes the ashes to clump together into a mass <note>original Latin: *massam*</note>; this same mass is called **soda** in our language, from which glass is made. But the salt that flows out during the boiling process of glassmaking is **sal alkali** <term>alkali salt</term>.

**Kali**, in Arabic called *Usnen* <note>original: *Vsnen*</note>. Rhazes <note>the famous 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist</note>, however, says that *kali* is *alumen asfur* <note>a specific type of mineral salt or alum</note>.

**Kalnos**, that is, smoke.

**Kamar** or **Camar**, that is, silver, *kyana*.

**Kamir**, that is, leaven or ferment.

**Kanfor**, that is, tin.

**Kaprili**, that is, sulfur.

**Kar**, that is, a gemstone shining like fire.

**Karabe**, that is, a gum similar to saffron; **Amber** <note>German: *Agstein*</note>.

**Karlina**, is wild dill.

**Kartina**, **Carline Thistle** <note>German: *Eberwurtzen*; historically used in medicine and alchemy</note>.

**Kasam**, that is, iron.

**Katimia**, called *Kadmia* in Greek, and in Latin *Calamina* or *lapis calaminaris* <term>Calamine: a zinc ore</term>. **Galmy** <note>a common name for calamine ore</note>, however, is a root of **Tutty** <term>Tutty: zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</term>; indeed, to speak more truthfully, it is the raw Tutty itself, for it is the stone [with which...]

## L

**Labrum**, a tub or vat <note>German: *Wanne*</note>.

**Læuigatio** or **Alcolifmus**, is calcination <term>reduction by fire</term> which, by pulverizing a substance, brings it into the state of "Alcohol." <note>In early chemistry, "alcohol" (Alcool) referred to any extremely fine, impalpable powder, not just spirits of wine.</note> In this context, it is the reduction of certain things through binding <note>original Latin: *glutinationem*</note>, and others through melting or "lightning" <term>a rapid refining process, typically for precious metals</term>.

**Lacuna**, a stroke-sump or collection pit <note>German: *Streich Sumppf*; likely referring to a pit used in mining or metallurgy to catch runoff</note>.

**Lacune**, that is, **terra sigillata** <term>literally "sealed earth," a medicinal clay traditionally from the island of Lemnos, stamped with a seal to guarantee its authenticity</term>.

<header>DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN [RULAND].</header>

...they have thought, and still dispute: But if you wish to consider it sharply, the **Arabian Stone** <note>original Latin: *Lapis Arabicus*</note> is none other than the **specular stone** <term>a transparent or translucent mineral, usually a variety of gypsum or muscovite mica, that can be split into thin plates</term>, or the **Moon-stone** <note>original Latin: *lapis Lunae*</note>, or **Mary’s ice** <note>original Latin: *glacies Mariae*</note>, called in German *Sperglass* <note>modern German: *Spiegelglas*, meaning mirror-glass or mica</note> or *vnser Frawen Eyß* <note>modern German: *Marienglas*, literally "Our Lady's Ice," a name for high-quality transparent gypsum</note>. From which windows were formerly prepared, with smoothed wooden frames placed in stead of lead. From which also the best **gypsum** <term>a soft sulfate mineral used for plaster</term> is made, according to the testimony of Pliny. And it is, as it were, the furthest refinement of gypsum, as Albertus [Magnus] maintains; he also calls this specular stone **Aphroselinum** <note>from the Greek for "moon-froth"</note>, because at night it reflects the image of the Moon, or because it is formed from dew like moon-froth. Some, however, argue that **selenite** <term>a crystalline variety of gypsum</term> is the specular stone, which Dioscorides also calls Aphroselinum. But of these things, we shall speak elsewhere. This specular stone is truly called the **Arabian stone** because it was first found in Arabia, though Albertus claims it was first found in Spain, in the city of Segundia, and in greater abundance; and later in many German locations. If you consider it, there are various species of this stone. First, this stone is found short and spotted in the Bolognese territory of Italy, as Pliny also testifies; it is perhaps similar to spotted ivory, which is how Dioscorides describes the Arabian stone. Second, it is found among us as a blackish variety, which is not sufficiently clear. Third, it is found among us as a very white variety, from which windows were once made. And this is the selenite which is discussed under the letter S. Fourth, it is found in Saxony similar to ivory, which is the Arabian stone of Pliny. Fifth, it is found with black or red spots, which could also be the Arabian stone of Dioscorides. Albertus, however, identifies three species of specular stone: one, namely, clear like glass, from which windows are made; a second, black, like ink; a third, yellow, which he calls **orpiment** <term>a deep orange-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</term> or **arsenic**. It is true that the Arabs said natural arsenic or orpiment was similar to the specular stone, looking at the flakes <note>original Latin: *crustas*</note>. But the specular stone, even if it is yellow, is not simply orpiment, as Albertus mistakenly believes. The specular stone does not have that same fattiness <note>original Latin: *pinguetudinem*</note> of orpiment. And what could be more foolish than to identify orpiment with the specular stone, when there is no similarity between them except in the flakes? Indeed, this specular stone is a distinguished stone and a humor, as if a solidified part of the earth, which does not dissolve; and while it is an earthly humor frozen in the manner of crystal, and...

<header>BY RULAND, PHYSICIAN AND PHILOSOPHER.</header>

...hardened into a stone; for this reason, our people call it **Mary’s ice** <note>original Latin: *glaciem Mariæ*; a name for clear, high-quality selenite gypsum</note>. Some say that it is celestial dew exposed to the brightness of the Moon, which has been coagulated and constricted into the appearance of a stone, especially that variety which is most brilliant white and is called **Aphroselinon** <note>literally "moon-foam" in Greek</note>. This **specular stone** <term>a mineral such as mica or selenite that can be split into thin, transparent sheets, formerly used for windows</term> is found among us in the mines themselves, as well as in many other places. The river Elbe <note>original: *Albis*</note> also sometimes carries this stone along with it, together with gypsum. For the rest, if you wish to know anything perfectly concerning that stone, see Pliny, Book 36, Chapter 22; a passage which I now omit for the sake of brevity. Finally, this also should be noted: although the specular stone has an affinity with **gypsum** <term>a soft sulfate mineral</term>, such that gypsum is its source, nevertheless its use in medicines is excellent, whereas gypsum is of doubtful use and poisonous, insofar as it causes choking. Indeed, our people use the specular stone in the quantity of a hazelnut for dysentery with great success. They also use it for drying hemorrhoids and in tooth-powders, as Dioscorides writes concerning the **Arabian stone** and Pliny in Book 36, Chapter 6. Concerning the Arabian stone, which we call the specular stone, see Avicenna on the **Moon-stone** <note>original: *lap. lunæ*</note>.

<margin>Stone from a crab</margin> There are also found in crabs themselves, especially in the females when they have shed and cast off their shell <note>original: *Syphar*</note>, white and round stones which the Germans call **Crab’s eyes** <note>German: *Krebsaugen*</note>, because they have the form of an eye, or **Crab-stone** <note>German: *Krebsstein*</note>. Their power is to break up stones in the bladder, and for this reason they are collected. But there is nothing more effective than these for breaking the "stone" <note>likely referring to internal blood clots or bruising</note> in those who have suffered a fall from a height. The Arabs call this stone **Roststein** <note>German for "roasting stone" or "rust stone"</note> or **grinding stone** <note>German: *reiben*</note>; it is of a cold and moist nature, though others maintain it is dry.

<margin>Stone of Magnesia</margin> 1. **Livonian Magnesia** <note>likely muscovite or mica; Ruland often uses "Magnetis" for glittering minerals</note>, of a silvery color and glittering, which can be split into the thinnest scales: **a transparent silver-white from Livonia.** 2. **Meissen Magnesia**, greenish within white, easily split. 3. Of a leaden color, not transparent, which likewise is split into scales: **lead-colored silver-white / not transparent.** 4. Clod-like, in which many small, hard, round, and heavy stones are contained, similar to impure carbuncles <note>red gemstones, usually garnets</note>: **A beautiful silver-white, containing genuine little stones not unlike impure garnets.**

**Clasp-stone** <note>original Latin and German: *Spangenstein*; these are fossilized segments of crinoid stems, also known as "Saint Cuthbert's beads."</note> 4. **Yellow.** 5. **White Hildesheim joint-stone** <term>Entrochus</term>, which is uniformly smooth and cylindrical, consisting of 14 wheel-shaped segments <term>trochites</term> covered in a crust. When the crust is broken, they can be removed, set one against the other. These are **clasp-stones joined together** <note>original German: *Spangenstein an einander*</note>. 6. Likewise, a **yellow** one, uniformly smooth, consisting of ten wheel-shaped segments. 7. An **ash-colored** one, composed of three segments. It is also smooth, but the middle part is swollen while the ends are narrower, featuring prominent ridges; where the ends meet, there is something like a belt or ring. 8. A **white, smooth** one that swells in the middle, having low rays and lacking rings. This is a **smooth clasp-stone** <note>original German: *Ein glatter Spangenstein*</note>. 9. A **rough, ash-colored stone** in which the wheel-shaped segment is formed. It is from **Spangenberg** <note>a town in Hesse, Germany</note>. It is found in a high mountain, from which it is believed the mountain and the fortress took their name.

<margin>Colored stones.</margin>
1. **Aldeberg stone**, ash-colored, smelling of **violets** <note>original German: *Violenstein*</note>. 2. **Red Aldeberg stone** smelling of violets, appearing **exactly like natural blue violets**. 3. **Lauenstein stone**, found by chance; when moistened and exposed to the Sun, it smells of **violets**; the same occurs when it is sprinkled with water and placed in a furnace, for the heat draws out the scent. 4. **Marienberg stone** found in the "Saints Fabian and Sebastian" vein; when struck with a hammer, it smells of **musk**. 5. **Thuringian stone** shaped like a **comb** <term>Ctenitae</term>, which was dug out of a tunnel for an aqueduct leading to the Beichlingen fortress; it smells of **wild thyme**. 6. **Zöblitz serpentine** <term>ophites</term> does not always have a scent; but that which does smells somewhat of **new wine** <term>must</term>, not only when shaped into cups but even in its rough masses. It **smells like must**. 7. **Echites** <note>likely an "eagle-stone" or a type of hollow geode</note>, according to Solinus, smells somewhat of **wine**, as he himself says: **Wine-ore, it smells like wine**. 8. **Hildesheim stone** mimics the odor of **burnt horn** if it is rubbed against another stone or struck with a hammer. It **smells like burnt horn**.

**Another stone** is excellent (according to Dioscorides, Book 5, Chapter 88) which has the color of **pumice** <note>original German: *Bleich Farb*, meaning a pale or sallow color</note>. It is light, spongy, and crumbly, having split veins of a yellow color running toward the bottom. It is called simply "the stone"...

### LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND ###

...on account of the color and substance of the stone. For it is not called a stone because of its hardness, but rather because it is light and spongy. It is called the **Asian stone** <note>original Latin: *Lapis Asius*</note> because it is born on Mount Assos in the Troad <note>an area in modern-day Turkey</note>, and not only in Asia generally. Its power is astringent, and it has the property of slightly eroding and gently eating away at **superfluous flesh**. For this reason, it is also called a **sarcophagus** <note>from the Greek *sarx* (flesh) and *phagein* (to eat); here referring to the stone's corrosive medicinal properties rather than a coffin</note>. It is one stone, called "sarcophagus" because of its power, and "Asian" from its place of origin. Although Pliny, in the same place (Book 36, Chapter 17), through some oversight, classifies them differently. For he says that the Asian stone, which is salty to the taste, relieves **gout** <note>original: *podagras*</note>, and that in those specific quarries all ailments of the legs are healed, whereas in all other mines, the legs are harmed. Earlier, he teaches that on Mount Assos in the Troad, the sarcophagus stone is split from a fissile vein, and that dead bodies placed within it are consumed within forty days, with the exception of the teeth. He also mentions this in Book 2, Chapter 98. What kind of stone that truly is, is generally unknown. However, we have it in Germany, right on the surface. Around it and under it a "flower" grows, a salty down or fuzz appearing like **nitre** <term>Nitre: naturally occurring potassium nitrate or similar salt crusts</term>, which is called the **flower of the Asian stone** <note>original: *flos Asiæ petræ*</note>. As Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> testifies in the place cited, it is a yellowish salt-crust sitting upon the top of the stone, of a thin consistency; in some places it is white in color, in others similar to pumice, tending toward yellow, and it stings the tongue somewhat when applied. Its powers are stronger than the stone itself; this flower is dried and washed, and has various uses in medicine. **Foam of nitre** <note>original: *Aphronitrum*</note> (that is, the froth of nitre), the **flower of the stone**, and the **flower of the Asian stone** seem to be almost the same thing. They differ slightly in substance, for this flower of the Asian stone is dissolved by fire and therefore does not burn; however, the foam of our local nitre does not dissolve. At **Jena** <note>a city in Germany</note>, a most beautiful species of foam-nitre is found, which corresponds very closely to the flower of the Asian stone described by Dioscorides. Indeed, the flower of the Asian stone is, as it were, a species of foam-nitre. Similar in color to this flower of the Asian stone is the **adarces** <term>Adarces: a salt-crust found on reeds in marshes</term>, which was discussed above. Furthermore, Pliny (in the location cited) says this flower of the Asian stone is also similar to **red pumice**. This variety is hidden from us. ...describes its species <note>original Latin: *eius species ponit*</note>. For one type of its flower is white, which is most often found around Jena <note>a city in Germany</note>; another is reddish or red, which is the one mentioned by Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*</note>; another is like pumice, leaning toward a saffron color, which is that "flower of the stone of Asia" described by Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note>. They claim that this flower of the Asian stone is born from the dew of the sea when rain falls upon it.

<margin>Carp stone.</margin> The carp <note>original: *Lapis carpionis*</note> is a well-known freshwater fish, extremely viscous; for this reason, it is cooked with wine to remove its viscosity; in German, it is called *ein Karpff*. In the jaws of this fish is found a gem or stone called *ein Karpffenstein* <note>German: "carp stone"</note> which is triangular in shape, its size proportional to the fish, white on the outside and yellow on the inside. This stone is also beneficial for those suffering from the stone <note>referring to kidney or bladder stones, also called calculi</note>, and it especially possesses this power: to resist the "boiling" of yellow bile. When one suffers from heartburn <note>original German: *Wann einen der Sodt seudt*—literally "when the heartburn seethes in one"</note>, the stone should be held in the mouth. It has other powers as well, which I omit now for the sake of brevity. It also protects against the pain of colic.

<margin>Phrygian stone.</margin> The Phrygian stone <note>original: *Lapis Phrygius*</note> is best when it is pale and moderately heavy, with a body that is not solid but rather interspersed with white segments, like **Cadmia** <term>Cadmia: a term used for various zinc-rich ores or the crusts that formed in smelting furnaces</term>. It took its name from the fact that fullers <note>workers who cleaned and thickened cloth</note> in Phrygia once used it for dyeing. See Dioscorides, Book 5, Chapter 87, who teaches its place of origin, its medicinal power, and the method of burning and washing it. Among us, various species of this stone are found. First, we have a sticky juice or earth which we call **washing earth** <note>German: *Wasch Erde*, commonly known as Fuller’s Earth</note>. Furthermore, in Saxony, we have sticky and pumice-like earths which they call **washing earth** from their effect, as fullers use them in washing cloths. Pliny, in Book 36, Chapter 19, says that the Phrygian stone takes its name from the nation and is a pumice-like clod, useful only for dyeing garments.

<margin>Thracian stone.</margin> The Thracian stone <note>original: *Lapis Thracias*</note>, also called *Thracius* or *Threicius* by Nicander <note>a Greek poet and physician</note>, is born in a river of Scythia named Pontus. It has the power of **jet** <note>original: *gagates*, a type of lignite coal used as a gemstone</note>; it is ignited by water and extinguished by oil, just as happens with bitumen. And that stone is nothing other than...

...because of the color and substance of the stone. For despite its hardness, it is not truly a stone, because it is light and spongy. It is called the **Asian stone** <note>original: *lapis Asius*</note> because it is born in Mount Assos in the Troad <note>a region in Northwest Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey</note>, and not only in Asia. Its power is astringent, and it has the quality of slightly eroding and gently corroding superfluous flesh. For this reason, it is also called **sarcophagus** <note>literally "flesh-eater." The ancients believed that coffins made of this limestone would dissolve the body while leaving the bones.</note>. Thus, it is one stone: called *sarcophagus* for its power, and *Asius* for its place of birth.

However, Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, Roman naturalist</note> in the same location (Book 36, Chapter 17), through some carelessness, posits a different view. For he says that the Asian stone, which is salty to the taste, soothes gout; and he claims that in these stone-quarries all ailments of the legs are healed, even though in all other metal mines, the legs are usually harmed. This is despite the fact that he earlier teaches that the *sarcophagus* stone is cut in a fissile vein in Mount Assos of the Troad, and that the bodies of the dead placed within it are consumed within forty days, except for the teeth. He also mentions this in Book 2, Chapter 98. 

What kind of stone that truly is remains commonly unknown. However, we have it in Germany, and even on its surface. Around it and beneath it, a "flower" is born—a salty down <note>original: *lanugo*</note> with the appearance of nitre <note>saltpeter or natron</note>, which is called the **flower of the Asian stone**. As Dioscorides <note>Greek physician and botanist</note> testifies in the cited passage, it is a yellowish saltiness sitting upon the top of the stone, with a thin structure. In some cases, it is white in color; in others, it is similar to pumice, verging toward yellow; when applied to the tongue, it is somewhat biting. It is stronger in its medicinal powers than the stone itself; this flower is dried and washed, and it has various uses in medicines. 

It seems that **Aphronitrum** <note>literally "foam of nitre"</note>, the flower of the stone, and the flower of the Asian stone are nearly the same thing. They differ only slightly in substance, for this flower of the Asian stone is dissolved by fire and therefore is not burned <note>calcined</note>, whereas the foam of our native nitre is not dissolved. A most beautiful species of *aphronitrum* is found at Jena <note>a university city in Germany</note>, which corresponds very closely to the Asian stone described by Dioscorides. Indeed, the flower of the Asian stone is like a species of *aphronitrum*. **Adarces** <note>a mineral crust formed on reeds in salt marshes</note>, which was discussed above, is similar in color to this flower of the Asian stone. Furthermore, Pliny (in the location cited) says this flower of the Asian stone is also similar to red pumice. This variety is hidden from us.

<meta>This page continues the "Lexicon Alchemiae" by Martin Ruland the Elder, moving from the previous entries on the Asian stone and Carp-stone to a detailed discussion of Thracian stone and jet (gagates). It explores the origins of these substances from bitumen and naphtha.</meta>

<page-num>280</page-num>

<header>MARTIN RULAND’S DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY</header>

...that other species of jet <note>original Latin: *gagates*</note>, the black kind, **black eye-stone / amber / fountain-stone** <note>original German: *schwarzer Augstein / Bernstein / Bornstein*; while *Bernstein* usually means amber, in this context it refers to a black, stony variety related to jet</note>; and it is formed from black <term>naphtha</term> <note>a volatile flammable liquid hydrocarbon</note> or liquid black <term>bitumen</term> <note>a viscous, tar-like mixture of hydrocarbons</note>: Just as yellow jet is formed from <term>petroleum</term> <note>literally "rock oil"</note>, that is, white liquid naphtha, when it drips or flows into the sea. It hardens into stone through both its own internal heat and the heat of the water. Its specific types are "stone-coals" <note>original Latin: *lithanthraces*</note>, **The Pit-coals** <note>original German: *Die Steinkolen*</note> / those stony coals, whether light or heavy. Then also that fissile <note>easily split into layers</note> stone, **Slate** <note>original German: *Der Schifer*</note>. That the Thracian stone is indeed made from bitumen is attested by its odor, its bituminous substance, and its black color, as well as being a rough, crusty, and light stone, as this stone is described by Dioscorides <note>a 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>. How it differs from amber <note>original Latin: *succinum*</note> itself has already been stated. In short, the Thracian stone and jet are stones of one kind from one and the same matter, differing only in color. The black variety is more "crusty" than the yellow, because the "mother-naphtha" <note>the source material</note> from which it comes is more impure and less refined, containing more earthiness than that more diluted white naphtha. Nicander <note>a 2nd-century BCE Greek poet and physician</note> in his *Theriaca* <note>a work on venomous animals and their cures</note>, from which Dioscorides borrowed his own material, describes this stone most beautifully when he says:

> Or you may burn the Thracian stone in the fire, which, when 
> sprinkled with water, shines and glows. But as soon as it feels 
> even a little sprinkling of oil, it is extinguished. This stone is 
> brought by shepherds from the Thracian river, which they call 
> the Pontos, where the low-born Thracian masters of the flock, 
> who feed on meat, accompany their sluggish herds.

These are the words of Nicander. The commentaries <note>original Latin: *scholia*</note> on Nicander, however, cite Aristotle, who says that such a river exists in Media and India, in which a stone of this kind is born, which burns in water, yet is extinguished when anointed or sprinkled with oil. Euax <note>a legendary king of the Arabs and author of a work on gems</note>, in his book of stones <note>original Latin: *lapidarium*</note>, has nothing of value regarding the Thracian stone. Pliny <note>the Elder, Roman naturalist and author</note>, in Book 33, Chapter 5, touches upon the nature of the Thracian stone. Likewise, in Book 36, Chapter 19, he describes what the Thracian stone is. This account agrees in all respects with our black jet: namely, it is black, flat, porous like pumice, not much different from wood, light, brittle, and of a heavy odor. If it is burned, it gives off a sulfurous smell...
