<header>MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.</header>

...is ignited by water and extinguished by oil. That Thracian stone is found in Libya, Britain, and upon the shores of the German Sea <note>The North Sea</note>. Furthermore, in former times, those who made the pilgrimage to Saint James <note>Santiago de Compostela</note> used to carry with them—on their cloaks and hats—images of the holy James artistically fashioned from this stone <note>original: *succinum* / *lapide isto*; here referring to jet or black amber</note>. Beautiful images can be shaped from it because it yields easily to the lathe. In ancient times, magicians also made use of the Thracian stone in <term>Axinomancy</term> <note>original: *Axinomantia*; a form of divination performed by balancing an axe on a post or throwing it into the ground</note>.

**Bezoar Stone** <note>original Latin: *Lapis bezaar*</note>, according to the testimony of Serapion <note>a 12th-century Arab physician</note> in the *Book of Aggregations*, chapter "Hager bezaar": first, it signifies any medicine suitable for counteracting a specific poison. Second, it specifically signifies a stone that is generated in the eyes of deer in the East. (Just as we read that the entire eyes of the hyena turn to stone; hence they are called "hyena-gems" by Pliny). In the spring, the stag tracks down the burrows of serpents and, with the breath of his nostrils, drags out those that resist and eats them, so that he may purge the weariness of the year. Soon after, he seeks out waters and rivers, in which he plunges himself up to his very head, staying there as long as he feels the power of the poison is being overcome. Meanwhile, through the force of the poison, he sheds tears from his eyes which coagulate into the **bezoar**, a remedy against all poisons. They are found in colors of lemon-yellow, dusty, greenish, and white, and it is said they are discovered in Syria, India, and the East.

In Germany, we also see something that often turns to stone near the eyes of our own deer; that hardened, bony matter—which is undoubtedly gathered from the tears—is collected by hunters and is a bezoar. That is to say, it opposes all poisons, benefits those with heart ailments, and conversely, aids in "failings of the soul" <note>likely referring to fainting, melancholy, or loss of consciousness</note>, and heals all venomous bites. The **bone from the heart of the stag** <note>original Latin: *os de corde cerui*</note> has the same power and is also a bezoar: **the little crosses found in the heart of the stag.** <note>original German: *die Creußlein die man findet in dem Herzen deß Hirſchen*</note>. As hunters know, these are shaped almost like the crosses found in the head of a "water-wolf" <note>original Latin: *lupi aquatici*; a common historical name for the Pike fish</note>, except that they are made of bone. Furthermore, such bones from the heart of a doe or a hind protect the birth and are wonderfully beneficial to pregnant women. The stone found in the stomach and intestines of a doe has the same power. But since mention has been made of the deer...

# LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND

Let us say a few things about its remaining virtues. Its marrow is beneficial for all inflammations, especially those of the womb. Its sinewy genital member, when dried and taken as a drink, soothes the pain <note>original OCR: *colorem*; likely *dolorem*, meaning pain</note> of the colon. Shavings of its private parts incite Venus <note>sexual desire</note>. Its blood halts a flowing bowel and benefits those suffering from stones <note>original: *calculosis*; kidney or bladder stones</note>. Its horn, acquired between the festivals of Mary <note>original: *intra festa... Mariæ*; referring to the "Frauendreißiger," the thirty days between the Assumption (Aug 15) and the Nativity of Mary (Sept 8), a period of traditional folk-medicinal significance</note>—especially the tips of the branches—is wonderfully beneficial for those with the falling sickness <note>original: *comitialibus*; epilepsy</note> and counters the effects of swallowed poison. Nothing is more useful for those with consumption <note>original: *phthisicis*; tuberculosis</note> than its lungs.

**The Stone from the Perch.** The perch fish <note>original Latin: *Perca*; German: *ein Barß* or *Persick*</note> has firm flesh. It is of two types: larger and smaller. The larger is called simply a "perch" or a "variegated perch" <note>German: *Buntel Barß*</note> because of its color. The smaller is called a "ruff" or "bull-head perch" <note>German: *ein Kaulparß*</note> by the Germans because of the roundness of its body. In its head, two very white, bony gems are found, about the size of linseed, though in proportion to the fish. Nothing is more effective than this gem in shattering stones in the bladder; therefore, it is carefully and deservedly collected by those who know its use. The gutted head of a loach <note>original Latin: *funduli*; German: *der Schmirlein*</note>—which resembles the face of an adorned maiden—is said to possess the same power.

**The Jewish Stone.** The *Thecolithos* <note>from the Greek *theke* (case/container) and *lithos* (stone)</note> is called the "Jewish Stone" because it is found in Palestine and the land of the Jews; it is now kept in apothecaries' shops. It is of two types: namely, the Greater and the Lesser. The Greater is similar to an acorn and marked with lines as if they were drawn on a lathe, just as it is excellently described by Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician and botanist</note>. He calls it *Phaenicites* because it is found in Phoenicia, or because it is similar to a certain type of acorn <note>original: *balano*</note>, as Pliny suggests in Book 36, chapter 10. Furthermore, it is called *Pyrena* because it resembles the pit of an olive, as the same Pliny testifies in chapter 11 of that book. It also has other names, such as *Thecolithos*, because it is like an olive pit and because, when licked, it breaks and expels stones. Moreover, it is called *Eureostriata* because it is striated like a seashell, though not so white. But Pliny, in the location cited above, was deceived by the names of these terms and thought there were several species, when there are not. These names signify one and the same thing: without a doubt, the Jewish Stone.

# RYLAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN

This stone is also found in Germany, such as along the Elbe, near the mouth of the Tanger. However, a smaller variety, which is shaped like a cylinder, shines when broken; it looks like a small well-stone <note>original German: *Wülstein*; likely referring to a small, smooth rounded stone or pebble</note>. This was undoubtedly unknown to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>. It is also found in Saxony near Hildesheim, and in the Old March at the mouth of the Tanger, along the banks of the Elbe, possessing remarkable beauty. Both types are wonderfully beneficial for difficulty in urination and for those suffering from stones <note>original Latin: *calculosis*; kidney or bladder stones</note>. Consult Dioscorides and Serapion <note>An influential 9th-century Arabic physician</note> in the *Book of Aggregations*, chapter on "Hager Aliendi," and Solinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman geographer</note>, chapter 40.

**Jewish Stones.** 1. These resemble an olive pit and are striated <note>original Latin: *striati*; marked with small ridges or grooves</note>. To this day in Palestine, these stones are called "stony olives" <note>original German: *Steinerinne Oliuen*</note>. <note>These are actually the fossilized spines of sea urchins, which were historically used to treat urinary ailments.</note>

2. Another variety resembles an olive but lacks striations; these are smooth stony olives <note>original German: *glatt steinerinne Oliuen*</note>.

**The Quiris Stone.** The hoopoe is a foul bird with a visible, folding crest that it draws together and smooths along the length of its head; the entire bird is associated with illusions and augury. In its nest is found a stone named *Quiris*, which is said to be a betrayer of secrets and a provoker of various images during sleep. <note>In medieval folklore, the hoopoe's nest was often associated with filth and magical properties; the Quiris stone was believed to reveal the thoughts of others if placed on their chest while they slept.</note>

A **lapillus** <note>a small stone</note> is a coagulum extracted by means of moisture, from which a friable and glassy substance arises by thickening. For moisture alone is the medium of this extraction. In moisture, the stone also coagulates, though at times it becomes thicker, like mud, and at other times more diluted. Thus it is: glassy in nature regarding its consistency, and fragile, although the particles are not always large, but often appear like common salt, or like snow-white concretions and frost.

**The Famous or Precious Stone:** these are the same as the "hair" <note>original German: *dieselben Haare*</note> or even the "salt of urine." <note>In alchemy, "salt of urine" or microcosmic salt was a vital substance in the search for the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

**Minute pebbles** which rivers wash down: *Affter* <note>original German: *Affter*; likely referring to mine tailings or residues found in riverbeds</note>.

**An aerous fossil stone** <note>containing copper</note>: Copper Shale <note>original German: *Kupffer Schifer*</note>.

**Large-ish black pebbles**: *Graupen* <note>original German: *Graupen*; literally "groats," used here to describe granular or barley-shaped ore deposits</note>.

**The Rebis Stone** is the "hair" of choleric or sanguine people. <note>In alchemy, *Rebis* usually refers to the divine hermaphrodite or the union of opposites; here Ruland links it to the human temperaments and "hair," a common alchemical metaphor for the fine, filament-like crystals that form during chemical reactions.</note>

### Stones that emit a juice when rubbed.
1. Morochtus <note>original: *Morochtus*; a type of light-colored clay or soapstone used by ancients for whitening linen</note>, or soft white-earth <note>original: *leucogea*</note> from Saxony.
2. Morochtus or hard white-earth from Saxony.
3. Black milk-stone <note>original: *Galactites*; a stone that creates a milky emulsion when ground with water</note> which, when rubbed against whetstones, yields a milky juice; it is dug out of the sandy pits of Hildesheim. **A black millstone.**
4. Ash-colored milk-stone.
5. Black hematite <note>original: *Haematites*; bloodstone</note>, which yields a black juice within a saffron-colored <note>yellow-orange</note> exterior.

### Other stones of various kinds.
1. Stem-stone <note>original: *Stelechites*; named for its resemblance to a tree trunk</note>, which has the appearance of a tree stump; it is found in clay near Meissen <note>original: *Misena*; a famous German mining and porcelain center</note>. **A stump-stone, which is found in clay near Meissen.**
2. Pentagon-stone, **a five-angled stone.**
3. A thirteen-sided stone <note>original: *Triskædecagonus*</note>, that is, of thirteen angles; it is white and from Hildesheim. **A white stone of thirteen corners.**
4. Armenian stone <note>original: *Armenius lapis*; often associated with azurite or blue carbonates, but here described as yellow</note>, yellow, which is found enclosed in true Armenian bole <note>a medicinal clay</note>, just as Samian stone is found in Samian earth.
5. Emery-stone <note>original: *Smiris*</note>, of an iron color and harder than iron. **Emery.**
6. A stone in the shape of an almond nut, found within flint. **A stone like an almond nut.**
7. Moon-shaped stone <note>original: *Menoides*</note>, or drug-stone <note>original: *pharmacites*; stones believed to have medicinal or chemical properties</note>.
8. A white, heavy, sandy stone, which is composed of pipes <note>tubular structures</note> made of very hard ash-colored stone; these pipes are touching one another and are filled as if with a honeycomb.
9. A yellowish stone, light like tufa <note>a porous volcanic or limestone rock</note>, which has large pipes full of sand; it is mined at Rabschütz <note>original: *Rabschicizii*</note> above Meissen. Its outer skin is sometimes tuberous and sometimes flat.
10. A white, hard, round stone, decorated on one side with many small round lines flowing from a single center; on the other side, it resembles the planks of ash-wood.
11. A very hard black stone of Sebnitz <note>original: *Zeblicianus*; referring to Sebnitz in Saxony</note>, in which many garnets are found.

**Ceraunian Stones.** <note>original: *Lapides cerauneæ*; derived from the Greek *keraunos* (lightning). In the early modern period, prehistoric stone axes and arrowheads found in the earth were believed to be the physical remnants of lightning strikes.</note> 1. **A black Ceraunian stone**, large and heavy, which completely resembles the shape of a wedge, and is perforated at its wider part. Its length is nine fingers, its width four, and its weight is three and a half pounds. This stone is said to have been driven twelve ells <note>roughly 24 to 45 feet deep, depending on the local measurement of an "ell"</note> into the ground by the force of a lightning bolt in Vienna, 1544, striking into a house and its wine cellar. **A black thunder-bolt.**

3. **Another, blackish-green**, which is entirely in the shape of a wedge and perforated through the middle; it is similar in size to the previous black-blue one. **A black-gray thunder-bolt.**
4. **One of a brownish-yellow color**, pointed, long, and rounded, perforated in the upper part like the others; it was driven into a tree by the force of lightning in the village of Sipfio in the territory of Torgau. It has the length of the black Ceraunian stone, and is so thick that it can be held by two fingers at the upper part. **A light-gray pointed thunder-bolt.**
5. Moreover, they are called **Ceraunian** from the word for lightning, and it is likely they are found in the Ceraunian Mountains of Epirus, which are frequently struck by lightning.

**Tongue-stones.** <note>original: *Lapides Glossopetræ*; from the Greek *glossa* (tongue) and *petra* (stone). These are fossilized shark teeth, which were historically believed to be the petrified tongues of snakes or dragons, often used as charms against poison.</note> 1. **A white tongue-stone** with blue lines on the surface. **A white adder’s tongue with blue lines.**

<meta>This page continues Martin Ruland the Elder's alphabetical encyclopedia of alchemical and mineralogical terms. ->### LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND<-

...[a piece of] wood of whatever size you wish, into those large bronze vats in which hops are boiled to make beer. When the hops have been thoroughly boiled, the same wood is removed and buried in sand or gravel within the cellars themselves for three years. When it is eventually taken out, it appears hardened into stone. From this material, whetstones are primarily made, which money-changers <note>or merchants</note> use for sharpening iron tools.

**Stones named after living creatures, likewise "pregnant stones" and whetstones.**
**From birds.** 
1. **Hieraclites**, which is similar in color to the softer feathers of hawks. **Hawk-stone.** <note>German: *Habichstein*. Likely a variety of jasper or agate with feather-like patterns.</note>
2. **Perdicites**, which represents the feathers that partridges have on their breasts. **Partridge-stone.** <note>German: *Rebhunstein*.</note>

**Thunderstones.** <note>Latin: *Lapides Brontiæ*; anciently believed to fall from the sky during storms, these descriptions actually refer to fossilized sea urchins (echinoids).</note>
1. **Brontias** or **Ombrias** <note>Rain-stone</note> of a brownish color, in the shape of a half-sphere, on whose surface ten lines appear. These descend from a single point, always joined in pairs, and are intersected by small holes. In the German language, this stone has received its name from the shape of a toad. **A grey toad-stone, upon which ten lines stand pair by pair, which are full of small holes.** <note>German: *Ein grawer Krotten Stein...* Toadstones were highly valued in folklore for their supposed ability to sweat in the presence of poison.</note>
2. **Yellow-colored**, twice as large as an egg, which has twenty lines, again descending from a single point, always joined in fours, which are likewise divided by points. **A large yellow toad-stone with twenty lines, every four and four together, which are full of holes.**
3. **Compressed and of the same color**, in which ten lines appear without holes. **A yellow, squeezed-together toad-stone without lines.** <note>The Latin specifies "without holes" (*sine foraminibus*), while the German text says "without lines" (*ohne Striche*).</note>
4. **Reddish**, in the shape of a half-sphere, in which ten lines appear without points, just as the previous one was without holes.
5. **Brownish color**, semi-round, lacking lines and points. **A smooth grey toad-stone.** <note>German: *ein glatter grawer Krottenstein*</note>
6. **Yellowish and flat on the surface**, but bumpy on the lower part.

**Pregnant Stones.**

4. **A white translucent variety from Thuringia**, mixed with ash-colored gypsum. **"Our Lady’s Ice" mixed with gypsum.**
5. **Mixed with gypsum** in the foundations of Stein-Wanzleben <note>original: *Steinii Vnicelebiorum*</note> near the Unstrut river in Thuringia.
6. **Burnt.** **Burnt spar.**

# OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.
Oo 3

## Augmentation of the Philosopher’s Stone, that is, The Increasing.

**Geber**: The increasing <note>German: *Die Mehrung*; the process of multiplication where the quantity and quality of the alchemical medicine is increased.</note> happens in two ways. 1. By repeating the <term>solution</term> <note>the process of turning a solid into liquid</note> and <term>coagulation</term> <note>the process of turning a liquid back into a solid</note>. 2. By projecting <note>original: *werffe*; the act of casting the alchemical powder onto molten metal</note> onto the white or red <term>body</term> <note>original: *corpus*; the base metal or the fixed material of the stone</note> in such a quantity that it also becomes an elixir. Then place both into its water and <term>solvent</term> <note>original: *menstruum*; a substance that dissolves a solid, named for the "monthly" cycles of digestion</note> to be dissolved; thus the first elixir becomes the <term>ferment</term> <note>a substance that acts like yeast, transforming the whole mass into its own nature</note> of this <term>tincture</term>.

Grind the medicine and dissolve it again in its mercury, and coagulate it gently, and <term>wax</term> it <note>original: *incerirs*; to bring a substance to a soft, waxy state so it can flow and penetrate metals</note> again like wax; thus its body is already doubled. If you dissolve and cook it once more, you have multiplied it a hundredfold, and so on; the more often, the better. **Rouil**, take heed of how much weight is missing in the medicine; for the more powerful it becomes, the more mercury you must add in the multiplication. For example, when it has double the strength it had at the start after the first multiplication, then add double the mercury. Likewise, when it has triple the strength: if you wish to increase the power and quality, take water. But if you wish to increase the substance and quantity, take **sulfur**, or the <term>prime matter of the stone</term> <note>original: *materiam primam lapidis*; the fundamental, unrefined substance required for the Great Work</note>, and cook it with the elixir. 

**Thomas of Toledo**: Take the 20th part of the elixir, add four parts of mercury, seal it, and cook it in the first degree of fire for 13 days. In the second degree, for 12 days. In the third, for 10. Put this back into mercury and cook it as before; you will complete it in 30 days; and thus for the third time even faster, up to the seventh. 

**Thomas Aquinas**: Take one part of the elixir and mix it with <term>virgin’s milk</term> <note>original: *lacte virginis*; a symbolic term often referring to mercurial water, a white precipitate, or a specific stage of the solvent</note>, add 7 parts of purifying mercury, mix, and wash as before; press it through a cloth or leather so that only the seventh part remains. <term>Fix</term> this <note>original: *figir*; to make a volatile substance stable under heat so it no longer evaporates</note>, and you have increased its power sevenfold. From this second powder, take one part, add 7 parts of mercury, press it through like wax and fix it, making it seven times more, and so on.

It cites recipes from historical alchemists like Geber, Thomas of Toledo, and Thomas Aquinas, focusing on the repeated cycle of dissolving the elixir in mercury and re-solidifying it.</summary>

# MARTIN RULAND’S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY.

**Solution of the Philosopher’s Stone** is a revelation of the hidden; it makes the coarse pure and thin, and the hard and dry liquid. For materials to be united <term>by their smallest parts</term> <note>Latin: *per minima*; the alchemical concept that substances must be broken down to their fundamental components to truly combine</note>, they must become water.

**Calcination** <note>the reduction of a solid to a powder by heat</note> happens through the first water. **Solution** happens through the second, which is the <term>Philosopher’s water</term> <note>Latin: *aqua philos.*; a specialized alchemical solvent, often a prepared form of mercury</note>. It does not happen with force—better raw than cooked, better moist than dry; it should be tempered, mild, gentle, bright, and clear. It transforms nature, breaks, and divides; black is better than red <note>referring to the *nigredo* or blackening stage, which must precede the final red stage</note>.

All common solution and sublimation are worth nothing; and everything happens through water without hands <note>a metaphor for a natural or self-operating chemical process requiring no manual interference</note>, and without the addition of any other things; and this is called <term>sharp vegetable water</term> <note>Latin: *aqua vegetabilis acuta*; an acidic spirit distilled from organic matter</note>. This is the <term>marble</term> <note>Latin: *marmor*</note> and the grindstone.

**Roger Bacon:** The first destruction of the world happened through water <note>the Biblical Deluge</note>; the second will happen through <term>fire</term> <note>German: *F:wer*, abbreviation for *Feuer*</note>; so it is also here in the Work.

**The Turba:** <note>Referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> Take iron, beat it into thin plates, sprinkle them with poison, and put them in a vessel well-sealed. Through this boiling, a third part of the water is consumed; the rest becomes wind, which the <term>Chambar</term> <note>an alchemical term for the "magnesia" or the chemical vessel that holds the spirit</note> carries in its body.

**Senior:** <note>Referring to Senior Zadith, a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose work was influential in Europe</note> In the beginning, it is dissolved with its water; at the end with <term>fire</term>, just as fruit in spring requires moisture, and thereafter heat to ripen.

The first solution is recognized when the body, together with the water, becomes equally yellow throughout, or a middle color between yellow and white.

**The Duration of the Philosopher’s Stone:** The time belonging to the necessary Stone: <term>heat</term> <note>Latin: *calid.* for *caliditas*</note> prepares the Stone until it reaches the white stage in 130 or 140 days.

**Bernard of Trevisan:** <note>A 15th-century alchemist known for his allegorical tales of the Great Work</note> Until the red stage, it takes nine and a half months; and he says the King lets himself be placed in the <term>fountain</term> <note>Latin: *fontina*; a metaphor for the solvent bath</note> after 130 days, and comes out after 282 days. **The Sound of the Trumpet** <note>Latin: *Clangor Buccinae*, a famous alchemical treatise</note> requires 280 days.

<meta>catchword: Day.</meta>

# OF MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.

Citation 40: until the white; 90: until the red; 150: the ferment.
*The Lily* <note>original: *Lilium*; refers to the alchemical text *Lilium inter spinas* or "The Lily Among Thorns"</note> says: Some have prepared it in 9 months, some in 12, some in 3, and even in eight days. **Mary the Prophetess** <note>a legendary foundational figure in alchemy, often identified with Miriam the sister of Moses</note> herself is said to have completed it in 3 days—that is, in three <term>works</term> <note>alchemical "days" often refer to completed cycles of distillation or sublimation rather than 24-hour periods</note>; for as a day follows a night, so must every imperfect work reach its perfection.

On the 6th day, a <term>solution</term> <note>the dissolving of the solid "body" into liquid</note> appears, and thereafter it looks like an <term>island</term> <note>original: *Insul*; a visual stage where the matter sits in the center of the vessel surrounded by liquid</note>, if it is governed correctly. For the <term>blackness</term> <note>the *nigredo* stage, representing the death and putrefaction of the matter</note>, 21 days are required, and this is half of the Work. Even if you find "21 weeks" written elsewhere, do not let it lead you astray; for to the philosophers, day, night, and month are often considered equal. Unequal time also chokes the unequal weight; for whoever takes too much water must cook all the longer. If it will not turn black in 40 or 50 days, then increase the **fire**; then the matter becomes liquid and appears like a <term>Hyacinth</term> <note>a reddish-orange zircon or gemstone; here referring to the color of the liquid</note>.

1st Degree of **Fire**. **Saturn** clothes the King in black in 40 days.
**Jupiter** clothes him with a gray robe in 20 or 24 days.
2nd Degree of **Fire**. **Luna** <note>the Moon, representing Silver</note> clothes him with white linen in 40 days.
**Venus** clothes him in yolk-yellow in 22 days.
3rd Degree of **Fire**. **Mars** clothes him in red in 40 days.
4th Degree of **Fire**. The **Sun** <note>Sol, representing Gold or the final perfection</note> completes it in 40 days; then he sweats for 3 days in a **potter’s furnace**, and the Work is finished.

**A shortcut for making the Stone.** From the *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarium Philosophorum*; a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note>: from the **black lead of the philosophers**, draw a gold-colored oil. Dissolve your Stone with this after the first <term>fixation</term> <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note> 2 or 3 times for 3 or 4 days. This will spare you many solutions and coagulations, so that you may be finished in 30 days, etc.

2. Cook the **white Magnesia** <note>in this context, a "mother" substance or primitive mineral, not modern magnesium</note> with a strong fire until it is blood-red. Then take out the <term>King</term> <note>the refined metallic core</note> and add to his part 3 parts of rubbed gold and 2 parts of **gold-water** <note>likely *aqua regia* or a specialized solvent for gold</note>. Mix until the body is hidden, then cook it until it reaches redness. Thereafter, increase it again with gold-water, and cook it; the more often this is done, the better.

### MARTIN RULAND’S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY.

**Putrefaction of the Stone** <note>original: *Lapis putrefactio*, *Faulung*</note>. This belongs to the <term>digestion</term> <note>a stage of the process involving slow, constant heat</note> as a principal part of the Work, of which all chemical books are full. It is, however, a true dissolution of natures and all their bonds, both of the form and the substance, so that a new form may be introduced. For without putrefaction nothing can grow; it is accomplished, as if in the shadow of <term>Purgatory</term> <note>original: *Fegfewr*; a metaphorical state of purification through intense heat</note>, in 40 or 46 nights. There the <term>union of the smallest parts</term> <note>original: *unio per minima*</note> occurs, and lasts perhaps 5 months, 156 days, etc. The coarse part dies in the fruits and creates the <term>blackness</term> <note>the *nigredo* stage, signifying the death of the old material</note>, which closes the door to the volatile spirits; thereafter, it passes out of Purgatory into Paradise, where there is Life, Light, and Glory.

**The Weight for the preparation of the Stone** <note>original: *Lapidis conficiendi pondus*</note>.
1. Some take 10 parts of the Water, and one part of the Body.
2. 12 parts of the Water to 1 part Gold <note>represented by the symbol ☉</note>.
3. 4 parts Water to 3 parts Gold.
4. **Lullius** <note>Ramon Lull, a 13th-century polymath and influential alchemical authority</note> takes equal parts.
5. 4 parts Water to one part Gold.
6. **Termis** <note>likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>: 12 parts with one x part.
7. **Theophrastus** <note>Paracelsus</note>: 2 and 7.
8. **Zenon**: 1 part and 3 parts, saying it does not depend especially on the weight, so long as the cooking is performed accordingly, as the practical manual work <note>original: *Handgriff*</note> teaches.
9. 3 parts Salt, 2 parts Mercury, 1 part Sulphur.

**Fermentation and Feeding of the Stone** <note>original: *Lapidis fermentatio, cibatio*</note>. Here Gold <note>original: *Sol*</note> is sown into the "foliated white earth," and it is called **our gold** <note>original: *aurum nostrum*; a term used to distinguish alchemical gold from common gold</note>. They feed the child at first with very little water or milk, and gradually more, as it grows stronger. In the beginning, divide your water into two parts; proceed with the one as has been taught. Thereafter, <term>imbibe</term> <note>the process of soaking a dry substance with liquid until it is saturated</note> the dry matter—ore, ashes, earth, rust, etc.—with the other part, not all at once, but [in]

# MARTIN RULAND’S ALCHEMICAL LEXICON #

...become loose and subtle / so that the other may enter to act upon it / and this is their true **calcination** <term>calcinatio: the process of reducing a substance to a dry powder through heat</term>.

It is turned into an immovable Earth / and is called **coagulation** <term>coagulatio: the thickening of a liquid into a solid</term>, **incineration** <term>incineratio: reducing a substance to ashes</term>, Separation of the Elements / **extraction of the quintessence** <term>extractio de quinta essentia: drawing out the fifth essence, the purest and most potent part of a substance</term>. Then the Body becomes spiritual / light / white / dry / and has [the names] **solution** <term>solutio</term>, **incineration** <term>incineratio</term>, **sublimation** <term>sublimatio</term>, for the **dregs** <term>fæces: the solid remains or impurities</term> are sublimated so that one may obtain the Oil: it is also called the White Killing / Understanding <note>German: *Verstand*; here likely referring to the 'clarification' or 'shining' of the substance</note> / Putrefaction / Expulsion / Boiling / **roasting** <term>assatio</term>.

<margin>**Sublimation of the Stone** <note>original: *Lapidis sublimatio*</note></margin> **Arnold** <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>: Our Sun must be raised from the Earth / onto the Cross in the Air / so that he becomes glorious through suffering <note>An alchemical metaphor where the "Sun" (Gold or the Spirit) is heated and vaporized (the Cross in the Air) to achieve a higher state</note>. **L. However, there are three types of **sublimation** <term>sublimatio</term>. 1. When the Body becomes volatile and united with **Mercury** <term>Mercurio: the fluid/feminine principle of liquidity</term>, even if it does not yet rise. 2. When the **Mercury** is united with the Living Lime <note>original: *lebendigen Kalck*; quicklime or a caustic mineral substance</note> / it becomes more noble and improved. 3. In the color and fixation, according to **Bacchus** <note>likely referring to an alchemical author or a specific Deckname (cover name) used in alchemical literature</note>. **Terniss. in his Epistle**: The red spirit / in the first sublimation / placed through the salted minerals / is of no use to us / that specific purification does not suffice.

### BY MARTIN RULAND, PHYSICIAN AND DOCTOR ###

->Pp 2<-

...perfection arrives when it becomes yolk-yellow / then it is elevated / thin and subtle / and is called Air / red Oil / and all the Names of Birds and Spirits. When it becomes red / then it is called Heaven / Gold / red Sulfur / Carbuncle / and it has every name for whatever is red and precious between Heaven and Earth / such as red Gold / our Gold / Gold-flower / the newborn King / the red Son / **Red Ethelia** <note>original: *Ethelia rubra*; a term for a volatile spirit or vapor</note> / red Earth / tingeing Poison <note>In alchemy, 'poison' often refers to the transformative power that 'infects' or changes base metals into gold</note> / **body of magnesia** <note>original: *corpus magnesiæ*</note> / **Theriac** <term>Thriack: a famous medicinal compound used as a universal antidote; here used metaphorically for the Stone</term> / the pure Body / Ashes / **Elixir** <note>original: *Olixir*</note> / **Kibrit** <note>original: *Kibrick*; an Arabic term for sulfur</note> / incombustible Sulfur / red and fixed Sulfur / **ferment of the Sun** <note>original: *ferment Solis*</note> / **gold of coral** <note>original: *aurũ coralli*</note> / overflowing-redness / red **philosophers' orpiment** <note>original: *auripigment philosophi*</note>: Ore / green vitriol / **Almagra** <note>a deep red ochre or earth</note> / **latten** <note>original: *laton*; a term for brass or an impure metallic body</note> / etc.

<margin>The **Whiteness of the Stone** <note>original: *Lapidis Albedo*</note></margin> When the Water covers the Earth / then the Whiteness is above the Blackness: but when the Air comes to the top / it becomes Saffron-colored / and when the Fire rules / it becomes red. Thus, when the Air floats upward / and the Earth sinks to the bottom / they call that the **Death of the Sun** <note>an alchemical metaphor for the dissolution of the "masculine" metallic principle</note> / and then **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> leads the Soul of the Sun with him into the Heights / and the **body** <note>original: *corpus*</note> lies in the Grave / like a dead man. <margin>The **Blackness of the Stone** <note>original: *Lapidis nigredo*</note></margin> If you make the fire too intense / the Matter becomes red too soon / and evaporates; however, first there appears a redness / a greenness / and almost all colors / before it becomes truly white / it often coagulates and dissolves itself / becoming black and white twice over.

### MARTIN RULAND'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY ###

**Blackness** is a sign of **Putrefaction**, **Marriage**, or **Conception**. In this stage, there appears an island in the sea, which gradually becomes smaller until the **Whiteness** gains the upper hand. This stage is called the **Raven’s Head**, **Pitch**, **Coal**, **Ethelia** <note>A term for a volatile spirit or vapor</note>, **Black Ore**, **Our Ore**, **Antimony** <note>original: *Spießglas*; a metallic element used in the purification of gold</note>, **Deadly Alkali**, **Penny**, and the **Dragon that eats its own tail** <note>The Ouroboros, an ancient symbol of the cyclical nature of the work</note>—which is its water. It is also called **Oath**, **Lead**, **Black Sulfur**, and the **Man**; it possesses every name of all black things on Earth.

Afterward comes the **Peacock’s Tail**, **Swan’s Feathers**; sometimes it appears as if the glass were plated with gold.

<margin>The **Digestion of the Stone** <note>original: *Lapidis digestio*</note>: to cook, ripen, divide, and join together again.</margin>

**Digestion** makes the humors thin and loose, ripens them, and makes them ready for their separation. About this, the philosophers speak marvelously and in many ways, more than about anything else; if you do not follow Nature, they will lead you astray. They perform a fourfold separation of the elements: of the **Oil**, the **Spirit**, the **Earth**, and the **Soul**; and it is all true and all one. Be warned. It is more pleasant to one who understands it, but deceptive to the beginner. *The Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba* (referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts)</note>, leaf 76. When the mixture has occurred, then you have the **Philosophers’ Tincture** <note>original: *tinctura philosophorum*</note> fermented and mixed; it is called **Heart of Salt** <note>original: *cor sussle*</note>, **Gold-Glue** <note>original: *colla auri*</note>, **Poison**, **Glitter of the Sea**, **Ethelia**, **Orpiment** <note>original: *auripigment*; a gold-colored arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, **Kanderich**, **Mercury from Chambar**, **Thick Gold** <note>original: *aurũ spissum*</note>, **Zendria**, **Absemech**, **Magnesia**, **Bismuth** <note>original: *Wißmath*</note>, **Chulut**, **Ore-like**, **Leech** <note>original: *hirudo*</note>, **Eye-Leech**, **Iron-Rust**, and **Stone**, leaf 67. One should not separate the water from the body in the glass, otherwise they would burn and perish.

Leaf 67. He flees from opening the door to him who does not wish to flee <note>This likely refers to the escape of volatile vapors if the vessel is opened prematurely</note>. Leaf 53. The water becomes powder, and the body becomes water. Therefore they call the water **Sand**, and the powder **Gold-Water**.

### THE WRITINGS OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN ###

**Stones named after animals or their parts.**
1. **Thuringian Mouse-stone** <note>original: *Myites*; from the Greek *mys* for mouse</note>, resembling a sitting and huddling mouse; it is full and rounded on its surface. (There is another Mouse-stone mentioned by Georgius Agricola <note>A 16th-century German scholar known as the "Father of Mineralogy"</note> that does not resemble a four-legged mouse, but rather a mussel shell.)
2. **Hessian Mouse-stone**, oblong and ash-colored.
3. **Onyx-stone** <note>original: *Onychites*</note>, which represents the fingernails of the human body, <gloss>Nail-stone.</gloss>
4. **Testicle-stone** <note>original: *Enorchis*</note>, similar to the testicles of living creatures.
5. **Triple-testicle stone** <note>original: *Triorchis*</note>, said to be formed in rivers with triple testicles.

**Geode Stones**, hard, of a reddish color, from Meissen; oblong, the size of an ostrich egg, containing within it hardened sand the color of natural ochre. When placed in water, it emits various hissing sounds. <gloss>A brownish stone containing a fine, yellow, hard sand.</gloss>
2. **The Chemnitz Geode**, of a brownish color; similar to iron-stone, which contains yellow earth within it. <gloss>An iron-colored stone containing yellow earth.</gloss>

**Demotive Fall** <note>original: *Lapsus demotivus*</note> is a seizure resulting in sudden death, more dangerous than an apoplexy.
**Bricks**, <gloss>Iron bricks.</gloss>
**Laterium**, lye, <gloss>Lye or a strong alkaline solution.</gloss>
**Later lectro**, Quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury</note>.
**Laton**, that is, brass <note>original: *aurichalcum*</note>.
**Laton**, <gloss>This is the unclean red body, says the *Clangor Buccinae* <note>A famous alchemical treatise, "The Sound of the Trumpet"</note>. It is the first stage of blackness; when that blackness is removed and it has become red again, it is once more called Laton, and it is composed of the Sun <note>gold</note> and the Moon <note>silver</note>. Thus, there are two Latons, before and after fermentation, and if it does not become white, it is of no use. However, it is whitened by means of *sal anatron* <note>native soda or salt</note>; the blackness is taken from it by the salt when it is cooked for a long time.</gloss>

**Later lictro**, quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>.
**Laton**, that is, brass <note>original: *aurichalcum*; an alloy of copper and zinc</note>.
**Laton** <note>In an alchemical sense</note>. <gloss>This is the impure red body, according to the *Clangor Buccinae* <note>An influential 16th-century alchemical text</note>. It is the "first blackness"; when this is removed and the substance has become red again, it is once more called Laton. It is composed of Sun and Moon <note>Gold and Silver</note>. Thus there are two Latons: one before and one after fermentation. If it does not become white, it is of no use. However, it is whitened by means of *sal anatron* <note>Natron or soda salt</note>; through this salt, the blackness is taken away from it, provided it is heated for a sufficient time.</gloss>

# MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND DOCTOR #

->305<-

**Liquefaction** is the dissolution of a mineral body by the force of a greater fire.
It is either **Simple** or **Probatory**.
**Simple Liquefaction** occurs when a body is melted for no other purpose than to be fused.
**Probatory Liquefaction** occurs when a melted body is tested <note>In this context, "probatus" refers to assaying or metallurgical testing to determine purity.</note>, and the imperfect is separated from the perfect: this is done either through **cupellation** <note>original Latin: *cinericium*. This is the process of refining gold or silver in a furnace using a cupel made of bone ash to absorb impurities.</note> or through **antimony**.
**Liquation** is fusion or melting.
**Resolved Liquid** is that which is liquid from its first entity, or by its own nature. <note>original German: *Was flüssig ist in seiner ersten Materi.*</note>
**Aquilegian Liquor**, that is, distilled wine. <note>original Latin: *vinum destillatum*. While "aquilegius" can refer to the columbine plant, in this alchemical context it refers to "water-gathering" or a specialized distilled spirit like brandy.</note>
**Liquor of Herbs** is made from herbs crushed with their entire substance, enclosed in a glass vessel, and cooked in a water bath <term>balneum maris</term> for several days; the juice is then strained through a cloth and, by the heat of ashes, acquires the thickness of honey.
**Essential Liquor** is that which is extracted from the internal members and is transmuted into flesh and blood. <note>original German: *Ist die feuchte/ so die innern Glieder an sich ziehen/ darauß Fleisch vnd Blut wachst* — "It is the moisture that the internal limbs draw to themselves, from which flesh and blood grow."</note>
**Liquor of Mercury** is the balsam of all things, in which the power of healing resides. Such mercury is very powerful in **tereniabin** and **nostoch**. <note>original German: *Ist der Balsam in allen Dingen...* Tereniabin refers to a medicinal manna or "celestial dew" found on plants. Nostoch (or Nostoc) was believed by alchemists to be a "star-jelly" or "celestial glue" that appeared on the ground after rain, containing concentrated vital energy.</note>
**Liquor of Salt** is the balsam of nature, by which the body is sustained so that it does not putrefy. <note>original German: *Ist der natürlich Balsam/ der den Leib behelt.*</note>
**Liquor**, and the oil of many things, is named by the addition of the substance from which it comes. The liquor of turpentine is its oil.
**Liquor of Gummy Mummy** is the oil of gum. <note>In alchemy, *mumia* refers to the vital essence or a resinous extract, not necessarily an Egyptian mummy.</note>
**Lithanthrax**, stone-coal <note>original Latin/German: *lapideus carbo, ein Steinkol*</note> (just as those stone coals are dug up among us, for example near **Zwickau** <note>original: *Cygneam*. Zwickau was a major coal-mining center in Saxony.</note>), is a species of jet: for it is nothing other than a hardened and boiled out...

# [BY RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.] #

**Liquefaction** is the dissolution of a mineral body by the force of a greater fire.
It is either Simple or Probative.
**Simple liquefaction** is when a body is melted for no other purpose than that it may be cast <note>Or "poured."</note>.
**Probative liquefaction** is when the melted body is tested, and the imperfect is separated from the perfect; and this is done by means of the cupel <note>original: *cinericium*, a vessel made of ashes used to refine precious metals by absorbing base metals</note> or by antimony <note>Antimony was used in the "trial by fire" to purify gold, as it would consume other metals but leave the gold untouched.</note>.
**Liquation** is a casting or a dissolving <note>original: *deliquium*. In alchemy, this often refers to the process where a salt absorbs enough moisture from the air to turn into a liquid.</note>.
**Resolved liquid** is that which is liquid from its "first being" <term>First Being (Prima Ens): the original, fundamental state of a substance before it takes a specific form</term>, or is liquid by its own nature. <gloss>That which is fluid in its first matter.</gloss>
**Aquilegian liquor**, that is, distilled wine <note>A term for high-proof alcohol or "spirit of wine," often used as a solvent.</note>.
**Liquor of herbs** is made from herbs crushed with their entire substance, enclosed in a glass vessel, and cooked in a water-bath <note>original: *balneum maris*, a double-boiler used for gentle, steady heating</note> for several days; the juice, strained through a cloth, acquires the thickness of honey through the heat of ashes.
**Essential liquor** is that which is extracted from the internal organs and transmuted into flesh and blood. <gloss>It is the moisture which the inner limbs draw to themselves, from which flesh and blood grow.</gloss>
**Liquor of mercury** is the balsam of all things, in which the power of healing consists. Such mercury is very potent in tereniabin and nostoch. <gloss>It is the balsam in all things, wherein all healing resides, and this mercury is powerful in tereniabin <note>A kind of manna or sugary dew collected from plants</note> and nostoch <note>A mysterious jelly-like substance found on the ground after rain, which Paracelsians believed was "star-jelly" fallen from the heavens.</note>.</gloss>
**Liquor of salt** is the balsam of nature, by which the body is sustained so that it does not rot. <gloss>It is the natural balsam which preserves the body.</gloss>
**Liquor**, for many things, is the same as "oil," with the addition of the name of the substance it belongs to. Liquor of turpentine is its oil.
**Liquor of gum mummy** is the oil of gum.
**Lithanthrax**, a stony coal, <gloss>a stone-coal</gloss> (just as those stone-coals are dug up among us, for example near Zwickau <note>original Latin: *Cygneam*</note>), is a species of jet: for it is nothing other than a substance hardened and boiled out...

...bitumen under the earth by heat. There are two kinds of such coals: namely, the light and rare ones, so that they sometimes float on water because of the earth being boiled away <note>The "boiling away" refers to the process where volatile components are removed, leaving a porous structure.</note>. ### BY RULAND, PHYSICIAN AND PHILOSOPHER ###

...a thread or net-string drawn through and through, fourfold or eightfold.

**Lye** <note>original Latin: *Lixivium*; German: *Laugen*. A strong alkaline solution used in cleaning and alchemical extractions.</note>.

**Sloping and hollow places**, pits where ash is made.

**Locust** <note>original: *Locusta*</note>, an insect with weak wings, so named from the scorching or "burning" of places <note>original: *uredine locorum*</note>; also called *acris*, *maxax*, *cornops*, *parnops*, *amoluris*, and *acamus*. Known in German as *Hewschreck*, *Juget*, or *Springhan* [grasshopper]. Furthermore, these are the tender extremities or young shoots of branches on trees. Paracelsus <note>The Swiss-German physician and alchemist (1493–1541) who revolutionized medicine with chemical treatments.</note> writes that Saint John used these for food, rather than those venomous winged creatures, as theologians have believed until now. These are the tips or young shoots on trees and herbs.

**Lorcha** is the complete sweetness of the locusts or the young buds, reaching into the very center of their substance.

**Lorindt** is a disturbance or commotion of the waters, accompanied by a sound or resonance which serves as a sign of change, just as a limit of alteration in the firmament <note>In alchemy, the "firmament" often refers to the upper part of the distillation vessel where "metereological" changes occur.</note>.

**Lorus**, that is, **Mercury** <note>The metal Quicksilver, or the alchemical principle of volatility.</note>.

**Lot** is urine.

**Lotium** is the urine of infants.

**Washers** <note>original German: *Seiffner* and *Wäscher*. In a mining and metallurgical context, *Seiffner* specifically refers to those who wash gold or tin from alluvial deposits.</note>.

**Luban** or **Luben**, that is, frankincense; the author refers to Lebanon <note>original: *Libano*; the region famous for its resins and aromatic woods.</note>.

**Slippery** <note>original: *Lubricum*</note>; that which is slick, but not oily like endive.

It is, however, dug out of the earth because the beast covers its urine, either because it envies its use by men or out of an innate sense of shame, as we see other animals do, such as wolves, dogs, and cats. From this urine, the *lyncurius* stone is coagulated by heat, as Pliny testifies in Book 37, Chapters 2 and 3, and Book 8, Chapter 38. I have proven this myself through experience. Why, then, should the urine of the lynx, or indeed of other animals, not be coagulated by natural and earthly heat?

**Magistery** <note>original: *Magisterium*. In alchemy, a "magistery" is a preparation that transforms a substance into a higher state without losing its original bulk or "wholeness," unlike an extract or essence.</note> is a chemical species [prepared] from the whole without extraction, worked and exalted merely by removing external impurities. Thus, all parts of the natural and homogeneous composition are preserved here. But they are so exalted that they nearly reach the dignity of essences. Hence, almost the same quantity or mass is left as nature herself gave; although it cannot always be avoided that some small amount departs along with foreign matter and things clinging to the outside; and sometimes something is even neglected by design for a specific purpose and use. From this, it is understood that what physicists call **alteration** <note>original: *alterationem*; a change in quality rather than essence.</note> is of the greatest importance here.
**Magistery** is of two kinds: one of quality, and another of substance.
**Magistery of Consistency** occurs when, while the essence is preserved, the consistency is changed to a more excellent state. This happens in several ways, not so much so that any nobility is added to the thing itself, but rather that it turns out more commendable and suitable for various uses.
**Magistery of Fixed Things** is when volatile and spiritual bodies are fixed to a state of constancy. "Fixed" is the opposite of "inconstant" and "volatile," and both are judged properly by fire; that which withstands its power is fixed; that which does not is volatile, since it flees from it and flies away like a spirit or a spark. Related to this is that which is hardened from a soft state; therefore, this is also included under the same title.
**Magistery of Scent** occurs when a thing is exalted by its smell. Craftsmen strive for this most especially in works where some unpleasant odor happens during the processing, as in the **burnt smells** <note>original: *empyreumatis*. Referring to the scorched or acrid odors produced when organic substances are heated in closed vessels.</note> of oils, waters, and the like; and then also in those things which otherwise by...

...nature, they have a foul, troublesome odor, or even none at all. Since, however, for the sake of the thing's utility, such qualities are to be exalted <note>The text implies that a substance's natural state—often dull or odorless—must be "exalted" or heightened through alchemical processing to make it useful or potent.</note>.

<margin>The Magistery of Paracelsus is a secret remedy [arcanum] extracted from natural things</margin>
without elemental separation <note>In traditional chemistry, substances were often broken down into the four elements (fire, air, water, earth). Paracelsus argued for a "magistery" that kept the substance whole but removed its "impurities."</note>, by which other things are usually prepared, but only by the addition of other things, from which that which is extracted is separated: *A masterpiece <note>original German: *Meisterstück*; Ruland uses this to translate "Magisterium."</note> is that which is drawn out from natural things without elemental contact, through an additive in which such matter is drawn and kept.*

<margin>The Magistery of weight occurs when a thing is exalted by its weight.</margin>
This is especially required in **gold** and **silver**, and it is one of the marks of perfection; since gold is the heaviest among metals, weight is also added to the external value in coins. If it is lacking, it is compensated by art. A mass of gold or silver that is lighter than it should be is boiled in urine with coralline precipitate <note>term: coralline precipitate; likely a red mercuric oxide used in alchemical refining</note>, or **mercury** <note>original: *hydrargyrus*</note> is rubbed onto the gold or silver until it becomes compatible and of the same color. Or they are boiled in a lye prepared from **sulfur** and **quicklime**; or they are cemented with sulfur or fixed precipitate, or this recipe: ♃ <note>The symbol for Tin or perhaps a specific recipe marker</note>. Mix four [parts], a half-ounce of powdered salt, the same amount of ground brick, and a quarter-ounce of **colcothar** <note>term: colcothar; the red-brown oxide of iron remaining after the distillation of vitriol, often used for polishing or as a pigment</note>. Smear gold leaf with egg white, sprinkle on **lime of the Moon** <note>term: calcis Lunae; silver that has been reduced to a powder through calcination</note>, and once dried, apply the previous powder. Layer these one upon the other, and "cement" them <note>term: cementation; a process of heating a metal in contact with a powdered reagent to change its properties</note> either in a box or between tiles. Gold usually turns white from this. Therefore, apply a coloring agent, hold it with tongs in the fire until it glows white-hot, and then extinguish it in urine.

<margin>The Magistery of color occurs when the color of any thing is brought to the best and highest degree in the sought-after kind.</margin>
Nor indeed is the present color only exalted from a lower to a higher degree, but also that which is in potential, or hidden, is called forth into action or manifest appearance. Sometimes even a foreign color is introduced after the example of that which is more excellent in its kind. If the color is both fixed and constant at the same time, the magistery is more noble.

<meta>This page continues Martin Ruland's Alchemical Lexicon, specifically expanding on the "Magistery"—the process of perfecting or "exalting" a substance. Having previously discussed the Magistery of weight and consistency, Ruland here moves into the Magistery of powders, principles, and the various qualities (hidden, manifest, and sensory) that a chemist can manipulate.</meta>

### ALCHEMICAL LEXICON OF MARTIN RULAND ###

**The Magistery of powders**, that is, of a continuous consistency reduced into a powder, is achieved most especially by methods of calcination <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical state, often turning it into a fine powder.</note>; from which it follows that they are not infrequently called by the name of **lime** <note>original: *calcis*</note>, or commonly **alcohol** <note>original: *alcoolia*; in early chemistry, "alcohol" referred to any extremely fine, purified powder (from the Arabic *al-kuhl*), not just distilled spirits.</note>. This is primarily intended so that the tenacity of the substance may be broken, allowing it to be easily crumbled.

**The Magistery of principles** occurs when a composite structure is resolved once again into its primary principles <note>Referring to the "tria prima" of Paracelsian alchemy: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note>.

**The Magistery of quality** occurs when a thing, having been processed through various forms, is exalted <note>To "exalt" a substance in alchemy means to raise it to a higher state of purity, potency, or perfection.</note>. This happens in two ways: either according to **hidden** or **manifest** qualities.

**The Magistery of the hidden quality** occurs when a perfect exaltation is achieved in those aspects pertaining to the density of the substance, which are only made evident through experience by their effects. If that quality is harmful for use, it is abolished entirely, or perhaps with some loss of the substance itself; in such a case, the perfection sought is not in the object itself, but in the *utility* of the object. In beneficial substances, both the substance and its use are preserved. If a harmful quality cannot be abolished entirely, it is repressed so that the substance may be employed without danger.

**The Magistery of the manifest quality** occurs when a thing is elaborated in its sensible forms. This is as varied as the types of sensory perceptions the Chemist <note>original: *Chymicus*; Ruland uses this to refer to the alchemist or practitioner of the chemical arts.</note> works to exalt within substances. Some of these aspects look more closely at the physical body of nature, while others are more formal.

**The Magistery of flavor** <note>original: *saporis*</note> occurs when the exaltation happens within the taste. Thus, the pharmacy <note>original: *pharmacopœia*</note>, the kitchen, and the wine-cellar can all be supplied by this art. However, the Chemist uses this most especially for correcting acrimony <note>Bitterness or sharp pungency.</note> and for removing qualities pertaining to a burnt taste <note>original: *empyreumatis*; empyreuma refers to the "smell of the fire" or the scorched taste resulting from overheating organic matter in a closed vessel.</note>.

**The Magistery of proper sensibles** occurs when things are exalted by their own sensible qualities. This takes place either in the "first sense," which is necessary for animals, or in those things which are for the sake of improvement. The first sense is **touch**. Therefore, of the primary tactile qualities...

### OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN ###

...of qualities, which are heat, cold, moisture, and dryness; from these the magistery arises.

<term>The Magistery of Sound</term> <note>original: *Magisterium soni*</note> is that by which a sound is corrected by the Chemist. This is achieved most especially in minerals, in which some mark of excellence is perceived from the sound; as in metals, or those substances which threaten danger in fires because of violent spirits breaking out with a noise and exploding everything in their way. <note>In early chemistry, the "clink" or resonance of a metal was a primary indicator of its purity and internal structure. "Violent spirits" refers to high-pressure gases produced during heating that could shatter vessels.</note>

<term>The Magistery of Volatiles</term> <note>original: *Magisterium volatilium*</note> is when a volatile substance is produced from one that was fixed. Related to this is **softening**, whereby a substance is made manageable and ductile, or even fluid (for "soft" is understood a little more broadly here than among the natural philosophers), being produced from that which was rigid, hard, and intractable. The techniques by which this is accomplished are quenching, macerations <note>Soaking a solid in a liquid to soften it or extract components.</note>, incerations <note>The process of adding liquid to a substance, typically by drops, until it reaches a wax-like consistency.</note>, sublimations, solutions, and similar methods. For here, one generally seeks the restoration of consumed or deficient moisture, or the removal of conquered harshness, etc.; whereas in volatility, the goal is for substances to take on the nature of spirits <note>In this context, "spirits" refers to the vaporous or gaseous state of a substance.</note> through the thinning of their essence.

<term>Magic</term> <note>original: *Magia*</note> is a Persian word, in Latin meaning "wisdom." It is twofold: **Natural and Lawful Magic**, which is the mother of true medicine; it is the hidden wisdom of nature, lying concealed and secret even to the very center. If you compare human reason with it, you will find nothing in the latter but sheer foolishness. It is truly a gift of God, through which He grants us the knowledge of supernatural things—not through the inspiration of demons, who possess nothing perfect and teach nothing. The other kind is **Unlawful Magic**, superstitious and forbidden by the entire Christian Church; this they call **Necromancy**, which is execrable and to be tolerated nowhere. From this comes "hidden wisdom."

<term>Metaphysical Magic</term> <note>original: *Magia metaphysica*</note> is an art permitted to Christians, neither sorcerous nor superstitious, but supernatural, through which any hidden secrets are revealed, just as manual labor is the work of mechanical industry.

<term>Large Wooden Chest</term> <note>original: *Magna capsa lignea*</note>, a *Schwángräber* <note>German: literally a "swing-digger," likely referring to a large wooden sifting box or a specific type of container used in mining or large-scale alchemical processing.</note>.

<term>Magnalia</term>, the works of God <note>German: *Gottes Werck*; in Paracelsian philosophy, *Magnalia* refers to the great medicinal or physical virtues that God has placed within nature for the use of mankind.</note>.

**The Magistery of Powders** <note>original: *Magisterium puluerum*</note> consists of a continuous consistency being reduced into a powder. **The Magistery of Quality** <note>original: *Magisterium qualitatis*</note> is when a thing, having been elaborated through its specific forms, is exalted <note>Refined or raised to a higher state of purity and power.</note>. **The Magistery of Occult Quality** <note>original: *Magisterium qualitatis occultæ*</note> is a perfected exaltation in those things which pertain to the thicker part of the substance, and whose effects are only made clear through experience. **The Magistery of Manifest Quality** <note>original: *Magisterium qualitatis manifestæ*</note> is when a thing is elaborated in its sensible forms. This is as many-fold as there are types of sensible qualities which the Chemist occupies himself with exalting. Some of these, however, look more closely at the body of nature, while some are more formal.

**The Magistery of Taste** <note>original: *Magisteriū saporis*</note> is when the exaltation occurs in the flavor. Thus, the pharmacy, the kitchen, and the cellar can all be supplied from this. **The Magistery of the Senses Proper** <note>original: *Magisterium sensilium proprium*</note> is when things are exalted in their own sensible qualities. This occurs either in the primary sense, which pertains to animal necessity, or in those qualities which exist for the sake of "better grace" <note>Aesthetic pleasure or refined presentation.</note>. **The Magistery of Volatiles** <note>original: *Magisterium volatilium*</note> is when a **fixed** substance is made **volatile**. <note>A "fixed" substance resists the fire and does not evaporate; a "volatile" one evaporates or sublimes easily.</note> Akin to this is the magistery of soft things, by which a substance is made manageable, ductile, or even fluid (for "soft" is understood somewhat more broadly here than among natural philosophers) from that which was rigid, hard, and unyielding. For here, one generally seeks the restoration of consumed or deficient moisture, or the removal of conquered harshness, etc. In the case of volatility, however, the goal is for substances to take on the nature of spirits through the thinning of their essence.

**Magic** <note>original: *Magia*</note> is a Persian word, in Latin meaning **wisdom**. It is twofold: First, **Natural and Licit Magic**, which is the mother of true medicine. It is the occult wisdom of nature, lying hidden and concealed even to the very center. If you compare human reason to this, you will find nothing in the latter but sheer foolishness. It is truly a gift of God, through which He displays to us the knowledge of supernatural things—not through the inspiration of demons, who possess nothing perfect and teach nothing. The other kind is **illicit**, superstitious, and prohibited by the entire Christian Church; this they call **Necromancy**, which is accursed and to be tolerated nowhere. From this comes "hidden wisdom."

**Metaphysical Magic** <note>original: *Magia metaphysica*</note> is an art permissible to Christians, neither sorcerous nor superstitious, but supernatural, through which any hidden secrets are revealed, just as a manual task requires mechanical industry.

**Large wooden box** <note>original Latin: *Magna capsa lignea*; original German: *Schwängräder* (flywheels or oscillating wheels).</note>

**Great Works** <note>original Latin: *Magnalia*; "the works of God," original German: *Gottes Werck*.</note>

## The Magnet — that is, Mercury.

The **Magnet** is named after its discoverer, according to Pliny (Book 36, Chapter 16). It is additionally called the Herculean or Heraclean stone. From this comes the proverb: "the Heraclean stone" <note>original: *ἡράκλεια λίθος* (*herakleia lithos*). This refers to something possessing an irresistible or "Herculean" power of attraction.</note>. It is called Heraclean after the city of Heraclea in Lydia; or, as others prefer, after Magnesia, where the most praised magnet is produced. Some believe it takes its name from there. On this subject, Lucretius says:

->*Which the Greeks call "Magnet" from the name of its home,*<-
->*Because its origin is in the native mountains of the Magnetes.*<-

Furthermore, the magnet is called the "siderite stone" because it attracts iron—for in Greek, *sideros* <note>original: *σίδηρος*</note> signifies iron. However, "siderite" is elsewhere used for iron slag, and also for a particular gemstone mentioned in Pliny (Book 37, Chapters 10 and 4). In German, it is called **Magnet** (derived from the Latin), and by the Saxons, it is called a **sailing-stone** <note>original: *ein Segelstein*. This is the "lodestone" used in compasses.</note>. It is the "nautical stone," so named because its use is immense in seafaring, as sailors know; for it is its nature to always turn itself toward the North. 

According to Dioscorides (Book 5, Chapter 93), it is a stone with a color verging on blue (the blue variety is always best), dense, not particularly heavy, and attracting iron by a certain natural power <note>original: *dynami*</note>, just as the *sagda* gem <note>A mythical green stone mentioned by ancient naturalists, said to attract wood.</note> attracts wood, or as jet <note>original: *gagates*</note> and amber <note>original: *succinum*</note> attract chaff and threads. Indeed, iron—which yields to nothing in its stubborn hardness—gives way to the magnet and is acted upon by it. Even more remarkably, iron touched by a magnet then draws other iron; iron, which stands as the tamer of all things, is stayed, held, and held fast in the embrace of the magnet. 

On the contrary—which I often marvel at—garlic and onions are the greatest enemies to the magnet. If the magnet is smeared with their juice, it will not attract iron at all. However, it recovers its strength if dipped in **goat’s blood** <note>A common medieval and Renaissance belief regarding the restoration of occult properties, also associated with the breaking of diamonds.</note>. The magnet stone is found in veins of iron, including in our own mines, such as on the borders of Bohemia at **Schwartzberg**; and without doubt at **Saalfeld** in the ancient iron mines, and at **Goslar** in a semi-collapsed old mine. The magnet even appears in its own distinct vein. So too in Spain (as is reported) and other places.

They teach that there is a great kinship between the **Magnet** and hematite <note>original: *haematite*; literally "bloodstone," an iron oxide mineral.</note>. For among the works of Pliny, the magnet is called hematite, specifically a species of Ethiopian hematite. Moreover, a magnet that has been "burnt"—whether by the natural heat of the earth or by artificial fire—becomes hematite and is sold as such. Pliny (Book 36, Chapter 25), following Sotacus <note>An early Greek writer on stones and gems whose works are largely lost except for fragments in Pliny.</note>, identifies five types of magnet and states that it takes its name from its discoverer, Magnes the Shepherd <note>original: *Magnete Armentario*. Legend states that the nails in his boots and the iron tip of his staff were pulled toward the earth as he walked over a deposit of lodestones.</note>. These are:

**Magnet** <note>original: *Magnes*, *Magneth*</note>. 
1. **Ethiopian.** This is held in the highest esteem. It is found in Ethiopia, in the sandy region of Zinuri, alongside the blood-red hematite magnet mentioned above. This Ethiopian magnet attracts not only iron but also magnets of every other kind. From this comes the verse of Silius <note>Silius Italicus, a Roman poet; the quote is from his epic poem *Punica*.</note>:

> *The Ethiopians came, a race well known to the Nile.*
> *They cut the magnet; the sole honor of that metal*
> *is to draw forged steel toward the nearby rock.*

2. **Magnesian**, from Macedonia, if it is red and black.
3. Found **in Echium of Boeotia**, which is more red than black.
4. Found **around Alexandria and the Troad** <note>The region surrounding ancient Troy.</note>. This type is black, considered "female," and of no practical use.
5. Found **in Magnesia in Asia**. This is white, of no importance, and does not attract iron.

The difference between these lies in whether they are "male" or "female" <note>In ancient mineralogy, "male" stones were typically darker, harder, or more potent, while "female" stones were lighter or weaker.</note>; they also differ in color. For more on the affinity between iron and the magnet, consult the same Pliny (Book 34, Chapter 24), where he also writes that the magnet is found in Cantabria <note>A region in Northern Spain.</note> in scattered bubbles <note>original: *sparsa bullatione*. This likely refers to the nodular or vesicular appearance of the iron ore.</note>; this variety also affects the edge of iron tools, just as other magnets do. Furthermore, the same Pliny teaches that in that same region of Ethiopia where the magnet is found, a stone named **Themanides** <note>Also known as *Theamedes*.</note> is discovered. This stone drives away and rejects all iron, possessing a nature contrary to the magnet. Likewise (Book 36, Chapter 26), he testifies to another property of the magnet: its ability to attract molten glass <note>original: *liquorem vitri*. This refers to the historical use of "magnesia" (manganese) in glassmaking to clear away impurities, which was often confused with the magnet.</note>. Just as the magnet attracts iron and molten glass by its natural power and force <note>original: *dynami*</note>—

Euax <note>A legendary king of the Arabs and author of a famous medieval treatise on the properties of stones.</note> says there is also a species of magnet that attracts flesh, especially human flesh. Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), the German philosopher-theologian known for his scientific observations.</note> says that a black magnet is found in our East Francia <note>Franconia, a region in modern Germany.</note>, appearing as if it were rusty iron burnt with pitch. The Franks should search for this. Doubtless, it will also be found in Thuringia, which borders Francia, if anyone should investigate. Moreover, the same Albert says that in his own time a magnet was found that attracted iron from one corner and repelled it from the other (which Aristotle, if I am not mistaken, mentions). If this is true, it corresponds well to what Pliny writes concerning the stone *Theamedes* <note>A stone from Ethiopia said to have properties opposite to the magnet, repelling iron.</note>. Thirdly, Albert adds that Emperor Frederick <note>Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, known for his curiosity regarding natural wonders.</note> possessed a magnet that did not attract iron, but was itself attracted by the iron.

**Magnesia**, that is, the shell <note>original: *testudo*; literally "tortoise shell," used metaphorically in alchemy for a protective crust or a specific vessel.</note> or sulfur.

It is also silver mixed with mercury, a highly fusible metal that liquefies as easily as wax and possesses a wondrous whiteness; this is called the **Magnesia of the Philosophers**. *When silver and mercury are united into a heavy, liquid metal...*

The Indian Ocean yields precious **pearls**, as does the Red Sea in the Persian Gulf near Arabia, and now the British Sea. A **Pearl**, or **Union** <note>original Latin: *vnio*. In antiquity, large, high-quality pearls were called "unions" because each one was said to be unique, with no two being exactly alike.</note>, is nothing other than the offspring or birth of the pearl-bearing shell. For these shells, at a certain time of year when the generative hour of the season stirs them, open themselves with a kind of gaping yawn. They thirst for dew as if for a husband; they gape with desire for it, and long to be filled by a dewy conception.

Soon, when the lunar drippings fall, they swallow the dew—the longed-for moisture—with their womb (as it were) wide open, and thus become pregnant. Afterwards, they give birth to **Pearls** according to the quality of the dew conceived. If they have conceived pure dew, a pearl of wonderful whiteness appears; but if they have conceived turbid dew, the offspring also becomes soiled. Pearls also turn pale when the sky threatens storms; if they are conceived when the shells are open in seasonable weather, the pearls grow large. If it lightens at the time of mating, the shells snap shut, and "unions" are born small in proportion to their "fasting" <note>This implies that because the shell closed early, it could not take in enough "celestial food" or dew to grow the pearl to full size.</note>. If it thunders, the frightened shells suddenly contract and then give birth to miscarriages, which they call *physemata* <note>original Greek: *physemata*, meaning "inflations" or "bubbles." These were hollow or light pearls of poor quality.</note>.

They also say that if frequent thunder is heard after their conception, the shells spit out the "unions" into the rivers, and thus they are frequently found in rivers, as some claim happens among the sands of the **Moselle** <note>The Moselle River, flowing through France, Luxembourg, and Germany, was historically famous for its freshwater pearl mussels.</note>. Furthermore, if at the time of mating a ray of the sun falls into the gaping shell along with the dew, the pearls are stained with redness, just as we see occur. Therefore, at sunrise, the shells submerge themselves; for they feel that they would otherwise become reddish and then, as it were, perish.

Finally, a pearl becomes clearer if the shells receive the "seeding" of the morning air—that is, the dew—rather than that of the evening. So great is the affinity of the heaven and the shell in this mating with the dew, which is, as it were, the seed of the air. Not without reason are pearls dedicated to **Venus** <note>The goddess Venus (Aphrodite) was said to have been born from the sea foam in a shell, linking her essence to the pearl.</note>, on account of this miraculous mating. Moreover, it is called a "union" because no two are ever found exactly alike. Its merit lies in its whiteness, size, weight, roundness, and smoothness. While in the water, every pearl is soft, just like **coral**; once removed into the air, it immediately hardens and becomes a stone. But concerning "unions" and the nature of these shells...

### White Marbles
1. White Lunense marble from Tuscany <note>Known today as Carrara marble, prized since Roman times.</note>, **a white marble stone**.

3. Another Laconic marble, blackish-green.

### Gray Marbles
1. Gray Hildesheim marble, which smells like burnt horn.
