<meta>This page continues Martin Ruland’s alphabetical dictionary of alchemical terms, moving from the entry on the onyx stone into a detailed classification of different types of "oils" (olea) and the methods of their preparation, such as distillation, fixation, and decoction.</meta>

### MARTIN RULAND’S DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY ###

**Spelt-grain oil** <note>original German: *Dinckelkornöl*</note> is made in two ways: namely, with a glowing metal plate, and through descending distillation <note>Distillation by descent involves heating the substance from above so the oil flows downward into a receiver, often used for heavy or thick oils</note>.

**Oil of sulfur** <note>original: *Oleum sulphuris*</note> consists of sublimated or elevated vapors from prepared sulfur.

**Fixed oil** <note>original: *Oleum fixum*</note> is that which, from substances dissolved and filtered until pure, has been reduced to an oily consistency, primarily through the frequent drawing off of spirit of wine. For we call "fixing" here the process of producing an oily and stable consistency from a diluted and thin one by drawing off or digesting the wateriness. However, it is necessary for substances to be dissolved in a liquid so that, once the thick parts are separated by filtration, the thin parts are deposited into the moisture, from which they are brought back through such fixation. The common practice is to dissolve the substance in some liquid, using maceration, boiling, or liquefaction <term>deliquio: the process where a solid substance absorbs atmospheric moisture and dissolves into a liquid state</term>, either alone or with other substances, etc. If the solution contains any dregs, strain it until it is clear; afterward, spirit of wine is poured on and they are digested together; then the spirit is drawn off again, and this is repeated until the oily consistency is satisfactory.

**Oil is either Distilled or Secret.**

**Distilled oil** <note>original: *Oleum destillatum*</note> is that which is extracted through distillation: and this is done either by ascent <note>rising as vapor</term> or by descent <note>flowing downward</note>, whether the oil was inherent in the substance or previously absorbed. Indeed, all absorbed oil is drawn out by distillation alone. Inherent oil, however, is also separated by other methods.

**Palestinian oil** <note>original: *Oleum palestinum*</note> is Vinegar <note>original German: *Essig*</note>.

**Descending distilled oil** <note>original: *Oleum stillatitium descensorium*</note> is that which is produced by distillation through descent.

**Oil extracted and boiled out by decoction** <note>original: *Oleum per elixationem extractum, & excoctum*</note> is that which is extracted by boiling. This is done either by boiling in a liquid or by the use of a dry flame.

**Oil from roasting** <note>original: *Oleum ex assatione*</note> is made by a dry flame, when substances are exposed by themselves to fiery heat without any solvent <term>menstruum: a solvent used to extract essence from a solid</term>, and they release the oil, which is collected by whatever means possible. This occurs in two ways: by roasting and by combustion.

### WORKS OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN ###

**Burning oil** <note>original: *Oleum ardens*</note> is the oil of tartar refined to the highest degree <note>original German: *corrigirt weinstein Oel*. Tartar is the potassium bitartrate crust found in wine barrels; its "oil" was a highly prized chemical solvent</note>.

**Gilded oil of vitriol** <note>original: *Oleum vitrioli aurificatum*</note> is that which has been skillfully sweetened with gold <note>original German: *Vitriol, Oel mit Goldsüß gemacht*. In alchemy, "sweetening" often refers to removing the corrosive or acidic nature of a substance, here combined with the properties of gold</note>.

**Colcothar oil** <note>original: *Oleum colcotharinum*</note> is the red oil derived from vitriol <note>original German: *das rot Oel auß Vitriol*. Colcothar is the brownish-red residue of iron oxide left after the distillation of sulfuric acid</note>.

**The oiliness of things** <note>original: *Oleitas rerum*</note> is the sulfur present in all things <note>According to the "Tria Prima" theory of Paracelsus, Sulfur represents the principle of combustibility, oiliness, and the soul</note>.

**Olympic spirit** <note>original: *Olympicus spiritus*</note> is the "star" or astral force within man, which enables him to project a shadow of himself <note>original German: *Das Gestirn im Menschen / das da macht / daß er ein Schatten von ihm gibt*. This refers to the Paracelsian idea of the "sidereal body" or astral self that connects humans to the heavens</note>.

**Oly** is the moisture or the slime of metals; it flows atop the solvent <term>menstruum: a general term for a solvent used to dissolve solids</term> once they have been dissolved.

**Onyx** is a gemstone which, according to Pliny <note>Book 37, Chapter 6 of his *Natural History*</note>, represents the whiteness of a fingernail <note>The name "Onyx" comes from the Greek word for fingernail</note>; however, it is of many species. At times it reflects the color of Chrysolite, Sard, or Jasper. Indian onyx is sometimes fiery, black, or horn-colored, surrounded by white veins, appearing like an eye with oblique veins intersecting. There are also Onyxes in Arabia with white bands and black bodies; to see how they differ from the Indian ones, consult the aforementioned passage in Pliny. From this we get the name **Sardonyx**, as if it were "Sarda" <note>a reddish-brown stone</note>, which name it shares with the onyx; they say that with the Sardian stone present, the onyx is bound. Furthermore, they say that onyx is formed by the petrification of the tears of a tree. When burned in a fire, it gives off an odor and appears with various impressions and forms. Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century scholar and alchemist</note> also distinguishes species of onyx as black, reddish, and white; all of these, however, when rubbed, dissolve into a substance that resembles the human fingernail. They say that onyxes excite sadness and fears. For they stir up the melancholic humors, provoke quarrels and turbulent dreams, and increase saliva in children. However, the Sarda stone joined to it—that is, the **Sardonyx**—softens that power and makes men chaste and modest.

**Onyx 1.** A pure, transparent, horn-colored chalcedony named for its location.

-> ### OF MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN ### <-

**Viper-stone** <note>original Latin: *Echites*; German: *ein Natterstein*</note>, which has spots like a viper: although it may also be considered a species of **Serpentine** <note>original Latin: *Ophites*</note>. It is neither the foreign **Dragon-stone** <note>original: *draconites*</note>, nor our own native kind—**the Dragon-stone, or our Snake-stone** <note>original: *der Drachenstein/oder unser Schlangen-stein*</note>—which is said to be formed from the brains of dragons or serpents, or from their coagulated foam. In short, it is called Serpentine solely because of its color—**a Snake-stone** <note>original: *ein Schlangenstein*</note>—because its color resembles that of serpents.

That species is entirely marked with ashen and blackish lines, just as our **water-snakes** <note>original: *Chelydri*</note> are in color. Near the mouth of the Tanger <note>original: *Tangra*, a river in Germany</note>, where the royal seat of **Charles IV** <note>Holy Roman Emperor, 1316–1378</note> once stood, there is a church within the fortress adorned with various gems, in which the walls on all sides shine with such Serpentine; a variety of this is the Viper-stone, which bears the markings of a viper.

There is also another species of Serpentine that more closely approaches the form of a snake, for it possesses scales like a serpent. It is a crusty stone. It is found in many places in Saxony, around **Hildesheim**. It appears quite dull, much like horn.

There is yet a third species of Serpentine found on the banks of the Elbe near the mouth of the Tanger. It is a thin and oblong stone, shaped exactly like a serpent, as if a snake had hardened into stone; inside it is black with a shimmering blue color, while the outside is whitish.

**Pliny** (Book 36, Chapter 7) teaches that Serpentine <note>original: *Ophiten*</note> also received its name from the spots of serpents. He describes two kinds: a soft white one and a hard black one. He notes that vessels and jars are made from the white variety; likewise, vessels could be made from our Serpentine if someone were to attempt it.

According to **Dioscorides** and also Pliny, Serpentine is beneficial for **lethargy** <note>a state of profound drowsiness or unconsciousness</note>, headaches, and the bites of serpents. Thus, Serpentine is of two types: regarding its markings and lines, and regarding the very shape of the serpents themselves. Furthermore, the ancient astrologers dedicated Serpentine to the planet **Saturn**.

**Workman** <note>original: *Operarius*; German: *Schomper*</note>.
**Refining-cover** <note>original: *Operculum*; German: *Treibhut*. A lid used in the cupellation process of refining metals</note>.
**Cover of a flask** <note>original: *Operculum ampullæ*</note>, a **Helm** or **Alembic** <note>the cap of a distilling apparatus</note>.
**The plug of the upper hole of the bellows-frame** <note>original: *Operculum superioris foraminis tabulati follium*; German: *Spund*</note>.
**Mineral spirits** <note>original: *Operimethioliin*</note> is the spirit of minerals, or the **smoke of the ore** <note>original: *den Rauch von Ertz*</note>.

**Opals** <note>original Latin: *Opali*</note> have their true motherland in India. It is a precious gem, for in it appears the subtle fire of the carbuncle <note>a red gemstone, often garnet or ruby</note>, the shining purple of the amethyst, and the green sea of the emerald. It also has certain distinct species. Some opals match the colors of orpiment <note>a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, others the burning flame of sulfur, and others the fire of ignited oil. Its size is that of a hazelnut. There are also certain defects in opals: if the color fades into the appearance of crystal or hail, or into the flower of the heliotrope herb, or if salt-like spots, roughness, or other visual blemishes are present. It is also recorded that opals are born in Egypt, Arabia, and in Pontus, but these are of very low value. They are also found in Galatia, Thasos, and Cyprus, but while these shine better, they are rough: see Pliny, Book 37, Chapter 6.

**Orale**, that is, a vessel.

**Orbis**, a drum or pulley; the disk or wheel upon which the ropes run <note>original German: *Scheibe/Scheiben darauff die Seil gehen*</note>.

**Orbis saxeus**, a round stone <note>original German: *Rondtstein*</note>.

**Orbiculi**, the valves or "suckers" of a pump <note>original German: *Pumpen Soge*</note>.

**Oriens**, the East; red oil; the Father; red vitriol; Ruby; the measure; salt of urine; the Sun; golden sulfur; the Ram <note>the zodiac sign Aries</note>; Summer; the Crab <note>the zodiac sign Cancer</note>; Tartar; Ashes; Ore; Wine; and Oil of Iron. <note>In alchemy, the "East" or "Rising" refers to a state of completion, redness, or the solar principle.</note>

**Ordoleum**, also written as *ordeolum*; a small abscess or swelling resembling a barley-corn; a stony growth like a grain of barley in the eyebrows <note>original German: *ein stein Geschwär/wie ein Gerstenkörnlein in Augbrauen*</note>.

**Orexis**, a burning sensation <note>heartburn</note> excited by tartar <note>original German: *der Sodtbrandt*</note>.

**Orichalcea fila**, brass brushes <note>literally "brass threads"</note>.

**Orizeum**, that is, gold.

**Orizeum foliatum**, gold leaf; gold beaten into very thin plates with a hammer <note>original German: *geschlagen Gold*</note>.

**Orizeum præcipitatum**, precipitated gold; this is gold reduced to its saffron <term>crocum: a fine, reddish-orange powder produced through calcination or precipitation</term> by the aid of the saffron of mercury.

**Oriza**, that is, rice.

**Orms**, that is, a hen.

**The mouth of the furnace**, the eye <note>original German: *Auge*</note>.

**The spiritual mouth**, the vent or bung-hole that catches the wind <note>original German: *Spundt/so den Wind facht*</note>.

**Ostracites** takes its name from oysters, though it is similar to a shell, being crusty and splittable into thin plates. Pliny, in Book 36, Chapter 19, states—as does Dioscorides—that one species of it is said to resemble a shell and is used in place of pumice stone. Furthermore, in Book 37, Chapter 10, he says that the *ostracea* or *ostracites* is harder than this first shell-like kind, and that the oyster gave it both its name and its appearance. He says another species of it is similar to agate <term>achates: a translucent variety of quartz</term>, except that Agate becomes greasy when polished with more force. Thus, there are three distinct species of *ostracitidis*: one that resembles a shell, a second that resembles an oyster, and a third that resembles Agate. The first, which is like a shell, is found with splittable veins in the mountains of Saxony that have been naturally burnt by fire. The second, which is like an oyster, is also found in the cliffs of Saxony. According to Dioscorides, these *ostrachites* are very effective for stanching menstrual flow, treating breast inflammations, and healing spreading ulcers <term>nomas: gangrenous or "eating" ulcers that spread rapidly</term>.

**Osoror**, that is, opium.

**Ossa paralleli** is a universal medicine for gout <note>original Latin/German: *podagra / ein sondere Artzney zu allen Podagra*</note>.

**Transplanted Masterwort** <note>original: *Ostrutium*</note>, that is, Angelica <note>a plant highly valued in the Middle Ages for its medicinal properties, believed to be a gift from an angel</note>.

**Othan**, the bird <note>original German: *Vogel*</note>, or the Mercury of the Philosophers <note>in alchemy, birds often symbolize volatile substances that "fly" or sublimate during heating</note>.

**The Egg**, that is, the blessed stone <note>the *Lapis Benedictus* or Philosopher's Stone</note>.

**The Philosophical Egg**, or the Egg of Hermes, is a vessel shaped like an egg used in philosophical <note>alchemical</note> operations.

**Oxos**, that is, vinegar; Palestinian oil, which is also vinegar.

**Oxy**, that is, sharp or acidic.

**Ozeman**, that is, the white of eggs.

**Ozo**, that is, Arsenic.

# THE WORKS OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN #

Those who wish to praise Man rightly have called him a **microcosm** <note>original Latin: *microcosmum*, meaning "little world," the idea that the human body reflects the structure of the universe</note>; they have compared him to the Elements, Heaven, Earth, Stars, and all creatures, as well as to the state of marriage and the birth of children, as the old saying goes:

> The Sun is his father, **Noah**, the **heavens** <note>original: *Noha, cœlum*</note>.
> The Moon is his mother, Aretia, **Noah’s** wife, or **Vesta** <note>Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth; in alchemy, she often represents the earth or its internal fire.</note>.
> The Wind carries him in its belly, the **air and spirit** <note>original: *aer, spiritus*</note>.
> The Earth nourishes him, etc.

For just as the Sun, with its warmth and power, is like a father to all growing things, and the Moon with its moisture is the mother, the Air must contain and carry everything, and the Earth must provide nourishment.

But there is something special in this Work, for the metallic Sun is truly the Father and provides the male seed. The Moon is the true Mother and provides the female seed. The Wind and Air must lift and guide it, as **Hermes** says <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the *Emerald Tablet* and the foundations of alchemy are attributed.</note>: Our **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> rises in the glass with the air; the Earth lies below and captures within itself the soul and spirit, so that a perfect Child and King may be born.

2. The Father is our **Sulfur** <note>original German: *Schwefel*</note>; the Mother is our **Mercury**, who carries the Sulfur in her body. For the Woman is pregnant with a red child—that is, a child hidden within the white. When it is born, the red becomes visible again, and the Woman is transformed into a red Man, becoming an **androgynus** <note>An "androgynous" or hermaphroditic being, symbolizing the perfect union of the male (Sulfur/Sun) and female (Mercury/Moon) principles in the alchemical Stone.</note>.

3. The Man, says **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century Arab alchemist Ibn Umail, whose "Chemical Tables" were widely cited in the Renaissance.</note>, has no wings, while the Woman flies and is pulled down from above when she is **coagulated** <term>Coagulation: the process of turning a volatile or liquid substance into a solid; in alchemy, this is "fixing" the spirit into a stable form</term>. The Moon is dark, which is why it is called **shadow** <note>original Latin: *umbra*</note>. The Woman is bright and is called **radiance** <note>original: *radius*</note>, a glow or ray of the Sun. Draw the shadow out of the radiance—that is, coagulate it—and make it bright.

<summary>This page explains the symbolic "parentage" of the alchemical Stone, identifying the Sun as the father (Sulfur) and the Moon as the mother (Mercury). It describes the process of "coagulation" and the creation of the philosophical "androgynus" through the union of these cosmic principles.</summary>
<keywords>microcosm, Sulfur and Mercury, Hermes Trismegistus, Senior Zadith, androgynus, coagulation, Emerald Tablet, alchemical generation</keywords>

# MARTIN RULAND'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY #

4. The Man is called Lead: Mars is the Man, and the Woman is Venus and Arsenic. The Man is from the Woman, and the Woman is from the Man, just as it was with Eve <note>The author uses the Biblical story of Genesis to explain the chemical separation and recombination of substances.</note>; the sleeping Adam lost his ribs, but he was not yet glorified because he did not die. Only after death and the Resurrection is he transfigured. So it is with our Adam: in his first sleep, he gives forth Eve; afterward, in the second washing <note>original Latin: *lotio*, a stage of purification in alchemy where the substance is "cleansed" by liquid</note>, he dies and rises again in glory, and then no Eve can ever be taken from him again. S. Ternesi <note>Likely a reference to an alchemical authority or specific manuscript.</note> says: The Father is the calcination <note>original: *calnatio*, likely a shorthand for *calcinatio*, the process of heating a substance until it reduces to powder</note>, and the Mother is the solution. The Fountain is his mother, and yet he is older than the fountain because he has been made perfect.

**Patias**, that is, a scale, a **metallic flake** <note>original German: *Metallschap*</note>; *lepida* is the same.
**Pedagra** is tartar <note>original: *tartarus*; in alchemy, this refers to the hard crust or sediment found in wine casks, often used as a source of potassium bitartrate</note>.
**Pegernus**, that is, the pilgrim or foreigner, which is Mercury.
**Pegernus** is **lime made from the whitest shells of the sea** <note>original German: *Kalck von den allerweissesten Ohren der Meerschen*, literally "lime from the whitest ears of the sea-creatures," likely referring to abalone or similar iridescent shells</note>.
**Pelecanus** <note>The Pelican</note> is a circulating vessel, named after the form of a Pelican that pecks at its own breast to restore its young with its own blood <note>A common alchemical allegory for a vessel that allows liquid to evaporate and then flow back down, "nourishing" the base material</note>. It has a wide belly that tapers into a narrow neck, which then turns back and re-enters the belly. This vessel has a tube at the bottom through which the liquid is poured; once the liquid is inside, it is closed with the Seal of Hermes <note>an airtight seal</note> and moved to the heat.
**Pelicide**, that is, cooked honey; also called *pelude*.
**Penates** are said to be the spirits of the element of fire and of the heavens, the indwelling ones, those born within us, the guardians of the larder, the household gods, the spirits of the hearth, the seasonal spirits, the honey-sweet ones: **the spirits of the fire or household gods.**
**Penetratio** <note>Penetration</note>, that is, submersion.
**Pentacula** <note>Pentacles</note>, amulets, signs or seals hung around the neck, believed to protect against evil spirits and any sort of spell: they are also called *periapta*, *apotropaics*, or *parartemata*: **that which one hangs about oneself against spirits and diseases.**

# THE LEXICON OF MARTIN RULAND, DOCTOR OF PHILOSOPHY AND MEDICINE #

**Perdonium**, herbal wine <note>original: "vinum ex herbis," German: "Kräuterwein." A medicinal wine infused with herbs.</note>.
**Perdettæ**, small yellow turnips <note>original German: "kleine gelbe Ruben."</note>
**Periodus** is the height or the muscle of life, the pulse running through the body <note>original German: "die Mauß/das Leben/das hin vnd wider im Leib laufft." In early medicine, "musculus" (little mouse) was often used to describe the movement of muscles or the pulse under the skin.</note>.
**Perones, water-boots** <note>original German: "Waſſerſtiffel." Likely heavy, waterproof footwear for laboratory or field work.</note>.
**Perpurgare, to burn clean** <note>original German: "Brennen." To thoroughly purify a substance through fire.</note>.
**Pertica, a staff.**
**Perticæ, hedge-poles** <note>original German: "Heckſcheiter." Stakes or poles used in fencing or for support.</note>.
**Pes metallicus, a work-foot** <note>original German: "Werckſchuch." A specific unit of measurement used by miners and metalworkers.</note>.
**Pes lucuſtæ**, that is, the foot of a locust, also called the foot of a *bruista*, which refers to Yemen alum <note>original: "alumen Iameni." Alchemists often used animal metaphors like "locust's foot" to refer to specific mineral formations or salts.</note>.
**Petra ſanguinaria**, that is, hematite <note>A iron-oxide mineral often called "bloodstone" because it appears red when powdered or immersed in water.</note>.
**Peucedanum**, which is wild angelica.
**Phanlec**, that is, iron <note>original Latin: "ferrum." An alchemical synonym for the metal Mars.</note>.
**Phantaſmata** are spirits found in deserted places and around the seashores; they are not diabolical, but very often speak with imaginative people. They sometimes cause terror and take their origin from the imaginations of men, such as those that the living have about or with the dead. **Wild spirits in the wilderness; they are not devils, according to the opinion of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus refers to Paracelsus. This entry reflects his theory that human imagination can give birth to "astral" entities or phantasms that are separate from traditional demons.</note>, but only the sons of the devil.**
**Phiala** is a glass vessel with a belly rounded like a sphere, with a slender neck rising to a great height; its use is frequent in coagulations and solutions <note>A vial or long-necked flask, a primary tool in the alchemical laboratory for the processes of thickening or dissolving substances.</note>.
**Phibit**, that is, rapacious or greedy.
**Phlotron**, a type of flow generated from the midriff <note>original Latin: "fluxus ex cooſtro," German: "ein Fluß in Mittel deß Leibs leiſt." Likely refers to a bodily discharge or "catarrh" originating in the center of the torso.</note>.
**Phœnix**, the quintessence of fire, or the most celebrated Philosopher’s Stone <note>The Phoenix is one of the most famous symbols in alchemy, representing the final stage of the Great Work: the Stone that has been "reborn" from its own ashes through fire.</note>.
**Phionitides**, persecutors or natural enemies who lay snares for one another and pursue each other unto death—just as the Stork pursues frogs, the cat pursues mice, or the spider pursues toads. **Whatever seeks to take the life of another, as dogs do to cats, or birds of prey do to other birds.**

# THE LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND #

**Green Phrasium**, that is, the flower of copper <note>original: "flos æris." Usually refers to verdigris or the green oxidation on copper surfaces.</note>.

**Phthisis**, or **consumption** <note>original: "tabes," German: "Abnemen deß Leibs/Schwindsucht."</note>, a wasting away of the body, the "drying-out" sickness, or a self-consumption. In other respects, **atrophy** is almost the same thing: a cessation of nourishment arising from fear or excessive greed; the wasting and falling away of the body until it is emaciated and the person can no longer flourish <note>original German: "grünen," literally "to turn green," implying the loss of youthful vitality.</note>.

**Physiognomy** is the art by which a person’s nature is known from the condition of the body; the art of natural recognition used to judge and understand a person based on their physical form.

**Pila**, a pillar <note>original German: "Pfeiler."</note>.

**Pilae**, pouches or pockets <note>original German: "Taschen."</note>.

**Pilizenii**, the white hairs growing around the tail and neck of a hare; the white patches found around a hare's neck.

**Pilosella**, or **Mouse-ear** <note>original: "auricula muris." A common name for Hawkweed, used in traditional medicine.</note>.

**Pilos**, that is, **clay** <note>original: "argilla," German: "Lått."</note>; moist earth or "fresh hearth."

**Pinguedinosa**, that is, any kind of fatty substances.

**Pilum**, a pump-rod <note>original German: "Pompenstange."</note>.

**Pilum**, a pestle <note>original: "pistillum," German: "Stößel."</note>.

**Pilum of the smelters**, a pounding-beam or mace <note>original German: "Stoßbaum/Stoßkolb." A heavy tool used in the refining process.</note>.

**Pilum**, a pole or beam <note>original: "tignum," German: "Gestenge."</note>.

**Pilum without teeth**, a club or mace <note>original German: "Kolbe."</note>.

**Pilum**, or the head of a pestle, with which copper cakes are broken <note>original German: "Kufferbrecher."</note>.

**Pirstein**, a type of copper cake or ingot <note>original: "panum æreorum species." A metallurgical term for a specific stage of copper smelting.</note>.

**Pisare**, that is, to strain or filter through a cloth or otherwise.

**Pistare**, that is, to pound or crush.

**Pistillum**, that is, a small pestle or a mortar-pestle.

**Liquid Pitch**, that is, turpentine <note>original: "terebinthina," German: "Glorian."</note>.

**Pixari**, that is, to treat with pitch.

**The plain of the mountain**, the face or flat surface of a mineral vein <note>original German: "Fleche eines Gangs."</note>.

**Plumbum** (Lead) is "the Man" and the "Impure Body." In our art, it is also called **Astrob** and **Our Copper** <note>original: "æs nostrū." In alchemy, "Lead" often refers to the raw, unrefined state of the Prime Matter, while "Our Copper" distinguishes the alchemist's material from common metal.</note>; it is our ore.

RYLANDI PHIL. ET MEDICI.
Zz 2

**Lead of Alkali** is a **Hermaphrodite** <note>In alchemy, a "hermaphrodite" refers to a substance that contains both "male" (sulfur/active) and "female" (mercury/passive) qualities, or one that can act as both an acid and a base.</note>.

**Lead** is assigned by chemists to **Saturn**, and it is called by his name. It is a metallic body: leaden-colored, earthy, heavy, and possessing very little whiteness. It contains a great deal of earthy substance, and through washing it is turned into tin. From this, it is clear that tin is somewhat more perfect than lead. Furthermore, lead has more of the substance of fixed sulfur in its composition than **Jupiter**—that is, tin. 

For lead is an unclean, imperfect body created from **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo," literally "living silver" or mercury.</note> that is impure, non-fixed, earthy, and dreggy; it appears somewhat white on the surface but is red within its hidden nature. It is also procreated in part from a type of combustible sulfur. It lacks purity, fixation, color, and the ability to endure fire <note>original: "ignitio."</note>. In short, it is made of a bad, coarse, foul-tasting, and stinking quicksilver of weak virtue; it is as if a **menstrual mother** <note>Alchemists used the term "menstrual" to describe the base, impure mercury used as the "womb" for the birth of metals.</note> were joined by a **leprous or livid husband** (the sulfur); from this union, that cold Saturnine son is born, whose name is lead. 

Note, however, that **pure lead** <note>original German: "gediegen Bley," meaning native lead found in a metallic state.</note> of any color is not found in mines; nor have I read of, seen, or heard of it being found in mines. The lead that is smelted is of three kinds: namely, **black lead**, which is true lead; then **ash-colored lead**, and **white lead**. Regarding **black lead** <note>original German: "von dem Bley."</note>, which we are discussing now, it is called *molybdos* by the Greeks <note>original Greek: "μόλυβδος."</note>. It is made and smelted from **galena** <term>Galena: Lead sulfide, the most important ore of lead.</term> (of which more later), or it is made from **pyrite** <term>Pyrite: A sulfide mineral; while usually iron-based, Ruland likely refers to lead-bearing ores associated with it.</term>, which has already been discussed.

Furthermore, for the method of making **washed lead** <note>original: "plumbum elotum."</note> and **burnt lead** <note>original: "ustum."</note>, and to learn their powers in medicine, consult **Dioscorides**, Book 5, Chapter 48. Washed lead is already available in certain pharmacies for use against inflamed ulcers and cancer. Some pharmacies lack it entirely. However, burnt lead has more effective powers than washed lead. Potters use it extensively for painting <note>glazing</note> their vessels. The **slag or dross of lead** <note>original German: "der Bleyſchlacken."</note> can also perform the same actions as burnt lead.

# LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND

...of which there is a great abundance at Goslar <note>A historic mining town in Germany famous for the Rammelsberg mines.</note>, and likewise in Meissen <note>original: "Misnia," a region in Saxony known for its mineral wealth.</note> at the workshops where metals are smelted. Consult Pliny, Book 34, Chapter 16, and the chapters following.

**Ash-colored lead** <note>original: "Plumbum cinereum."</note> is a species of lead called by the Germans **Bismuth, Mythan, or Counterfeit.** <note>original: "Wyßmut/mythan, oder Conterfeyn." Ruland is describing Bismuth, which was often mistaken for a type of lead or tin. "Counterfeit" refers to its use in alloys that mimic silver.</note> It differs from black and white lead in its color. It is, so to speak, a metal of its own kind. It is more noble than lead, yet inferior to silver, and stands as a middle ground between the species of lead and silver itself. The ore from which it is smelted is similar to galena <note>A natural mineral form of lead sulfide, the primary ore of lead.</note>, from which black lead is cooked; but it differs from galena in that it stains the hands of the person handling it with blackness, unless it is entirely solid. Furthermore, when it is solid, it is not brittle like galena, but can be cut. It is also somewhat darker than the second species of raw silver, which is lead-colored, although the ore of ash-colored lead itself not infrequently contains some silver. In whatever place it is dug up, it usually signifies that silver lies beneath; and for that reason, it is called the "Roof of Silver" <note>original: "tectum argenti."</note> by miners. From this is smelted what they call **Counterfeit, Bismuth, or Mythan.** From this, various things are now crafted and cast, just as from silver—such as cups, vessels, and other items. A type of blue pigment is also prepared from it. The Arabs were entirely ignorant of this metallic substance, as were the ancient chemists; otherwise, they would have recognized more metallic bodies.

Just as black lead is called by the Germans **Lead** simply, or **Black Lead** <note>original: "Bley oder Schwartzbley."</note>, so white lead is called by them **White Lead or Tin.** <note>original: "Weißbley oder Zin."</note> However, our white lead is improperly called **Tin** <note>original: "stannum."</note>; they are not the same thing, though until now people have claimed that *stannum* and white lead (**our Tin**) were the same. *Stannum* is one thing (which will be discussed in its own place), and our white lead—**our Tin**—is another; it is, as it were, something purer and more perfect than black lead. Pliny called this *cassiterium*, named after the Cassiteride islands <note>The "Tin Islands," likely referring to the British Isles, specifically Cornwall.</note>, where it was first discovered by...

**Mydacritum.** <note>original: "Mydacryto." A term used by Pliny the Elder to refer to certain types of tin ore or lead-like minerals.</note> It is smelted among us now just like black lead, both from pyrite <note>A common iron sulfide mineral with a metallic luster.</note> and from galena <note>original: "auß dem Kyß vnd Glantz." Lead sulfide, the primary ore of lead.</note>. It is also cooked from small black stones varied with whiteness (as Pliny also states in Book 34, Chapter 16), which black stones are found in large sizes in some places, but sometimes are found only as sand. Within these black stones, pyrite and a sandy type of rock and other mixtures are also found; sometimes they are mixed together, and sometimes they remain distinct. Pliny writes that white lead <note>original: "plumbum candidum." In the ancient and Renaissance world, this term specifically referred to Tin.</note> occurs in Britain, and likewise in Galicia <note>A region in northwest Spain.</note> and Lusitania <note>A Roman province roughly corresponding to modern Portugal.</note>, although Galicia produces almost no black lead. Julius Caesar, in the fifth book of *The Gallic War*, also testifies that white lead occurs in Britain.

### Black Lead <note>original: "Plumbum nigrum." This is the common term for Lead.</note>

1. **Native lead**, of its own color, but impure. <note>original: "Gediegen Bley." Naturally occurring metallic lead.</note>
2. **An ore of black lead** found among the Ubii <note>A Germanic tribe in the region of Cologne (Köln), Germany.</note> that is white, similar to white non-transparent spars. <note>original: "Bley auß dem Stifft Cöln/weissen durchsichtigen Flüssen gleich." Referring to lead ore found in the Diocese of Cologne resembling white fluorspar.</note>
3. **A white ore of black lead**, similar to white transparent spars, which is exceedingly rich. For from a hundredweight of this ore, more than sixty pounds of black lead are produced.
4. **Caldebornia**, which is similar to ashen-colored marl <note>A lime-rich mud or mudstone.</note>.
5. **Similar to white sandy stone.**
6. **Similar to metallic flint**, in which small veins of live sulfur appear.
7. **From Poland**, mixed with native ochre.
8. **Flowers of black lead**, similar to white corals. <note>In alchemy, "flowers" usually refer to the powdery sublimate or oxidation products formed during heating.</note>
9. **Yellow lead**, full of lines of yellow sulfur, hence the name derived from lead and sulfur. <note>original: "Bley/Schwebel/ein gelber Bleyschwebel." Likely referring to a lead-sulfur compound like lead glance or anglesite.</note>
10. **Smelted black lead from Villach**, <note>original: "Plumbum nigrum Villacense coctum." Villach in Austria was a major historic lead-mining center.</note> which is pure lead and contains no other metal. <note>original: "rein Bley/ das kein ander Metall hat."</note>
11. **From the Palatinate**, which is very soft lead. <note>original: "ganz weich Bley."</note>
12. **Depleted lead**, <note>original: "Depauperatum."</note> which is fresh lead but not rich in lead content. <note>original: "Frisch Bley/ nit reich am Bley." This likely refers to a lean ore or a specific stage of processing.</note>

<meta>This page continues Ruland's detailed lexicographical entry on lead ores, moving from the physical descriptions of bismuth and lead varieties into a philological debate. He attempts to synchronize the contemporary German mining term "Glantz" with the classical terms used by authorities like Pliny, Dioscorides, and Galen, specifically focusing on "galena" and "molybdenum."</meta>

<page-num>371</page-num>

->**THE WORKS OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN**<-

They call it galena; we now call it *Glantz* <note>original: *Glantz*. A German mining term meaning "luster" or "brilliance," referring to the shiny, metallic appearance of lead sulfide ore.</note>. It is not, however, called galena because it comes from Galicia <note>a region in northwest Spain</note>, as Marcellus—an otherwise learned interpreter of Dioscorides—would have it. For Pliny denies in Book 34, Chapter 16, that **black lead** <note>original: "plumbum nigrum." To the Romans, this was common lead, while "plumbum album" or "white lead" referred to tin.</note> is produced in Galicia. Yet, it is produced from galena.

Thirdly, our **lead-ore** <note>original: "plumbago." While this now means graphite, in Ruland’s time it referred to various lead-bearing minerals.</note> is primarily the color of lead; for that reason, it is called *molybdenum* <note>original: "molybdena," from the Greek "molybdos" for lead.</note> by the Greeks and rightly called *plumbago* by the Latins, or the stone from which lead is made. Just as it can be called a **lead-stone** (to mention this in passing), it is also correctly called lead-vein, lead-earth, and the matter from which lead is made.

Fourthly, Pliny says nothing of the **lead-like stone** <note>original: "molybdoide."</note>, about which Dioscorides nevertheless writes, and was content with the name galena. Therefore, galena and also the "lead-like stone" of Dioscorides are one and the same.

Fifthly, Galen says that he himself saw **natural molybdenum** <note>original: "molybdenam nativam."</note> in the form of a stone, cast up by rivers; he makes no separate mention of "lead-stone," because he considered them to be the same thing. Therefore, molybdenum and lead-stone are the same.

Sixthly, the same Galen, in the book titled *On the Composition of Medicines*, says that an <term>oil-and-water mixture</term> <note>original: "hydrelaion" (ὑδρέλαιον), a pharmaceutical preparation of water and oil.</note> is prepared from white lead and litharge <note>lead monoxide</note>, and from brownish-dark molybdenum, and those which are ash-colored. And this can be prepared from our galena—not indeed the yellow kind, but the leaden-colored one. Therefore, galena and molybdenum are one and the same.

Seventhly, to Dioscorides, our galena, which is the color of lead, is called the <term>lead-like stone</term> <margin>molybdoid</margin> <note>original: "molybdoides" (μολυβδαιδης).</note> because it has the appearance of lead and contains the matter of lead within itself. It possesses the same powers as washed lead and the dross of lead, and is washed in the same manner. It differs from the natural molybdenum of Dioscorides only in color, not in substance: for he writes that his mined molybdenum is yellow and shining. But the color can easily be changed in lead-ore by various vapors raised from the bowels of the earth. Thus, among us in our mines, galenas are found of black, blue, and liver-colored <note>original: "iecinoris." A reddish-brown hue similar to the organ.</note> varieties. So too, yellow can be found pro-

->### MARTIN RULAND'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY ###<-

without doubt in warm regions, and galena is found among us in mines, which is covered with a yellow color, which is perhaps that molybdenum <note>original: *molybdena*. In early modern mineralogy, this term referred to various lead ores, specifically lead oxide or litharge, before it was identified as the distinct element molybdenum in the 18th century.</note> mentioned by Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD, author of *De Materia Medica*.</note>. And this yellow substance, with which that galena is sprinkled or stained, is sometimes found separately in veins; it is occasionally so tempered by the heat of the earth that it shines—especially if it is split open—so that it seems to contain something of metal within itself.

The Arabs knew nothing of molybdenum, or they believed it to be the same as litharge <note>original: *lithargyro*. A secondary mineral formed from the oxidation of galena ores, often used as a pigment or in glassmaking.</note>. For they are similar in temperament <note>constitution or physical nature</note>. Molybdenum, however, is a little colder and consists of denser parts, nor does it have the power of cleansing. Serapio <note>likely Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century Arab medical author</note> has nothing or very little to say concerning molybdenum. See the *Book of Aggregations*, chapter *Hasas*. 

If indeed you wish to hold some distinction or some difference, call the stone "plumbago" <note>lead-ore</note> or "molybdenum" when it contains only lead; on the contrary, when it contains both lead and silver, say it is "galena." Since, therefore, molybdenum, plumbago, and galena are one and the same, note that galena or molybdenum is twofold: namely, Native and Artificial.

**Native** [mineral] found by digging is again twofold, namely: 1. **Fruitful** <note>original: *frugifera*. In a mining context, this means ore-bearing or productive.</note>, which is a vein or leaf of lead; and then it is truly called a **lead-stone** <note>original: *lapis plumbarius*</note> by Pliny and Galen. Pliny, in Book 33, Chapter 6, identifies galena as a vein of lead, and calls it that which is found near veins of silver. Next, it is either a vein common to silver and **black lead** <note>original: *plumbo nigro*. The Roman term for common lead, as opposed to *plumbum album* (tin).</note>, <term>from which one smelts lead and silver</term> <note>original German: *man schmelzet Bley vnd Silber darauß*</note>, and then it is truly galena. 

This "fruitful" variety is again twofold: regarding its color, not its substance. For they are of the same substance, namely, one is of the color: 1. of shining lead, and this is our plumbago, or galena, or the molybdenum of Pliny. To Dioscorides, however, it is the <term>lead-like</term> <note>original Greek: *μολυβδοειδής* (molybdoeidēs)</note> stone; by Galen it is called a vein, earth, or lead-stone. And it is sometimes found in streams. 2. The other is of a yellow and shining color: just as it is described and celebrated by Dioscorides. It is found near Sebaste and Corycus <note>Ancient cities in Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey)</note>, and is also mentioned by Pliny.

In Book 34, chapter 18, Pliny states that molybdenum or galena <note>original: *molybdenam seu galenam*</note> is of better quality when it is more golden in color, less leaden and friable, and moderately heavy. In hot regions, it is perhaps stained with such a color by the dried vapors from the bowels of the earth. For if you sharply consider our lead-ore <note>original: *plumbaginem*</note> regarding its color—how it is stained by colors in the bowels of the earth through vapors—you will find in our mines lead-ore of these colors: 1. **Black Luster** <note>original: *Schwarzer Glantz*</note>. 2. **gray Luster** <note>original: *grawer Glantz*</note>. 3. **Liver-colored Luster** <note>original: *Lebarfarb Glantz*</note>. 4. One covered with a yellow color, which is perhaps that of Dioscorides. Among the Germans, all these species are called by the general name **Lead Ore / Luster** <note>original: *BleyErtz / Glantz / *</note> due to its brightness, or **Lead-sweat** <note>original: *Bleyschweiss*</note>.
II. There is a sterile kind of no importance, which is not unlike the fruitful kind in color, but is entirely sterile and consumes the whole strength of the fires <note>meaning it requires much fuel but yields no metal</note>.

The **Artificial** variety, which is produced by the work of furnaces, clings to the gold and silver furnaces. Pliny (Book 34, ch. 18) calls this "metallic," which was once highly praised when found in Zephyrium. By the Germans, it is called **Tjest or Hearth-scum** <note>original: *Tjest oder Herdfiehen*. *Tjest* refers to the refractory clay or cupel material in the furnace, while *Herdfiehen* refers to residues or litharge swept from the smelting hearth.</note>. By some, it is called **Silver-litharge** <note>original: *Silberglöde*</note> because of the relationship it has with the "froth of silver" <note>original: *spuma argenti*, a term for litharge or lead oxide produced during the refining of silver</note>; however, it is improperly called so. Pliny also, in Book 33, chapter 6, describes a species of silver froth which he calls *molybditis*. Dioscorides also treated this artificial lead-ore in Book 5, chapter 50, noting that it rivals silver froth and is produced from gold and silver; it is the dross of silver <note>original: *fæx argenti*</note>. From this is also made an **oil-and-water plaster** <note>original: *ὑδρέλαιον* (hydrelaion), a medicinal preparation of oil and water</note>, just as from native galena. But note that this metallic variety melts when it is cooked with fire. Furthermore, this metallic kind, when cooked in oil (as Dioscorides teaches), takes on the color of liver—not the native kind, as Pliny suggests in the place cited; Pliny translated that passage of Dioscorides poorly when he said: "Native lead-ore, cooked in oil, takes on a liver color." Finally, note that Sylvaticus <note>Matteo Silvatico, a 14th-century physician and botanist known for his medical encyclopedia *Pandectae Medicinae*.</note> in his *Pandects* calls molybdenum "burnt lead" and "lead dung." <meta>This page continues the technical classification of lead-bearing minerals. Ruland is refining the distinctions between "molybdena," "galena," and "plumbago" (lead-ore), drawing heavily on the metallurgical descriptions of Pliny the Elder and the medicinal observations of Dioscorides to correct contemporary misunderstandings.</meta>

-># MARTIN RULAND'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY #<-

You may see for yourself how these things agree. That molybdenum <note>original: *Molybdena*</note> is by no means lead, nor is it the "dung" of lead—that is, the slag <note>original: *scoria*</note>. Rather, it is the residue (if it may be so called) from lead-ore <note>original: *plumbagine*</note>, which contains silver and lead and adheres to the walls of the furnaces. Pliny agrees that when it is cooked <note>refined</note> a second time, it becomes lead. Sylvaticus <note>Matthaeus Silvaticus, a 14th-century medical writer</note> is in error on this point, etc. As for the medicinal virtues of lead-ore, and likewise how it should be burned or washed, see Dioscorides himself and Pliny in the cited passage. Likewise, regarding its smelting <note>original: *excoctione*</note>, consult the same author in Book 34, chapter 16, where he says: "Black lead <note>original: *Plumbi nigri*; in antiquity, this referred to lead, while 'white lead' referred to tin</note> has a double origin: it either comes from its own vein and produces nothing else from itself, or it is born with silver and is smelted from mixed veins. The first liquid that flows from it in the furnaces is called *stannum* <note>a lead-silver alloy, not to be confused with modern tin</note>, which is second to silver. That which remains in the furnaces is called *galena*, which is the third portion of the added vein. When this is smelted again, it yields black lead, two parts having been removed." Among us, if I am not mistaken, silver is separated in the first cooking, and the lead is coagulated into a stone; this is then cooked again and becomes lead.

1. **Metallic or native lead-ore**, called by the Spanish word *galena*, that is, **a common vein of lead and silver, Luster** <note>original: *Glanz*</note>.
2. **Simple lead-ore**, which contains nothing in itself but lead, **pure Luster / which holds nothing but lead** <note>original: *reiner Glanz / der nichts dann Bley helt*</note>.
3. **Rich lead-ore**, **fine-grained Luster** <note>original: *kleinspeissiger Glanz*</note>.
4. **Mixed with white pyrite**.
5. **Tessellated in limestone**, **cubic Luster in white limestone** <note>original: *würfflichter Glanz in weissen Kalckstein*</note>.
6. **Tessellated in long, white, transparent fluors** <note>original: *fluoribus*; refers to fluorspar or flux-stones</note>.
7. **Mixed with yellow fluors in white stone**, which glows in the fire, **intergrown with yellow fluxes in a white fluid stone** <note>original: *mit gelben Flüssen durchwachsen / in einem weissen flüssigen Stein*</note>.

It is cooling to the hands, with powers similar to <term>Cimolian earth</term> <note>Cimolian earth (from the island of Kimolos) was a type of medicinal clay or "fuller’s earth" used in antiquity for its cooling and cleansing properties.</note>. It is a blackish earth. We certainly possess a black earth, yet it is not *pnigitis*, for it is of the deepest black. This seems entirely to be *pnigitis* hardened by heat, sometimes of immense size, and light in proportion to its bulk. Or it is simply <term>Ochre</term>, which, having been scorched by the heat of the Sun or the earth, passed into a <term>red earth</term> <note>original: *rubricam*</note>, and consequently, being over-burnt, became such a *pnigitis*. Or it is a species of <term>Ampelitis</term> <note>A bituminous or coal-like earth; the name derives from the Greek word for "vine," as it was used to treat vine-parasites.</note>, though I have not made the experiment to see if it may be dissolved by oil. Let the investigators of such things judge soundly of these matters. That stone can be reduced into a very fine, well-digested, and very soft powder, which contains the least bit of sand. Whatever it is, it is something most beautiful, although it lies rejected and despised by the inhabitants of those places. Sometimes it is even found shimmering with tiny little sparks, so that it seems by no means a sterile stone or matter.

<header>->OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.<-</header>

**Nothing is [so] good for the eyes.** <note>original German: "Nichts ist in die Augen gut." This likely refers to the medicinal reputation of zinc oxides for treating eye ailments.</note> They also roughly call it **white pompholyx**. <note>original: *pompholigem*. Pompholyx is a historical term for zinc oxide produced in smelting furnaces.</note> Conversely, **spodium** <note>A term used for various metallic ashes or residues, often more impure than pompholyx.</note> is the same as what they call **black pompholyx** in pharmacies, or **gray nil**. <note>original: *nil gryseum*. "Nil" is an old name for furnace calamine or zinc oxide deposits.</note> By **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician and philosopher.</note> it is called, unless I am mistaken, **succudus**. Thirdly, **antispodion**, which is used in place of spodium, is an ash made from the leaves, flowers, and unripe berries of the styptic **myrtle**, or even the branch of the wild **olive** and others, just as **Dioscorides** and **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, *Natural History*, Book 34, Chapter 73.</note> teach in the cited passages.

**Note A:** You should not give any of our **spodos** nor **antispodos** by mouth to anyone now, because we truly do not know what they are or from what they are made in our time.

But let us come to the things themselves. **Pompholyx** is a metallic ash which forms at the top or on the walls of furnaces or the small houses where furnaces are located—**in the smelting huts** <note>original German: *in den Hütten*</note>—from the extinguished sparks. This ash differs according to the variety of the metals and the place where it is produced. For that which is ash-colored and made from **pyrite** is more effective than that made from **lead-stone**. Hence, that from **Goslar** <note>A famous mining town in the Harz Mountains of Germany.</note> is better than all those from **Meissen**, as it naturally contains silver, lead, and copper within itself. Just so, Dioscorides says the **Cyprian** variety is the best.

That part which adheres to the walls of the small houses and furnaces is **spodion**. Conversely, that which hangs at the top is **pompholyx**. It differs from spodium in its whiteness and lightness, as Dioscorides notes that pompholyx differs from spodium only in appearance, not in kind. Specifically, **spodos** is:
1. black,
2. heavy,
3. full of clusters, <note>original: *pileis*. Likely referring to the tufted or capped shape of the deposits.</note>
4. swept from the floors of the workshops.

**Pompholyx** is a substance that is:
1. white, like a bubble or a blister (whence it also takes its name among the Greeks), <note>From the Greek *pompholyx* (πομφόλυξ), meaning "bubble."</note>
2. fatty and light,
3. pure,
4. collected and produced at the top of the furnaces.

Furthermore, pompholyx is properly of two species: the first is somewhat fatty and of an airy color; this is properly called **gray nil**. The other species is exceptionally white and of the greatest lightness; this is produced either during the refining of copper, when crushed **Cadmia** <note>A term for zinc ores or the crusts that form in the furnace; furnace calamine.</note> is sprinkled over it more abundantly by design, or it is produced from the Cadmia itself when blown by bellows. The reason for which—

<page-num>378</page-num>

### LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND

Dioscorides <note>A first-century Greek physician and botanist, author of *De Materia Medica*.</note> teaches how to produce it in a long sequence of steps. The thin, lightest part of the matter rises to the highest point, flies off, and adheres to the walls and the roof of the furnace; this is called **pompholyx** <note>original: *pompholix*. A light, white zinc oxide often called "philosopher's wool."</note>. The heavier part, however, which settles in the lower areas, is called **spodion** <note>original: *spodion* or *spodos*. A more impure metallic ash or slag.</note>.

Furthermore, for information on which pompholyx is good and which is adulterated, how it ought to be washed, and what its powers are for astringing, cooling, filling, purging, obstructing, and drying, you should consult Dioscorides himself, who teaches all these things. Additionally, he adds the method of burning, or what he calls "torrefaction" <note>original: *torrefactionis*. A process of roasting or parching a substance over fire.</note>, and from what metals it is chiefly made—namely, from **gold, silver, lead, and copper**. And after discussing the variety from Cyprus, where the **pyrites** stone is most abundant, he says the leaden variety is also effective. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist and author.</note> agrees with these points. Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire.</note> attributes more effective powers to **Pompholyx** than to **spodion**. Indeed, pompholyx possesses composite powers, much like the rose itself.

Moreover, we taught above concerning **Cadmia** <note>A term used both for zinc ore (calamine) and for the deposits found in smelting furnaces.</note> that the variety called **botryitis** <note>original: *botryitin*. A form of cadmia named for its resemblance to a cluster of grapes (Greek *botrys*).</note> is called **Arabic tutia** <note>original: *tutia*. Also known as "tutty," a crude zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces.</note>, just as the Alexandrian variety is called hard or solid tutia. However, **botryitis cadmia** is a different thing than tutia, as the Arabs testify, and specifically Serapio <note>Likely Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century Arabic medical author.</note>. For the **spodium** being discussed here is tutia, and it is a "thing of nothing" <note>original: *res nihili*. This is a pun on "Nil," a common name for these oxides, and the Latin word for "nothing."</note>; yet **botryitis** is not tutia. Dioscorides mentions spodium and not tutia, so as not to appear to be listing the same thing twice.

In summary: that which the Arabs call **Tutia**, the Greeks call **pompholyx**, and we call **spodion**. This is testified by Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian "Prince of Physicians."</note> and Serapio regarding tutia, and by Dioscorides in his chapters on pompholyx. There has been an error in the names of the things, but not in their powers. We can use **Botryite Cadmia** in place of tutia (that is, spodium) if it has been properly prepared.

However, **Botryitis**, **capnitis** <note>A variety of cadmia found near the "smoke" or mouth of the furnace.</note>, **Cadmia**, **Pompholyx**, and **spodos** differ from one another—even though they are made from the same material—only because of the locations where they are formed. **Botryitis Cadmia** is formed on the sides or in the upper chambers of the furnaces; on the other hand, the interior **capnitis** is formed specifically at the mouths of the furnaces.

True **Pompholyx** is "white nothing" <note>original: *nil album*. Also known as "nihili album," a historical name for zinc oxide.</note>, a thing of nothing, the lightest metallic ash.

But these substances are also found at the top of the furnaces or on the walls, or even on the outside of the small collection-houses. If it is found at the mouth of the furnace, then the <term>Cadmia</term> <note>A term here referring to furnace deposits of zinc oxide.</note> is called **capnitis** <note>original: *capnitis*, from the Greek for "smoke-like."</note>; if it is on the sides and the upper chambers, it is **pompholyx**; the part that hangs down from the top is **pompholix**; conversely, the part that adheres to the walls is **spodion**. Students ought to observe these distinctions diligently.

Furthermore, note that the Arabs identify two kinds of **tutia** <note>original: *tucia*. A medicinal zinc oxide.</note>: namely, the native kind found in mines—white, green, and yellow—which is found on the shores of the Indian Sea; and then the artificial kind made in furnaces, which is discussed here. 

Note also that there are other types of ash besides that soot, such as the **spodion** mentioned by Serapion, Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen. Galen remarks, "I have never used spodion, because I had enough pompholyx." The Arabs have a twofold definition of **spodion**: 
1. **Spodium** from reeds and the roots of a certain overseas reed that has been burnt. This is found in the writings of Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> regarding spodium, where he says: "Spodion is the root of burnt reeds, cold in the 2nd degree and dry in the 3rd degree." Paul <note>Likely Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note> also describes spodion as being of a cold and dry temperament. 
2. The other kind is that which is, or is made from, genuine burnt ivory; secondly, from the bones of elephants, dogs, and other animals. This ash is burnt until it is light, being made from bones— <insert>from the bones of a carcass</insert> <note>original German: *Aus dem Schelmknochen*.</note>—and <insert>one still finds bone in there</insert> <note>original German: *Man findet noch Beyn darinnen*.</note>, whereas it ought to be made from burnt ivory. 

And note well, you should never administer either **spodos** or **antispodos** <note>A substitute for spodium, often made from different ashes.</note> by mouth to anyone, for we no longer know what spodos or antispodos truly are in our apothecary shops. We cherish foreign things and despise our own. Physicians ought to reclaim our own **spodon** from the furnaces, but "I am telling a story to the deaf" <note>A Latin idiom meaning his advice is being ignored.</note>. 

Moreover, some people call copper rust—both **aerugo** <note>Verdigris, the green pigment/crust formed on copper.</note> and **ios** <note>Greek for rust or poison, here referring to copper oxide.</note>—by the name of **spodon**. Finally, observe what Pliny has to say on these matters in Book 34, Chapter 13, when he says: **pompholyx** and **spodos** are found in copper-smithies, and the difference between them is that **pompholyx** is produced by washing, while **spodos** is produced unwashed. Furthermore, he says that **pompholyx** is that which is whitest and lightest, being indeed the ash of copper and Cadmia, while **spodon** is...

**Pompholyx** 1. is soot that is collected in the chambers where metal is smelted; <note>original German: **Hütten Rauch**</note>.

2. **Pompholyx** derived from silver; <note>original German: **Silver-bearing flock-dust**</note>.

3. Yellow [pompholyx] which adheres to the walls when silver is separated from lead; <note>original German: **yellow, poisonous smelter-smoke**</note>.

4. Mansfeld <term>Aetis</term> <note>likely a local term for furnace residues from the Mansfeld mining region</note>; <note>original German: **Copper-dust**</note>.

5. That which is collected when silver is separated from copper; <note>original German: **Copper-dust**</note>.

6. That which is collected in the chimneys where white lead <note>likely referring to tin</note> is smelted; <note>original German: **Tin-dust**</note>.

<header>### DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND</header>

...leaves; it also bestows the secret effect and virtue, and is marked with this figure: <note>A symbol for Mercury (☿) is depicted here. Alchemists believed this symbol was a composite containing the signs of all other planets, particularly the circle of the Sun (Gold) and the crescent of the Moon (Silver), signifying its universal nature.</note> which contains and encloses within itself the signs and figures of all the planets, especially of gold and silver.

**Principles** <note>original Latin: *Principia*</note> are those primary things from which every kind of mixed substance is made. Because they are inherent, they already possess a certain fixed nature within them in which they flourish and from which they can be drawn out. These principles differ from those of Aristotle; they are not understood as the absolute first principles of all things, but as the first in any specific category, though they are analogous to the Aristotelian ones. The powers of these principles are founded both in their elemental parts and in the celestial realm. Thus, in one way they lean toward the elements, and in another toward the essences. There are three principles: **Mercury, Salt, and Sulfur.** <term>Tria Prima</term> <note>The 'Three Pillars' of Paracelsian alchemy. Sulfur represents the soul and flammability; Mercury represents the spirit and volatility; Salt represents the body and stability.</note>

**First temperature** <note>original Latin: *Prima temperatura*</note>; <note>original German: *Vorpleyen auff ein frischen Einstrich*—the process of adding lead to a fresh charge of ore or a new smelting cut.</note>

**Primal beings** <note>original Latin: *Primales*</note> are deceptive bodies placed before our eyes by the stars; otherwise known as **optical illusions** <note>original German: *bedrognr leib*—deceptive or phantom bodies</note> which the sight places before the eyes.

**Projection** <note>original Latin: *Proiectio*</note> is the exaltation of a substance through a "medicine" <note>the Philosopher's Stone or Elixir</note> cast upon the material to be changed, resulting in a sudden entry and transformation. It is similar to fermentation because it changes the substance internally; however, it differs because it does not happen through slow digestion—where mixed materials are gradually altered and reach a balanced state <term>crasis</term> <note>a Greek medical term for the healthy blending of humors or qualities</note>—but rather through a violent penetration occurring almost in the moment of contact, which transfigures the body. That medicine is also called a **tincture**, rather than a ferment.

**Landowner**; <note>original German: *Grund-Herr*—the lord or proprietor of the land where mining occurs.</note>

**Inherited shares**; <note>original Latin: *Proprietarii partes*; original German: *Erblusus*—shares in a mine or estate that are passed down through inheritance.</note>

**Proscription**; it delays or retards.

**Prolectation** <note>original Latin: *Prolectatio*, a drawing out or enticing</note> is extraction by the thinning <note>attenuation</note> of subtle parts, so that when they are rarefied by the inclination of their own nature, they are carried away from the thicker parts in a different direction and remain there. Therefore, those substances from which we extract something in this way are called thinning agents, or rarefiable.

...refractory: and before it solidifies as a projection <note>original Latin: *prolectatum*—the alchemical goal of transforming base metal into gold</note>, whether it be of a fiery, airy, or watery nature, it is sufficient that the form of these elements intervenes. **St. Anthony’s Fire** <note>original: *Pruina, pruna, ignis Persicus, S. Antonis Feuer*</note>. **Pumice**, called *famechi* or *fenec* in Arabic, is the "Stone of Vulcan" <note>referring to its volcanic origin</note>. The Germans call it **a *Byhms* or *Byhmsstein*, or *buems*.** There are two species: the black and the white. The black variety is also called *tophus*, or **black bath-stone.** This type is most excellent and is found in Melos, Scyros, and the Aeolian Islands; it is very well suited for smoothing the skin, as the poet Catullus mentions. On the other hand, there is the white variety, or **white bath-stone**, which Dioscorides describes in Book 5, Chapter 74. He notes that it is light, spongy, easily split, not sandy, easy to grind, and bright white. He further adds the method for burning it and its medicinal powers, for which one should also see Pliny, Book 36, Chapter 21. Finally, Theophrastus is cited (if I am not mistaken, in *On Plants*, Book 9, Chapter 18). Pumice is called a "stone" because of its hardness, yet because of its porosity <note>original Latin: *raritatem*</note> it is not truly a stone, and it deviates clearly from the nature of a stone because it floats upon water. Pumice is found wherever alum and sulfur are produced. I believe it is earth that has been entirely burnt away on islands, which is then carried by the waters as far as Barce, a city in Libya. For this reason, it is also called the "Stone of Barce" or "Barchin."

...it also grants or yields the secret action and virtue, and it is designated by a figure that contains and includes the signs and figures of all planets, primarily those of Gold and Silver. <note>The author is likely describing the "Monas Hieroglyphica" or the universal symbol of Mercury, which was believed to incorporate the symbols of the Sun, Moon, and other celestial bodies.</note>

**Principles** <note>Latin: *Principia*</note> are those first things from which every kind of mixed substance is created. Because they are inherent within the substance, they already possess a certain fixed nature underlying them in which they thrive and through which they can be drawn forth. These principles differ from those defined by Aristotle; they are not understood as the primary elements of all things in general, but rather as the primary elements within each specific category, though they are analogous to the Aristotelian ones. Furthermore, the powers of these Principles are founded both in their elemental parts and in the celestial realm. Thus, in one sense, they relate to the elements, and in another, to the essences. **Projection** <note>Latin: *Proiectio*</note> is an exaltation of a substance being transformed, achieved by throwing the medicinal agent <note>The Philosopher's Stone or Tincture</note> upon it, resulting in a sudden entry and transformation. It is similar to fermentation because it changes the substance from within its core; however, it differs in that it does not occur through slow digestion (by which mixtures are gradually altered and receive their temperament), but rather through a violent penetration that transfigures the substance almost at the moment of entry. This medicine is also called a **tincture** rather than a ferment.

**Proprietor**, <note>German: *Grund Herr*</note> a landlord or lord of the soil.

**Portions of the Proprietor**, <note>German: *Erblusus*</note> the shares of an heir or an ancestral inheritance.

**Proscription**, that which hinders or delays. <note>Latin: *Retardat*</note>

**Prolectation** is an extraction performed by the thinning of subtle parts, so that once they are rarefied by the inclination of their own nature, they are carried away from the thicker parts in a different direction and settle there. Therefore, the types of things from which we draw something in this manner are called attenuators, or **rarefiable** substances. <note>Latin: *rarefactiles*</note>

<meta>This page continues Martin Ruland's Lexicon, moving from the definition of various mining and purification terms into a philosophical and technical discussion of "Putrefaction"—a core alchemical process of breaking down matter to release its essence.</meta>

<header>### THE LEXICON OF MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN</header>

1. Some are purified through sublimation <note>original: *sublimiren*; the process of turning a solid into vapor to leave impurities behind</note>, such as spirits.
3. Some through dissolving <note>original: *solviren*</note>, as with salt.

7. Some through liquation <note>original: *seygern*; the process of separating metals with different melting points</note> and filtering.

**To Pulverize** / To turn into sand. 
**Potent Powder** / Parting powder <note>original: *Scheidpulver*; a corrosive powder or acid used to separate gold from silver</note>.

**The Well** / An engineered shaft <note>original: *Kunst Schacht*; usually a shaft equipped with machinery or pumps</note>.

**Straight Shaft** / A main or perpendicular shaft <note>original: *Richt schacht*</note>.

**Decayed** / Brittle or crumbling earth <note>original: *Schwediger*</note>.

**Putrefaction** <note>original: *Putrefactio*</note> is the resolution of a mixture through natural decay in a warm, moist environment. For it is necessary that moisture overcomes the dry boundary, driven by external heat. Once this is done, the innate heat—along with its substantial moisture—is separated from the mixed components and preserves its own homogeneity, existing apart. Therefore, if the substance to be putrefied abounds in moisture, it is crushed and left in that very moisture, then placed for digestion in the warmth of a dung-bed <note>original: *fimi*; horse manure was a standard source of steady, gentle heat</note> or a warm bath—that is, by applying moist heat from the outside. If, however, the substance has little or no moisture of its own, it is ground and sprinkled with a proportional amount of moisture, and then placed in its own vessel to rot.

**Putrefaction** is the resolution of things mixed together, occurring when the mixed parts—their internal enclosures having been unbolted—depart as they are dissolved by heat acting through moisture. And this is the path to those most excellent operations of Alchemy; it produces not so much the elements as it does the celestial essences, now separated from their elementary composition. ### ALCHEMICAL LEXICON: M

<page-num>383</page-num>

->**PUTREFACTION**<-

When the pores are closed, the essence—in which the substantial temperament <note>original: *crasis*; the unique internal balance of qualities in a substance</note> is rooted—is released, and the process takes place. From this, it is evident that in mixtures which deviate significantly from the simple nature of the elements, there exists something internal beyond the elements themselves. This internal thing is considered incombustible; it produces a new substance through natural putrefaction as it establishes itself. This type of resolution <note>the breakdown of a substance into its components</note> is twofold: Putrefaction and resolution through medicine.

There is another kind of Putrefaction that lies between corrosive calcination <note>the reduction of a metal to powder through heat or acid</note> and putrefaction proper; this is called dry and Philosophical Putrefaction. Indeed, it takes its name from whatever process it most closely resembles, such as sublimation, the separation of the elements, coction <note>original: *coctio*; ripening or "cooking" through steady heat</note>, solution, and so on. It takes place in the "dry water of the Philosophers" <note>original: *aqua Philosophorum sicca*; often a reference to mercury or a specific corrosive agent that does not "wet" the hands</note>, or in the sharpest vinegar, and it is applied to no other substances but the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note>.

Putrefaction is a form of digestion that dissolves the substance of a thing by retaining its vapors and applying external heat, in order to generate a more excellent thing. It is the specific property of putrefaction to consume the old nature of things, to introduce a new one, and occasionally to produce the fruit of a different generation. Through this process, corrosive spirits become sweet and mild, and all colors are transformed into others. Likewise, the pure is separated from the impure (with the impure settling at the bottom). This is achieved by placing the matter in a vessel, which is then set in dung <note>original: *fimum*; a common alchemical method for providing steady, gentle heat</note>, maintaining the heat of the dung for a predetermined time. However, it is often better to place the vessel in a water bath <note>original: *balneum*</note>.

Putrefaction <note>original: *Fäulung*</note> occurs when the matter turns black; at that point, it also stinks, like dung or a carcass. Here the true dissolution of the body <note>original: *solutio corporis*</note> takes place: the elements are pulled apart and disrupted, acting and suffering upon one another. This produces various colors until the victory is won <note>the stage where the process is completed</note> and everything is unified once more.

Putrefaction is defined as corruption leading to alteration—the rotting of one thing <note>original: *Ein Fäulung eines Dings*</note> into a different essence.

<vocab>Putrefaction, Rotting, calcination, corrosive, sublimation, digestion, spirits, of the Sun (Gold), of the Moon (Silver)</vocab>

### OF MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN. 389

Pusta <note>a term likely referring to a type of corrosive residue or dross</note> is an innate digestion of waste matter, **An innate wasting away of iron.** <note>original Latin/German: *Pusta digestio saniei innata, Ein angebohrne Verzehrung deß Eisens.*</note>

**Pygmies**, mannikins, or subterranean spirits, whom they also call little torches and sparks. It is claimed that they are not born and have no parents, but are generated from the corruption of the earth, just as beetles are generated from putrefied horse dung. **Earth-men or little mountain-men / spirits.** <note>original Latin/German: *Pygmæi homunciones vel subterranei spiritus... Erd oder Bergmändlein / Schröttelin.* Spontaneous generation was a common belief in the 16th century to explain the presence of small creatures or "spirits" in mines.</note>

**Pyrites** and **marcasite** are the same thing. For what the Latins and Greeks call pyrite, the Arabs call marcasite and black *zeg* <note>original: *Zeg nigrum*; a term used for vitriol or substances used in making ink</note>. By others it is also called the "stone of light," due to its effect; also "capparosa marcasite," and "copper stone," and even *calcitis* <note>a term for a copper-bearing mineral or roasted copper ore</note> in its primary meaning. Everything the Greeks wrote concerning pyrite, the Arabs translated into their own language under the name of marcasite.

It is called pyrite because fire is easily struck from it <note>from the Greek *pyr*, meaning fire</note>; for this reason, it is now known among our people by the general name **Firestone**, and soldiers use it to ignite their cannons. Furthermore, it is called pyrite because its color is often fiery. Otherwise, among Germans, pyrite is simply called **Kies, or copper-stone / copper-ore.** <note>original German: *Kyß oder Kupferstein / Kupfferertz.*</note> Although these names are more general in nature.

There are various species of pyrite found in our mines: specifically, pyrite of a silver color, a near-golden color, a truly golden color, one resembling galena <note>lead ore</note>, an ash-colored one, and even an iron-colored one, etc., which we shall now discuss.

**Pyrite of a silver color**, the first species of pyrite found in our mines, is called by the miners **Water Kies / or White Kies.** <note>original German: *Ein Wasser Kyß / oder weisser Kyß.*</note> This is argentiferous <note>silver-bearing</note> pyrite, silver in color, from which silver is smelted, as can be seen in the valley. Pliny (Book 36, Chapter 19), if I am not mistaken, mentions this; but he did not know that silver could be smelted from it, as was the case with all the ancients.
