### LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND. 390

...nevertheless, it was undoubtedly known that it could be smelted from it: just as Serapio <note>an influential 9th-century Arabic medical writer</note> testifies that copper is smelted from marcasite; and Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> clearly testifies that copper is smelted from pyrite. Therefore, that pyrite of a silvery color contains silver and copper; sometimes only silver, sometimes only copper, sometimes silver and copper together, sometimes silver and **black lead** <note>original: *plumbum nigrum*; usually referring to lead ore or galena</note>, sometimes several metals, and sometimes it is found to be entirely sterile <note>barren of any precious metal</note>. Moreover, it seems to me that this pyrite possesses more **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> than the other species.

Pyrite of a nearly golden color is the second type of pyrite, called by the Germans **Yellow pyrites / or yellow copper-pyrites / copper-stone / copper ore.** <note>original German: *gelber Kieß/oder gelber Kupfferkieß / Kupfferstein / Kupffererz.*</note> This is not infrequently found in our silver mines, but more frequently in copper mines. Copper is smelted from it. It is properly pyrite, and a pyrite of copper in the form of copper; or as Pliny says, having the appearance of copper. It is specifically that **marcasite** of the Arabs from which copper is smelted. This pyrite is chosen by Dioscorides in Book 5, Chapter 89, above all others for medicinal use, especially the kind that easily emits sparks and is solid; he also teaches how it should be roasted and washed. Truly, even the first type of pyrite is not to be despised in medicine. When Dioscorides mentions *chalkitis* <gloss>copper-stone</gloss> <note>original Greek: *χαλκῖτιν*</note> in the passage cited, he signifies a type of copper more in its form than its color. Now, this type, like the former species, contains silver and copper; sometimes only copper, sometimes silver and copper together, sometimes silver and black lead, sometimes also other metals, and sometimes it is entirely sterile. Pliny testifies that these two species were found of old in Cyprus and in the mines around Acarnania—or as some read, Acamania—and they are found among us in many places in our mines. Furthermore, note that Pyrite, both of golden and silvery color (as was also said before), is often found in silver mines, and more often in its own vein as entirely sterile; the same pyrite is also not infrequently found in streams, such as in the Gamersdorf torrent, and also by rivers, like the Elbe <note>original: *Albim*</note>. If, however, much is found...

->RYLANDI PHIL. ET MEDICI. 391<-

...[is smelted], a certain kind of stone is forged therefrom, whose use is great in the smelting process. Such sterile pyrite <note>ore that contains no precious metals</note> has been found in its own vein in great abundance at Havelberg on the Havel <note>a town in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany</note> of wondrous beauty.

Pyrite of an entirely golden color is the third species of pyrite, <gloss>A pyrite that has an entirely golden color</gloss> <note>original German: *Ein Kieß der gantz ein Farb hat/ wie Goldt/*</note> and this seems to have more sulfur; to this is sometimes mixed that fourth following species, <gloss>The shiny pyrite</gloss> <note>original German: *Der glantzichte Kieß:*</note> and it is such that it delights the sight vehemently. Pyrite which is similar in color to galena <term>galena|lead glance or lead sulfide, the most important ore of lead</term> is the fourth species of pyrite, <gloss>A shiny pyrite.</gloss> <note>original German: *Ein glantzichter Kieß.*</note> But the miner <note>original Latin: *agricola*; likely a reference to the mineralogist Georgius Agricola, or a general term for a field worker</note> perhaps feels it is neither galena nor pyrite, but has its own certain kind. And it is true, for this pyrite has neither the color nor the hardness [of typical pyrite], yet from galena, whose color it shares, it differs entirely in its substance. Gold and silver are smelted from it, and it is found in great abundance at Reichenstein <note>modern Złoty Stok in Poland, historically known for gold mining</note> in a very fine form; and it is sometimes mixed with the preceding species, as has been said. It is also found larger at Rauris <note>a market town in Austria</note>, but this contains more silver and less gold; on the contrary, that which is found at Reichenstein contains more gold and less silver, or gold alone.

Pyrite of an ashen color is the fifth species of pyrite. This is found quite fine also at Reichenstein, and is called <gloss>a gray pyrite</gloss> <note>original German: *ein grawer Kieß/*</note> and it is mixed with the preceding species, so that gold can also be smelted from it. This same species, in a slightly different manner, is also found at Altenberg <note>a town in Saxony</note> even in Silesia, from which gold and silver are likewise forged.

Pyrite of an iron color is the sixth species of pyrite, of which Avicenna <note>a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age</note> makes mention; it presents entirely the appearance of a mass of iron. It is found in iron mines: not however in all, but in certain ones. Miners call it <gloss>an iron-stone, not that it is an iron-stone...</gloss> <note>original German: *ein Eiſenſtein/ nit daß es ein Eiſenſtein*</note>

### LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND ###

...it is; rather, that it is similar to ironstone <note>original German: *sey/ sondern daß er dem Eisenstein gleich ist*</note>. From these six species of pyrite, fire is struck from most of them, and they are heavy—some even very heavy—and most suitable for kindling fire. Therefore, these are also understood by **Pliny**, who, in the passage cited, describes them when he says: "Some also make one genus of pyrites which contains the most fire, which we call 'living' <note>original Latin: *vivos*</note>, and they are the heaviest. These are most necessary for camp scouts," etc. Indeed, it must be denied that there is any other genus of pyrites. Just as fire is easily struck from the first two species of pyrite, which are almost of a silver and gold color, if they are dense, thick, and compact; so too, whenever they are thin, subtle, and dissolved into the smallest parts, they do not give off even a spark, just like the subsequent types, because they themselves are not compact and sufficiently solid.

**Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar renowned for his works on natural philosophy and alchemy.</note>, who was a learned man in his time, errs significantly regarding pyrite, even though he is said to have written most diligently of all concerning metals. For he says that every kind of pyrite, or as he himself calls it, **marcasite**, consumes fire. Thus, Albertus denies that metals are smelted from marcasite, whereas **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and alchemical works were foundational in the West.</note> teaches that there is marcasite of gold, silver, copper, and iron. **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> teaches that copper is smelted from pyrite, and **Serapio the Arab** repeats that copper is cooked from marcasite; and we see this being done in countless places in Germany. In **Silesia**, at **Kupferberg** <note>a historic mining town in modern-day Poland</note>, shoemaker’s black is also manufactured in the same place <term>shoemaker’s black|Latin: *atramentum futorium*; a type of vitriol or iron sulfate used historically for making ink and dyeing leather</term>. If Albertus had read and observed these things, he would never have fallen into that error. I believe Albertus easily gave ear to the Chemists <note>likely referring here to laboratory practitioners or 'pseudo-alchemists'</note> and was not so diligent in investigating the mines and the metals themselves; for that reason, he slipped easily.

Finally, pyrite has a remarkable power of dispersing, cleansing, and heating; but for how it should be burned and washed, consult **Dioscorides**, book 5, chapter 89. **Pliny**, in book 37, chapter 11, says that black pyrite burns the fingers when rubbed. Whence also those ancient verses speak:

# THE WRITINGS OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.

> It seeks a gentle touch and to be held with a kind hand,
> For if pressed too hard, it burns the fingers of the one touching it.
<note>This couplet likely refers to the corrosive or caustic nature of certain mineral ores, such as those containing arsenic or vitriol, which can irritate the skin.</note>

As far as I know, I am unaware of a "black pyrite." Furthermore, I have not put it much to the test whether pyrite possesses such a nature that it burns the hand—unless **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author and naturalist whose *Natural History* was the standard reference for minerals in the Renaissance.</note> intends that to be understood simply as our black cobalt, which burns, that is, corrodes, the hands of the workmen. **Solinus** <note>Gaius Julius Solinus (3rd century AD), a Latin grammarian and compiler of geographical wonders.</note> also subscribes to Pliny's view in his *Polyhistor*, chapter 46. But I leave these matters undecided. Furthermore, the same Pliny, in book 36, chapter 19, calls coral "pyrites," because there is a great deal of fire in it. In truth, "pyrite" is treated as a broad genus by Pliny; thus, according to Pliny, the **Chalcedonian** <note>A variety of quartz or silica from the region of Chalcedon.</note> stone would be a pyrite because of its effect, as would **flint** <note>original Latin: *silex*</note>, from which fire is commonly struck in our time. Finally, lest I seem to have passed over this, there are some who wish that fossil stone called <term>shale</term> <note>original German: *Schyfer*; a fine-grained, clastic sedimentary rock.</note> to be a species of pyrite, from which copper is also smelted. That fissile stone is most suitable for subterranean impressions. *For in it we have sometimes seen fish, serpents, scorpions, cicadas, and once even a most beautiful cock, adorned with flesh-colored feathers and a double crown.* <note>Ruland is describing fossils found in slate or shale. The "cock" may have been a particularly well-preserved fossil bird or a misinterpreted fossilized plant or crustacean.</note>

### Pyrites of a silver color from which fire is not drawn.

1. Pyrite of a silver color, surrounded by yellow cubic spars: **yellow cubic fluors coated with water-pyrite.** <note>original German: *gelbewürfflichte Flüsse mit Wasserkies vberzogen*. "Water-pyrite" (*Wasserkies*) often refers to marcasite, which is prone to decomposing in moisture.</note>
2. Mixed with yellow spars.
3. Fissile and wedge-shaped in metallic marble, which continually exudes an acrid juice: **shale-like water-pyrite found in a spar like a wedge, and it gives no fire.** <note>original German: *Schiffrichter/ Wasserkies bricht in einem Spaht wie Keile/ vnd gibt kein Feuer*.</note>
4. Mixed with white spars and metallic marble, resembling a brain.

### Pyrites of a gold color.

1. Pyrite which is solid and reflects the color of gold entirely; it is called by the Spanish name **Marcasite**. <note>original German: *Marchasit*.</note>
2. Found at Mansfeld <note>A famous mining region in Germany known for copper shale.</note> in white hexagonal spars that are not transparent: **a golden-yellow copper-pyrite in white hexagonal fluors.** <note>original German: *ein goldgelber Kupfferkies / in weissen sechseckichten Flüssen*.</note>

# THE LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN

**Pyromancy** <note>original Latin: *Pyromantia*</note>, an art of predicting the future from fire, occurs when the stars reveal themselves to humans through flames so that the knowledge of the truth being sought might break forth, removing all doubt or suspicion. An example of this is what is said of the boxwood tree <note>original: *buxo*</note>; it is reported that if its leaves are cast into a fire after being inscribed with the names of individuals under suspicion, the leaf belonging to the guilty party will crackle and leap out. In the same way, many believe that conjectures about the future can be made collectively. *When one predicts something from the fire.* <note>original German: *Wenn man etwas auß dem Fewer vorsaget*</note>

**Pyronomia** is the science of applying heat to one's works and the governing of fire. In this field, the industriousness of Alchemy shines most brightly. It is the highest praise for an artisan to be skilled more through the practical use of things than through mere rules; indeed, some aspects of this art are such that they require the eyes and the hand rather than words. The external agent which the artisan uses as a primary tool in this science is heat, which we designate by the word "fire." However, cold is not to be excluded, nor moisture, nor dryness; these qualities, whether acting alone or in combination, greatly assist the master in their various works and locations.

**Pyrotechnics** <note>original Latin: *Pyrotechnia*</note>: this operates solely in the preparation of natural things with the aid of fire, used as a middle and most powerful instrument. *The art of what is made in and with the fire.* <note>original German: *Die Kunst was inn vnd mit dem Fewer gemacht wird*</note>

**Pyramis** (called by others a cone-shaped vessel, or *a casting-mold* <note>original German: *Gießbuckel*; a conical mold used to separate metal from slag</note>) is a metallic vessel hollowed out in the fashion of a pyramid, such that its upper part is wide while the lower part tapers to a point. It is designed so that molten minerals can be shaped into a "regulus" <note>A "regulus" is the metallic heart or "little king" that settles at the bottom of a mold as it cools</note>.

<note>A large, elegant, handwritten calligraphic letter Q centered on the page serves as a decorative divider for the start of the 'Q' alphabetical section.</note>

**Quandros** is a stone or gem of a white color which is found in the brain and head of a vulture. It is said to fill the breasts with milk and to be effective against harmful accidents.

# THE LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND

**Quanli**: lead.

**Quars**: gallstone <note>original Latin: *petra fellis*</note>.

**Quartatio** <note>Quartation</note> is the separation of gold and silver from one another when they have been mixed together. It is called "quartation" because enough silver is added to the mixture of gold and silver so that there are three parts of silver to one part of gold, making four parts in total.

**Quartura**: Quartation, the highest assay of gold <note>original German: *höchst Prob deß Goldes*</note>. It is performed in this way: nine parts of silver are mixed with all the gold through melting in a fire; then both are dissolved together using *aqua stygia* <note>literally "Stygian water," a term for corrosive acids</note> or *aqua fortis* <note>nitric acid</note>. All the silver flows into the water, while the gold settles at the bottom in the form of a reddish-black powder.

**Quadratum**: A square <note>original German: *Vierung*</note>.

**Quadrangula contignatio**: A quadrangular timbering or framework <note>original German: *Schrot*; in historical mining, this refers to the square timber frames used to line and support a shaft</note>.

**Quadrans fodinae**: A quadrant of a mine; also a work shift <note>original German: *Schicht*; a "quadrans" or quarter-day shift of six hours</note>.

**Quebricum**: Used for *febrit*. Some say it is arsenic <note>original Latin: *Arsenicum*</note> and should be written with a "K." But Stephanus says it is sulfur.

**Quebrit**: That is, sulfur; *quibrith* is the same.

**Qui harpagone laborat**: One who works with a grappling hook or a brake <note>original German: *Prembser*</note>.

**Quianos**: That is, a vein of the earth, also called *Cuperosum* <note>likely referring to copperas or vitriol minerals</note>.

**Quinta essentia** <note>The Fifth Essence or Quintessence</note>: This is the nature, power, virtue, color, life, spirit, medicine, and specific property of things drawn out from their physical body through the Art <note>referring to Alchemical extraction</note>. To others, it is the "specific form" which, if removed from the species, returns to its genus and progresses higher until it rests in a certain state. <note>The German text repeats this definition: "The Fifth Essence is the nature, power, effect, virtue, color, life, spirit, and property of things drawn from their body through the Art."</note>

**Quintum esse**: The "fifth being" of any element produced by itself alone; it is the animal belonging to that single element <note>original German: *Ein jedes Elements Thier*; a reference to the idea that each element has a corresponding life form, such as the Salamander in fire</note>.

**Quinta essentia**: Is the Heaven; it is neither cold nor warm, nor...

# PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN RULAND

...neither moist nor dry, but tempers the soul and gives strength; it is an unquenchable burning water, the *aqua vitæ* <note>original Latin/German: "aqua vitæ / ein brennend Wasser unstörlich"; literally "water of life," usually referring to concentrated alcohol or a highly purified solvent</note>.

**Quintessence** <note>original Latin: *Quinta essentia*</note> is a mystery, exalted to the purity of the ethereal nature and its most excellent powers. Hence it is usually called "Heaven," and "Celestial Substance," in which the purest and most sincere temperament and substantial root resides, as if it were an outflow of the ether, or a ray of the firmament, dispersed through the lowest things by the voice of the Creator and an offspring <note>original Greek: ἀπογέννημα (*apogennēma*)</note> of the world-soul.

**Quintessence of Vegetables** is that which is extracted from plants and their parts. This is most especially made from the extracted juice. The foremost position here is held by the quintessence of wine, which Lullius <note>referring to Ramon Llull, a 13th-century polymath and supposed alchemist</note> also calls Vegetable Mercury; others call it the Water of the First Entity, the Heaven, and the Key of the Philosophers.

**Quintessence of Animals** is that which is extracted from the parts of animals, by reason of a natural and vegetable mixture; therefore, the practice differs little from the preparation of vegetables.

**Quintessence of Minerals** is that which is fashioned from minerals. The quintessences of metals and gemstones are preeminent here.

# MARTIN RULAND'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY

### R

**Rhagades** <note>original Latin/German: *Ragadiæ*; fissures or sores</note> are marks or abscesses of the private parts, occurring as ulcers in the buttocks, the womb, or the male member.

**Rhapontic Mercury** <note>original: *Rhaponticum ☿*</note> occurs when the "Body" is transformed into water and a black color.

**Rama** is an abscess under the tongue, also called a "frog" <note>original Latin/German: *Ranula / Frosch*; a medical term for a cyst on the floor of the mouth</note>.

**Realgar** is properly the fume of minerals; it includes anything of an arsenical nature or anything that acts as a covering. Metaphorically, it refers to a corrupted nature within the body, from which ulcers are primarily born. It is fourfold, according to the number of the elements:
1.  **Realgar of Water**: the foam floating upon the waters.
2.  **Realgar of Earth**: arsenic.
3.  **Realgar of Air**: *tereniabin* <note>a term for "manna" or a sweet dew believed to fall from the air</note>.
4.  **Realgar of Fire**: the Saturnine conjunction <note>likely referring to a specific alchemical alignment or lead-based reaction</note>.

**Rebis**, the excrement of the bowels.

**Rebis**, that is, the "Stone Rebis," which refers to hair <note>original German: *die Haar*</note>.

**Rebisola** is a secret remedy <note>original Latin: *arcanum*</note> derived from urine for the treatment of jaundice <note>original Latin: *icteritia*</note>. If the urine is boiled and the foam thoroughly skimmed off, and it is then left to rest for three days, it gives forth small stones called *rebisoleos*. It is a secret remedy for jaundice made from urine; when one boils the urine and removes the scum, letting it stand for three days, the remedy is found in the form of small stones.

# MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN

### R

**Rebus** is the ultimate matter of things, the final substance of all things <note>original German: *die letzte Matery aller Ding*</note>.

**Rebolea** is mummy <note>a medicinal substance derived from preserved or embalmed bodies, used in various remedies</note>.

**Rebona** is burnt dung, whether from humans or cows.

**Recha** means marble.

**Rebis** <note>from the Latin *res bina*, meaning "double thing"</note> is Man and Woman, Body and Spirit, the first part of the Great Work. It is a subtle, pure sand that adheres to Mercury; two-fold seeds mixed together are called Rebis. Senior <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, an influential alchemical author</note> states on page 79 that it is the Elixir, the Ferment, the Medicine, the Tincture—a composite thing.

**Receptaculum** (The Receiver) is a large, spherical vessel designed to receive distilled fluids; it is commonly called a receiver <note>original German: *ein Vorlage*</note>. However, the receiver varies according to the nature of the substance being distilled. For if the materials are vaporous, flatulent, and spiritual <note>volatile</note> when dissolved, the vessel must be large; otherwise, the great force of the spirits will cause it to burst with a loud bang and crash, shattering into pieces and endangering those standing nearby. If the substances are hot and thin, it should be shaped with a long neck. If they are of a moderate nature, a medium receiver is required.

**Recrementa** are dross, slag, or furnace residues.

**Recrementa of Iron** are iron scales or cinders <note>original German: *Sinder*</note>.

**Rector of the Machine** <note>original German: *Hengstiezer*; likely a technical term for a regulator or a specific component within a furnace setup</note>.

**Redux** is a powder used to melt calcined <note>burned to ash or powder</note> metals and minerals so they return again to a metallic state (regulus).

**To Reduce** <note>original German: *Reduciren*</note> means to make dry, to bring back, or to make fatty like butter so that it flows like wax. In the context of "drinking and nourishing," alchemists call this pouring water onto dry earth.

**Rel** or *Rebus* signifies acidity or sour milk.

**Relollium** is a power arising from a substance's constitution, as seen in St. John’s Wort (*hypericum*). Its primary virtue is that it is warm and healing; its accidental and hidden virtue is that it resists worms and decay. It is a hidden, incidental power: in St. John's Wort, its first virtue is that it expels heat—this is *relollium*—its second is that it is warm and healing.

## MARTIN RULAND'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY

**Remanere** means to remain behind, as if in certain whirlwinds or eddies <note>original German: *Bleibe/bleiben*</note>.

**Repercussives** are medicines so called because they drive back flows or humors <note>original German: *was hinder sich treibet*</note>.

**To withdraw and pour back excavated things from the channels** refers to throwing the mountain-ore back <note>original German: *Bergk zu rück stürtzen*; a mining term for backfilling or moving earth</note>.

**Fossil substance** (a mined mineral), resembling silver dross, refers to a dross or slag of the second degree <note>original German: *trüß Pückel im zweyten Grad*</note>.

**Resolution** <note>dissolution or separation</note> in medicine occurs when mixed substances are violently separated by the addition of a dissolving agent, which segregates each part of the mixture. Following the authority of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century father of alchemy</note>, we call this dissolving agent a "medicine," although even if it is liquid, it can be called a dissolving water <note>a solvent</note>. It happens in the same way that vinegar or similar agents cause the separation of milk through curdling. Therefore, the work itself could also be called *empyriasis* <note>from the Greek for "setting on fire," referring here to a heat-driven separation</note>. In some instances, it is closely related to coagulation, as the two often occur together.

**Restis** is a cord or rope <note>original German: *Pestener strick*, likely a specific binding used in mining or medicine</note>.

**Quenching** <note>Restinctio</note> is a method of gradation in which glowing-hot objects are quenched in an "exalting" <note>enhancing</note> liquid; by this means, they attain the highest nobility of their kind. Indeed, this is the primary and chief purpose for which the art of quenching was invented.

**Resin** is a beautiful yellow pitch, such as opopanax, sagapenum <note>OCR reads *serapinum*</note>, or ammoniacum; it is a fine yellow resin like galbanum <note>these are all aromatic plant resins used in ancient pharmacy</note>.

**Resin of Gold** is the "Saffron of Gold" <note>a chemical precipitate, usually an oxide or chloride of gold</note> extracted from gold.

**Resin of Pine**, that is, of the fir tree <note>original German: *Danenharz*</note>.

**Resin of the Earth** is sulfur.

**Potable Resin of the Earth** is sulfur sublimated into a liquid, or reduced into a balsam or oil <note>original German: *Schwefel in ein Safft oder Oel gebracht*</note>.

**The Retort** is a spherical vessel whose neck proceeds gradually from the belly and passes by degrees into a reflected, oblong tube <note>a staple of the alchemical laboratory used for distillation</note>.

**Reverberation** is a process of ignition where bodies are heated by a "living" <note>active</note> flame that reflects and—

# RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN

...by striking, reducing it into a finer powder <term>calx: a powder produced by roasting or oxidizing a metal</term>; it is either closed or open.

**Closed Reverberation** occurs when the bodies to be reverberated are calcined in a closed reverberatory furnace. In this type of reverberation, the degrees of fire can be administered with great precision, so that the heat can be increased or decreased at will—something that does not happen in common furnaces.

**Open Reverberation** occurs when the material is calcined in a reverberatory furnace with all the vents or openings left open. This form of reverberation is extremely intense, and we use it for dissolving hard and stubborn bodies.

**Rex** <note>The King</note>, a spiritual soul-water <note>original German: *Seel geistlich Wasser*</note> that moistens the Earth for the Woman <note>In alchemical allegory, the "Woman" often represents the passive or mercurial principle</note>, and is given back to the Fountain from which it was originally drawn; it is the Spirit within the water, an aqueous Spirit.

**Reverberatorium** is the furnace in which materials are calcined by means of a flame.

**Rinar** means filings. **Rion** is the same: filings or shavings <note>original German: *Feyleten / oder Feyl*</note>.

**Rillus** is a chemical instrument into which molten metals are poured to form oblong shapes; an ingot-mold <note>original German: *ein Inguß*</note>.

**Robes** means vinegar; **roscod** is the same. According to some authorities, *robes* refers to Saturn <note>In this context, likely "Sugar of Lead" or lead acetate, made by dissolving lead in vinegar</note>.

**Ron** means a pound; **rotula** is the same <note>literally "a small wheel," used here as a weight or measure</note>.

**Rosa** <note>The Rose</note> means tartar <note>the potassium bitartrate crust found in wine barrels</note>.

**Rosea** refers to erysipelas <note>a bacterial skin infection</note>, also called "the beautiful red-run" <note>original German: *Rothlauffen / die schöne*; "the beautiful" was often used as a euphemism for dangerous inflammatory diseases</note>.

**Rota** <note>The Wheel</note>, or **Rade**, refers to *Rotingenius*, which is colophony <note>a type of resin or rosin</note>.

**Rotætheca** means a wheel-case or wheel-box <note>original German: *Radschube*</note>.

**Rotæ** refers to basket-disks or sheaves <note>original German: *Korbscheiben*</note>.

**Rotumha** is a vessel similar to a cucurbit <note>a gourd-shaped glass flask used in distillation</note>.

**Rub** is a thickened juice; a sap that is boiled down until it reaches a certain thickness.

**Rubedo de nigro** <note>Redness out of the black</note>, that is, the redness extracted from black talc; the extracted redness coming out of the black calx <note>original German: *die außgezogene Röthe auß dem schwarzen Kalck*</note>.

<meta>This page continues Martin Ruland’s alphabetical dictionary of alchemical and medical terms. ### MARTIN RULAND’S DICTIONARY OF ALCHEMY

**False Red Gold** <term>Rubeum aurum falsum</term>: This is tinted copper, a gold-colored copper produced by alchemists.

**Rust** <term>Rubigo</term>: Known as the "leech" <note>original Latin: *hirudo*</note> in other works; it is a "sweet gall" and is prepared from gold.

**Sinopian Earth** <term>Rubrica sinopica</term>: Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD whose work was the primary source for European herbals for 1,500 years</note> in Book 5, Chapter 61, writes: "Some wish to call Sinopian earth 'Lemnian,' while the Greeks call it *magram* or *mogan*, and the Latins call it *sinopidam*." One should select that which is heavy, dense, liver-colored, free of grit, consistent in color throughout, and which spreads out extensively when diluted. 

Next, he explains the location where it is excavated and the origin of its name: it comes from the city of Sinope <note>A port city on the Black Sea coast of modern-day Turkey</note>, where it was once sold, or through which it was transported. As Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist</note> reports, it was first discovered in Pontus. 

Such Sinopian earth is brought from Byzantium <note>Modern-day Istanbul</note> to Venice in the form of clods or lumps, though rarely. Sometimes from the same city, tablets <note>original Latin: *pastilli*</note> of an almost tawny color are brought, marked with Turkish letters; because of this, merchants call them **Sealed Earth** <term>terra sigillata: a medicinal clay pressed into cakes and stamped with an official seal to guarantee its authenticity and prevent forgery</term>. 

In ancient times, Lemnian earth was similarly marked with the image of a goat because goat's blood was mixed into it. Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a millennium</note> traveled there himself to observe how much goat's blood was being mixed with that earth. Those marked tablets were called *Sphragida aegos* <note>Greek: *σφραγῖδα αἰγός*, meaning "the Seal of the Goat"</note>. 

Indeed, the island of Lemnos, where that earth was mined, is not far from Thrace, and the Turks also hold dominion over it; therefore, it can easily be transported to Byzantium. If the color of the tablets brought from Byzantium corresponds less to "red earth" than it should, the reason perhaps is that when the earth is diluted to be formed into tablets, it changes somewhat. Furthermore, it is now dug from deeper in the earth, and thus it is less scorched by the sun's heat. 

The Turks value such tablets highly for curing the plague. The Arabs also attribute the greatest power for curing the plague to **Armenian Bole** <term>gleba Armeniaca: a reddish-yellow clay used in both medicine and as a base for gold leaf</term>; as can also be seen in Galen, who records that it is pale. Indeed, that clay is not much different from this...

### MARTIN RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN

Cc 4

...it is not unlike **Sealed Earth** <term>terra sigillata</term>, except that it is nowhere recorded that a seal is ever impressed upon **Armenian Earth** <term>Armeniaca terra</term>. Beyond these, whether the earth is finally marked and formed into tablets <note>original Latin: *pastillos*</note> with Turkish letters, or whether it is diluted **Sinopian Red Earth** <term>rubrica Sinopica</term>, or **Lemnian Earth** <term>terra lemnia</term>, or Armenian earth, I do not think it matters much, since all such earths possess the same medicinal powers. One would have to inquire at Byzantium <note>Modern-day Istanbul</note> whether it was brought from Lemnos or Armenia, or transported from Sinope to Thrace. Formerly, this type of red earth was undoubtedly distinctive; today, due to the madness of the Turks, it is not imported as frequently. For the rest, concerning that Sinopian earth, see Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist</note>, Book 35, Chapter 6, where he identifies three species of it: red, a less-red variety, and a middle type between these. See also Serapion <note>An influential 11th-century Arabic physician</note> in the *Aggregator*, chapter *Mezgred*, where he also lists its species, and likewise Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine medical writer</note> on the subject of "mogra" Sinopian earth.

**Artisan’s Red Earth** <term>Rubrica fabrilis</term> is of two kinds. In German, both are called **Red Crayon / Red-stone / as used by carpenters and stonemasons /** <note>original German: *Röttel / Röttelstein / wie die Zimmerleut vnd Steinmetzen brauchen*</note> and in Greek, they are called *miltos tektonikē* <note>original Greek: *μίλτος τεκτονικὴ*, literally "architectural red earth," used for marking wood or stone</note>. For one variety is native, and the other is man-made. The native variety is properly called **Mountain Red Crayon** <note>original German: *BergkRöttel*</note> by the Germans. Among us, it is a fossil <note>In the 16th century, "fossil" meant anything dug out of the ground</note> and is sometimes found near the Elbe River. 

Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and author of the famous herbal *De Materia Medica*</note>, in Book 5, Chapter 62, testifies that the native variety is produced in Iberia <note>The Iberian Peninsula, modern Spain and Portugal</note>, toward the west, from ochre that has been scorched and has deteriorated into red earth. Pliny, Book 35, Chapter 6, writes of the same native variety that it is found in iron mines. Of this, we have several other species. One is found in a marble-like form at the mines in the valley; another, by contrast, is notable for being suitable for paintings, as Pliny writes concerning the variety found in iron mines. Furthermore, there is the manufactured artisan’s red earth, called **Brown Red Crayon** <note>original German: *braun Röttel*</note> by the Germans, which is made from burnt ochre, as Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note> and Dioscorides testify. Pliny, however, in Book 35, Chapter 6, through some negligence, reverses this, saying that red earth is made from ochre. For he says that ochre is made from red earth by burning it in new pots smeared around with clay. But the opposite is true. And nature also testifies to this, as he himself ob[serves]... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "seru-", which leads into the next page's "servatur".</note>

**Sagda** or sagdo is a gemstone of a leek-green color according to Albertus Magnus, Euax, Solinus (chapter 40), and Pliny (Book 37, chapter 10). By its nature, the sagda stone attracts straws and threads just as jet <term>gagates</term> does, or as a magnet attracts iron. Indeed, it clings so strongly to wood that it cannot be torn away unless it is cut off. It is found firmly fixed to the planks of ships. From this, it may be inferred that its homeland is the sea itself. I saw a specimen of it in the possession of a sailor, though it was of altogether weak power, for it could scarcely attract even the smallest twigs; its color was not truly leek-green. **It was pale green** <note>original: "Er war bleichgrün"</note>, the size of a bean. Solinus, in the place cited, says that among the Chaldeans the sagda gem is commonly found. Pliny says that in Samothrace a variety of this gemstone is black, similar to wood, and without weight.

**Salt** <term>Sal</term>, called *Alas* in Greek and *Melech* in Arabic; also called *selenipum*, it is the saltiness or the brine <term>muria</term> of salt produced when salt is dissolved by cold or by the humidity of a cellar. It is also the earthy principle <term>principium terreum</term> possessing the power of bounding, coagulating, and thus also preserving. Therefore, it is very close to nature and easily works in harmony with it. It is also Mercury.
1. The **Salt of Metals** is the Philosopher's Stone. Because of this, some wish to extract the salt from all metals and create the Art <note>The Great Work of alchemy</note> from it. This is not at all necessary, as Hermes says: "All salt is contrary to this Art, except for this single one, by which the souls are drawn out of the metals."
2. **Prime Matter** <term>Prima materia</term> is liquid salt, as the name *Halchymia* indicates. <note>Ruland suggests a linguistic link between 'Alchemy' and the Greek word 'hal' (salt)</note> This salt is everywhere, and in every house; it moves in the sea and is within all people.
3. There is one kind of salt from plants, another from animals, and another from minerals—and this last kind is the sharpest of all.
4. It is the best balm; it purges, contracts, thins, washes away, divides, alters, and awakens the power of the seed. Therefore, it is said that Venus was born from the sea. <note>Referring to the salt-water of the ocean as a creative, generative force</note>
5. Senior and Gratianus <note>Ancient alchemical authorities</note> say: From all things, lime <term>calx</term> and salt can be made; from ash, salt; from ash, water or Mercury; and from Mercury, gold. For this reason, they have sought gold in all things.

6. Now, everything that you wish to exalt and change, you must turn into Salt and Alum; and this is the Key: to **calcine** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter</term> the prepared Salt.

7. Everything that allows itself to be **dissolved** <term>solviren</term> takes on the nature of Salt and Alum, and after **putrefaction** <note>original: "Fdulung," likely a typo for "Faulung"</note>, it takes on the nature of the Stone.

And our Salt, which is the **tincture** <note>The active, coloring, or transformative principle</note>, is drawn out from the metals through putrefaction, until the entire composition sheds its own nature and assumes another.

9. **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval alchemy</note>: The Art must have **Lime** <term>Kalch or Calx</term>, which is its own Earth, wherein lies the greatest power of the minerals to harden the **Mercury**.

10. The Salt of the metals dissolves the Mercury into a clear water in **dung** <note>original: "Mist"; often referring to the *venter equinus* or horse-dung heat, a method of providing gentle, consistent warmth for digestion</note>; and when this same water is mixed and **coagulated** <term>turned from a liquid to a solid state</term>, the perfect **Medicine** <note>The Elixir or Philosopher's Stone</note> is produced from it. Therefore, whoever knows Salt and its dissolution possesses the Secret of the Ancient Sages. For this reason, place the entire foundation upon Salt, and pay no heed to any other thing. For Salt alone is the foremost Mystery that all Sages have kept hidden. 

**Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the father of Islamic alchemy</note>: You should know that this is a Salt, although in the beginning it does not have the form of a Salt; but through the work, it becomes a congealed leaf, and long duration makes it white, pure, translucent, and clear. And this is a good, noble Salt, which of its own accord becomes impure and then pure again; it dissolves and coagulates itself; it opens and shuts itself.

**Paracelsus** in the *Paramirum*: Salt provides the **Coagulation**, so that it flows together and becomes tangible; for without Salt, nothing is tangible. However, there are many kinds of Salt, just as there are many kinds of **Sulfur** and **Mercury**. <note>See above, folio 19.</note>

->### MARTIN RULAND'S ALCHEMICAL LEXICON.<-

**Sal alabrot**, <note>original: "id est, nitrum atrum"</note> that is, black niter: It is made from the juice of three herbs and is called the Master of all things. It works this wonder: that it transforms **Mercury** <term>quicksilver</term> into true **Luna** <note>the alchemical name for Silver</note>, or **Sol** <note>the alchemical name for Gold</note>. **Sal albus**, <note>original: "id est, borax"</note> that is, borax.

**Sal allocaph**, <note>original: "i. e. sal Armoniacus"</note> that is, Sal Ammoniac <term>ammonium chloride salt, often used as a flux</term>.

**Sal alkali**, <note>original: "id est, sal vitri"</note> that is, salt of glass. It is made from the ashes of **Cali** <note>alkali-rich plants, often used to create potash</note>. Also called **Salt of Bitterness** <note>original: "amaritudinis sal"</note>, or the Dregs of Bitterness. It is also called **Oil of the Philosophers** and the Salt of Wisdom. It ensures that the **Spirits** <term>volatile or gaseous substances</term> enter well and penetrate the **Bodies** <term>the solid, metallic aspects of a substance</term>.

**Sal aluminosum**, <note>original: "i. est, ex alumine plumoso tractum"</note> that is, salt extracted from plumose alum <note>a fibrous or feathery form of alum, sometimes confused with asbestos</note>.

**Sal amarum**, bitter salt; <note>original: "alkali, & nitri"</note> alkali and niter.

**Sal anathron**, <note>original: "vel anatron est sal ex vinea lapidea tractum"</note> or anatron is salt extracted from the stone-vine; glass-gall <term>the scum or dross found on the surface of molten glass</term>, or salt of niter.

**Sal armoniacus**, <note>original: "id est, sal saparicius, vel defossum, vel sal de Arabia"</note> that is, saparicious salt, or salt that is dug up, or salt of Arabia: the dissolved stone.

**Sal atrum**, <note>original: "sal thaber idem"</note> black salt; the same as salt thaber.

**Sal colcotharinum**, <note>original: "vel colcothacium"</note> or colcothacian salt: the salt from **Vitriol** <term>sulfate minerals, usually of iron or copper</term>.

**Sal congelatum** <note>original: "nascitur in thermis, fontibus & aquis medicatis"</note> is born in hot springs, fountains, and medicinal waters: that which grows in wells, as in thermal baths.

**Sal cristallinum**, <note>original: "quod ex urina hominis decoquitur"</note> which is boiled down from human urine: that which comes from human urine is called Crystalline Salt.

**Sal de Vngaria**, <note>original: "i. e. sal nitri"</note> that is, salt of niter <term>saltpeter or potassium nitrate</term> from Hungary.

**Sal enixum**, <note>original: "id est, resolutum"</note> that is, resolved: that which has dissolved itself.

**Sal Entali**, is a type of salt similar to a **Fixed Saltpeter** <term>niter that has been rendered non-volatile by heat</term>.

**Sal ex herbarum falsarum cinere factus**, <note>original: "i. e. sal alkali"</note> that is, salt made from the ash of salty herbs; that is, alkali salt.

**Sal gemma**, <note>original: "id est, Cappadocius"</note> that is, Cappadocian salt <note>common rock salt or sodium chloride</note>.

<header>BY RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.</header>

**Rock salt**, <note>original: "Sal gemma"</note> that is, Adrom salt, Fendar, or Sabachi; also known as mineral salt, Hungarian salt, or transparent salt.

**Greek salt**, <note>original: "Sal graecum"</note> that is, alum of Alaph or of Lacaph <note>specific types of alum used in alchemical preparations</note>.

**Indian salt** is named after its place of origin, **and it is red.** <note>original: "vnd ist roht"</note>

**Indian salt**, <note>original: "Sal Indicus"</note> that is, Mercury <term>quicksilver</term>, **which has been dissolved and coagulated.** <note>original: "der soluirt & coagulirt ist"</note>

**Salt of lye**, <note>original: "Sal lotii"</note> that is, salt of urine.

**Sea salt**, <note>original: "Sal marinus"</note> that is, rock salt; mineral salt is the same thing.

**Salt of Mercury**, <note>original: "Sal Mercurii"</note> that is, Spirit of Wine <term>alcohol or ethanol</term>, which intoxicates, **the spirit of wine which makes one drunk.** <note>original: "der Geist deß Weins / der truncken macht"</note>

**Artificial salt** <note>original: "Sal factitium"</note> is that which is boiled or produced by art <note>meaning chemical or industrial processes</note>, and this is again twofold: namely,

1.. **Sea Salt**, of which Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> makes mention in the place cited above; he praises that which is white, uniform, dense, and from the region of Cyprus, etc. This sea salt is produced in ponds filled with seawater and dried by the burning sun, through a process of evaporation <note>original: "coctione," literally "boiling" or "cooking" by the sun</note>, and by the addition of rain or fresh water. For no salt is made without fresh water, as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of *Natural History*</note> asserts in Book 2, Chapter 106. They mix fresh water with the salty water when preparing the salt to wash away the intensity of its bitterness; it is said that this is still done in several places in Spain and France, and Pliny reports in Book 31, Chapter 3, that it is made and dried this way in Lake Taranto and in Lake Cocanico in Sicily.

2.. **That which is boiled by art** from the natural brine <term>muria; concentrated salt water</term> of springs: just as our salt is now boiled at Halle in Saxony, and in other places in both Thuringia and Saxony. However, one surpasses the other in quality according to the nature of the brine: **depending on whether the salt-water is good, or has much "wild" [impure or diluted] water:** <note>original: "Darnach das Saltzwasser gut ist / oder viel wildes Wasser hat"</note> as we see happening in a certain place in the March <note>the Margraviate of Brandenburg</note>.

In the regions near Lisbon, as they are now called, there are great marshes by the sea where seawater stagnates in many places, just like those which sailors otherwise call **A Harbor**, <note>original: "Ein Hafen"</note> and in those places, such salt is also produced.

### LEXICON OF ALCHEMY BY MARTIN RULAND ###

...lake-like sea salt <note>original: "sal marinum lacustre"</note> found at the shores where the waves recede. This occurs through the action of the sun, which "cooks" <note>meaning evaporates or boils away the liquid</note> this sea water into salt. The inhabitants—mostly poor peasants—soon collect it using a specific technique, making little chests <note>original: "cistulis," likely small wooden frames or crates</note> so that it is not carried away again by the returning waves. They pile it into great heaps on the shore; there, it is further dried and processed by the sun in the open air, forming pieces of immense size, as if they were alum or even the ice of rivers, except that these pieces of salt are not translucent like alum or ice, but are pale, green, or black in color. This same salt is then carried by ships to various maritime nations and is ground by a certain device until it becomes like coarse sand. It is used to salt fish, such as whales, seals, herring, the hides of dogfish <note>original: "canum marinorum," literally "sea dogs," often referring to sharks or dogfish</note>, scallops, flounder, dories, rays, salema, catfish, and other fish. When this lake salt is boiled again, it becomes the finest and whitest salt.

The various powers <note>medicinal or chemical virtues</note> of salt are listed at length by Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> in the place cited, and by Pliny in Book 31, Chapter 9; and regarding the different kinds of salt in Chapters 7 and 10 of the same book. One may also consult Serapion in the *Book of Aggregations* <note>a medieval medical compilation</note>, in the chapter on "Malk" <note>likely referring to a specific mineral or salt in Arabic-derived medical terminology</note>. Furthermore, Dioscorides adds the method for burning salt, whether it be mined salt <note>original: "fossilem"</note> or manufactured salt; they call this burnt salt *saltaculum* or *cotulum*. He also mentions "foam of salt" <note>original: "spuma salis"</note>, which to him is nothing other than the frothy "down" <note>original: "lanugo"</note> of the sea, or the scrapings found on thin rocks in maritime areas along the shore washed by the sea. It is a certain coagulated substance, having the taste of salt and a strong, fishy smell of the sea (others call it both "foam of salt" and *Alcyonium* <note>a term used for sea-foam or certain porous marine organisms</note>, which was discussed above). Indeed, Pliny records this foam of salt or of the sea among the types of natural salt when he says in the place cited: "Another kind is born spontaneously from the waters of the sea, as foam left on the furthest shores and rocks. For all of this is thickened by the dew, and that which is found on rocks is more pungent." The commentator on Nicander <note>an ancient Greek poet who wrote on poisons and remedies</note>, in the *Alexipharmaca* <note>a work on antidotes</note>, defines this foam of salt as that which people...

<meta>This page continues Martin Ruland’s Lexicon of Alchemy. The previous page discussed the natural production of sea salt by solar evaporation and its use in preservation. Here, Ruland distinguishes between natural and artificial "sea foam" salt and provides a catalog of various specialized salts used in medicine and alchemy.</meta>

### BY RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN ###

Those preparing salt mix fresh waters with the salty ones to wash away the intensity of the sharpness. While they mix both, as Pliny also indicates, a certain foam is produced from the mixture, which is called *halos achne* <note>original Greek: ἁλὸς ἄχνη</note>, that is, the foam of the salt and the sea. If this is true, we have a double "foam of salt": one produced by the sea, which is that described by Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician</note> and which Pliny calls a species of native salt; the other is the artificial kind described by the interpreter of Nicander <note>a Greek poet and physician</note>. Just as salt and the foam of salt are related to each other, so too are nitre <term>historically referring to either saltpeter or native soda</term> and its foam, which we discussed above. Finally, it should be noted that there are infinite species of salt if you wish to consider their locations, origin, color, mineral source, quality, and other factors. If I wanted to touch upon all these species, my work would grow longer than the *Iliad*. 

We will briefly run through some species: Cappadocian salt, bread salt, lump salt, usual salt, and common salt are all one and the same. Second, Sodom salt is a salt generated in the Dead Sea, where the water is bitter. It is called "of Sodom" from the mountains adjacent to that sea. It seems to me that this salt is a species of sea foam or hardened salt. Third, there is another species of salt called alkali salt <term>from the Arabic 'al-qaly', referring to the ashes of plants</term>, or *alkal*, which is artificial and is made from the herb *Kali* <note>Saltwort</note> or *usuen*, which we mentioned above; they claim it is made by burning the herb *anthyllis* <note>likely Kidney Vetch</note> in a pit. There is also a clear salt named nitre, and Alexandrian salt, and the salt of Anderena known as *baurach* <note>Arabic term for borax or nitre</note>, and *aphronitrum* <note>literally 'foam of nitre'</note>, for nitre is a species of salt. There is also "priestly salt," which is included in the *antidotarium virili* <note>a collection of remedies for men's ailments</note>, and there is Tragefic salt, which we currently lack, and there is arsenic salt—that is, sublimated arsenic—and there is *Sal Alebroth* <term>a "salt of art" or "salt of wisdom," usually a double salt of mercury and ammonium chloride</term>, which is the salt of the chemists; see the entry for "Chemists" regarding this.

Flower of salt, or *Alosanthus* <note>original Greek: ἅλος ἄνθος</note>, seems to me to be derived from the sea. It is a certain efflorescence <note>a powdery or crystalline crust</note> of the sea, and the sea yields this medicine. It is kept in the apothecary shops under another name; namely, it is called *spermaceti* <note>original: "sperma vel semen ceti," literally whale seed or sperm</note>, or whale seed, or whitish amber. The Saxons call it *Walrat* <note>literally "whale-fat" or "whale-counsel"</note>.

# MARTIN RULAND’S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY #

...or Waldraht <note>original German: *Waldraht*; a folk name for a medicinal substance, likely spermaceti or a similar fatty salt</note>, perhaps so named from its effect in several diseases. The ancients made no mention of *sperma ceti* <term>literally "sperm of the whale," a waxy substance found in the head of sperm whales, often confused with ambergris in this era</term>, but rather of *flos salis* <note>original Latin: "flower of salt"</note>, and that is what it is. It is found in the sea itself, as sailors and merchants have reported to me several times (although some claim it is found upon the rocks in the Nile), or in marshes near the sea, and in stagnant parts of the sea. Dioscorides <note>a 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> in Book 5, Chapter 77, says it swims in the Nile and in lakes; its color is saffron or brick-red. However, so that it may lose its redness and become white, it is purified; for this reason, reddish bits, like husks, are still found in the mass itself, so to speak. It is a substance smelling of a fatty poison <note>original Latin: *pinguedine virus olens*</note> and of an unpleasant odor, which does not dissolve in water, but only in oil. 

In the place cited, Dioscorides teaches its origin, quality, adulteration, and harmfulness. He then describes its medical powers. For the rest, see Cassius Felix <note>a 5th-century Latin medical writer</note> regarding *halosachne* <note>original Greek: ἁλὸς ἄχνη, "sea-foam"</note>. Pliny, in Book 31 <note>OCR says 37, but Pliny discusses salts in Book 31</note>, says that the primary "flower of salt" is a thing of a different nature, being more humid and of a saffron or reddish color, like the rust of salt, and also differing from salt in its smell, not just from the foam. He says it is found in Egypt and carried by the Nile, and floats in certain springs, and is formed when north winds are blowing. In Saxony, its use is so common that I do not know for which disease they do *not* use it. I know that because of its excessive use, a most honorable matron perished at the gates of Tangra. 

Some call this *sperma ceti* "amber" (*ambra*); others say amber is the fruit of a tree, or a gum growing under the sea; others say it is the liver of a fish; others the dung of a certain fish; others a certain foam of the sea; others say it grows in the form of mushrooms under the sea. You should consult Serapion <note>an Arabic physician</note> in the *Book of Aggregations*, the chapter "Hambara"; Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina</note> *On Amber*; and Al-Mazuni in Tract 3, the chapter on Amber. 

Thus, "flower of salt" is twofold:
1. The finest ash and the whitest part of salt.
2. *Sperma ceti*. 
*Waldraht* or *Baldrah* <note>German folk etymology: "quick help" or "quickly helping"</note>.

**Salt-nitre** <term>saltpeter</term> is boiled out of the earth in which urine has been cast for a long time, as in sheepfolds and the stables of horses and oxen; <gloss>which one boils out of the earth and is made from the urine of humans and cattle</gloss> or it is alkali salt.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of various types of salts. Having previously covered "flower of salt" and saltpeter, Ruland now moves into a systematic classification of "Natural Salt" (rock salt and lake salt) and its various regional subspecies and medicinal properties.</meta>

# OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN #

<note>The text on this page is organized using a hierarchical classification system indicated by large curly braces. A primary heading "Natural Salt" branches into two main sources: mines and water bodies (lakes, springs, rivers). The "mines" category further branches into four distinct numbered species of rock salt.</note>

Natural Salt—called *Milck* in Arabic, *Sal* in Latin, and **Saltz** by the Germans—is the best of seasonings. It is of two kinds: Natural (that is, found in nature) and artificial (made by art, which was discussed a little earlier). Natural salt, also called fossil or mineral salt, is either:

1. Dug out of mines; this is what the Greeks call "salt of the earth" <note>original Greek: ἅλμες γαῖας, *halmes gaias*</note> or "a clod" <note>original Greek: βῶλαξ, *bolax*</note>, meaning salty earth or sterile brine. Of this type, I recognize four species:
    1. **Cleavable Salt**, also called *Sal Armoniacum* or *Sal Sagaraicum*. Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician and botanist</note> mentions this first in Book 5, Chapter 75. It is white, free of pebbles, transparent, equally dense in all parts, and similar in color to the alum they call *Schiston* <note>meaning "split" or "cleavable" stone</note>, appearing in long lumps. Ovid also mentions this salt in his *Medicaments for the Female Face* when he says: "And masculine incense with Ammoniac salt." <note>original Latin: *Cumque Ammoniaco mascula thura sale*</note>. However, some do not call it *Ammoniacum* but *Armoniacum* salt, because it is found in Armenia. Some say it is made from the herb *Salmoniaca* which grows in the mountains of Spain and resembles dill; Avicenna <note>a Persian polymath and physician</note> mentions this. Serapio <note>an 11th-century Arabic medical writer</note> says its species are red, white, black, dusty, or clear; he describes it as hot and dry in the fourth degree.
    2. **Stony Mined Salt**, which is found again in Africa and India. In Cappadocia it occurs in the manner of "specular stones" <note>transparent or reflective stones like mica or selenite</note>; it is also called *Sal Gemmæ* <term>Gem-salt; high-purity halite that is clear like a gemstone</term>.
    3. **Mined Salt in Poland**, which is black, though sometimes white or blue. Lumps are dug out that are as large as millstones. Elsewhere it is called Black Salt or Naphthic Salt, as it is found with naphtha <note>a flammable liquid hydrocarbon</note>. Others also call "Indian Salt" a black salt. However, Indian Salt is not a salt by its own nature, but is called salt because of its color. It is actually Sugar (*Zuccarum*), which is found congealed upon the honey-cane in India just like salt; it is the sugar of the cane. In our time, this is called "Sugar Candy" <note>original Latin: *Zuccarum candi*</note>, which is an artificial product made in imitation of that which occurs naturally on the canes of India like salt.
    4. **In Transylvania**, a **Green Salt** is dug up. It is crystalline and has a square body; this is also a type of *Sal Gemmæ*. It is otherwise known as *Sal Cappadocium* [Cappadocian Salt], *Sal Costum*, *Sal Metallinum* [Metallic Salt], or *Sal Taburen*. It is called *Sal Gemmæ* [Gem-salt] because it is as clear as a gemstone. It is a "vein of the earth," and possesses the heating and drying powers of *Sal Armoniacum*.

2. **From lakes, springs, or rivers**, the surfaces of which are condensed into salt. See Pliny <note>a Roman naturalist</note>, Book 31, Chapter 7.

---

These species would be called **Bergk Saltz** <note>original German: "Mountain Salt" or Rock Salt</note> by the Germans, and they are related species to alum. Their medical powers are to corrode and to dry.

### MARTIN’S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY ###

**Sal Napta** (Naphtha Salt) is extracted from petroleum <note>original Latin: *petrole*. A naturally occurring liquid bitumen or rock oil</note>.

**Sal Nominis** (Salt of the Name) is Gem Salt <note>original Latin: *sal gemmæ*. A transparent, crystalline rock salt often used in chemical operations</note>.

**Sal Panis** (Bread Salt) is common salt that has not been prepared.

**Sal Petræ** (Salt of Stone or Saltpeter) is that which grows in the vaults of cellars as long cones, formed from dissolved lime or from the foam of salt. When it has been prepared, it is then called **Sal Nitri** (Salt of Nitre).

**Sublimating Sal Petræ** is called *aqua arctens* <note>original Latin: "constricting water," a term often used for corrosive acidic waters or solvents used in the "locking" or fixing of substances</note>.

**Sal Plumosum** (Feathery Salt) is the "Shadow of Mercury." <note>This refers to a volatile or hair-like crystalline form, sometimes identified with asbestos or a specific mercurial sublimate</note>.

**Sal Practicum** (Practical Salt) is made from a mixture of saltpeter and Sal Armoniac in equal parts, placed in an unglazed earthenware pot and hung by a cord in a wine cellar. Through the process of resolution <note>dissolving due to the moisture in the air</note>, the salt penetrates through the pot and sticks to the outside; this should be scraped off every 10 or 12 days like frost.

**Sal Resolutum Externum** (External Dissolved Salt) occurs when one judges that what they are eating is salt. <note>This may refer to the physical sensation of salt on the palate or a specific medicinal application</note>.

**Sal Rubeum Indiæ** (Red Salt of India) is red nitre.

<margin>(Alembroth)</margin> **Sal Sapientum** (Salt of the Wise) is Sal Armoniac; it is a "weighed salt" <note>original Latin: *sal pensum*. Alembroth is a laboratory-made double salt of mercury and ammonium chloride used as a powerful solvent</note>.

**Sal Scissum** (Split Salt) is Salt of Entali, or split alum; our Germans call it **Our Lady’s Ice** <note>original German: *Vnser Frawen Eiß*. This refers to selenite or translucent gypsum, which can be split into thin, ice-like sheets</note>.

**Sal Tabarzet** is the whitest of all tartar <note>A potassium salt found in wine barrels</note>.

**Sal Tartari** (Salt of Tartar) is white calcined tartar.

**Sal Tripollinus** (Tripolitan Salt) is also called Syrian salt, Thabor salt, metallic salt, or hail-like salt; they are all the same thing.

**Sandaraca** (Sandarac): Regarding what this might be, see Pliny <note>the Elder</note>, Book 11, Chapter 7. In this context, however, native Sandarac is a certain metallic substance which Dioscorides discusses in Book 5, Chapter 75. The Germans call it **Mountain Froth**, **Reissgelb**, or **Rossigelb**. It is Arsenic and red orpiment <note>original Latin: *auripigmentum rubeum*</note>, which has been more thoroughly "cooked" or refined by nature. It is also known as **Red Sulfur**, **Fire Sulfur**, or **Red Orpiment**. It is hot and dry in the second degree. But it is not raw red silver ore, as some have dreamed and as we taught above. Sandarac is a metallic substance and a purple earth, as we shall say shortly. It is found in those...

<meta>This page continues the entry for Sandarac (realgar/red arsenic sulfide), further detailing its relationship to Orpiment and its classification by classical authorities such as Pliny, Dioscorides, and Theophrastus.</meta>

### THE WORKS OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN ###

...from the metals in which native **orpiment** <note>original Latin: *auripigmentum*. A deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note> is found. It is a species of orpiment, similar to it in all respects—in odor, substance, and power—except for the color, which is red <note>original Latin: *russum*</note> and matches the color of **cinnabar** <note>mercury sulfide</note>. Hence *Pliny* says that **arsenic** is made of the same material as **sandarac** <note>original Latin: *sandaraca*, usually referring to realgar or red arsenic</note>; by arsenic, he understands orpiment.

Alchemists strive to distinguish this arsenic from orpiment and sandarac, but they are mistaken. For they are one and the same, and are formed by nature from sulfur and a weak **quicksilver** <note>original Latin: *argento vivo*</note>. In summary, sandarac is a red, purple, or fiery metallic earth, smelling of the poison <note>original Latin: *virus*</note> of sulfur. Occasionally, red or flame-colored lumps are found within orpiment; and if one were to examine it closely, they would perhaps find the true sandarac within that orpiment. *Pliny* writes in Book 34, Chapter 18, that sandarac is found in gold and silver mines; it is red, smells of poison, and is pure and brittle. Something of this sort is not rarely found in our mines as well, but it does not smell of the poison of sulfur as *Dioscorides* claims. It is like a fine sand; and *Theophrastus*, if I am not mistaken, writes that orpiment and sandarac are sand or powder. 

Our substance might be called sandarac because of the similarity in color, following the custom of *Vitruvius*, who also calls sandarac that which is made from **ceruse** <note>original Latin: *cerusa*, or white lead</note>, which *Dioscorides* calls *sandix* <note>a bright orange-red pigment</note>. However, according to *Pliny*, **sandix** is made differently; just as our adulterated, artificial **minium** <note>red lead</note> made from lead is a species of artificial sandarac. Thus, our substance may be called sandarac—the sandarac of *Pliny* which is found in gold and silver mines. Thirdly, our sandarac could be called the sandarac of *Theophrastus* because it is a fine sand. Whether it truly possesses the virtues that *Theophrastus* attributes to his sandarac—namely, uniting with orpiment—I do not know.

# MARTIN'S LEXICON OF ALCHEMY #

Salt of naphtha, *is extracted from petroleum.* <note>original: *Sal naptæ / wird außgezogen von Petrole*</note>

Salt of the Name, that is, rock salt. <note>original: *sal gemmæ*. A common name for halite or pure crystalline salt.</note>

Salt of bread, that is, common salt that has not been prepared.

Salt of the stone <note>original: *Sal petræ*, referring here to saltpeter or potassium nitrate</note> is that which grows in the vaults of cellars in oblong cones from dissolved lime or from the foam of salt; *and when it is prepared, it is then called Saltpeter.* <note>original: *Sal nitri*</note>

To sublime Salt of the stone *is called binding water.* <note>original: *aqua arctens*. Likely a term for a restrictive or concentrated acidic solution used in the distillation process.</note>

Feathery salt <note>original: *Sal plumosum*, typically referring to fibrous alum or asbestos</note> *is the shadow of Mercury.*

Practical salt <note>original: *Sal practicum*</note> is made from a mixture of Salt of the stone and Sal Ammoniac in equal parts in an unglazed earthenware pot, suspended by a wire in a wine cellar: through dissolution, the salt penetrates and adheres to the outside of the pot, which must be scraped off every 10 or 12 days like frost.

External dissolved salt is when someone considers what they eat to be salt. <note>This likely refers to common table salt as it is perceived by the senses in everyday use.</note>

Red salt of India, that is, red saltpeter.

<margin>(Alembroth)</margin> Salt of the Sages, that is, Sal Ammoniac, a weighed salt. <note>original: *Sal sapientum* / *sal pensum*. Sal Alembroth was a famous alchemical "salt of art" used as a solvent, often identified as a double salt of mercury and ammonium chloride.</note>

Split salt, salt of Entali, split alum, *Our Lady’s Ice.* <note>original German: *vnser Frawen Eiß*. A historical name for selenite or transparent gypsum, which peels off in thin, ice-like sheets.</note>

Tabarzet salt is the whitest tartar of all. <note>original: *Sal tabarzet*. In historical pharmacy, "Tabarzet" often referred to a high-quality white sugar or crystalline substance.</note>

Salt of tartar, that is, white calcined tartar. <note>Potassium carbonate, produced by heating the tartar deposits found in wine barrels.</note>

Tripolitan salt, Syrian salt, Thabor salt, metallic salt, and granular salt are all the same.

Sandarac <note>original: *Sandaraca*. Not the modern resin, but the mineral realgar (arsenic sulfide)</note>, otherwise called *Erythace*; for what it is, see Pliny, Book 11, Chapter 7. However, in this place, native sandarac is a certain metallic substance, which Dioscorides discusses in Book 5, Chapter 75. It is called by the Germans *Mountain-red, Travel-yellow, or Horse-yellow.* <note>original German: *Bergroͤht / Reißgelb / Rossigelb /*</note> It is Arsenic and red orpiment <note>original: *auripigmentum rubeum*</note>, more thoroughly cooked by nature; *red sulfur, fire sulfur, red orpiment;* <note>original German: *roter Schwefel / Feuer Schwefel / roht Operment /*</note> it is hot and dry in the second degree. ### THE WRITINGS OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN ###

...concerning the metals in which native orpiment <note>original: *auripigmentum natiuum*. Orpiment is a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note> is found. It is a species of orpiment, similar to it in every way—in its scent, its substance, and its properties—except for its color, which is red and matches the color of cinnabar <note>original: *cinnabri*. Mercury sulfide, known for its bright vermilion color.</note>. Hence Pliny says that arsenic is made of the same material as sandarac <note>original: *sandaraca*. In this context, it refers to Realgar, the red mineral form of arsenic sulfide.</note>; by the term arsenic, he means orpiment.

Alchemists strive to distinguish this "arsenic" into orpiment and sandarac, but they are mistaken. For they are one and the same thing, and are formed from sulfur and mercury that has been weakened by nature. In short, sandarac is a red, purple, or fiery metallic earth, smelling of the stench of sulfur. Within orpiment, red or flaming clods <note>original: *glebæ*</note> are sometimes found; and if one were to examine it closely, one might perhaps find true sandarac within that orpiment. Pliny writes in Book 34, Chapter 18, that sandarac is found in gold and silver mines; he describes it as being red, smelling of poison <note>original: *virus*</note>, and being pure and brittle. Now, a substance of this kind is found not rarely in our own mines, but it does not smell of sulfurous poison as Dioscorides claims, and it is like a fine sand. Theophrastus, if I am not mistaken, also writes that orpiment and sandarac are sand or powder.

This substance of ours might be called sandarac because of the similarity of color, following the manner of Vitruvius, who also applies the name sandarac to that which is made from white lead <note>original: *cerusa*</note>, which is what Dioscorides calls *sandix*. However, *sandix* according to Pliny is made differently; just as our adulterated, manufactured red lead <note>original: *minium*</note> made from lead is a species of artificial sandarac. 

Furthermore, this substance of ours could be called sandarac in three ways:
1. It could be the sandarac of Pliny, which is found in gold and silver mines.
2. It could be called the sandarac of Theophrastus, because it is a fine sand. 
3. Whether it possesses the virtues which Theophrastus attributes to his sandarac—namely, that it combines with orpiment—I do not know.

### OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN. ###

-> Ggg 2 <-

...from the metals in which native orpiment <note>original: *auripigmentum*. A deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note> is found. And it is a species of orpiment, similar to it in all things—in odor, substance, and power—except for the color, which is reddish and matches the color of cinnabar <note>Mercury sulfide, known for its bright scarlet color.</note>. Hence Pliny says that arsenic is made from the same material as realgar <note>original: *sandaraca*. A ruby-red arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>: by "arsenic," he understands orpiment.

Alchemists strive to distinguish this arsenic (that is, orpiment) from realgar; but they are in error. For they are one and the same, and are produced by nature from sulfur and a weak quicksilver <note>original: *argento vivo*</note>. In summary, **realgar** is a red, or purple, or fiery metallic earth, smelling of the stench of sulfur. Among orpiment, red or flaming clods are sometimes found: and if one were to consider it closely, they would perhaps find true realgar within that orpiment. Pliny writes in Book 34, Chapter 18, that realgar is found in gold and silver mines, and that it is reddish, smells of a poisonous odor <note>original: *virus*; here referring to the pungent, toxic smell of sulfurous fumes</note>, and is pure and brittle. Now, such a thing is not rarely found in our own mines, but it does not smell of the sulfurous poison as Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist whose *De Materia Medica* was a standard reference.</note> claims; it is like a fine sand, and Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, known for his work *On Stones*.</note>—if I am not mistaken—writes that orpiment and realgar are a sand or powder. 

And this substance of ours could be called realgar because of the similarity in color, following the manner of Vitruvius <note>A Roman architect and engineer.</note>, who also calls that "realgar" which is made from ceruse <note>White lead, often used as a pigment.</note>, which is what Dioscorides calls *sandix* <note>A red pigment, often confused with orpiment or red lead in antiquity.</note>. However, according to Pliny, *sandix* is made differently; just as our adulterated, manufactured minium <note>Red lead (lead tetroxide).</note> made from lead is a species of artificial realgar. Furthermore, this substance of ours could be called "Pliny's realgar," which is found in gold and silver mines. Thirdly, our realgar could be called "Theophrastus's realgar" because it is a fine sand. Whether it truly possesses the virtues that Theophrastus attributes to his realgar—namely, that it combines with orpiment—I do not know.

# LEXICON OF ALCHEMY #

-> 420 <-

Perhaps a good color might be produced from it, if anyone were to make the experiment. I do not believe that the variety described by Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note>, which gives off a poisonous stench of sulfur, is found in our mines; our mineral and that <term>sandaraca</term> <note>original: *sandaraca*; a ruby-red arsenic sulfide mineral now known as realgar.</note> of Dioscorides differ greatly. Presently, even the common sort of physicians believe sandaraca to be a gum, which is a very great error. And almost all apothecary shops, erring in this matter, now stock gum or juniper resin in place of true metallic sandaraca. It is also hot and dry in the second degree <note>A classification from Galenic medicine used to describe the intensity of a substance's effect on the body's humors.</note>. I believe, however, that the error arose from this: the Arabs simply call juniper resin or gum "sandarax" or "varnish" <note>original: *vernix*</note>, while they called that metallic sandaraca a "red orpiment" <note>original: *auripigmentum*; a yellow or orange-red arsenic mineral.</note> or a species of orpiment. Conversely, the Greeks called this metallic substance of a fiery color "sandaraca." Thus, when the unlearned heard or read "sandaraca" in Greek texts, they immediately understood it according to the Arabic usage as juniper resin, whereas they ought to have understood it as this metallic mineral we are discussing here. Furthermore, because that juniper resin is called *sandarax* and *varnish* among the Arabs, one error led to another. Certain unlearned men soon took this artificial substance which we call **Varnish or Vernisch** <note>original: *Bernis/ oder Bernisch/*; Middle High German terms for varnish.</note>, which is used by painters and other craftsmen and made from oil and gum, for true metallic sandaraca. Consequently, if you were to write "Take <term>sandaraca</term>," they understood it in the Arabic sense as "Take gum" or juniper resin, or that artificial varnish of the craftsmen, even though the metal [mineral] was meant. In our apothecary shops, metallic sandaraca is no longer kept; **bookbinders now use it for sizing.** <note>original: *Die Buchbinder brauchen es nun zum Grunde*; "zum Grunde" refers to a base coat or primer used in bookbinding or gilding.</note> In summary, this non-metallic sandaraca is juniper gum to the Greeks and Arabs; the Greeks and Arabs have different meanings for "sandaraca." For the rest, concerning this metallic sandaraca—that is, the red variety of orpiment—see Serapion <note>An influential medieval Arabic medical writer.</note> in the chapter on *Harnceh*, Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician and philosopher Ibn Sina.</note> in Book 2 on Arsenic, and Pliny <note>The Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder.</note> in Book 35, Chapter 6. Pliny says that native sandaraca is produced on the island of Topazos in the Red Sea, but it is not exported. Regarding the artificial kind, consult Pliny and the chemists themselves.

He claims, however, that the Oriental and Indian varieties are the best, and that one species of these is of a transparent color like a clear sky, in which a yellow tint almost prevails; another has dark clouds declining toward redness; and another, conversely, has small white clouds. Furthermore, the virtues of the Sapphire are said to be: to make a man chaste, pious, and stable. Even today we use Sapphire to comfort the heart and to cool the inner body. -> OF RULAND, PHILOSOPHER AND DOCTOR. <-
423

...it is called Carniolus <note>Cornelian</note> according to Pliny (Book 37, Chapter 7). Formerly, drinking vessels were made from it. This gem exchanged its name with the sardonyx; it takes its name from Sardis, where it was first found, though the most praised variety is found in the "heart of the rock" in Babylonia. It is also found in other places, such as Epirus and Assos. In India, there are three types. Albertus Magnus proclaims that the *Sarda* <note>Cornelian</note> sharpens the wit and makes men joyful, because it purges the blood and generates good spirits <note>In the medieval sense of vital humors or "vitality"</note>. Regarding the sardonyx, see elsewhere in Solinus (Chapter 36) and Pliny (Book 37, Chapter 6). The following species of *Sarda* are enumerated:

1. Indian Sard, transparent: which is very red, and is called the male. (A transparent Cornelian).
2. Transparent, less red (a pale red Cornelian).
3. Transparent, similar to human flesh (a flesh-colored Cornelian).
4. Transparent, similar to flesh, full of red dots (a flesh-colored Cornelian with little red dots).

**Inverted stone**, a stubborn or refractory stone <note>original German: "widerporstig Stein"</note>.
